title: The Celebrity Traitors final review – more muted but still thrilling to the last | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: The endgame came with perfect touches of turmoil, from last-minute wobbles to yet more wilful wrongness
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The endgame came with perfect touches of turmoil, from last-minute wobbles to yet more wilful wrongness
Content: The Celebrity Traitors’ five-week, 10-show run attracted record-breaking viewing figures.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertView image in fullscreenThe Celebrity Traitors’ five-week, 10-show run attracted record-breaking viewing figures.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertThe TraitorsReviewThe Celebrity Traitors final review – more muted but still thrilling to the lastThe endgame came with perfect touches of turmoil, from last-minute wobbles to yet more wilful wrongnessLucy ManganFri 30 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey took it right down to the wire but in the end we finally got a moment of true treachery in this series of Celebrity Traitors where none of the contestants seemed to have understood the brief. Or the title. At the final round table, King Kenny turned on the queen and voted Maya – with her Cruella de Vil cheekbones but without the villainous heart to match – out.Sky-high ratings – for a lacklustre series: The Celebrity Traitors has become too nice for its own goodRead moreAs if that were not unexpected excitement enough at the end of a five-week, 10-show run whose record-breaking viewing figures have somewhat belied its comparatively muted nature, we had a last-minute wobble from Romesh that threw the endgame into turmoil. Turmoil! TURMOIL!As Maya left, you see, a shimmering, furious vision in jade, she added to her goodbye, “Good luck. You’re going to need it.”Romesh considered James Blunt to be uncharacteristically dismissive of what that might mean and – à la Nick Mohammed with Joe Marler last year – was suddenly convulsed by doubt and voted to banish the man who could not have been more clearly a Faithful than if he’d been … well, Joe Marler.Blunt, who had remained so consummately untouched by self-doubt throughout the show despite being 100% wrong 32bn times – “God give me the confidence of a perfectly pleasant white man” could become his new family crest – was shattered by the volte-face.Kenny, meanwhile, silently rejoiced because it left him in pole position to win. Until Bash – Bash, that tiny sweet wisp of a child! – stepped up, split the vote, talked sense into Romesh and got the last remaining Traitor banished instead.View image in fullscreenLeigh-Anne Pinnock, Romesh Ranganathan, King Kenny and Sebastian Croft during the final task.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertThen it was just the three Faithfuls left, and all were set to call it quits and split the prize money three ways. Except there was one last chance for Blunt to be wrong again and so he looked once, looked twice, and seized it. And was duly voted off.Perhaps “Consistency in all things” will do, in Latin, under a berk rampant. Bash and Romesh split their prize money between two charities for refugees and displaced persons. It was a result everyone could enjoy.And it was some form of oblique justice for Leigh-Anne, who had only ever been cheering up Miranda with her impromptu choreography and it hurt all our hearts to see her suffering for it.And if that last sentence makes no sense to you – well, that is sort of the point ofThe Traitors, in its celebrity incarnation or otherwise. You need to get into it. You have to commit to the run.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere’s no point dipping in and out – you either get to know the personalities, the ebbs and flows in popularity, the alliances made and broken, the tiny moments that become pivotal (or the huge blunders – hope you’re OK, Richard E G, or the massive curveballs – hi, James A, we’re still processing that one) and join in the fun, sign up to the temporary national pastime, or you don’t.The latter type will piss and moan about its existence and the former will enjoy that rarest thing – a few hours of respite from the world that is too much with us, by immersion in a game that doesn’t matter and that harms precisely no one.It’s true this season is unlikely to go down as a classic – too few twists, not enough suspense, too few metaphorical jugulars severed, not enough Celia Imrie farting in a shack – but it still got its main job done.And left us with the hope that one day Maya will turn to politics, ideally on a joint ticket with Joe Lycett, rise again and come to rule us all.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsBBCreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ceilidh renaissance’ lures gen Z offline in search of real-life joy | Folk music | The Guardian
description: Young dancers at the Ivy House in south-east London join the older crowd amid a renewed appetite for authentic, community events
Author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
Headline: Young dancers at the Ivy House in south-east London join the older crowd amid a renewed appetite for authentic, community events
Content: ‘It’s really lovely to come together in spaces with lots of different people,’ said one dancer at the ceilidh at the Ivy House in Nunhead, south-east London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s really lovely to come together in spaces with lots of different people,’ said one dancer at the ceilidh at the Ivy House in Nunhead, south-east London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianFolk music‘Ceilidh renaissance’ lures gen Z offline in search of real-life joyYoung dancers at the Ivy House in south-east London join the older crowd amid a renewed appetite for authentic, community eventsRosie Peters-McDonaldFri 30 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheIvy House pubin Nunhead, south-east London, has long been associated with raucous music, with the rock legends Ian Dury and Elvis Costello gracing its stage in the 70s, and indie favouritescarolineandKiran Leonardpulling in crowds today. But last Friday, it was a traditional Scottish ceilidh dance rather than a grassroots gig luring London’s cool kids to its sticky dancefloor.The event is emblematic of a renewed appetite for analogue, in-person experiences among a younger generationplagued by a loneliness epidemicandfatigued by meeting people on dating apps.“We spend a lot of time looking at screens,” said Matt, who saw the event as a refreshing way to spend time offline. “It’s really lovely to come together in spaces with lots of different people.”View image in fullscreen‘It just makes you feel alive.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianThe popularity of the ceilidh is evidenced by the launch of Ceilidh the Musical, which promises a “heart-warming party” with no experience required and started its tour at Shoreditch town hall, eastLondon, last week.According to the ticketing platform Eventbrite, from 2024-25 ticket sales for ceilidh events in the UK grew by 16%, while there was 15% growth globally. Page Dudley, a spokesperson for the platform, said young people were looking for events that were “communal and a lot less polished”.“It’s my first time at a proper ceilidh,” said George, 35, at the Ivy House. “I just like how silly it can be. It just makes you feel alive.”His partner, Louise, 32, was also a ceilidh first-timer. She said she liked how nobody was judging other people’s dance abilities. “It’s nice that it’s all ages,” she said. “When you strip away the ego, everyone just becomes their childlike selves.”View image in fullscreen‘Everyone just becomes their childlike selves.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianJamie, 19, is a seasoned ceilidh attender and said they were becoming much more popular among his peers. He has even bumped into schoolfriends unexpectedly at ceilidhs. “Everyone is just laughing at the same stuff, especially when people get confused [with the dance moves],” he said.Anna Spree, the communications, events and fundraising assistant atLink Age Southwark, which raised money from ticket sales at the Ivy House dance, said the “ceilidh renaissance” had allowed the local anti-loneliness charity to reach new people.“[The dances] were accessible enough that anyone could join in, but also slightly complex, which made them a lot more fun,” she added.View image in fullscreen‘It’s nice that it’s all ages.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianCeilidh, which comes from the Gaelic word for “visit” or “gathering”,originatedin Scotland and Ireland in the 19th century.“I’ve noticed the ceilidhs we’ve been putting on have been attended by a lot of under-30s,” said Alison Craig, a guitarist in the South East London Folk Orchestra (SELFolk), which provided the music on Friday.The ceilidh was organised after a successful dance in the same pub last year, which Craig recalls was bustling with young ceilidh newcomers. “The last time I saw the Ivy House bouncing like that was in about 1975,” she said.Although this particular ceilidh took place in a bar, Craig maintained that ceilidhs could be good for dry nights out, too: “You think, bloody hell, I’ve just had a Saturday night out and not had a drink.”View image in fullscreenSELfolk – the South East London Folk Orchestra – provided the music.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianEd McCabe, the founder ofLondon Ceilidh Club, has also noticed the shift. “Ever since Covid, it’s really boomed,” he said. “People just want to be in a room together.” He believes ceilidhs have “low barriers to entry” and are a great place to meet new people – or even find love.“There’s a whole aspect that you can’t look cool while you’re doing it,” he said. “You’re sweaty, you can’t stop smiling … it’s a great place to meet someone.”Craig echoed this: “It’s not about trying to look sexy or really cool,” she said. “Not to say ceilidhs aren’t sexy or cool, because they can be. You just need to get into it and enjoy it.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s the opposite of not being picked for sports at school.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianRichard Jones, who plays the accordion in SELFolk, suggested another great thing about ceilidhs was that they weren’t heteronormative. “It’s non-gender, if you like,” he said.His bandmate Neil McLean, who plays the flute, agreed. “We don’t really do men and women, we do ones and twos,” he said. “It’s the opposite of not being picked for sports at school.”SELFolk hosts regular ceilidhs which attract a crowd across all ages, according to Jones. “[People] know it’s safe, they know they can have a good time, and they don’t need to come in groups,” he said. “Very quickly the group becomes its own community.”Explore more on these topicsFolk musicFolk dancingYoung peopleLondonPubsLonelinessCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League
Content: Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this.Illustration: Nathan Daniels/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGuéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this.Illustration: Nathan Daniels/The GuardianManchester CityHow can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe?Barney RonayClub’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier LeagueFri 30 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 18.59 EDTShareI felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.Not my words. Also not the words of theManchester Citycentre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.This passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead moreNow the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.There have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking: “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”Football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have said, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?View image in fullscreenThe physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight.Photograph: Matt West/ShutterstockAgain, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.The first issue is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.And maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary issue derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.What are the consequences of this new fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.Manchester City guilty over Premier League charges after £900m of ‘sham’ contractsRead moreAnd here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to issues of personal principle.The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?There are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest issue here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been said out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.Explore more on these topicsManchester CitycommentShareReuse this content

title: The White House Farm massacre phone calls: could a single disputed digit set Jeremy Bamber free? | Jeremy Bamber | The Guardian
description: He has been in prison for 41 years for killing five members of his family. But if a phone call was made to the police by Bamber’s father on the night of the murders – as his team believes – one of the UK’s most notorious criminals could be exonerated
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: He has been in prison for 41 years for killing five members of his family. But if a phone call was made to the police by Bamber’s father on the night of the murders – as his team believes – one of the UK’s most notorious criminals could be exonerated
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; Sinenkiy/GettyView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; Sinenkiy/GettyThe Bamber filesJeremy BamberThe White House Farm massacre phone calls: could a single disputed digit set Jeremy Bamber free?He has been in prison for 41 years for killing five members of his family. But if a phone call was made to the police by Bamber’s father on the night of the murders – as his team believes – one of the UK’s most notorious criminals could be exoneratedSimon HattenstoneFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTShareOn7 August 1985,fivepeople were found dead atWhite House Farmin Essex, England:28-year-oldSheila Caffell(known to her family asBambi); hersix-year-old twin sons,Daniel and Nicholas; and her61-year-old adoptive parents,June and Nevill Bamber. All five had been shot with a rifle. Caffell’s24-year-old brother,Jeremy Bamber, who was also adopted, had calledto alertEssex police to a disturbance inside the farmhouse – he said his father had called to tell him – and had been outside with the police forfourhours before the bodies were discovered. Caffell, who had recently been hospitalised withschizoaffective disorder and is said to have feared her children were going to be taken into foster care, was found with the rifle lying on her chest, pointing towards her neck. There were two gunshot wounds to her neck and chinand a bloodiedBibleby her side.The case was initially thought to be open and shut, a tragic murder-suicide committed by Caffell. But a month later,Bamberwas arrestedafter relatives went to the police to voice their suspicions about him; his former girlfriendJulie Mugfordthen told police he hadmade a confession to her. The relatives went on to inherit from Nevill and June Bamber’s considerable estate after Bamber’s convictions. It was later discovered that Mugford had agreed to sell the story of their relationship to the News of the World for £25,000 if Bamberwas convicted. Essex police andcrown prosecutors had also agreed to drop charges against her forburglary, chequebook fraud and selling cannabis, because “prosecuting her could jeopardise her availability or credibility as a key witness” against Bamber.View image in fullscreenBamber arrives at Chelmsford crown court for his murder trial, October 1986.Photograph: Peter Case/Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesBamber was found guilty of the murdersand has now been in prison for41 years,but questions have always been asked about the safety of his conviction. These have grown recently. The proper body to examinethese is the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), but it has already taken the CCRCfouryears to consider less than half the evidence that Bamber has submitted to them. InJuly 2025, it concluded that thefirst four of 10 pointsdid not meetthe high evidentiary threshold needed to refer the case back to thecourt ofappeal.In the third piece inour series considering discrete pieces of evidence, we analyse discrepancies in timelines recorded by Essex police that could prove Bamber’s innocence.“Imagine how stupid I’d have to be to put myself in the frame for murdering my family by telling the police I’d received a phone call when I hadn’t,” Jeremy Bamber says. “Like most people, I assumed the police would have been able to trace the call. If it turned out Dad hadn’t called me, I’d have basically been handing myself in.”View image in fullscreenBamber with his girlfriend Julie Mugford at the funeral of his sister, his adoptive parents and his two nephews in August 1985.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyBamber is writing to me from Wakefield prison. For the past 41 years, he has been locked up for the murder of five members of his family, while always protesting his innocence.In his letter, he is referring to a phone call he made to Essex police from his cottage in the middle of the night on 7 August 1985. Bamber, now 65, told the police his father, Nevill, had just called him to say Bamber’s sister, Sheila Caffell, had “gone crazy” at the family home, White House Farm, and got hold of one of Nevill’s guns. Bamber said the line had then gone dead. His call to Essex police has never been disputed. What has been disputed is his claim that Nevill called him.At Bamber’s trial, the prosecution claimed he had made up the call to provide himself with a false alibi. They argued that he had killed the five members of his family at White House Farm between 12am and 3am, before cycling back to his cottage and calling the police himself.This is a story about telephone calls, technology and timings. It is also a story about a single disputed digit in police logs, which could prove Bamber’s innocence. A digit that, at the time of the trial in 1986, neither the jury nor Bamber’s defence team could possibly have understood was so significant. It was only 25 years later, when347,000 documentsrelating to the case were released, that its importance became clear.The digit relates to the time Bamber called the police. At trial, there was confusion about whether it was 3.26am or 3.36am. The presiding judge, Sir Maurice Drake, told the jury to accept a timing of 3.26am. But a series of police logs and statements that were not disclosed at trial suggest Bamber made the call at 3.36am.View image in fullscreenA crime scene photograph of White House Farm, with the telephone left off the hook.It appeared to be an obscure time-keeping argument in court, of little real significance. But it seems there is evidence that the jury was misled and that the differing times in fact refer to two different calls – the first made by Nevill and the second by Jeremy Bamber. And if Nevill did call the police to report his daughter had gone “berserk” with a gun, his son should not be in prison.The trialChelmsford crown court, October 1986. PC Michael James West, who took Bamber’s call at Chelmsford police station in the early hours of 7 August 1985, takes the stand to give evidence for the prosecution. He explains that he works in the control room, a radio and telephone hub for the Chelmsford division, where the unit’s calls are received and officers are allocated their tasks. PC West says he filled out an event log, called a C1, as the conversation took place with Bamber, and that the practice is to log the time at the beginning of the conversation. Surprisingly, that C1 call log is not available to the jury. West tells Anthony Arlidge, the QC for the prosecution, that he recorded the time of 3.36am using the digital clock on the wall in the control room.Arlidge doesn’t mention the time again. It is only when Geoffrey Rivlin, counsel for the defence, cross-examines West that he is challenged about the purported inconsistencies in his record-keeping.View image in fullscreenNevill and June Bamber, who were found dead at White House Farm.Photograph: HandoutIn his first statement, made two days after the murder, West said he received the call from Jeremy Bamber at 3.26am. In a more detailed statement a month later, the time had changed to 3.36am. Rivlin suggested in court that West had got the time wrong when he changed it and that the call was made, as he had said in his first statement, at 3.26am.Rivlin: I would like to ask you about times first, if I may. The time you have recorded was 03.36.West: That is correct.Rivlin: Is it right that you may have misread the clock and the time may have been 03.26?West: I was informed I actually spoke to theinformationroom at a time prior to the one that I have recorded so I can only assume that I have wrote – I actually recorded the wrong time, as it were.But then West, it seems, becomes defensive. He is reluctant to say he made a mistake or that the clock was inaccurate.Rivlin: The situation is, you looked at the clock and recorded 03.36. You were told subsequently that was almost certainly wrong and you said you may have misread the clock.West: Well, there is a dispute over the times. I don’t know whose time is right and whose time is wrong.Rivlin: Let me ask you this question. As regards the clock in thecontrolroom at thepolicestation, is that accurate?West:. Yes, it is.Rivlin: Are you sure about that?West: It has on occasion been inaccurate, but on very few occasions.Rivlin: Would you agree with this, that thecontrolroom wall clock rarely shows an accurate time?West: I would have to disagree with that.Rivlin: You disagree?West: Yes.Rivlin: At all events, perhaps we need take it no further than this, that you did subsequently agree you may have misread the clock?West: It is possible, although certainly there is a variance in times, yes.This exchange must have been baffling for the jury. West appeared unwilling to concede that he got the time wrong. Rivlin seemed to suggest the difference between 3.26am and 3.36am was highly significant, but never explained why. He was determined that 3.26am should be recognised as the correct time, but the jury was given no explanation for his insistence.The reason Rivlin was adamant that the call was made at 3.26am is simply because he thought it looked better for the man he was defending. Bamber had said he received the call from his father at about 3.15am, then rang his girlfriend, Julie Mugford, before calling the police. What kind of man waits 20 minutes and speaks to his girlfriend before contacting the police in such an emergency? Ten minutes, Rivlin thought, would seem more acceptable to a jury.But Bamber says that is looking at it with the benefit of hindsight: “The last thing I thought when Dad called me was that this was going to end up with my whole family killed.” There had been previous incidents with Caffell, who had a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder and had been hospitalised after a psychotic episode five months before the murders. But none had ended in disaster.The evening before the killings, Bamber had been at White House Farm and had taken out his father’s .22 rifle, to try to shoot rabbits. When he returned to the farmhouse, he had removed the magazine and the bullet in the breech of the rifle and left those items, and the gun itself, on a bench in the annexe of his parents’ kitchen.View image in fullscreenThe C1 call log made by PC West, which wasn’t available to the jury in this case, noting the details of a call from Jeremy Bamber at 3.36am on the night of the massacre. The call log was eventually disclosed, 25 years later.He didn’t fear for the worst when he got the phone call from Nevill, he tells me, because he knew the gun was unloaded. “I assumed my dad, who was 6ft 4in and a strong man, would take the gun off Sheila and that she would calm down.”As for waiting 20 minutes before calling the police, Bamber has always claimed his father was cut off in the middle of their conversation and that he tried a number of times to call him back, but kept getting the engaged tone. He says he then called Mugford at 3.30am and asked her what she thought he should do. Mugford – who told police a month after the murders, just after Bamber ended their relationship, that he had confessed the killings to her – advised him to “go back to bed”.He ignored her and at 3.36am, he says, he called the police. “If I’d made up the call from Dad, why on earth would I have said I took 20 minutes to call the police? I would have said I called the police immediately.” Bamber is telling me this in letters sent a few months ago, before the prisonbanned him from discussing his case with journalists.But the 3.26am timing of the call appeared to be supported by a rolling log made by a civilian phone operator, Malcolm Bonnett. He was situated at Essex police HQ, a building roughly a mile away from Chelmsford police station, where West was stationed.Bonnett’s job was to log radio messages and send help from the police and other emergency services. Emergency 999 calls came in to Bonnett, but he also took phone calls from local police stations and officers such as West.The Bonnett logwasshown to the jury at the trial – exhibit 29. It was presented to the court as his record of a call West made to him about the phone call he had received from a Mr Bamber. The jury was told that the Mr Bamber in question was Jeremy. Bonnett’s rolling log starts with an entry at 3.26am. The subject line for this call is “Daughter gone berserk”. This is the only document the jury were shown in regard to the time of the call. It was never explained why West’s C1 log of the phone call was not included in the bundle given to the jury. They had no idea why West had logged the time as 3.36am or why the confusion in court when it was suggested he had got it wrong.Something didn’t add up. At the trial, it was unclear whether West or Bonnett actually sent out the police cars. Both appear to claim to have done so. West said he radioed the officers asking them to attend the scene, but Bonnett also said that after receiving the call from West about the incident he sent the first police car, CA7, to White House Farm at 03.35am, followed by another car, CA5, at 03.36am. These timings only made sense if West had taken the call from Bamber at 3.26am.After West and Bonnett’s evidence, the time of Bamber’s call played no part in the trial until the summing up, in which Drake stated that the clocks in the information room were later checked and found to be correct. He advised the jury to accept the true time of Bamber’s call as 3.26am. “You would, in effect, be giving the defence case the benefit of a doubt, and I will suggest that you may – although it is always a matter for you – work on the timing of 03.26 as the time when the phone call was made to Chelmsford police station, and accept thatPoliceConstable West quite simply made a mistake when reading the clock, or writing down 03.36.”View image in fullscreenThe Malcolm Bonnett log shown to the jury at the trial – exhibit 29. This rolling log starts with an entry at 3.26am, with the subject line ‘Daughter gone berserk’.In fact, though, insisting that the call was made at 3.26am gave Bamber anything but the benefit of the doubt. Instead, it put him in the time frame for the murder, because the chronology now made sense: Bamber called West at 3.26am, and West called local officers, who set off for White House Farm at 3.35am.After a month-long trial, the jury came back with a 10-2 majority on 28 October 1986. Bamber was convicted of one of the most notorious crimes in British history and sentenced to life with a recommended minimum of 25 years. This was later extended to a whole-life tariff by the then home secretary Douglas Hurd in 1988, although Bamber was not made aware of this until 1994.Fast-forward 25 years. It’s 2011 and Bamber now spends most of his life in prison searching for exculpatory evidence. There is also a campaign team working on his behalf to try to get his conviction overturned. He belatedly receives 347,000 pages of documents, initially withheld by Essex police, after public interest immunity laws are amended in favour of greater disclosure.This is when Bamber’s team becomes convinced it has found the smoking gun. Amid the myriad documents is the C1 form that West filled in as he was speaking to Bamber on 7 August 1985. Astonishingly, this log wasn’t even included in the exhibit list, which includes every document that can potentially be shown to the jury. The time recorded on it is 3.36am, as he stated at trial. At the top, it clearly states who has made the call and from what address – Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger. The subject is “Distress call”.When West’s C1 log is compared with Bonnett’s log, important differences, apart from the times of the call, become obvious. In West’s C1 log of Bamber’s call, it says: “Father phoned (aged 62). Please come over your sister has gone crazy and has the gun. Phone went dead. Sister Sheila Bamber age 27 has history of mental illness.” This is clearly Bamber relating the call from his father – hence the reference to father and sister.By contrast, the opening of Bonnett’s rolling log, which begins at 3.26am, is told from a wholly different perspective. For a start, it refers to Caffell as “daughter” rather than “sister”. The subject of the log is “Daughter gone berserk” and it says “Daughter Sheila Bamber aged 26 yrs has got hold of one of my guns”. The guns at White House Farm belonged to Nevill. In West’s C1 log it refers tothegun. Both logs get Caffell’s age wrong. Bonnett’s says she is 26, West’s 27. In fact, she had celebrated her 28th birthday a couple of weeks earlier. In West’s log, Bamber has mistakenly added an extra year to his father’s age. In Bonnett’s log, no age is given.Then there is the different way in which the caller’s name and address is logged. The convention in police logs is to start with the informant’s name and address, because it immediately establishes who is providing the information, and it means they are traceable if contact is lost. Bonnett’s log of West’s call refers to “Mr Bamber, White House Farm, Tollshunt D’Arcy”.West’s log refers to “Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger”. Next to the address for White House Farm is the phone number. Bonnett’s rolling log doesn’t have a number for the farm till 03.56am, when the police confirm that the phone is off the hook.In addition, Bonnett’s 3.26am log makes no mention of Caffell’s history of mental health problems, a crucial fact that any officers dispatched to the scene should have been informed of. The differences in perspective and facts between Bonnett’s log and West’s log would surely have been spelled out by Rivlin for the defence if both had been available.There is a line space in Bonnett’s log after the initial paragraph, and then it states: “Message passed on to CD [Control Chelmsford, the code used to refer to the central radio control room where West was stationed] by the son of Mr Bamber after the phone went dead”. The line space suggests it could be a new entry.View image in fullscreenThe presiding judge, Sir Maurice Drake, told the jury to accept a timing of 3.26am.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyWhen Bamber’s team came across West’s C1 form, they were convinced that this explained the confusion between 3.26am and 3.36am and why the first police car had been dispatched before Bamber’s call: there had been two distinct calls. They believed that the first section of Bonnett’s log referred to a call from Bamber’s father, Nevill, and that this was the information the police appeared to have responded to. This would finally explain how a car had been sent to White House Farm before West said he took Bamber’s call. And, crucially, it would prove Bamber’s innocence.“At the trial, I had no idea why they were making such a fuss about whether I’d made my call at 03.26am or 03.36am,” Bamber writes. “It was only when we finally saw the log from West 25 years after I was first jailed that it became obvious there must have been two calls. The language is different, the perspective’s different, the information provided is different. It can only be two different people reporting the same incident as they see it.”In 2016, a documents expert, Dr Chris Davies, studied the new evidence and concluded that the most likely reason for the inconsistencies was that there were two phone calls. “I consider that this would be my preferred explanation for them,” he said. If Nevill called the police at 3.26am to say his daughter had “gone berserk” and had the gun, it puts Bamber in the clear.If there was an earlier call from Nevill Bamber, there are various theories about who may have taken it, including Malcolm Bonnett (who died in 2023) and officers who were in the control room with PC West (there were at least two others).Bamber’s team felt that the 3.26am and 3.36am logs finally enabled them to make sense of a mystery from the original investigation: why had the police devoted so much energy to trying to prove that Bamber could have cycled from White House Farm back home to Goldhanger in 10 minutes, before finally concluding that it was impossible? This early police theory appears to have allowed for two calls – one from White House Farm at 3.26am and the other from Goldhanger at 3.36am, both made by Bamber.Fifteen years on from the disclosure of West’s C1 log, Bamber’s team are still scouring the 347,000 documents that were released to them. In 2020, they came across “pocket book no.49”, belonging to DC Stephen Myall, one of the three officers originally radioed, alongside PS Bews and PC Saxby, asking them to attend the incident at 3.30am, six minutes before West stated on his C1 log that he received the call from Bamber. At the time, they were on an undercover foot patrol of an industrial estate after a spate of burglaries.View image in fullscreenBamber’s home in Goldhanger, Maldon, Essex. It was from here that he called the police on the night of the murders.Photograph: Steve Douglass/ANL/ShutterstockIn his pocketbook, Myall wrote that he, Bews and Saxby immediately returned to Witham police station when, at “03.37am approx”, they received a phone call from West about the incident at White House Farm. “The Officer (PC West) at CD Control was on the phone and told us that he was relating information to us and still had the informant (Jeremy Bamber) on the other telephone.” Myall wrote that Bamber had told West that his father had said “words to the effect of ‘Come quick, your sister’s gone berserk. She’s got a gun’. The telephone had then gone dead.”Bamber’s team believes it is now clear that Bews, Saxby and Myall were contacted by radio at 03.30am, as a result of a call from Nevill at 03.26am. The police officers were not at Witham police station at that point, but immediately returned from the nearby industrial estate to collect the police car, which they hadn’t taken with them on the undercover job. West then contacted Witham police station, by telephone, at 3.37am, having spoken to Bamber for a minute, from 03.36am.The CCRC, the body that investigates alleged miscarriages of justice, has examined Bamber’s convictions three times. In 2002, it sent the case back to the court of appeal, butthe judges concluded: “The more we examined the detail of the case, the more likely we thought it to be that the jury were right.”In 2011, the CCRC refused to refer the case, stating that the evidence did not raise a real possibility that the court would find Bamber’s convictions unsafe. In 2021, his legal team made a new submission, consisting of 10 points. The CCRC has been widely criticised in recent years for its tardiness and its poor referral rate. In 2024/25, only 2% of cases – 31 out of 1,541 applications – were referred back to the court of appeal. (This rate has improved considerably since Dame Vera Baird became interim chair in June 2025.) By July 2025, the CCRC had examined four of the 10 points in Bamber’s submission and declared that, on the basis of these four points, it would not be referring the case back, although it would continue to explore the remaining six points.One of the four points that was dismissed was the discrepancy between 3.26am and 3.36am being recorded as the time of Bamber’s call to the police. The CCRC remains adamant that the different timings are a result of police error and that there was only one call, from Bamber, at 3.26am. This is despite the C1 log from West stating it was at 3.36am and despite Myall’s record stating that West had Bamber on the phone at 3.37am.The CCRC also claims that the issue of the call timings “had been dealt with at trial”. This is plain wrong. At trial, and at his 2002 appeal, Bamber’s team had no idea that there were two logs suggesting two calls to police about the same incident.Since the 2021 submission to the CCRC, more valuable evidence has been uncovered. After the trial, Drake ordered the Dickinson review, an internal inquiry by Essex police into what the Times called the “blunders, omissions and ineptitude” of the force’s early investigation into the murders. The review would examine, for example, why the crime scene was grossly contaminated; the destruction and mismanagement of vital evidence; and the timeline and call-log inconsistencies.The findings of the inquiry have never been made fully public. However, some documents from the review were released to Bamber’s lawyers in 2011 after a legal challenge. His defence team only recently discovered that the Dickinson review supports the 3.36am timing of Bamber’s call in its timeline of events on the day. It states that Bamber called West at 3.36am and, at 3.37am, “PS Bews, PC Myall & Saxby [were] at Witham. Receive telephone message from PC West. Despatched to White House Farm.” All these references are consistent with the first call to the police having been made by Nevill at 3.26am, officers being asked to attend White House Farm, then West taking a second call from Bamber at 3.36am.View image in fullscreenAn extract from the internal Essex police Dickinson review showing Bamber’s call at 3.36 and police leaving at 3.37.Today, West works for the Masons. I contact him to suggest that his original log, which stated that Bamber called the police at 3.36am, was in fact accurate and consistent with the statements provided by other officers. He tells me he cannot recall the details, 41 years on, without seeing the specific documents and suggests that we meet face to face.After this conversation, West does not respond to my calls. I text him with an explanation of why I believe his initial record of 3.36am was correct and suggest that a separate call may have been made at 3.26am. But he is having none of it: “Simon, I have nothing to add to anything that has been said and absolutely no comment on any of your rather ridiculous postulations. Jeremy Bamber was found guilty and remains a convicted felon. No one seems to ask: ‘What if that was the correct decision?’”Meanwhile, Bamber’s team continue to try to piece together the missing pieces of the jigsaw. A few months ago, they re-examined PC West’s trial transcript and came across an astonishing exchange between him and defence council Geoffrey Rivlin.Rivlin: You made it clear to him [Bamber] that police officers would be sent to the house.West: Police officers had already been sent when I spoke to him, yes.Here, PC West states that police officers had already been sent when he was speaking to Bamber. But if the police only received one call alerting them to the incident and the time of it was 3.26am, as the CCRC and Essex Police now insist, that would mean the first car had left before then. Yet the earliest mention of a radio call to officers is 03.30am and officers leaving is 03.35am. On the other hand if we stick with the 03.36am timing on West’s log, it only makes sense if there had been an earlier call because of the radio call to local officers at 03.30am and the leaving time of 03.35am.This was the closest the jury ever came to hearing that the police appeared to have received two different calls about the incident. Unfortunately, neither the defence nor the jury picked up on West’s answer that officers had already been sent to White House Farm when he spoke to Jeremy Bamber.View image in fullscreenBamber in jail in 2008.Photograph: Obtained by Guardian FilmsWhen asked to comment about the failure to disclose evidence and inconsistencies in officers’ logs, a spokesperson for Essex Police said: “In August 1985, the lives of five people, including two children, were needlessly, tragically and callously cut short when they were murdered in their own home by Jeremy Bamber. In the years that followed, this case has been the subject of several appeals and reviews by the court of appeal and theCriminal Cases Review Commission– all of these processes have never found anything other than Bamber is the person responsible for killing his adoptive parents Nevill and June, sister Sheila Caffell and her two sons Nicholas and Daniel.”A CCRC spokesperson said:“Mr Bamber has made three applications to the CCRC. The first application led to a referral to the Court of Appeal in 2001. His conviction was subsequently upheld. The second application to the CCRC in 2004 did not result in a referral. A third application received in 2021 is currently under review. A provisional decision on part of this latest application was issued to his legal representatives, and they responded to us in January this year. Work now continues to consider additional matters which were raised in Mr Bamber’s application. It would be inappropriate for us to discuss the case or make any further comment while the application is being reviewed.”Those convinced of Bamber’s guilt maintain that Nevill Bamber’s calls to his son and the police never happened. Which takes us back to the first statements Bamber made when he was arrested. At the end of an aggressive 11-hour interrogation by Essex Police on 10 September 1985, Bamber is getting frustrated with all the questioning about the phone call he claims to have received from his father. He suggests there is one easy way of settling the issue. Get hold of British Telecom’s records. Bamber is apparently convinced this will provide him with an alibi and prove that he is telling the truth. If his father never called him, this is a kamikaze defence. All Essex Police need do is check BT’s records, and if there isn’t a call from White House Farm, he has implicated himself.Bamber: Telecom must be able to tell you the times of phone calls on my parents’ phone.Officer: What d’you mean by that?Bamber: It would be proof that I received a phone call from my father.Officer: If I tell you that Telecom can’t give such details then your theory can’t be checked.Bamber: I thought Telecom could.But it couldn’t. Or at least that’s what he was told. Despite an extensive advertising campaign in Essex stating that phone records were being digitised at the time, Essex Police said that calls in the area could not yet be itemised and bills still relied on an anonymised meter system. Years later, documents emerged showing that Telecom did indeed have itemised bills of earlier calls made from Bamber’s home phone number, though these were long-distance calls.An Essex police document showing BT records were destroyed.One aspect of the Bamber case that must have shocked the judge was how much evidence was destroyed on the day of the murders. At the time, the police believed it to be an open-and-shut murder-suicide. But that can never excuse the destruction of bloodied mattresses and bed linen.However, in 1996, 11 years after the murders, an even more shocking obliteration of evidence took place. Although it was known that Bamber was preparing an appeal for the Home Office (which was subsequently inherited by the newly formed CCRC, in 1997), Essex police unilaterally destroyed vital evidence. Among the list of exhibits that were destroyed are bullets, blood samples and swabs, all of which may have provided exculpatory evidence for Bamber as DNA testing became ever more sophisticated. It was particularly alarming that Essex Police destroyed Sheila Caffell’s heavily bloodstained night dress, which may have shown her to have been in contact with the other victims, who were also very bloodied.As so often in Bamber’s case, the document listing the evidentiary material and whether it was to be filed or destroyed is incomplete. Here it starts at number 167 and finishes at 661. At numbers 598 and 599, it says “British Telecom extract of calls”, citing the telephone numbers for Bamber’s home and White House Farm. By the side of both entries, it says “Destroy”.Explore more on these topicsJeremy BamberThe Bamber filesCriminal Cases Review CommissionUK criminal justicePoliceShare

title: This is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop nationalist populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rules | Jonathan Freedland in Tel Aviv | The Guardian
description: The opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in power, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in power, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Partnership for Peace (Shutafut LaShalom) calls for the Yashar party leader, Gadi Eisenkot, to form an alliance with Israel's Arab parties, Herzliya, 29 October 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPartnership for Peace (Shutafut LaShalom) calls for the Yashar party leader, Gadi Eisenkot, to form an alliance with Israel's Arab parties, Herzliya, 29 October 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelThis is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop nationalist populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rulesJonathan Freedlandin Tel AvivThe opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in powerFri 30 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.59 EDTShareIt’s less an election result than a philosophical puzzle: what happens when a win contains a loss, a loss contains a win and the two collide? That’s the question posed by the confused and confusing outcome of this week’s Israeli election, one that, despite its murky uncertainty, offers clear, sharp lessons – both for that country and for those locked in combat with nationalist populists across the globe.Start with the result that has simultaneously handed Benjamin Netanyahu a devastating defeat and a strong chance of staying on as prime minister, extending a run that has seen him lead Israel, on and off, for more than 19 of the past 30 years. The defeat is clear enough. At a stroke, his parliamentary majority was wiped out. Before Tuesday, the parties that together comprised his ruling coalition controlled 68 of the Knesset’s 120 seats: that tallyhas now shrunk to just 53, far short of the 61 seats needed for power. That’s a loss in anybody’s language.And yet, Netanyahu does not look or sound like a man defeated. That’s because he knows that while the parties arrayed against him won many more seats than he did – 67 to his 53 – their chances of forming a government are slim. If they fail, one or two of them might peel away and enter a so-called national-unity government – under Netanyahu as PM – or there will have to be fresh elections, ones from which, most analysts agree, Netanyahu would emerge stronger.The opposition’s problem is not arithmetical. It goes much deeper. Put simply, a big chunk of the anti-Netanyahu seats were won by parties that chiefly represent the one in five Israeli citizens who are Palestinian. This was the big twist of Tuesday’s election, a huge surge in turnout for what Israelis refer to as the Arab parties. Usually, far more Jewish than Arab Israelis participate in the country’s elections, but this year that pattern was flipped:turnout in Palestinian communities inside Israel hit 80%. The result is a record total of 19 seats for Arab-led parties. The anti-Netanyahu bloc cannot form a government without them. In today’s Israel, Palestinian politicians are the kingmakers.On paper, the next step might look straightforward enough. All Netanyahu’s Jewish opponents need do is team up with their Arab colleagues and they can send the PM packing. But such an alliance would mark a watershed in Israeli history. It would mean breaking a taboo that has endured, with only fleeting exceptions, since the founding of the state, a taboo rooted in mutual suspicion.On the one hand, Israel’s Jewish-led parties have long shunned the mainly Arab parties because the latter identify as anti- or non-Zionist, meaning they reject Israel’s self-definition as a Jewish state. For that same reason, Arab-led parties have maintained a boycott, refusing to legitimate the Israeli state by participating in its government.In 2021, a short-lived “government of change” broke the taboo by including in its ranks Ra’am, an Islamist party regarded, improbably enough, as the most moderate of the Arab groupings. But after the Hamas massacres of 7 October 2023, the taboo was restored – and hardened. Netanyahu cast Palestinian-Israeli politicians as an enemy within, as tacit allies of the Hamas killers, a framing buttressed by a crude anti-Arab racism voiced most explicitly by his coalition allies – the likes of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – and which sought to delegitimise Israel’s entire Arab minority.This was Netanyahu’s core message throughout the campaign: you can’t trust my opponents because, when the moment comes, they will sit with “the Arabs”. In recent days, he and his allies have doubled down on that message, claiming high Palestinian turnout means that “the Arabs are stealing the election” – rather than merely exercising their democratic rights – and, on Thursday,alleging that Qatar paid Palestinian-Israeli citizens to vote, thereby rendering the entire result void.Instead of challenging Netanyahu’s framing, and insisting that the vote of every citizen, Arab or Jewish, is of equal worth, most of the main opposition parties –Yair Golan’s Democrats were the exception– bowed to it, pledging that they would not forge a coalition with the largely Arab parties, and certainly not with any group more radical than Ra’am. Now they find themselves in a bind. On their own, the Jewish-led opposition cannot form a government. Unless they somehow manage to lure defectors from Netanyahu’s bloc –perhaps one or both of the ultra-Orthodox parties– even Ra’am’s support won’t be enough to reach the magic number of 61. They need Arab partners – and probably several of them.This, then, is the big lesson for Israel. That group that has long opposed Netanyahu – Jewish-Israelis who despise a PM on trial for corruption, who has mounted serial assaults on Israel’s institutions, including the supreme court, and brought isolation, if not pariah status, upon the country – are now confronted with a fact that has long been true but which they have preferred not to see: that they are a minority in the land they once dominated. As Aluf Benn, editor of the liberal daily Haaretz, told me: “The Jewish vote is predominantly rightwing in Israel and has been for decades.”That means the Jewish Israeli opposition cannot win alone. This week stands as proof, because this was their perfect opportunity. Netanyahu was at his lowest ebb, the leader on whose watch the most calamitous day in Israeli history took place, the leader who promised to destroy Hamas in Gaza, but who succeeded only in turning that place into a ruin, killing tens of thousands and, in the process, destroying Israel’s standing in the world. He faced in Gadi Eisenkot, his lead challenger, a decorated former general rooted in the Mizrahi working class, a man universally regarded as honest and decent, a bereaved father whose own son fell in the Gaza war – a man, in other words, who might have been designed to appeal to the very voters who for so long have been beyond the opposition’s reach. And yet none of that was enough to win.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe only way the opposition can succeed is by making common cause with their Palestinian fellow citizens, just as Democrats in the US –who have not won a majority of the white vote since 1964– could never win the presidency without the support of Black Americans. No one should underestimate the scale of the task, which requires a deep cultural shift as much as a political one. It should have been the work of decades, rather than a panicked scramble in a few rushed weeks of coalition horse-trading. It demands a reshaping of Israeli society, breaking a pattern of systemic discrimination and inequality within the country that has existed since the founding of the state (to say nothing of the post-1967 occupied territories where, of course, millions of Palestinians have no vote at all in Israeli elections). That task was always essential, but this week has confirmed that, if the right’s lock on power is ever to be broken, it can be delayed no longer.Much of this is peculiar to the unique political terrain of Israel. But there are broader lessons for all those fighting nationalist populism, whether that be Donald Trump innext week’s US midterms, Marine Le Pen in France or Nigel Farage in Britain. First, don’t accept the terms laid down by the other side: that was the cardinal error made by Netanyahu’s challengers. Second, mere opposition and criticism is not enough. The nationalist populists will always tell a compelling story; you have to tell an equally compelling one of your own. And, last, you need to be every bit as determined as they are. Too often you play by gentlemen’s rules, when those you are fighting are anything but gentlemen. Netanyahu is without shame and will do anything – cross every line, cut any deal – to keep power. The opponents of such a man will prevail only if they show an equal resolve in seizing it.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael-Gaza warcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s been a whirlwind’: the Essex lawyer who quit her job and became voice of Netflix’s hit show Spike | Children's TV | The Guardian
description: Emily McGonagle was watching cartoons with her sons when she decided to embark on a career change. A decade on, she is a star of a globally popular children’s series
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Emily McGonagle was watching cartoons with her sons when she decided to embark on a career change. A decade on, she is a star of a globally popular children’s series
Content: Emily McGonagle plays eight characters in an animated series called Spike about a young dragon and his friendsPhotograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmily McGonagle plays eight characters in an animated series called Spike about a young dragon and his friendsPhotograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianChildren's TV‘It’s been a whirlwind’: the Essex lawyer who quit her job and became voice of Netflix’s hit show SpikeEmily McGonagle was watching cartoons with her sons when she decided to embark on a career change. A decade on, she is a star of a globally popular children’s seriesEsther AddleyFri 30 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmily McGonagle was on maternity leave from her job as a lawyer, juggling the care of her new baby and her toddler son, when the daily diet of TV cartoons made her think about an unlikely career change.Watching Peppa Pig and Paw Patrol, her older son’s favourites, “it occurred to me: who does this job?”, says the 42-year-old fromEssex. “How do you get into it? Even when I was watching TV commercials, I’d think: well, how do you do that?”McGonagle had been commuting to her demanding legal job in London from the family home in Colchester, but was ready for a more flexible work-life balance. She had always loved performing in school plays and knew she had a talent for accents – so why not look into how to become a voice actor?A decade on, she is voicing one of the most popularNetflixTV shows in the world. McGonagle plays eight characters in an animated series called Spike about a young dragon and his friends. When the programme launched on the streaming network on 12 October it quickly became the seventh-most-watched programme globally in any genre.“These past few weeks have been a bit of a whirlwind and very surreal,” says McGonagle. “It’s just amazing to me that one day I was watching Peppa Pig with my kids wondering how you get into it, and today I’m turning on Netflix and seeing Spike next to Peppa Pig in the top 10. It is honestly amazing. I could never in my wildest dreams have imagined that I would get to this point.”Video from Emily McGonagle’s YouTube channel.When first looking into the industry as a young mum, she says: “I realised that with the right training and setup with professional audio equipment, I could do it from home – which was a revelation to me because I had assumed everything was done in a studio.”With the support of her husband, Ciarán, she converted a large wardrobe into a soundproofed vocal booth and began auditioning for voiceover jobs that were offered online. She started with a few corporate training videos, before getting some commercial TV and radio adverts, even voicing a Formula One-themed go-kart ride.But the ambition to work in children’s animation never wavered, so she looked into drama classes at her local theatre, then took some specialist courses in acting for voice animation. The roles in Spike came about when McGonagle saw the project advertised “on LinkedIn, of all places” by the Lithuanian animation company behind it. Originallyscreened on YouTube, its snowballing popularity among hard-pressed preschooler parents eventually attracted the attention of Netflix.Voicing multiple different characters in the same project can be a challenge, says McGonagle (She provides the voices for 20 in the video game Game of Thrones: Kingsroad, “and that was a lot”).How does she keep them distinctive? “I write a bio for my characters and think about what they look like, how old they are, where they might be from and give them some backstory in order to bring that character to life. And then I will adapt my voice to make it younger, make it older, or I might add an accent. It’s all about the way in which you move your body and even your mouth itself.”‘You’re stealing my identity!’: the movie voiceover artists going to war with AIRead moreThe characters she voices in Spike include the main character’s mother, a girl giraffe, a boy elephant, and the canine police officer. Some speak with various English accents, some American. “Those were just the accents and characters I put forward when I auditioned,” she says. “It’s not ultimately my decision.”“It’s a very international team and we do all communicate online but there haven’t been any in-person meetups. We have spoken on Zoom calls but nobody has ever met in person because we all have our own home studios,” she says.McGonagle’s sons, Finn and Jack, are now 11 and nine, and far too old for preschool dragons. They must be proud of her unusual career path, though? “They’re not really that bothered by it, which is probably a good thing,” she says. When she read them bedtime stories when they were younger, “honestly, they would just tell me: ‘Ah stop, don’t do the voices’.“Quite often I’ll be going around the house talking in different voices just to practise and they do get annoyed with it.”Explore more on these topicsChildren's TVAnimation on TVWork-life balanceEntertainment TVTelevisionWomenNetflixfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade | Commonwealth of Nations | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: UK PM to launch drive to restructure debt of poorest Commonwealth countries but rejects demands for reparations
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Exclusive: UK PM to launch drive to restructure debt of poorest Commonwealth countries but rejects demands for reparations
Content: Andy Burnham said he wanted to share his ‘sorrow and regret’ for the pain and suffering of millions of people due to slave trade.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said he wanted to share his ‘sorrow and regret’ for the pain and suffering of millions of people due to slave trade.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/AFP/Getty ImagesCommonwealth of NationsAndy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave tradeExclusive: UK PM to launch drive to restructure debt of poorest Commonwealth countries but rejects demands for reparationsBritish people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy BurnhamPippa CrerarandNatricia DuncanFri 30 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has gone further than any previous prime minister towards offering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, in a Guardian article ahead of a Commonwealth leaders’ summit where the subject is expected to dominate.As he prepares to fly to theCaribbeannext week, the prime minister said he was open to calls for an official apology on behalf of the state and offered formal talks to those affected, including individual countries and campaign groups at home and abroad.Burnham wrote: “The Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”While any formal statement will depend on that dialogue, Burnham gave what amounted to a personal apology, saying he wanted to share his “sorrow and regret” for the pain and suffering of millions of people, and to recognise the way the slave trade still shapes the world now.However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries and campaigners for the UK to pay financial reparations for its role in the slave trade, maintaining the position of successive governments that British people today could not be held liable for the past.He wrote that reparations were not the “right answer”, adding: “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, which happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”‘We want a full apology for slavery’: Commonwealth at a crossroads as king heads to the CaribbeanRead moreInstead, Burnham said he would launch a new drive to restructure debt for the poorest Commonwealth countries – led by former prime minister Gordon Brown and expected to eventually include organisations such as the IMF – helping them repay debt over a longer period and with better interest rates.Debt servicing costs for the poorest and most vulnerable Commonwealth countries are at their highest in more than 25 years, he added, with more than 40% of those spending more on interest repayments than on health.Burnham’s intervention follows years of pressure from Caribbean states, backed by some African countries, for European nations including the UK, France and Spain tooffer reparations– including monetary compensation, a full formal apology, support for health and education and debt cancellation.As recently as last week, the Commonwealth secretary general, Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey,said a formal apology for slaveryfrom King Charles, who will attend the heads of government summit, “wouldn’t hurt” and the “time has come” for a serious conversation on reparations.Writing for the Guardian, Burnham said: “The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths.“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.”He added: “We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.”View image in fullscreenA protester from the Guyana reparations committee holds a placard as people demonstrate on the day King Charles visited Georgetown, during a tour of Caribbean nations that will also take him to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersBurnham’s intervention received a cautious welcome from leading figures in the Caribbean. Dorbrene O’Marde, the chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations support commission, said his organisation welcomed the statement as “a movement in the correct direction in the interest of reparatory justice and humanity generally”.But, he added: “We reject the decision that financial reparations will not be on the table.”Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure inthe Repair campaign, told the Guardian that an apology was the first point in the Caribbean community’s 10-point reparations plan but “though necessary, is insufficient”.He added: “We are pleased to hear that [the UK] comes into a conversation. But it can’t be a conversation about nothing. It has to be a conversation about something. If they are not going to entertain reparations, what is the conversation about? Nothing.”Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caricom reparations commission, said he believed Burnham “is carrying the broad middle of British opinion on this matter”.He said the call for financial reparations need not be a stumbling block to progress: “There are much broader issues that can occupy that dialogue. So you don’t know what you will emerge out until you have a conversation of decency.“I think the prime minister will find that Caribbean leaders are very reasonable people on the matter of developing a new Anglo-Caribbean bond … words are important, but the spirit of collaboration is more important.”In a statement, the Barbados prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground” but said she and the UK government “are not yet on the same page on every element”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully. Honest disagreement on some questions should not hold back progress on the many others where we can readily agree.“An apology, a commitment to eradicate a mindset that is anchored in Afrophobia and against all things “black”, investment in health and education, development partnership that fights systemic poverty and institutionalised inequality, and fairer terms on debt for vulnerable states, as called for by the Bridgetown Initiative, are a few of the areas where we believe understanding can be reached and settled,” her statement said.“I thank prime minister Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, for breaking new ground and recognising that this is the right thing, and the moral thing, to do by ensuring that we move to the next stage of engagement on this difficult and emotional issue,” it added.The UK government has taken a cautious approach to the issue amidpressure from leftwingMPs to offer a formal apology and engage in reparatory justice, alongside concerns over the potential fiscal and electoral impact, withpolls suggesting most voters are opposedto financial compensation.The Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), which King Charles will also attend, runs from Sunday 1 November until Wednesday 4 November.At the previous Chogm summit in Samoa two years ago, Britain’s former colonies agreed “the time has come” for a dialogue about reparations – even though then-prime minister Keir Starmer said it would not be on the agenda.Officially, this year’s theme is “accelerating partnerships and investment”, with discussions on climate, youth employment, growth and trade between the 56 member countries, which between them represent 2.7 billion people.Some inside the UK government had questioned whether Burnham should even attend after the reparations row dominated the 2024 gathering.
