But his decision to address the issue head-on is likely to be welcomed in Antigua and Barbuda.Campaigners see the summit as the culmination of decades of advocacy from Caribbean leaders for a deeper acknowledgment of the UK’s historic responsibility for the enslavement of millions of Africans.Advocates say the UK had been under increasing pressure to act after a UN resolution in March which described the trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.The UK was among the 52 countries that abstained, saying that while it recognised the gravity of the issue, it disagreed with thefundamental propositionof the text which it said risked creating a hierarchy of historical atrocities.In June, Mottley,announced a new manifestofrom Caribbean leaders asserting the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations over damage caused by hundreds of years of enslavement.The 10-point plan argued that repair could include international debt cancellation and that climate justice and slavery reparations were “inextricably linked”.Burnham also referred to the history of Manchester as “the cotton capital of the world” which grew in part thanks to cotton picked by enslaved people.In 2023 the owner of the Guardian apologised for the role the newspaper’s founders had in the transatlantic slave trade, and launchedthe Cotton Capital seriesand a 10-year programme of restorative justice.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth of NationsAndy BurnhamReparations and reparative justiceCommonwealth summitSlaveryBritish empireColonialismShareReuse this content

title: Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries | European Union | The Guardian
description: Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’
Content: Antonio Costa, the European Council president, with Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister and, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in Montreal.Photograph: Graham Hughes/EPAView image in fullscreenAntonio Costa, the European Council president, with Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister and, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in Montreal.Photograph: Graham Hughes/EPAEuropean UnionCanada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countriesAlliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’Leyland Ceccoin TorontoFri 30 Oct 2026 15.42 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada andEuropehave announced a new alliance of like-minded nations toserve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president,Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.As they concluded their two-day summit,Canadaagreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever betweenEuropean Unionand a non-European country”.Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionCanadaAmericasEuropeMark CarneyUrsula von der LeyennewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspicious bets returning £149,000 for predicting Ballon d’Or under investigation | Ballon d'Or | The Guardian
description: A series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order of this year’s Ballon d’Or and generated almost $200,000 is being investigated
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: A series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order of this year’s Ballon d’Or and generated almost $200,000 is being investigated
Content: Harry Kane was crowned the winner at this year’s Ballon d’Or.Photograph: S Stingl/FC Bayern/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarry Kane was crowned the winner at this year’s Ballon d’Or.Photograph: S Stingl/FC Bayern/Getty ImagesBallon d'OrSuspicious bets returning £149,000 for predicting Ballon d’Or under investigationBets predicted exact top-five men’s finishing orderOrganiser France Football has contacted policeEd AaronsandRomain MolinaFri 30 Oct 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 17.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order ofthis year’s Ballon d’Orand generated almost $200,000 (£149,000) in winnings is being investigated by the event’s organisers, France Football, who have also contacted the police.It has been alleged that 12 Polymarket accounts – an American cryptocurrency-based prediction market – placed the bets, with more than $264,000 wagered on the outcome before Monday’s ceremony. Their extraordinary accuracy has raised serious questions about a potential leak of confidential results before football’s most prestigious individual award.Harry Kane was crowned the winnerat the ceremony at the London Palladium, finishing ahead of Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Lionel Messi. Remarkably, this was the exact order predicted by the group of accounts identified in French media outletUpside’s investigation.According to Raphaël Pautard, the co-founder of Upside, his team identified 12 Polymarket accounts created between 1 October and 20 October. The accounts displayed strikingly similar patterns of activity, leading investigators to suspect they could be connected to the same individual or group. Seven of the 12 accounts had not participated in any other betting markets, while six placed their first bets 15 minutes after being created.Pautard revealed that his team managed to trace one transaction back to a French platform. After sharing the relevant blockchain transactions and wallet addresses with the company’s team, the platform reportedly confirmed it had identified the individual behind one of the accounts involved in funding the suspicious bets. The identity of that individual has not been publicly disclosed, but the development could prove significant in establishing connections between the accounts and tracing the money behind the wagers.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Upside passed its findings to France Football, which Groupe Amaury owns and which has organised the awards since 1956. It is understood to have received confirmation on Friday afternoon that an investigation has been opened, with the French police also to be informed. France Football has been contacted for comment.Rather than spreading their money across different outcomes, the accounts concentrated their wagers on a specific scenario: Kane winning, followed by Mbappé in second, Yamal in third, Rodri in fourth and Messi in fifth. Every position subsequently matched the official results, generating nearly $200,000 in profits.According to the investigation by Upside, one account purchased a contract predicting Kane would win at 37 cents before selling it when the price reached 67 cents. The funds were subsequently redirected towards bets on specific finishing positions, including Yamal finishing third. This sequence of transactions has attracted attention because it suggests the account holder adjusted their strategy as the relevant markets developed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBefore the ceremony, France Football had indicated that only a handful of people knew the winner in advance. The possibility that confidential information could have reached betting accounts before the official announcement is therefore a serious concern, particularly given the precision of the predictions and the amount of money involved. “How do we keep the winner’s identity hidden? I think a well-kept secret is one that is shared with as few people as possible,” said the former France Football editor Pascal Ferré last week.Explore more on these topicsBallon d'OrnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police Scotland investigate Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s visit to Balmoral | UK news | The Guardian
description: Force says it has received ‘information’ on pair’s stay at royal estate as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Force says it has received ‘information’ on pair’s stay at royal estate as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor
Content: Undated photo appearing to show Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell near Balmoral in Scotland.Photograph: US Department of JusticeView image in fullscreenUndated photo appearing to show Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell near Balmoral in Scotland.Photograph: US Department of JusticeUK newsPolice Scotland investigate Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s visit to BalmoralForce says it has received ‘information’ on pair’s stay at royal estate as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-WindsorMatthew Weaverand agencyFri 30 Oct 2026 08.11 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 05.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDetectives in Scotland are investigating Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s stay at Balmoral castle as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor amid allegations that women were trafficked to the royal estate.Police Scotland said it had received “information” and inquiries were at a “very early stage” into the time the disgraced royal spent with the child sex offender at Balmoral.The late Epstein, who was convicted in 2008 of soliciting sex from girls, and Maxwell, who was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking a minor, stayed at Balmoral in 1999.Pictures previously released by the US Department of Justice appear to show Andrew and Epstein shooting on the estate.View image in fullscreenJeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell stayed at the royal estate in Balmoral, Aberdeenshire, in 1999.Photograph: John Bracegirdle/AlamyThe Daily Express has reported that the inquiries relate to claims that women were trafficked to the estate.A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing, but these are at a very early stage. All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries. We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”Other investigations linked to the release of the Epstein files were ongoing within several forces, including Thames Valley police, the Metropolitan police and Surrey police, the National Police Chiefs’ Council confirmed.An NPCC spokesperson said: “Identifying any further potential offending, suspects, victims or witnesses is a complex process and will take time, but UK policing remains committed to carrying out a meticulous assessment of the material released by the US Department of Justice.”There was no national investigation at present, the NPCC said.The former Duke of York was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office on 19 February this year, his 66th birthday, after allegations he had shared sensitive information with Epstein during his time as a UK trade envoy. He was interviewed under caution before being released under investigation. He denies wrongdoing, with the police investigation continuing.View image in fullscreenThe former Duke of York being driven away from Aylsham police station after his arrest in February.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersAn email released in a tranche of the Epstein files last year and signed by “A” asked the disgraced British socialite Maxwell for “inappropriate friends”. In one of four emails sent to Maxwell in August 2001 by someone using the name the Invisible Man, the sender told her their “valet” had recently died and they had “left the RN”.Mountbatten-Windsor left the Royal Navy the month before the email was sent. Another email from the same individual, dated 16 August 2001, said they were at “Balmoral summer camp for the royal family” before asking Maxwell: “Have you found me some inappropriate friends?”In March 2002, an email from Maxwell to the Invisible Man said she had passed on a message to an unnamed individual, with that message beginning: “I just gave Andrew your telephone no.”The message from Maxwell to the unidentified person also said “Andrew” would be “very happy” if he did some “two legged sight seeing”.Andrew was the UK’s special representative for international trade and investment from 2001-11, when he stepped down amid controversy over his friendship with Epstein.He received no salary for travelling around the world and the UK promoting Britain’s business interests, but criticisms were made about the thousands of pounds spent each year on his expenses and travel costs.His decision to quit the role came in the same year he was pictured with his arm around his primary accuser, Virginia Giuffre, who said she had been trafficked to the former duke at the home of Maxwell.Andrew paid Giuffre, a woman he has claimed never to have met, millions of pounds to settle a civil suit in the US in 2022.Giuffre died by suicide, aged 41, in April 2025.Explore more on these topicsUK newsScotlandEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand trial: accusers have ‘nothing to gain’ and were not led by media, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: In closing speech, prosecutor says six women had ‘bravely’ come forward after realising they were not alone
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: In closing speech, prosecutor says six women had ‘bravely’ come forward after realising they were not alone
Content: The women were ‘haunted’ by their encounters with Russell Brand, the prosecutor said.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe women were ‘haunted’ by their encounters with Russell Brand, the prosecutor said.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsRussell Brand trial: accusers have ‘nothing to gain’ and were not led by media, court toldIn closing speech, prosecutor says six women had ‘bravely’ come forward after realising they were not aloneEmine SinmazFri 30 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix women who have been “haunted” by their encounters with Russell Brand came forward to give evidence against him with nothing to gain and no appetite for fame, a court has heard.The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said the women, who do not know one another, had not been compelled to make police complaints by the “magic force” of media reporting on Brand’s alleged misconduct.In her closing speech, she told jurors at Southwark crown court that the women had “vivid recollections” and had “bravely” come forward to the tell “the truth” after realising they were not alone.Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Karmy-Jones denied that a 2023 Dispatches documentary about Brand had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.She said the complainants had described a similar pattern of behaviour, saying: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not looked out for some form of publicity, who have not taken part in a documentary, not made claims for compensation.“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago.”She said the women described how Brand’s “demeanour changed” before he assaulted them. “Listen to their accounts,” the prosecutor told the jury. “Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change. A pivot. His eyes changed, he snapped from charming to frightening and nasty.“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting. In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim.”She said the women had given the court “specific details” about Brand’s conduct. “What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago.“The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years,” she said.The prosecutor also accused Brand of using “gaslighting” to “good effect” by asking some of his accusers for their telephone numbers or emails after the alleged assaults.She said women were a “disposable commodity” to Brand and later added: “He was a defendant who was rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever her wished, whenever he pleased.”Karmy-Jones described the account of the youngest witness, a fan then in her early 20s who accused the TV personality of anally raping her at his London townhouse after meeting her at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.He cared only about his “birthright orgasm” and ignored her pleas for him to stop, the prosecutor said, adding that she was “just another number to add to his 5,000 notches which he was marking up”.The court heard Brand had a “flavour of disdain” towards the allegations, which the prosecution suggested was “a reflection” of his “whole approach to the female species at that time”.“Women as a whole were disposable, they didn’t matter to him. He didn’t even need to know their names. They were just a means to an end.“As he said in a 2017 interview, they were the amusements in what he described as his playground of orgasms,” Karmy-Jones continued.Earlier on Friday the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, gave legal directions to the jury in which he pointed out that they would have “rival arguments” to consider.Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.His barrister, Ian Winter KC, is due to deliver his closing speech on Monday.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’ | Binance | The Guardian
description: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses
Content: North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn from a different exchange last year.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenNorth Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn from a different exchange last year.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersBinanceNorth Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so farQ&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?Dan MilmoandKalyeena MakortoffFri 30 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifyingNorth Koreaas the likely culprit.Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars.Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the$1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.Trump says he doesn’t know who crypto tycoon is despite having pardoned himRead moreTRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack.Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets.The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who wasjailed for four months in 2024after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.Donald Trump pardoned himin 2025.The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”View image in fullscreenBinance was founded by Changpeng Zhao.Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMarkets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.”Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m.The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic.View image in fullscreenRichard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance: ‘Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg/GettyWorld Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers.Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.Share your experienceShare your experiencePlease share your response in the form below, anonymously if you prefer. We will contact you before we publish any of your submission.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhere do you live?Tell us a bit about yourself (e.g. age, background, what you do)OptionalIf you've been directly affected by the Binance hack, we'd like to hear about it herePlease include as much detail as possible.How did you hear about the hack? How has communication been so far?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.Has your confidence in crypto altered in any way?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.Do you have concerns?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.If you are happy to, please upload a photo of yourself hereOptionalPlease note, the maximum file size is5.7 MB.Choose fileCan we publish your response?Yes, entirelyYes, but contact me firstYes, but please keep me anonymousNo, this is information onlyPhone numberOptionalYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.You can add more information hereOptionalIf you include other people's names please ask them first.Would you be interested in speaking to our audio and/or video teams?Audio onlyVideo onlyAudio and videoNo, I'm not interestedBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreA spokesperson for the FCA said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.”The Bank of England is also monitoring the hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment.Coinbase, another major cryptocurrency exchange, said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarilyhalted trading after a security incidentinvolving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsBinanceCryptocurrenciesHackingNorth KoreaBitcoinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man accused of sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband says he thought it was ‘their kink’ | UK news | The Guardian
description: Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been drugged
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been drugged
Content: From left, top: Connor Sanderson Doyle, 32, and Norman Macksoni, 48; bottom, from left: Mohammed Hassan, 38, and Richard Wilkins, 62.Composite: PAView image in fullscreenFrom left, top: Connor Sanderson Doyle, 32, and Norman Macksoni, 48; bottom, from left: Mohammed Hassan, 38, and Richard Wilkins, 62.Composite: PAUK newsMan accused of sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband says he thought it was ‘their kink’Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been druggedSteven MorrisFri 30 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMen accused of sexually assaulting a woman whose then husband drugged her for years and allowed her to be abused have described being invited to the couple’s home via online adverts and a swinging website.One of those accused of assaulting Joanne Young, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, as she lay restrained and blindfolded said he was a young man “trying out things” and had no idea she was drugged.A second said there was a large “cuckold community” of men who watched their wives having sex, claiming his encounter was “just a sex meet” and she seemed “fine”.Philip Young, 50, has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and sexually abusing his former wife, 49, at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, over a number of years. The prosecution has said he advertised his wife online and “loaned” her out to other men.Four other men are on trial at Winchester crown court, including Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, who denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016.In police interviews read out to the jury, Sanderson-Doyle said he contacted Philip Young via Craigslist after seeing an ad in its adult section for a woman tied and blindfolded. He said he thought he had met a couple “trying to live out whatever their kink is”.He said he went to the Youngs’ house on his motorcycle. He asked if he should take his shoes off when he arrived, but kept his balaclava on throughout. He saw there were toys in the house so assumed the couple had children.Sanderson-Doyle, then 21, said he found Joanne Young “tied up and blindfolded” as she had been pictured in the online ad. She did not say anything but seemed awake.The defendant said that at one point he heard her say “No” but he thought she wanted him to do something different rather than stop completely.Sanderson-Doyle told police he started to get a “vibe she wasn’t enjoying it or was not comfortable” and left soon afterwards.He continued: “I thought I had her consent. I didn’t know she was drugged,” adding: “I was just a young guy trying out things.” He called the encounter a “non event”.A second man, Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. He told police he worked as an MC and went by the username “dark stranger” on the swingers’ site where he made contact with Philip Young.He said the site was “about couples living out fantasies” and there was a thriving “cuckold community”. Macksoni told police he had never had sex without consent and Joanne Young was “totally coherent”. He said: “It was just a sex meet and then I left.”The defendant told officers he did not wear a condom and added: “He specifically said she didn’t like them.”Also on trial are Richard Wilkins, 62, of Toothill, Wiltshire, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, of Swindon, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘His honesty gave courage to survivors’: domestic abuse charities praise Patrick Stewart’s legacy | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: Actor shared his childhood experiences as part of an Amnesty International campaign on violence against women
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Actor shared his childhood experiences as part of an Amnesty International campaign on violence against women
Content: Stewart speaking in Amnesty International’s Stop Violence Against Women campaign in 2004.Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreenStewart speaking in Amnesty International’s Stop Violence Against Women campaign in 2004.Photograph: Ian West/PAPatrick Stewart‘His honesty gave courage to survivors’: domestic abuse charities praise Patrick Stewart’s legacyActor first shared his childhood experiences as part of Amnesty International campaign and became Refuge ambassadorRachel HallFri 30 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenPatrick Stewartwas growing up in the 1940s, he witnessed how, after his father beat his mother, home doctors and ambulance workers would tell her: “You must have done something to provoke him.”Stewart knew the violence was never warranted, a conviction that became the spark for a lasting commitment to campaigning for greater understanding of domestic abuse.Asnews emerged of his death, aged 86, domestic abuse campaigners praised his legacy and said his contributions had helped raise awareness of domestic abuse and its impact on children.Patrick Stewart: the legacy of domestic violenceRead moreKerry Moscogiuri, Amnesty International UK’s chief executive, said that although Stewart, asCapt Jean-Luc Picardin the sci-fi TV series Star Trek, was “best known for playing heroes on screen … one of his bravest acts was telling the truth about his own childhood”.“For many years, he stood with Amnesty. He spoke openly about the violence his mother suffered at home to support our campaign to stop violence against women. His honesty gave courage to survivors around the world,” she said.“Our thoughts are with his wife, family and friends. The best way to honour him is to carry on the fight he believed in. It should appal us all that the scourge of violence against women and girls continues and governments must do far more to end it.”Stewart shared his storyfor the first timein 2004 as part of Amnesty International’s global campaign to cut violence against women.At the time, he recalled: “I saw the self-loathing of my father, due to his inability to control his violent outbursts. I saw society, police, doctors and neighbours conspire to hide the abuse with comments like: ‘She must have provoked him’, and: ‘It takes two to make an argument’.”He was moved to speak out about his childhood in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, after his 79-year-old brother said that “what happened had blighted his life”, and was spurred by a conviction that “violence must be controlled. If you fail to raise your hand in protest, you are part of the problem.”The most recent government figuresshowalmost one in 10 adults in England and Wales experienced domestic abuse in the last year, prompting domestic abuse charities to warn that the government was “not on track to fulfil its pledge” to halve violence against women and girls in a decade.In 2007, Stewart became an ambassador for the charity Refuge, a role he continued in for the rest of his life. His work included attending events and fundraising, as well as contributing his lived experience to policy discussions, with the result that children were recognised as victims of domestic abuse in their own right in the Domestic Abuse Act 2021.Sir Patrick Stewart obituaryRead moreHetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge’s chair of trustees, said the charity was “deeply saddened” to hear of his passing.She added: “I was privileged to watch his endless devotion and passion to the cause. He told me he did the work in honour of his mother, and in lending his voice he raised much-needed awareness of the cause and broke down barriers and taboos on the subject.“He empowered other survivors to come forward to speak out about the domestic abuse they had experienced and raised vital awareness of the longstanding impact domestic abuse has on children. He was very proud of the work he did with us and leaves an important legacy behind. He will be sorely missed by Refuge colleagues past and present.”Cherie Blair KC, who is also a Refuge ambassador, said she recalled being “profoundly moved” when she first heard Stewart’s account of his father’s violence towards his mother, and the “devastating impact it had on him as a child”.Describing him as a “powerful advocate”, she added: “At that time, it was unusual for a man, particularly someone as famous and respected as Patrick, to speak so openly about domestic abuse. His courage in sharing such painful personal experiences helped to break the silence surrounding domestic violence and reminded us that its consequences extend far beyond the immediate victim to the children who witness it.“Patrick understood how important it was for men to speak out against violence towards women. His support for Refuge was not simply lending his famous name to a worthy cause. It was a deeply personal commitment, sustained over many years.”The domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, Nicole Jacobs, said:“Patrick was a powerful advocate for women’s rights, using every opportunity to courageously share his experience and give a voice to survivors and child victims of domestic abuse. His loss will be deeply felt by all of us working towards a world free from domestic abuse. My thoughts are with his family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”The chief executive of Women’s Aid, Farah Nazeer, described Stewart as a “true ally” for speaking out.She said: “Eradicating domestic abuse, and wider violence against women and girls, requires a whole-society approach and champions like Sir Patrick were instrumental in raising awareness of domestic abuse and its long-lasting impact on women and children alike.”In the UK, the nationaldomestic abuse helplineis 0808 2000 247, or you can visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartDomestic violenceViolence against women and girlsAmnesty InternationalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed | Poundland | The Guardian
description: With the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conduct
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: With the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conduct
Content: Gordon Brothers said this week that options for the business ‘are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyView image in fullscreenGordon Brothers said this week that options for the business ‘are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyPoundlandPoundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposedWith the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conductSarah ButlerFri 30 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It was a very successful and simple proposition,” laments one formerPoundlandboss. With every product in the shop sold at £1, and the price in its name, its proposition to shoppers was the clearest of any UK high street chain.Now the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer could disappear amid heavy competition and inflation that has eaten into its ability to offer bargains.Its potential collapse has brought distress for its up to 12,000 staff in the run-up to Christmas, and as shoppers head to the chain for Halloween costumes and treats.Meanwhile, its low-profile owners are facing questions from the prime minister over their behaviour in the week his government’s budget attempted tooffer support to the high street.Poundland’s future hangs in the balance – and not for the first time – after the 36-year-old retailer filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.The legal measure protects Poundland, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland, from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the prospect of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers hold back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.The chain’s potential demise comes after Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring specialist which bought Poundlandfor a nominal £1from its previous owner in June last year, rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the whole chain by Martin Property Group.While the Northern Irish firm is still in talks about taking on Poundland, it is understood its offer amounts to about £15m. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood.This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, Poundland’s former owner, which holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News.One source who knows Poundland well said that Gordon Brothers had already taken about £10m in fees and interest out of the chain in the last year and that wanting another £30m was “egregious”. Gordon Brothers did not respond to a request for comment and has not confirmed this figure.View image in fullscreenIn the past, Poundland removed products if it could not sell them profitably for a pound, but its choices have become more limited.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianGordon Brothers said earlier this week that options for the whole and parts of the business “are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland’s people and all relevant stakeholders”.Sources close to the process said Gordon Brothers was unwilling to accept the Martin deal as the latest offer includes only about £7.5m up front and the rest over the next two years, leaving uncertainty for creditors, staff and suppliers.One source said Gordon Brothers had sought bidders for the whole of Poundland but “the market had spoken” and only one little-known financial bidder with no history of running a large retail chain in the UK had come forward who might only go on to break up Poundland itself.Instead, the restructuring specialist is understood to believe that suppliers and staff would be safer with the “trusted established retail operators” who have already put forward firm offers for parcels of outlets that amount to about half of Poundland’s stores, which could be converted to their formats.A deal may yet be agreed with Martin over the next 10 days, especially with political pressure from Andy Burnham. On Friday, he told the Telegraph: “We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.”For now, Gordon Brothers appears more keen on a break-up after losing faith in the likelihood of Poundland finding a route to long-term profitability amid tough times on the high street and heavy competition.UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price risesRead moreRapid inflation on the cost of goods and labour, energy and business rates in recent years has forced Poundland to take a hit on profits and sell products for more than £1, including items for £5 or more.In the past, Poundland removed products if it could not sell them profitably for a pound, but its choices have become more limited. High inflation – triggered first by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and then the Middle East conflict – has exposed a business model which always appeared to have a shelf life.In most supermarkets a two-litre bottle of milk costs over £2, a pack of KitKats is at least £1.50 and a tin of Heinz baked beans is about £1.40, according to the price comparison site Trolley. Cutting the size of Poundland has, meanwhile, reduced its scale, making it harder to get good deals from suppliers to protect margins.Poundland has also admitted that it made mistakes in recent years, including putting its Pepco clothing ranges into stores, which proved unpopular with UK shoppers.The expansion of cut-price chains such as Savers, The Range, B&M, The Works and Home Bargains alongside budget online rivals such as Temu, Shein and Amazon means the cheaper end of the UK retail market is now very crowded.Meanwhile, the low-wage shoppers that make up the core of Poundland’s clientele have little spare cash for non-essentials amidrising household bills. Those with more to spare have more options in their supermarket shop, where they are increasingly locked in by loyalty-card-linked discounts.Poundland’s pre-tax losses widened to £85.3m in the year to September 2025, from a loss of £45.4m in 2024, as sales at its outlets in the UK, Republic of Ireland and Isle of Man slid almost 12% to £1.55bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House.View image in fullscreenGordon Brothers was likely to come out looking like the worst version of a restructuring firm, said one expert.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianIn September Poundland said its revenues had returned to growth, up 3.3% at established stores in the latest three-month period, but sources said the business was not generating enough cash to pay off its loans.US-headquartered Gordon Brothers has a long history of involvement in selling off the assets of UK high street businesses, including offloading the stock and and fittings of failed retailers such as Toys R Us.It previously owned the British fashion brands Laura Ashley and Ben Sherman, where it oversaw the closure of their stores, and it recently bought LK Bennett, which has also closed its stores this year.One advisory expert said Poundland’s owners had intended the buyout to be a rescue operation rather than a break-up but ultimately: “Gordon Brothers has ended up doing what Gordon Brothers do. Leopards do not change their spots.”He said Gordon Brothers was likely to “come out looking like the worst version” of a restructuring firm. The number of stores likely not to find an immediate buyer “might not be as catastrophic as half” but it was unlikely buyers would be found for all, he added.Poundland’s possible demise is part of a wave of consolidation of similar outlets over the past decade.Poundworldclosed its 350 stores in 2018, and Poundland bought its rival99p Storesin 2015. Poundland thenclosed about 200of its then 800 UK stores in a restructuring last year.Poundstretcher was boughtby Majestic Wine’s owner, Fortress, in 2024.Poundland itself has a rocky history during which it has passed in and out of the hands of investment firms. Founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, the company was listed on the London Stock Exchange in 2014 at a value of about £750m by its then owner, the buyout firm Warburg Pincus.Just two years later, Poundlandagreed to a £597m takeover by Steinhoff, the South African retail conglomerate, after the British chain struggled to digest the takeover of 99p stores.By 2018, Poundland had toseek new investmentafter an accounting scandal at Steinhoff and was hived off into Pepco, a company formed from Steinhoff’s European retail business. Poundland was then preparing to rejoin the London stock market when the Covid pandemic hit in 2020, scotching those plans as high streets across the UK closed down for months.Last year, with costs rising, Pepcowas looking to sell. Gordon Brothers stepped in, snapping up the struggling chain with its £1 deal. It remains unclear whether someone new will flip another coin to bet on turning Poundland around.Explore more on these topicsPoundlandRetail industryUK cost of living crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sky-high ratings – for a lacklustre series: The Celebrity Traitors has become too nice for its own good | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Too many recruitments, frustrating confessions and an underwhelming murder in plain sight … this series has failed to take off
Author: Louis Staples
Headline: Too many recruitments, frustrating confessions and an underwhelming murder in plain sight … this series has failed to take off
Content: At the round table … James Acaster.Photograph: Euan Cherry/PAView image in fullscreenAt the round table … James Acaster.Photograph: Euan Cherry/PAThe TraitorsSky-high ratings – for a lacklustre series: The Celebrity Traitors has become too nice for its own goodToo many recruitments, frustrating confessions and an underwhelming murder in plain sight … this series has failed to take offLouis StaplesFri 30 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis article contains spoilers for theepisode of The Celebrity Traitors on 29 October. Do not read on if you have not seen it.What happens when a game that revolves around secrets and lies gets derailed by the truth? That’s what played out last night in the penultimate episode of The Celebrity Traitors, when – spoilers ahead! –James Acasterwas dramatically confronted at the round table about his role in murdering Ross Kemp. After being grilled by Michael Sheen in a soliloquy that felt borderline Shakespearean, Acaster did something we have never seen before on this show: he fessed up to the entire thing, falling on his sword and revealing his true identity.Acaster’s reveal is one of the defining scenes in a series that has broken the show’s sky-high ratings records. Yet watching the episode – and this celebrity series as a whole – I can’t shake the feeling that it’s been underwhelming. The grand finale could provide some big twists, but the show so far has felt tentative and lacked a certain spark. If Acaster’s confession had happened last year, it would have been merely a blip. But here, it feels emblematic of a series that, no matter what happens in the final, hasn’t quite lived up to the hype.The selection of the Traitors is one of the most important parts of the game because these players have an outsized influence on its direction and, as a result, often take up more airtime. They also become the unofficial narrators of the show as they are the only ones who know what is really going on.Part of the reason this series has felt lacklustre is because most of the Traitors were selected by the Traitors themselves, rather than producers who make a living from creating addictive TV. It all started with Richard E Grant’s epic blunder in episode one, when he told Joe Lycett that he was a Traitor and was quickly banished from the game. Not only did this deprive the audience of watching Grant and fellow Traitor Maya Jama scheming in the turret, but it set in motion a chain of events in which most of the Traitors were recruitments.The problem here is that some of the recruited Traitors didn’t seem up to the task of murder and betrayal. Acaster made no secret of the fact that he didn’t want to be a Traitor, and Hannah Fry didn’t seem fully comfortable in the role, either. I have no problem with these players being authentically themselves, but it’s more fun to watch characters such as Alan Carr (from the 2025 series) gleefully plotting in the shadows – to witness supposedly “nice” celebrities mastering the dark side. That’s what the game is about.The number of recruitments has also made the show feel stilted. Being a Faithful is a tricky task at the best of times, but it’s borderline impossible to have consistent theories or a sense of momentum when someone is being recruited every few episodes, rendering many events from earlier in the game null and void. The “original” Traitors making it deep into the game isn’t just satisfying for the audience; it’s also important for how the game functions. Too many recruitments can erode narrative cohesion.As a format,The Traitorsis close to being the perfect gameshow, which is why it has become a smash hit in almost all its international versions. But one flaw that’s baked into the game is that the biggest characters are often murdered or banished first, because they are seen as a threat to either the Traitors or the Faithful.This has an even greater impact on the celebrity version because we already know the players. For the audience, there is a sense of disappointment when a celebrity they really like gets eliminated early on. (Myha’la, I will avenge you!) This doesn’t exist in the same way on the civilian version, because we don’t necessarily know what we’re missing out on.Richard E Grant admits Traitors mistakes: ‘I never thought they would take me seriously’Read moreI can’t shake the feeling that the celebrities are just a little too nice to each other. Perhaps this is because they have been on TV before and are wary of how they will be perceived, or don’t want to fall out with someone they might see again in a professional setting. As someone who watches many international versions of The Traitors, I prefer the charm of the British show to the American version: the latter is far more conflict-filled and glitzy. But with this series, we’ve gone too far in the opposite direction. It’s become too nice and Acaster falling on his sword encapsulates that.On social media, there is a lot of anger towards Acaster, with some accusing him of making a mockery of the game. That was my initial reaction, too – and his confession has somewhat taken the wind out of the show’s sails ahead of the finale. But nobody watching at home can know how they would react in such a high-pressure situation.The backlash against the comedian is really misplaced frustration that this series hasn’t delivered many of those “OMG!” moments we have been accustomed to. Even the murder in plain sight – usually a box-office highlight – felt underwhelming. You can fill a castle with celebrities and engineer all kinds of twists, but sometimes it just doesn’t pan out the way you would hope. That’s reality TV for you.The Celebrity Traitors finale airs on BBC One at 8pm on 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsThe TraitorsTelevisionRichard E GrantJames AcasterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandma | Television | The Guardian
description: The star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filming
Author: Coco Khan
Headline: The star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filming
Content: Food for thought … Awkwafina aka Nora Lum.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFood for thought … Awkwafina aka Nora Lum.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTelevision‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandmaThe star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filmingCoco KhanFri 30 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m embarrassed I didn’t bring anything. It’s 10-something in the morning, and I’m meeting Nora Lum, 38 – best known as rapper, comic actor and writer Awkwafina – the morning after the Bafta TV awards. I feel that I should have brought her a pastry pick-me-up. Yet here I am empty-handed. “It could have been Chinese buns,” she playfully suggests.Yes, it could have been. Especially because we are meeting to discuss her new series on Apple TV, Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook. It sees the star of box-office hits Crazy Rich Asians and Marvel’s Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings travel across the US to learn from a new generation of Asian American chefs, in the hope that she might revive her own family’s long-closed Cantonese restaurant. But there’s one problem: she can’t cook.Or so she says. “Unlikely” cook? There’s nothing unlikely about it, I wager. Sure, in the first episode, Lum looks genuinely alarmed by the triple threat of hot oil, high heat and sharp knives in wok cooking. But she does very well. She clearly has a knack for food.“Well, I think it was the easiest knack to develop, because all it really takes is to eat at a ton of restaurants and order food constantly,” she pushes back.“But look, I was raised by immigrant Chinese people – I did eat all the weird Chinese stuff,” she says, understating her family’s impressive culinary credentials. The full story is thus: back in the 50s, Lum’s great-grandfather Jimmy opened one of New York’s first Chinese-American restaurants in Flushing, Queens. Called Lum’s, it became something of an institution, helping to popularise the Chinese-American food beloved today (think: orange chicken and BBQ ribs).“The restaurant is how we came to this country,” she explains. “It closed in 1982, so I wasn’t born. But it was so important. The way they talk about it is like a family member that passed away.”View image in fullscreenHigh steaks … Awkwafina and Jimmy O Yang (right) with Andrew Samia of Curry Boys BBQ in The Unlikely Cook.Photograph: Christina Belle/Apple TVLum’s new TV show about it is pleasingly warm and personal, with much of its gentle humour coming less from the supposedly awkward personality that inspired Lum’s stage name than her deep appreciation for food and hospitality. Have you ever seen someone scream “Oh my God, not the cilantro!” in ecstatic anticipation of a herb? I have, and it’s charming. But ultimately, Unlikely Cook is a love letter to Lum’s magnetic, occasionally foul-mouthed, paternal grandmother; the woman who raised her when she lost her mother at just four years old.Several months after I meet Lum, I see the Instagram post announcing her grandmother’s death. But, for now, I ask about the woman who has loomed so large over her creative work, and regularly steals the show in Unlikely Cook. How easy is it working with your own grandma?“It’s crazy. I’ve been asking my grandma to be in things since my first [TV] job, which was on MTV’s Girl Code,” Lum explains. Grandma obliged, starring in the brilliantly named episode Bad Sex, Grandparents, Eating Habits.“I’m always a little worried, thinking: ‘Oh my God, what are you going to say?’ But she has such a lovely on-camera affect. It just kind of clicks.”“With this [project], she’s calling me at all hours of the night, we’re staying up talking. Actually, she called me a week ago and was like, ‘I’m just thinking about the menu, and we should put a pu pu platter – but we shouldn’t call it pu pu, because, you know, it means shit so we should call it the volcano platter.’ It’s giving her excitement again.”View image in fullscreenFry hard … Awkwafina in The Unlikely Cook.Photograph: Christina Belle/Courtesy of AppleBetween the family appearances and actor Jimmy O Yang’s star turn (Lum’s real-life best friend) Unlikely Cook may be Lum’s most biographical work yet. Which is saying something given her hit 2020 comedy television show was literally called Awkwafina Is Nora from Queens, and starred her as directionless, awkward Nora living in – you guessed it – Flushing, with her widowed father and boisterous grandmother.For fans of Nora from Queens, there may be a particular, parasocial joy in watching Unlikely Cook. The sitcom could be absurd (Nora’s grandma accidentally growing cannabis, for instance), but you always sensed some emotional truth beneath it. Now we get the real Nora Lum.“Oh my God, yeah,” she exclaims. She refers to an episode where she is stressed. “That episode was bizarre to watch. Because I have never seen myself be serious, be panicked. That’s never been recorded.”“There was something about it where I actually felt bad. I felt bad for my exes, my friends. I was watching myself back like, ‘Chill out, girl!’”I didn’t have her pegged as the self-conscious type, I say, what with working so frequently from her real life. “I’ve never been documentarised in quite this way,” she explains. “There’s a part of me that’s like, oh my God, you let people see this crazy, unbridled version of you?! I still don’t know how to deal with that. But I do feel that whatever is honest, it can’t be the worst.”To be fair, foodisemotional stuff, and so often bound up in questions of identity, history and, especially in the immigrant context, family sacrifice. I ask Lum about her observation in the documentary that a generation of elders grafted in restaurants so their kids didn’t have to. They could be lawyers instead.“The truth is that a lot of the [older] people we met didn’t want their children to go back into the restaurant business. For my great-grandpa’s generation, when they came over they were relegated to either laundromats or restaurants, cooking food that has historically been demonised,” Lum says. “But then again, it’s also something that people love. There are more Chinese restaurants in America than there are McDonald’s, KFC, Burger King, all of that.”But while the restaurant business gave Lum’s family life, it also took a lot of it. Her grandmother had her own restaurant for a time, but when it failed, Lum’s grandparents were forced to file for bankruptcy, losing both their business and home. For a while, the whole family lived in a one-bedroom apartment.View image in fullscreenAll smiles … Awkwafina.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian“I think her business failing was really hard on her. She would fold the napkins in the back. She would launder napkins in our home. And she would be the most amazing maître d’ that the whole town knew. I don’t think she ever really recovered from it.”Would opening a permanent Lum’s be a way of rewriting that history?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I think giving back – if I’m in a position to do that – does feel like this full-circle moment where I could still make my family proud in that way. It would definitely be something for her.”All this talk of making family proud and honouring their sacrifices is something I know well, having also been raised in an immigrant household. Did Lum agonise over her choice of a creative career as much as I did when I chose English lit over law – something I loved over something that might more reliably make good on what my family gave me?“No, because I don’t think I was smart enough to get into law school,” she laughs.“Oh, I doubt that’s true,” I reply.“I’m actually not a good student. I went to summer school for gym.For gym. If you fail a class during the year, you can make it up over the summer. But it’s like a punishment, right? Every day I was taking two periods of gym, because I had failed so many times.”She continues: “Do you know what Earth science is? The rock one? It’s the easy rock one. It’s not even chemistry. I had to take the Earth science [exam] five times, dude.“So I think my family were just thinking, well, she has nothing to lose. Besides I wasn’t doing it off their dime, so I think maybe they were just happy I was doing something. But my dad really wanted me to be a meat inspector. I’m still on those government job registries that he signed me up for. He’s like, “Meat inspector, that’s a really good job.”“Itisa good job,” I concur.“It is! Great entry level salary. And you always, always need a meat inspector,” she says.“You could start now,” I offer.“I know, I know,” she laughs, and I wonder if she has the same idea I have.Awkwafina is the Meat Inspector, coming soon to Apple TV.OK, back to business. Watching Unlikely Cook, I couldn’t help thinking about the politics of America right now. After all, a show celebrating the work of immigrants feels significant in the age of Trump and ICE. Was that intentional?“No, not at all. But if you want to tell the story of Chinese-American food, immigrant culture is something you can’t ignore. It’s also a deep part of our identity as second-generation Asian Americans, it’s part of how we see the world. And it’s a hard thing to see right now in America.”Our time is nearly up. But wait, I’m still not sure, does this mean someday there will be a permanent Lum’s? “It’s still in the works of being figured out,” she says.But clearly, in Nora Lum herself, something has stuck. “After this show, I did start dabbling a little,” she says. While shooting a film in Kentucky, she took to cooking her own breakfast, “a four-egg omelette with spinach and cheese”, she says with faint pride. It’s not quite as impressive as Chinese buns. But maybe they’ll come soon.Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook is on Apple TV from Friday.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionFood TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Buy a wind-up radio – and don’t forget the chocolate: survival experts on how to prepare for an emergency | Emergency planning | The Guardian
description: UK government guidance says we should be ready for the unexpected, but what’s actually helpful to have at home? We ask the specialists
Author: Isabelle Aron
Headline: UK government guidance says we should be ready for the unexpected, but what’s actually helpful to have at home? We ask the specialists
Content: Just in case: a few essential supplies can make all the difference if everyday services are disrupted.Photograph: HanaHa/GettyView image in fullscreenJust in case: a few essential supplies can make all the difference if everyday services are disrupted.Photograph: HanaHa/GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterEmergency planningBuy a wind-up radio – and don’t forget the chocolate: survival experts on how to prepare for an emergencyUK government guidance says we should be ready for the unexpected, but what’s actually helpful to have at home? We ask the specialistsThe best power banks – testedIsabelle AronFri 30 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow prepared are you for an emergency? Do you have a few extra tins of beans in the cupboard, or a full-on preppers’ kit in the cellar? While no one likes to think about worst-case scenarios, you can’t have failed to notice the growing noise around being sensibly, practically ready for floods, power cuts, cyber-attacks and other events.The government launched itsBe Ready campaignin October withguidance on how to prepare for emergencies, including a list of suggested items to have at home.To help you understand what to buy, and where to buy it from, we asked survival, medical and nutritional experts for their advice. “There’s lots of panic about upcoming floods, El Niño and AI attacks, but this emergency preparedness is something we all should be doing anyway. It’s just a good idea to look after yourself and your family like this,” says Hannah Cloke, regius professor of meteorology and climate science at the University of Reading. And if you are in a position to do so, consider donating to a charity likeTrussellto help support one of thealmost one in 10 UK householdsalready experiencing food insecurity.From wind-up radios to water filters, here’s what the experts recommend adding to your list.Are you stocking up onessential items at home? What products have you found useful for past eventssuch as power cutsor being without water?Please let us know how you’re following government advice atthefilter@theguardian.com.What to keep at home in case of emergenciesView image in fullscreenReady for anything: a little planning can help you cope with the unexpected.Photograph: Natalia  Lebedinskaia/GettyFirst aid kit“Top of my list is a good first aid kit with sterile dressings that you can cut to size, not just little plasters, and some kind of tape to secure it with,”says John Hudson, chief survival instructor to the UK military and author ofHow to Survive: Lessons for Everyday Life from the Extreme World. “Zinc oxide tape is good because it’s super sticky and can be used for blisters. Other basics include crepe or elastic roller bandages, sterile eye pads, blunt-ended scissors, tweezers, safety pins or clips, alcohol-free antiseptic wipes and gloves for if you’re helping someone else.Lifeventure makes good travel-sized first aid kits.”Will Duffin, an NHS GP working in urgent care who runs theExtreme MedicInstagram account, also stresses the importance of a good first aid kit. “I recommend buying an off-the-shelf first aid kit, and then you can add bits into that,” he says. “One of the main things for families is a thermometer and some Calpol.” Duffin also suggests having supplies of basic, over-the-counter medication that might come in handy, such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, antihistamines, Imodium and rehydration sachets.“The other day-to-day one is wound care – cuts, aches and sprains. So have some antiseptic, sterile gauze, basic dressings such as plasters and medical tape,” he says. As well as getting the gear, you need to have some idea of what to do with it, which is why Duffin recommends going on a basic first aid course. Organisations such asSt John AmbulanceandBritish Red Crossoffer various options.View image in fullscreenTravellerfirstaidkit£37.99 at Lifeventure£37.99 at LifesystemsView image in fullscreenBraun ThermoScan 7ear thermometer£36 at Lloyds PharmacyFrom £44.85 at AmazonView image in fullscreenTommee Tippee 2-in-1thermometer£14.99 at John Lewis£15 at BootsWind-up radiosIn case channels of communication go down, the government has advised buying a battery or wind-up radio, some of which also have a torch and a USB slot to charge your phone. “It’s such a simple piece of kit. The wind-up versions are great because in an emergency, you can use the power of your own arm to power the battery,” says Cloke.View image in fullscreenImmverwind-upradio with 10,000mAh battery and LED torch£34.02 at B&Q£28.99 at AmazonA wool blanket and jumper“If you haven’t already got some kind of woolly throw or blanket in the house, get one. It doesn’t have to be expensive merino wool or anything like that; it just needs to be wool,” says Hudson. The same goes for woolly jumpers, too. “People have probably got enough clothes in their house, but make sure you have something that’s got a lot of wool in it. A jumper is brilliant because if it’s chucking it down with rain and you get caught out, wool will keep you warm even when it’s wet,” he says. Both are helpful if you have no way to heat your home, and are one of the best ways to keep you warm even if it’s damp.View image in fullscreenRecycledwoolblanket£30 at the RNLISupplies for your car“[Many of us] are in our cars all the time, and what happens if you get stuck? Put some blankets and warm clothes into it, have a torch, some batteries, jump leads, a small shovel, a hi-vis jacket so you can safelyask for help at night, some basic water and long-life food, and a first aid kit. A mini version of what’s in your house,” says Cloke. It’s also a good idea to have a sleeping bag in the boot of your car, so that if you’re driving and you get stuck or your car breaks down, you can stay warm in the car, says Hudson. “The sleeping bag can help stop you from becoming hypothermic. You want a hollow-fibre one because it will still keep you warm if it gets damp.Snugpak does great stuff, and several of its products are used by the military. You can also get secondhand sleeping bags from military surplus stores,” he says.View image in fullscreenSnugpakthesleepingbag£42.95 at Outdoor ActionFrom £41.06 at AmazonView image in fullscreenAAwintercarkit withfoldingsnowshovel£21 at Argos£15.73 at AmazonA torch“Most of us have got torches on our phones, but in an emergency you will want to save the battery for contacting people and other things. A basic torch and some spare batteries are a very useful thing during a power cut,” says Cloke. You can also buywind-up torches, which save on batteries.View image in fullscreenEnergizer 1,000-lumenmetaltorch£20 at Tesco£20 at B&QView image in fullscreenDuracell Plus AAalkalinebatteries (30pack)£27.95 at B&Q£22.49 at AmazonSpace blanket“Some of the cheap space blankets take up no space, but they’re like wrapping yourself in something thinner than a crisp packet, so they will rip if there are any sharp edges or wind. Reinforced ones are really robust. They’re a big sheet that’s silver on one side and brightly coloured on the other, with rivets in the corner, so you can do all sorts with them,” says Hudson. “Space blankets are lined with very thin, highly reflective aluminium so any radiated body heat is reflected back to you rather than being lost to your surroundings. Plus, the orange colour is a great way to get spotted by any potential rescuers if you’re outdoors.”View image in fullscreenRedcampheavy-dutyemergencyblanket£17.99 at AmazonHead torches“Head torches are great because you’re still able to use both hands while being able to see in the dark,” says Hudson. “You can spend a fortune on them, but you don’t have to. I bought an Energizer one recently, and it’s all that you really need.
