That one needs batteries, but you can get rechargeable ones too – I have one from Everbeam.”View image in fullscreenEnergizer Vision400-lumenheadtorch£19.99 at Argos£24.99 at Robert DyasView image in fullscreenEverbeam650-lumenheadtorch£16.99 at AmazonFor more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest head torchesWater“Having water stored is really important for a whole range of emergencies. The [mains] water might go off or get contaminated in some way. The key thing is to make sure you’ve got enough for the number of people in your household. My advice is to have 10 litres per person per day for hygiene, cooking and drinking,” says Cloke. The governmentguidancesuggests having enough bottled water for three days. It says you should have “three litres per person per day for drinking. More would be needed for other tasks such as cooking and washing”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWater filterHudson recommends a water filter bottle such as Pure Hydration’s Aquapure Traveller, which has a clever purifier cap to reduce harmful substances and microorganisms in water.You put in any fresh water, screw the cap on, and drink the water you squeeze through the purifier. “They’re amazing,” Hudson says. “The filter takes out a lot of the things in water that can harm you, from large things such as pathogens – worms and snail eggs – through to bacteria and tiny viruses, so you can more safely drink from any fresh water source you can find, such as rivers or rainwater. We’ve used them for 20 years in all sorts of environments with the military.” It’s a good idea to buyextra filters, too, although Hudson says they’re “good for 350 litres, so enough water at least 10 days if you’re not somewhere super hot and/or humid”.View image in fullscreenAquapure Traveller£49.50 at Pure HydrationPower bank“I think a power bank is more useful than batteries,” says Hudson. “You can buy big ones [he recommends the size below] that will also jump-start a car, which is quite handy, and also charge things such as head torches and phones. These days the bigger, the better if you don’t have to carry it; so many items need juice.”View image in fullscreenPortablecarbatteryjump-starterpowerpack£39.99 at AmazonFor more, read the Filter’s guide tothe best power banks and battery packs in the UK for reliable charging on the goHand sanitiser“Basic alcohol hand gel is important. If the water supply goes out, things like coughs and colds can spread within the family. Having a supply of hand sanitiser is good preparedness,” says Duffin. Cloke also recommends stocking up on “packets of wet wipes for basic hygiene, particularly if you’ve got babies”.View image in fullscreenCuticuraantibacterialhandgel£1.55 for 100ml at Boots£9.30 for 6 x 100ml at AmazonView image in fullscreenWet Ones Be Fresh Originalantibacterialwipes£2 for 40 wipes at Boots£9.43 for 6 x 12 wipes at AmazonCandles“Candles provide light without burning through your power supply. Go for stocky, fat ones because they’ll fall over less easily and last longer. Tea lights are also good – they don’t burn for ages, but you can buy sackfuls of them for not much money. You need matches too, like the big chunky boxes of Cook’s matches. Don’t leave unattended, and make sure you’ve got a fire extinguisher or a fire blanket,” says Hudson.View image in fullscreenVotivepillarcandles,four pack£3.50 at DunelmPulsesView image in fullscreenCupboard staples: tinned and jarred foods are handy when fresh supplies or cooking facilities are limited.“Tinned beans, chickpeas and lentils all have a long shelf life and are rich in fibre, nutrients and protein,” says Dr Federica Amati, head nutritionist at Zoe, nutrition lead at Imperial College London’s school of medicine and author ofThe Appetite ResetandEvery Body Should Know This. “Getting a variety is good for flavour reasons, but also for micronutrient content. Dried lentils are easy to cook, but if there’s a power cut or a shortage, tinned and jarred lentils will serve you better.” Oh, and don’t forget a tin opener.View image in fullscreenOxoGood Gripssoft-handledtin opener£19 at John Lewis£16.15 at AmazonGrain pouches“Microwaveable pouches are fantastic. If you’ve got a few ready to go, then if for whatever reason you don’t have enough water or can’t use the hob but you have a microwave, you can have these. Some of them you don’t even need to microwave, and you can just eat them out of the packet,” says Amati.View image in fullscreenMerchant Gourmetbrown,redandwildrice,250gx 6£9 at AmazonTinned fish“Get a variety of tinned fish, like mackerel, sardines, anchovies and sprats. Tinned mackerel is one of the easiest to integrate, and you can get them tinned with tomatoes, which a lot of people prefer if they don’t like fish. Find something you like, and then buy a couple more of those in your next shop, so you can build up a supply,” says Amati.Frozen fruit and vegetables“Buy frozen fruit and vegetables, if you have the space. Frozen veg is picked ripe and blanched within hours. Have some frozen berries and veg – broccoli, cauliflower and peas. You can get jars and tins of vegetables too, like roasted peppers, sweetcorn, carrots or beetroot,” says Amati. It’s also worth noting that, in the case of a power outage,food should stay frozen for up to 48 hours in a full freezer, or 24 hours if it’s half full, provided you keep thedoor closed.UHT milk, teabags and chocolate“UHT milk is worth getting, and make sure you have enough teabags, because you might be able to have a cup of tea, and those things are still important. Dark chocolate is also awesome – it keeps for months, needs no cooking or power, and offers plenty of energy in a small square, mostly from cocoa butter fats that sustain you rather than causing a rapid rise and crash in energy,” says Amati. She suggests opting for 70% cocoa or above so that “you also get more fibre, magnesium, iron and cocoa flavanols, plant compounds that support healthy blood vessels”.For more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest supermarket dark chocolateOats“Oats are fantastic,” says Amati. “You can just add hot water, mix them up, and then you’ve got something to eat. And you can eat them raw, mixed into yoghurt or milk.”Vacuum-packed bread“If you can’t buy fresh bread and you can’t freeze it, unopenedvacuum-packed rye bread can last about six months, and it’s super nutritious,” says Amati.View image in fullscreenBionaorganicryebread, 500g£3 at WaitroseOther tipsView image in fullscreenBe prepared: keep your first aid kit stocked and make sure you have enough of your regular medication.Photograph: Riska/GettyHave some cash“If there’s been some kind of tech outage and things are slowly coming back up, you might not be able to use your cards or phone to pay for stuff, so it’s worth having a little bit of cash,” says Hudson.Write down numbers“Everyone’s got people’s numbers in their phones, but what if the phone’s broken? Have some numbers written on a piece of paper, like people that you care about that you want to check in with and a number for a local medical centre in case you need to get your prescription,” Hudson says.Stock up on vital meds“If you’ve got some extra regular medication, that’s great. Sometimes people struggle to get that prescribed for them. But if you can stay a few days ahead, that will really help in case of emergency. I like to suggest having enough for a week or a month if you can, or at least two days if you’re struggling,” says Cloke.Duffin suggests having “at least seven to 14 days of your vital repeat medications in hand”, and that this is a useful thing to do anyway. “Request your script early, not just because of a severe weather event or a nuclear attack. If supply chains become more volatile, the medicine you need may not be in stock and might need to be ordered in.” Thegovernment guidancesays that “it’s important to request prescriptions up to five working days before you need your medicine”. The NHS also has anonline formyou can use to request emergency supplies of prescription medicine if you have run out, but note that they advise against ordering more than needed.For more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest camping stovesand thebest power banksIsabelle Aron is a lifestyle and culture journalist who’s written features on everything from the secrets of superagers to chefs on their favourite kitchen gadgetsExplore more on these topicsEmergency planningThe FilterGadgetsExtreme weatherClimate crisisHackingFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I wrote a book about death. Here’s what people really think about dying | Well actually | The Guardian
description: In the eight years since my graphic novel on death published, I’ve learned readers of all ages want to talk about loss and preserve their family’s stories
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In the eight years since my graphic novel on death published, I’ve learned readers of all ages want to talk about loss and preserve their family’s stories
Content: ‘What to Do When I’m Gone: A Mother’s Wisdom to Her Daughter is a lighthearted, emotional and illustrated ode to moving forward and living life fully while grieving the loss of a parent or anyone you love.’Illustration: Hallie Bateman/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘What to Do When I’m Gone: A Mother’s Wisdom to Her Daughter is a lighthearted, emotional and illustrated ode to moving forward and living life fully while grieving the loss of a parent or anyone you love.’Illustration: Hallie Bateman/The GuardianMemento mori: a series about deathWell actuallyI wrote a book about death. Here’s what people really think about dyingIn the eight years since my graphic novel on death published, I’ve learned readers of all ages want to talk about loss and preserve their family’s storiesSuzy HopkinsFri 30 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTShareBecoming an author in my late 50s was unexpected, the result of my daughter Hallie’s own existential anxiety in her early 20s.Fearing my untimely demise, she begged me to write down advice that would cover all of life’s bases going forward. I agreed, but put the project off for years; it wasn’t until she cornered me with a laptop on vacation that I gave in. She asked countless questions, and I found, to my surprise, that I had plenty to say. Hallie helped shape the manuscript, and then spent a year painting its warmly emotional gouache illustrations.Our graphic novel,What to Do When I’m Gone: A Mother’s Wisdom to Her Daughter, was published in 2018. Though marketed for mothers and daughters, it holds my advice to all three of my children on moving forward after I die. Included are notes on grief and loss and life, plus a few recipes – not because I’m a great cook, but because food is so integral to family heritage. The book is a lighthearted, emotional and highly illustrated ode to moving forward and living life fully while grieving the loss of a parent or, really, anyone you love.What we’ve learned in the eight years since its release is that readers of all ages have a deep hunger to know more about their parents’ backgrounds, beliefs and values, including around grief and loss.They want to talk about all of it.View image in fullscreenWhat to Do When I’m Gone: A Mother’s Wisdom to Her Daughter by author Suzy Hopkins (Author) and illustrator Hallie Bateman.Photograph: Courtesy of Hallie BatemanGone wasn’t exactly a hot property. All but one publisher rejected it, uncertain who would buy a book on death and grief. But Bloomsbury editor Nancy Miller saw potential for broad readership. Eight years later, it has been published in seven languages and continues to find new readers.The book has brought us comments from around the world. The most common:I lost a parent (or other loved one, including spouse or beloved pet) and your book helped me through.I gave the book to my kids and wrote my own notes in the margins.I can’t bear the thought of my mom or dad dying, but they don’t want to talk about it. I’m hoping that sharing the book with them will start some conversations.But the most frequent sentiment we hear is: My mom or dad died, and I wish they had left me something like this.In book events in New York and on the west coast, invariably, someone in the audience was crying. Sometimes, it was because of the person’s fractured relationship with their mother, and grieving the loss that represents. Most often, it was because they missed their mom or dad, and did not have a record of their unique voice and wisdom to lean on.There is science behind this hunger to know more, to deepen this vital connection between the generations.Studieshave shownthatknowing moreabout family history, including weathering hard times, is good for mental health and identity formation.I understand that hunger to know more, both as a longtime journalist and as a daughter. Years before Hallie coaxed me into doing our book, I wanted to capture my own mother’s story and did a series of interviews with her. Two decades after her death at 85, the slim memoir that resulted preserves her voice, wit and love for family.At the moment she died, I was at her bedside holding her frail hand when, suddenly, I was swept into an invisible cyclone of memories and feelings that lasted for several minutes – and left me stunned.Years later, that otherworldly experience helped me pen the closing pages of our book.But this isn’t an ad for Gone. You, like some readers, might even hate it: “It just rambles on about recipes and driving a car off a cliff and being trampled in a Black Friday sale and replacing your mother with someone else,” wrote one Amazon customer called Christine. “Is there even a point to the book?”View image in fullscreenYes, Christine, there is a point. Two, actually:Love endures long after the person we love dies.Talk about your beliefs, history and values with the people you love while you’re alive; share the stories that are yours, and in turn, theirs.Thankfully most readers seemed to understand, given all the feedback we’ve received. Some found themselves “ugly crying” in bookstores (though the book is funnier than it sounds) and many sent notes or wrote emotional reactions online.“As someone who has lost their mom, it’s something I reach for often when I need a hug from her,” Dara wrote. Natsu shared the book with her mother, who then wrote her own book – each section named after a favorite song – which Natsu spent a year illustrating. Some readers acknowledged that their parents would have very different advice from mine, but echoed that universal desire for help finding their way forward.My twin grandchildren may need such help.At two and a half, they are little human yardsticks by which I measure my remaining years. I may be around for their high school and perhaps college graduations, but clearly, the first decades of their lives will be the last decades of mine. And the older I get, the more I appreciate simple days, simple problems: hangry toddlers, high grass that needs mowing.I can fix these, unlike the world’s larger problems: the climate crisis, injustice, greed, the othering and abuse and killing of entire populations.These children, and their children, will need help making their way through chaos we cannot yet fully imagine.But there is a book.In it, they will see the sense of humor and worldview Hallie and I share, and perhaps better understand their own. When they hit hard times, I hope they will find comfort in its pages.After being dumped at 58, I realized I was not equipped for the griefRead moreSo, Christine, the underlying message is this: Think about what you will leave behind.Hallie and I always intended that Gone would encourage other families to have these deeper conversations: why you chose the paths you did, what you truly care about and why, how you think about death and grief and what’s beyond. The only real requirement is willingness to examine what you believe.Each person’s life leaves an imprint, and that imprint most affects the people we love – those who are here and those yet to come. Tell them what really matters.Because, as many people around the world have told us, it all matters more than you will ever know.Suzy Hopkins, a former newspaper reporter and magazine editor, is the author of What to Do When I’m Gone and What to Do When You Get Dumped. She lives in Cincinnati, Ohio. She previously wrote aboutthe unique grief of divorcefor the Guardian.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyMemento mori: a series about deathParents and parentingFamilyDeath and dyingBereavementShare

title: ‘It really was the idiots in charge’: inside the TV sketch show that launched a generation of stars | Television | The Guardian
description: It influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its due
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its due
Content: Astonishingly talented cast … back row, L-R: Catherine O’Hara, Joe Flaherty, John Candy, Dave Thomas and Harold Ramis. Front row, Andrea Martin and Eugene Levy.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenAstonishingly talented cast … back row, L-R: Catherine O’Hara, Joe Flaherty, John Candy, Dave Thomas and Harold Ramis. Front row, Andrea Martin and Eugene Levy.Photograph: NetflixTelevision‘It really was the idiots in charge’: inside the TV sketch show that launched a generation of starsIt influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its dueDale ShawFri 30 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSCTV – short for Second CityTelevision– is one of most influential comedy shows ever created. In the 1970s and 80s, while North American comedy fans worshipped at the altar of Saturday Night Live, the comedy nerds loved SCTV. The Canadian sketch show was weird. It was dark. It was multilayered and years ahead of its time.Dave Thomas, head writer and an original cast member, was there from the start. “Conan O’Brien said that he used to watch and he thought, ‘This show is being written specifically for me,’” Thomas tells me. “There were references in it that he was absolutely sure only he got. We wrote at the top of our reference level. And the idea was to see if the audience would meet us there.”Thomas was part of an astonishingly talented cast that included John Candy,Eugene Levy,Catherine O’Hara, Rick Moranis, Joe Flaherty, Martin Short, Harold Ramis and Andrea Martin. They wrote and starred in the series, which ran intermittently in Canada from 1976 to 1984. At a time when American shows dominated the airwaves, and homegrown content tended to be earnest factual programmes along the lines ofHinterland Who’s Who, Canadian audiences were delighted to see a show that reflected their culture while being – to everyone’s surprise – actually funny. It even went on tofind a late-night audience in the US.View image in fullscreenFormer cast members Catherine O’Hara (left) and Andrea Martin in SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of.Photograph: NetflixTo celebrate its legacy, Netflix has just added 134 episodes of SCTV to coincide with its release of a new documentary – SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of. Like many of the show’s fans, Thomas isn’t exactly enamoured with the title.“Yeah, the title is kind of insulting in a way,” he says.That’s not the only problem. While it’s a decent primer for revisiting the show, featuring new interviews with the surviving cast members, including Thomas, the documentary could have been so much more. Many things are skipped over, such as the musical acts, including bands like the Boomtown Rats and the Plasmatics, who didn’t just perform but also appeared in sketches. And while the cast took care of the writing in the show’s early days, they were later joined by talented staff. These omissions rankle with Thomas.“Tom Hanks and Bob Odenkirk doing the narrative on how it was written? I thought, what the fuck? Why don’t you ask some of the people who wrote it? We had some really good writers on that show.”SCTV’s Leave It to Beaver parodyThere is a cracking story to be told. For the uninitiated: the cast of Chicago’s legendary Second City improv theatre had already been plundered by producer Lorne Michaels to create Saturday Night Live in 1975. It seemed to make perfect sense to use Second City’sTorontooutpost to create a Canadian version of SNL. Gilda Radner and Dan Aykroyd had already been poached by Michaels, so the remaining cast members were asked to make a television sketch show without knowing the first thing about it.“For the first two seasons, SCTV was a failure,” Thomas remembers. “It was the poor brother of SNL. Our greatest weakness was that our show looked cheap as shit. So we made it about a small television station, and that’s why it looks so cheap.”Each episode of SCTV covered one broadcast day for a run-down TV station in the fictional rural Canadian town of Melonville. As well as parodying the film and TV of the time, the backstage dramas of the station also played a part.“We were learning,” Thomas tells me. “We were being paid to learn how to produce television while doing it. It really was the idiots running the asylum for the first two years. There are a lot of things we got credit for that were just horrible mistakes.”View image in fullscreenJohn Candy, who would later go on to star in Planes, Trains and Automobiles with Steve Martin.Photograph: NetflixThe naivety of the cast and the low budget, paradoxically, freed up the sketch-writers: without shiny sets and special effects, they focused on characters. There was the overbearing station managerGuy Caballero, the cheapskate’s cheapskate; the garrulous variety starJohnny LaRue, who was an extension of John Candy’s party-loving nature; Catherine O’Hara’s showgirlLola Heatherton; Eugene Levy’s appalling standup,Bobby Bittman; and Harry, the Guy With a Snake on his Face. Sketches were smart, sharp and featured startlingly accurate impressions (Thomas’s Bob Hopewas a standout).As time went on, the show found its feet, started gaining an audience, increased its budget and grew more sophisticated.“I was particularly proud of the evolution of the comedy,” Thomas remembers. “Like the parody of the television show Fantasy Island, which was also a parody of Casablanca, and also a parody of Road to Morocco, and also a parody of The Wizard of Oz, all weaved in and out. A lot of the Simpsons writers said that’s what they loved about SCTV, that it brought in a kind of a multilayered writing. And they said: that’s the way we write The Simpsons.”But as the money came in, the creators’ freedom dwindled. Used to having everything their own way, the cast and writers baulked when threatened with any outside interference.“I remember one of the producers that NBC had sent up was in the cafeteria one morning, crying,” recalls Thomas. “I said, ‘What’s the matter?’ He goes, ‘The goddamn cast, they shut me out. They stonewall me. I’ve got a good mind to quit.’ And I said, ‘Well, you probably should quit because you’re here in the cafeteria, crying. Is that what you had in mind when you got into showbiz?’”View image in fullscreen‘We thought, screw this press conference, let’s go to Studio 54!’ … Dave Thomas.Photograph: NetflixBeing produced in isolation gave SCTV a distinct personality and a legion of devoted fans. But the team were still very much on the outside.“We went to New York for a press conference,” Thomas says. “There were only three people there and two of them were student journalists. But we thought, well, screw this press conference, let’s go to Studio 54. We’re on television. We should be able to get in. They wouldn’t let us in.”Thomas and Rick Moranis (later to star in Ghostbusters, with Harold Ramis, and Honey, I Shrunk the Kids) were part of SCTV’s most surprising breakout success. Asked to include more specifically Canadian content in the series, they improvised two-minute pieces to camera featuring two dim-witted, beer-swilling, hockey-watching Canucks, Bob and Doug McKenzie. The characters caught on: Canadians, so used to watching American stereotypes played for laughs on TV, loved seeing two of their own get the same treatment. The documentary shows Beatles-like levels of hysteria at McKenzie brother appearances. They went on to record albums and make a film.Not everyone in the cast was delighted by all this, as Thomas admits. “There’s no question that the success of the McKenzie brothers was a divisive factor and played a role in Rick and I leaving. There were little things like that which definitely sowed some seeds of division, but we were still family.”The show shifted networks, time slots and cast members until it eventually fizzled out in 1984. But the SCTV family went on to greater heights. John Candy became a Hollywood star. Eugene Levy and Catherine O’Hara featured in many of Christopher Guest’s comedies (including Best in Show and A Mighty Wind), as well as starring in Schitt’s Creek together. Martin Short is, well, Martin Short.And Thomas has a wildly varied career: he starred in the sitcom Grace Under Fire, wrote Spies Like Us with Dan Aykroyd, started an animation company and is now developing an Amazon show with his son. But Thomas will always be fiercely proud of his SCTV achievements.“I loved that show because, I thought, nobody’s doing this. Nobody is doing a show like this. There was a network tendency to dumb everything down to the stupidest person in the room. And we didn’t do that.”SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of streams on Netflix from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionCanadaTV comedyTorontoCatherine O'HarafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why M&S director Kathryn Turner is the ultimate ‘Gay Halloween’ costume idea | Halloween | The Guardian
description: Product development boss at Marks & Spencer inspires niche outfits after unexpected success on social media
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Product development boss at Marks & Spencer inspires niche outfits after unexpected success on social media
Content: Kathryn Turner has been a hit on Instagram with her insider knowledge of the retailer’s upcoming snacks.Photograph: Marks and SpencersView image in fullscreenKathryn Turner has been a hit on Instagram with her insider knowledge of the retailer’s upcoming snacks.Photograph: Marks and SpencersHalloweenWhy M&S director Kathryn Turner is the ultimate ‘Gay Halloween’ costume ideaProduct development boss at Marks & Spencer inspires niche outfits after unexpected success on social mediaLauren CochraneFri 30 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShe is not the most likely viral star. But with 310,000 followers onTikTokand 270,000 on Instagram, Marks & Spencer Food’s director of product development, Kathryn Turner, has suddenly become one of the year’s big hits on social media. Her videos take the viewer with her as she goes in-store to look at new dessert launches, including its banana, caramel and pecan pudding, or taste test its latest products, such as itscherry and chocolate cookies.Turner is part of Marks & Spencer’s wider social media strategy implemented in 2020 as a way of attracting younger shoppers. Instead of using traditional influencers, M&S now champions 100 of its own employees onTikTok.Turner, who launched her account in May, now regularly receives more than 1m likes on her videos, with celebrities including Nigella Lawson and Stormzy among her followers. Part of the appeal is Turner’s insider knowledge and expertise: she has worked at M&S since 1995.This weekend, she will gain another prestigious accolade as fans spurn ghosts, witches and vampires and instead dress up as her forHalloween. The formula is simple. Some Turner-esque glasses, a blond wig and a packet of M&S cookies.The content creatorLiam Gleedhas been posting videos of himself as Turner in the run-up to Halloween and plans to wear the costume this weekend. “To be very real, I love a sweet treat and I work close to an M&S so I follow her socials to find out what snacks I’ll be getting every Friday at work,” he says. “The more niche you go for Halloween, the better. Why go as basic characters when you can dress as your current fixation or icons of the internet?”View image in fullscreenThe mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani, filling a pothole this year have also fuelled niche costume ideas.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGleed says it is the “real person” element that appeals to him. “I think it’s quite hilarious that someone who works as a product developer at M&S can become this on social media,” he says. “That’s what made the content work so well – it is so random that she is this popular figure from quite a normal job.”Dressing like someone such as Turner – an improbable online star – rather than a spooky character or a movie star fits into the idea of Gay Halloween. This is a way of approaching the dress-up holiday that utilises an online pop culture reference – the more specific the better. It taps into “if you know, you know” culture.This year, that could be anything from an iced coffee at a job interview, based on aviral storyabout whether or not it is acceptable, to Chappell Roan’s security guard,who allegedly made a fan cry, or the prenup papers for Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s marriage.View image in fullscreenGassed to be grass? Dancers at Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl half-time show may also provide costume inspiration.Photograph: San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesAccording to the websiteKnow Your Meme, the term Gay Halloween dates to 2023 but had a precursor in “jokes about ‘Gay Halloween’ costumes being absurdly niche” on X. The idea has now spread to everyone online, however.“I don’t think that gay people are exclusively culpable for this,” says James Greig, features editor of Dazed. “I can remember around 2016 finding it really annoying when straight guys were going [to Halloween parties] as very, very niche memes.”Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernaturalRead moreIt is well documented that Halloween hasbeen embraced by queer peopleowing to the holiday providing the freedom to dress up without judgment – it is sometimes called “gay Christmas” – and Gleed argues that its origins remain here.“Personally, as a gay man, I think it’s just another way for us to express ourselves,” he says. “We aren’t afraid to be our authentic selves after coming out, and to dress as someone so niche makes it comedic gold. I think the gays are doing it best because we don’t feel that shame of getting judged because we have been anyway.”As for which Gay Halloween costumes may be popular this year, José Criales-Unzueta, style correspondent at Vanity Fair,wrote aboutthe trend recently. They have a few predictions beyond Turner, including references to Heated Rivalry and Drake’s recent viral poncho.The internet is also championing a New York potholefilled by the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and the foliage duringBad Bunny’s Super Bowl performance. “But the best ones are the ones you cannot foresee,” says Criales-Unzueta. “Part of the magic of Gay Halloween is the unexpected.”Explore more on these topicsHalloweenMarks & SpencerFancy dress and costumeTikTokfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: On Star Trek, Patrick Stewart could make anyone feel hopeful for humanity | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: As Jean-Luc Picard in seven seasons, four films and a sequel, Stewart made us believe the most interesting person in the room might also be the most humane
Author: Ben Child
Headline: As Jean-Luc Picard in seven seasons, four films and a sequel, Stewart made us believe the most interesting person in the room might also be the most humane
Content: Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.Photograph: George Rose/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.Photograph: George Rose/Getty ImagesPatrick StewartOn Star Trek, Patrick Stewart could make anyone feel hopeful for humanityBen ChildAs Jean-Luc Picard in seven seasons, four films and a sequel, Stewart made us believe the most interesting person in the room might also be the most humanePatrick Stewart dies age 86His life in picturesPatrick Stewart brought gravitas and complexity to the screen, from Star Trek to X-Men‘He stood for the best of us’: William Shatner and more pay tributeFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 15.34 EDTShareWhat might humanity look like in 400 years’ time if we really do become wiser and more compassionate with each passing decade? The creators of Star Trek: The Next Generation clearly felt the answer closely resembled Patrick Stewart,who has died aged 86 after a short illness. Their decision may well have opened up an entirely new future for Gene Roddenberry’s enduring, resolutely utopian space saga.Patrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86Read morePrior to the casting of the classically trained Yorkshireman in 1987,Star Trekwas best known for the interplay between William Shatner’s charismatic, impulsive Captain Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s drily logical Spock. Stewart brought something of both men to the captain’s chair as Jean-Luc Picard, combining analytical rigour with a depth of feeling his imposing formality could never quite conceal.The bald, cerebral Englishman was a bold choice to succeed Shatner’s swaggering Canadian alpha male – but his ability to bring quiet authority and conviction to even the most outlandish of scenes gave the Enterprise an entirely different centre of gravity. Through seven seasons and four feature films, Stewart made audiences believe that the most interesting person in the room might also be the most thoughtful and humane.9:59Shakespeare to Star Trek: Patrick Stewart’s extraordinary life - The LatestThe difference between the two captains is perhaps best exemplified in the famous 1989 episode The Measure of a Man, in which Picard must defend the android Data against an overzealous Starfleet scientist’s attempts to dismantle him in the name of progress. Where Shatner might have chewed up all the available scenery before challenging the prosecution to a shirtless fistfight in a nearby space quarry, Stewart lets the legal arguments themselves become the drama. His measured questions on the nature of sentience expose the enormity of what is being proposed, the gathering anger in his voice conveying a civilised man discovering how much barbarism still lurks within his supposedly enlightened society.Stewart also gave Star Trek an emotional scale to match the extravagance of its ideas. In the 1992 episode The Inner Light, an alien probe from a long-dead civilisation entrusts Picard with decades of another man’s existence so that it might live on in his memory. He acquires a wife, children and a whole domestic life, even entering old age, before suddenly awakening aboard his ship to discover that only minutes have passed. The premise has something of Borges about it, an entire existence unfolding in a few minutes. Stewart makes us feel the weight of years that nobody else aboard the Enterprise has lived; he later called it his favourite episode.View image in fullscreen‘Patrick Stewart gave Star Trek an emotional scale to match the extravagance of its ideas’ … in Star Trek: The Next Generation (centre).Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockIt was perhaps inevitable that this blend of intellectual ambition and emotional intimacy didn’t always translate so effectively to the more bombastic world of the big screen, where Picard and his crew arrived in 1994 with the uneven Star Trek Generations. At times it was tempting to wonder if Stewart might have been better suited to the pre-blockbuster science fiction of the early 1970s, when Solaris and Silent Running could build entire worlds around questions of memory or conscience. The Star Trek films sometimes seemed uncertain about what to do with an actor who could make deliberation so compelling, handing him a phaser when unpicking a moral conundrum may have better suited his skills. It didn’t help that the Picard-era movies were made on substantially lower budgets than many of their contemporary sci-fi rivals, and often really looked like it.double quotation markStewart’s years performing Shakespeare prepared him for men whose public authority conceals private tormentAnd yet, even here, there were victories that only Stewart could have pulled off. First Contact (1996) cast Picard as a Captain Ahab-style avenger pursuing the technological white whale known as the Borg, which had briefly assimilated him into its remorseless hive mind during the TV show. Few other actors could have taken their best-known character into such unfamiliar territory unscathed, but Stewart’s years performing Shakespeare had prepared him for men whose public authority conceals private torment. He understood how eloquence could give destructive passions the appearance of reason, and how frightening rage becomes when it erupts from someone we have spent years watching display formidable self-control. By disrupting the qualities that had made his Picard so reassuring, Stewart was able to show how profoundly the Borg had wounded him.View image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard/Locutus of Borg in Star Trek: The Next Generation.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/Getty ImagesThe final Next Generation-era movie was 2002’s poorly received Star Trek: Nemesis, by which time Stewart had found a new multiplex audience as Charles Xavier in 2000’s X-Men. Despite his continuing prominence in genre fare, he never returned for the rebooted film series that began with 2009’s JJ Abrams-directed Star Trek, which instead turned to Nimoy for its elder-statesman gravitas.Patrick Stewart – a life in picturesRead moreTelevision eventually welcomed him back in Star Trek: Picard, which ran for three seasons from 2020, reuniting him with his old Enterprise colleagues for its highly acclaimed final run. Once a gamble on Star Trek’s future, Stewart had become one of the great reasons to revisit its past. His success helped establish that the saga could flourish beyond its original cast, opening the way for the political intrigue ofDeep Space Nineand the stranded explorers of Voyager. And his legacy is perhaps even more apparent today in the tonal confidence ofStrange New Worlds, which shares The Next Generation’s willingness to move between moral inquiry, cosmic peril and outright whimsy.As much as anyone, Stewart gave Roddenberry’s faith in progress a persuasive human form. If Star Trek was always about showing us how far humankind might travel in the next four centuries, he helped us believe we might actually have grown up by the time we got there.Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartStar TrekTelevisionUS televisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Arteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memories | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but the Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of the club’s greatest nights
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but the Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of the club’s greatest nights
Content: Mikel Arteta takes Arsenal to Liverpool, having never won there in the league as the Gunners’ manager.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta takes Arsenal to Liverpool, having never won there in the league as the Gunners’ manager.Composite: Guardian DesignArsenalArteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memoriesArsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of club’s greatest nightsEd AaronsFri 30 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta used a Spanish word to describe what it felt like to be helpless at Anfield while playing for Everton in 2011:bajar. “It’s when a cyclist is going up and looks amazing, then in one kilometre he goes ‘boom’ and he’s struggling again,” he said in Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary. “The game was going well and then suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around. The game is passing all over me and I cannot react. I only had that feeling in my career once, and it was at Anfield.”Given Arteta’s record at Liverpool, Sunday’s showdown with his childhood friend Andoni Iraola – five days after Arsenal weredumped out of the Carabao Cup by Fleetwood– could be expected to fill him with dread. Arteta finally tasted victory there as a player with Arsenalin September 2012, after five failed attempts in the Merseyside derby, but ended up spending the night in hospital with concussion after colliding with Jordan Henderson in an incident he has described as “the biggest fear of my life”.Fantastic Fleetwood seal shootout success in Carabao Cup shock against ArsenalRead moreArteta was part of the Arsenal side thatwon at Anfield again six months laterthanks to goals from the new signings Lukas Podolski and Santi Cazorla. That was the last time the club triumphed there in the Premier League. They have not won at Anfield for 13 league matches, equalling the club’s worst run at Liverpool. Arsenal’s one victory at Liverpool in the interim came in the League Cup on penalties in 2020 on Arteta’s second visit as a manager.The Spaniard tried to prepare his players for a trip to Anfield in November 2021 by playing You’ll Never Walk Alone over the training ground speakers butthat ended in a 4-0 defeat. He was criticised after last season’s loss in late August, when DominikSzoboszlai’s late free-kickended a sequence of three Arsenal draws at Liverpool, for a perceived failure to take off the handbrake, having started Mikel Merino as his No 10. Gary Neville went as far as to say Arsenal lacked “the mentality to go and win big matches at big away grounds”, an assertion that will have hurt Arteta but does have credence: they have not beaten Manchester City in the Premier League at the Etihad since 2015 under Arsène Wenger.Arteta will be keen to disprove such perceptions, especially after Arsenal struggled so badly against a team 84 places below them in the pyramid in a stadium that holds fewer than 6,000 people. The strikers Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres surprisingly started in tandem at Fleetwood, presumably in an attempt to lighten the load on Martin Ødegaard, although both look badly out of form. Bukayo Saka isout with a thigh injury, there are concerns over Noni Madueke’s ankle and Arsenal’sfailed appeal over Max Dowman’s red cardrules out the teenager for three matches.View image in fullscreen26 May 1989: the Arsenal manager George Graham hugs Alan Smith after they won 2-0 at Anfield, clinching the league title in the most dramatic circumstances.Photograph: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty ImagesWith that in mind, Arteta’s best chance of beatingLiverpoolis probably by taking the cautious approach that has served him so well and was the cornerstone of last season’s Premier League title triumph. He can take inspiration from one of the most famous nights in Arsenal’s history 37 years ago when George Graham’s side arrived at Anfield needing a 2-0 victory to be champions.“I told my players to keep things tight in the first half – it was imperative we did not concede,” said Graham in an interview to mark the 20th anniversary of that dramatic finale to the 1988-89 season, when Michael Thomas scored in stoppage time to end Arsenal’s 18-year wait for the title. “The papers were saying we’d have to attack from the off, but I was adamant that was wrong. If Liverpool had scored an early goal it would have been over. But they did very little attacking and played into our hands.”Before the 1989 game, Arsenal’s players ran to all four corners of the ground to hand flowers to Liverpool fans as a show of sympathy after the Hillsborough disaster the previous month – an idea proposed by their longstanding director Ken Friar, who died this month.Graham and Arteta were 44 when they won their first league titles and the similarities do not end there. The former Scotland midfielder, who scored almost 80 goals for Arsenal and helped them win the Double in 1971, was known for his emphasis on defending as a manager and “1-0 to the Arsenal” became synonymous with Graham, especially towards the end of his reign. Arteta has revived that tradition since he took over in December 2019, recording 1-0 victories32 times in the Premier League, more than any club apart from Everton.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsak applies finishing touch as Liverpool bring Brighton’s winning run to an endRead moreArsenal scored their first set-piece goal of the season ina routine 2-0 winat home to Everton last Saturday and targeting Liverpool’s weakness from set plays while keeping things tight at the other end could be the most effective tactic against a team who have been finding their feet under Iraola in recent weeks.“Collectively, we acknowledge the importance of defending,” said Arteta last year when asked about comparisons between his team and Graham’s. “We know that if we excel in that part of the game, the chances and the probabilities to win more matches is going to be very, very high.”Arsenal flew back to London after losing to Fleetwood on penalties in a shootout that will have revived bad memories of May’sChampions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain.The Carabao Cup has stretched Arteta’s squad in the past two seasons, when they reached first the semi-finals then the final, so that is one potential positive from their elimination – not that the ultra-competitive Spaniard would agree. For him, the only way to respond to the most embarrassing night of his managerial career will be to follow in Graham’s footsteps on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsArsenalLiverpoolfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carrick tells players ‘hard truth’ in attempt to turn Manchester United’s season around | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: The head coach, who said the players were ‘hurting’ after eight games without a win, reflected on ‘not always rosy and nice conversations’
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: The head coach, who said the players were ‘hurting’ after eight games without a win, reflected on ‘not always rosy and nice conversations’
Content: Michael Carrick is under intense pressure after defeats by Atlético Madrid, Como and Bournemouth in October.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick is under intense pressure after defeats by Atlético Madrid, Como and Bournemouth in October.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester UnitedCarrick tells players ‘hard truth’ in attempt to turn Manchester United’s season aroundHead coach reflects on ‘not always rosy’ conversationsPlayers ‘hurting’ after eight games without a winWill UnwinFri 30 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick said he has had difficult conversations with theManchester Unitedhierarchy and his players during their turbulent start to the season.United have not won in their past eight games and start the weekend in 16th place of 20 in the league, one point above the relegation zone.The academy system needs a refresh but now is the time for Carrick to trust in youthRead moreCarrick’s position was under threat after losing last Sunday to Bournemouthbut he has held on to his jobfor the time being and been given the chance to turn things around, starting at Chelsea on Saturday.The head coach suggested he had spoken with the club’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the chief executive, Omar Berrada, this week.“It’s pretty clear, it’s not always rosy and nice conversations between anyone, whether that’s between me and the players, whether that’s between me, Jason, Omar or the owners,” Carrick said. “It’s the truth, it’s the hard truth at times and it’s what we need to move forward. Whatever we need to move forward, we will do.”The supporters cheered Carrick off after he did a lap of the pitch in the aftermath ofSunday’s 3-0 defeat, but once he entered the tunnel they booed the players after a poor performance and perceived lack of effort. Carrick said the players are “hurting” but are “hungry” to turn things around.“I’ll be totally honest, it was mixed feelings for me,” Carrick said. “To have the appreciation from the supporters and that connection and that respect is something I feel strongly about.“It wasn’t a nice situation but to feel that was important, of course, but it didn’t make me feel better in the fact that I’m with the players 100% and we’re all in it together. I’ve told the players that, I’m happy to say that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I didn’t feel comfortable being in any way, shape or form, a separation from that. That’s my group, my players and this is my football club so we have to all be in it together, and that’s the supporters included. As hard as it is at the moment, I totally get that, I get their feelings, but when we get through this then we’ll be a lot stronger as a whole.”Gary Neville questioned some of the players’ professionalism on his podcast this week. “I’ve got no time for them,” Neville said. “There’s a few of them that don’t go to bed at the right time. Don’t eat the right things.” Carrick laughed off the allegations with the remark: “Gaz says a lot of things.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarricknewsShareReuse this content

title: Aston Villa to take legal action against Jamie Carragher for ‘unacceptable insults’ | Aston Villa | The Guardian
description: Aston Villa have announced plans to take legal action against Jamie Carragher following his “unacceptable insults” about the club and its supporters
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Aston Villa have announced plans to take legal action against Jamie Carragher following his “unacceptable insults” about the club and its supporters
Content: Jamie Carragher upset Aston Villa with comments he made on the Stick to Football podcast.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenJamie Carragher upset Aston Villa with comments he made on the Stick to Football podcast.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAAston VillaAston Villa to take legal action against Jamie Carragher for ‘unacceptable insults’Villa chair announces plan on social mediaCarragher said club will ‘never be Man United’Press AssociationFri 30 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAston Villa have announced plans to take legal action againstJamie Carragherfollowing his “unacceptable insults” about the club and its supporters.Carragher told Villa fans to “shut the fuck up” after facing criticism for suggesting Unai Emery should consider taking the Manchester United job. Villa responded on Friday evening with a statement on X signed by their chair, Nassef Sawiris.“Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the club and its fans,” the statement said. “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, chairman.”Former Liverpool defender Carragher made his remarks on the Stick to Football podcast while discussing the prospect of Emery replacing Michael Carrick at Old Trafford. The 48-year-old Sky Sports pundit argued there was a hierarchy in football, saying “Aston Villa will never be Man United”.“I’m not trying to annoy Villa fans but there is a chain in football, whether you like it or not,” said Carragher. “So Real Madrid will take Man United’s best player, they’ll take [Cristiano] Ronaldo. There’s very few above United, the same with Liverpool.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But there will be teams below Aston Villa and they [Villa] will take their manager or they will take their players, so shut the fuck up Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Man United.”Explore more on these topicsAston VillaJamie CarraghernewsShareReuse this content

title: Red Roses put defeats behind them by crushing USA to extend 35-year streak | Women's rugby union | The Guardian
description: England bounced back after two defeats with a comprehensive 55-12 win over USA
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: England bounced back after two defeats with a comprehensive 55-12 win over USA
Content: Claudia Moloney-MacDonald was in fine form on her return to the side.Photograph: Caean Couto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenClaudia Moloney-MacDonald was in fine form on her return to the side.Photograph: Caean Couto/Getty ImagesWomen's rugby unionRed Roses put defeats behind them by crushing USA to extend 35-year streakUSA 12-55 EnglandClaudia Moloney-MacDonald runs in four triesSarah RendellFri 30 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 21.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland have seen a lot of records crumble around them in this WXV Global Series but the world champions were not going to let a 35-year winning streak go against the USA. The last time the Eagles claimed a victory over the Red Roses was in the 1991 Rugby World Cup and since then England have won all 22 matches they have played. The Red Roses got back to winning ways and while their recent losses to Canada displayed the top sides had caught up with the world No 1 team, Friday’s outing against the USA evidenced that outside the top three there is still a gap to be closed.The USA headed into the match in good form with five consecutive wins, including victories over Wales and Ireland, and their No 8 Freda Tafuna has been one of the standouts across all of the teams during the WXV. However, England were able to contain the bright spark and despite good performances from Alev Kelter and Hope Rogers, the hosts did not have enough firepower.Red Roses suffer back-to-back defeats for first time in 10 years as Canada make statementRead moreThere were two key elements to England’s win: Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and a strong second-half performance from the front row. The wing Moloney-MacDonald may have been dropped from the matchday 23 against Canada last time out but she responded perfectly with four tries. It will be the exact retort John Mitchell would have wanted and the head coach praised the Exeter star afterwards for her consistency. Breaks by players such as Maud Muir gave the visitors the extra few percentages they needed.It was far from a polished performance by England though. Wasted chances against Canada contributed to both defeats and an error-strewn attack was on display again in the first half on Friday. The Red Roses had some great plays, namely Moloney-MacDonald’s first try, but they could have punished the USA more often had it not been for knock-ons and rogue passes.A disappointing note throughout the match was the empty-looking stands in the 25,000-capacity stadium in New Jersey. The official attendance was not announced but much of the ground had no fans. That was not helped by a 5pm kick-off time but a game of this magnitude deserves a bigger audience than the one that showed up.The last time these two nations met was in the opening game of the World Cup last year. The Red Roses won that 69-7, and once again England got the scoreboard ticking early on. It was less than five minutes before Moloney-MacDonald acrobatically finished, and she added another shortly after.Rogers got a try back and in doing so closed in on the American women’s all-time points record with the score bringing her just four points away. But it was England who held a 17-7 half-time lead after the captain, Meg Jones, scored and Moloney-MacDonald secured her third and fourth tries early in the second period.Kelter put in a huge hit on Jones and despite the tackle producing momentum for the world’s sixth-ranked side, it was England who went over through Mia Venner. The Gloucester-Hartpury wing has been impressive in her two starts in this away leg of WXV and she will give Mitchell a selection headache in 2027 if she continues her current form.The loss will leave a sour taste for the USA, not just because England’s replacement hooker Bryony Field, Maddie Feaunati and Sadia Kabeya turned a narrow win into a thumping one, but the hosts’ co-captain Georgie Perris-Redding hobbled off with injury.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis game was both teams’ last of the calendar year so the USA will have to wait to bounce back at the 2027 Pacific Four tournament. England will hope they have started a new winning streak to take into the Women’s Six Nations but the important things they will take forward, according to the captain Jones, are the lessons learned from this tour.“We have gained so much feedback from where we want to keep growing and getting better,” she said. “Ultimately teams are getting better, that is the nature of it. It happened in the men’s game, it’s happening in the women’s game and we just have to start being more unpredictable.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's rugby unionEngland women's rugby union teamUSA women's rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Searle makes difference as Leicester battle to Prem top spot at Bristol  | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Leicester scored four tries at Ashton Gate in a 22-16 win against Bristol that took them to the top of the Prem
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Leicester scored four tries at Ashton Gate in a 22-16 win against Bristol that took them to the top of the Prem
Content: Adam Radwan crosses for Leicester’s second try of four.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAdam Radwan crosses for Leicester’s second try of four.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesPrem RugbySearle makes difference as Leicester battle to Prem top spot at BristolBristol 16-22 LeicesterVisitors score four tries in error-strewn gameRobert Kitsonat Ashton GateFri 30 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the end there was a relatively clear winner of this straight shootout for top spot in the Prem.Leicestertook the spoils in an error-strewn contest between two sides who began the night in second and third position, scoring four tries to one and being masterfully steered to a bonus point victory by their alert fly-half Billy Searle.Following on from their commanding second-half display in the wet at home to Northampton, the Tigers were far from perfect but had the game’s outstanding player in Searle, whose left boot set up three of his side’s tries in addition to landing two conversions.Bristol, reduced to 13 players in the second quarter by a brace of yellow cards, had their moments but ultimately coughed up possession far too often.Exeter’s Tom Hooper: ‘Sometimes you’ve just got to suck up a little bit of pain’Read moreThe game’s stylistic highlight was a quite brilliant sixth-minute solo try by Louis Rees-Zammit, back to his sharpest on the wing for the Bears, but it takes more than the occasional flash of talent to tame the Tigers. In Adam Radwan they had their own high-speed danger man, with the former Newcastle wing and full-back Freddie Steward both registering first-half tries.Of the England international contingent on view, though, the most eye-catching was Ellis Genge who was a handful in all areas during his 63 minutes, only for the visitors to ruin the prop’s night with a bonus point try from Jamie Blamire within moments of his departure. Modern-day Leicester are not yet an irresistible force but they still have the ability to grind out crucial results. “That was a good gritty win,” stressed Geoff Parling, Leicester’s head coach. “I’m really proud of the team … we’re really pleased with the spot we’re in.”There was something of a throwback feel to the whole evening, with Bristol’s players wearing old-school letters in tribute to the club legends of yesteryear. Leicester were invited to do the same until league officials stepped in and deemed it too confusing. The Tigers’ rugby alphabet used to run the other way, with ABC denoting the front row rather than the outside backs, and asking them to abandon that tradition was borderline heresy.There was a timeless beauty, either way, to Rees-Zammit’s early score. The England tighthead Joe Heyes – entertainingly listed on the teamsheet as ‘Joy Heyes’ – was minding his own business in midfield when the Welsh wing accelerated past him from a standing start before slaloming all the way to the line.Leicester’s response was clinical in a different way, Searle’s cross-kick finding an unmarked Steward who dived over to mark his 100th Prem start in style. The visitors also had a close-range ‘try’ by Chessum scrubbed out for an earlier knock-on but, for a good while, there was little to separate the teams.If Leicester had a slight edge at the scrums the Bears were the more fluent attacking team and Rees-Zammit came close to adding another stunner to his collection,only for his deft chip ahead to elude his grasp. The momentum soon shifted significantly, though, courtesy of two quickfire yellow cards in three minutes for Matías Moroni and Tom Jordan for misjudged tackles.With a two-man advantage Leicester duly went ahead courtesy of another smart kick by Searle, drilled perfectly in behind the cover for the electric Radwan to outpace the cover and slide over. The half-time score of 12-7, even so, still gave the Bears some wriggle room in the closing 40 minutes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe omens did not look great when the Tigers scored again, Searle’s precise boot this time finding Ollie Hassell-Collins in acres of space on the left. But a penalty from Jimmy Williams provided some breathing space and, now restored to 15 players, a massive penalty for the hosts’ scrum altered the mood again.Blamire’s maul score, however, finally settled things, Searle again having an input with a raking kick to the corner. At a time when England’s fly-half pecking order is once again in the spotlight, here was another reminder of his match-winning qualities.On a night full of frustrating moments for both sides, his contribution was even more striking. Bristol huffed and puffed but chances came and went and the steady boot of Williams was ultimately not enough. While Leicester are now top dogs going into the weekend they will need to perform better than this to remain ahead of the chasing pack through the upcoming winter.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyBristolLeicesterRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fiesta awaits in Mexico City as Kimi Antonelli speeds towards F1 history | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Italian 20-year-old is on the verge of becoming the youngest world champion with Mexico City ready for a carnival coronation atmosphere
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Italian 20-year-old is on the verge of becoming the youngest world champion with Mexico City ready for a carnival coronation atmosphere
Content: Kimi Antonelli will have no shortage of support from the fans in Mexico as he closes in on his first title.Photograph: Manuel Velasquez/Formula 1/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli will have no shortage of support from the fans in Mexico as he closes in on his first title.Photograph: Manuel Velasquez/Formula 1/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Fiesta awaits in Mexico City as Kimi Antonelli speeds towards F1 historyItalian 20-year-old is on the verge of becoming the youngest world champion with the Mexican Grand Prix ready for a carnival coronation atmosphereGiles Richardsin Mexico CityFri 30 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn undeniable highlight of this Formula One season, marked by discontent at the new regulations, has been getting swept along by the sheer joy that the world champion-in-waiting,Kimi Antonelli, has displayed on his way to a title he will almost surely secure this weekend at the Mexican Grand Prix.Antonelli was still a teenager for the first half of the year and it seemed fitting to describe him as such. His exuberant embrace of competing for Mercedesat the sharp end of F1in just his second season was that of any 19-year-old. Like discovering a life-changing new band or how much fun can be had with a cold beer, a wide grin was barely off his face.George Russell determined not to let disappointing F1 season define careerRead moreHe is 20 now, still but a stripling and on Sunday at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez if he finishes in ninth place or better he will be F1’s youngest world champion, and the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.Antonelli has confessed that as a four-year-old he did not recall when Sebastian Vettel became the previous youngest title winner in 2010. “I remember I was playing with Hot Wheels, but I don’t remember him clinching it,” he said.This weekend he will likely embrace an unforgettable moment. Antonelli has shone on track, at home with the complex requirements of the new energy-managed cars, extracting a pace and control such that even his more experienced Mercedes teammate George Russellhas been left flailingin his wake. To which traits he has allied a sharp and incisive driving style that has been extraordinary at times and a judgment that has belied his years.That he has done so with such alacrity, especially after a difficult rookie season last year, has surprised many. Not least those team principal Toto Wolff pointedly observed had been questioning whether Antonelli should even be in F1 after his debut season. Doubts now assuredly consigned to the dustbin of history, in the city where Leon Trotsky, who coined the phrase, was killed in 1940.It has been clear how much the Italian loves what he does and how that has informed his performances. At his shoulder through the trials of last season and the triumphs of this, has been Peter Bonnington. Bono, as he is known, was Lewis Hamilton’s engineer across the British driver’s six titles with Mercedes. He and Antonelli have established a close relationship, a friendship, with the Italian taking on board his colleague’s experience and cool head, often referencing him and the importance of their interaction.During Antonelli’s run of five successive victories in the opening period of the season, the last of them was astriking performance in Monaco. Taking an exceptional pole position to deny Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who was in fearsome form on the streets of the principality, he then delivered a remarkable race win, including seeing off two restarts.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli is likely to be celebrating his historic title triumph this weekend in Mexico.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockAfter this, Bono, who often has the avuncular air of an older brother with his young charge, gave an almost disarmingly straightforward explanation of what made his driver so quick.“As soon as he’s happy in the car: happy driver, fast lap time,” he said. The team have adopted an approach to allow Antonelli the opportunity to ensure he could drive in a way that allowed him to truly embrace being himself and in so doing, taking the pressure off.Bonningham described this as “giving him the freedom to do what he enjoys, giving him the freedom to enjoy driving the car, that’s a real big thing and not stressing too much. He’s just a joy to work with.”To trust the youngster’s instincts and talent, when the temptation to micromanage him must have been overwhelming, has worked brilliantly. Even as the opposition caught and at times surpassed Mercedes, Antonelli was able to deliver when a win was off the table. When it was, as at the last round in Austin, he stepped up to sweep it away with a nonchalance that typified why he is world champion elect.This makes the atmosphere in Mexico City all the more febrile in what is already one of the most vibrant venues on the calendar. Antonelli could barely have chosen a better location to enjoy the celebration of his childhood dream. The fans here embrace F1 with the same passion the Italian has for his trade.With the race coinciding with Mexico’s Day of the Dead, the city and the paddock are adorned with the bright orange Mexican marigolds, the“flor de muerto”. Skulls and skeletons, candles and colour are plentiful to welcome the return of the departed in a joyful, festival lending the weekend an already celebratory air.View image in fullscreenThe race coincides with Mexico’s Day of the Dead.Photograph: Marcel van Dorst/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockThe F1 faithful are also in good cheer in welcoming home hero Sergio Pérez back to the grid, with Cadillac and his image everywhere in Mexico City. On occasion he appears as a lifesize cardboard cut-out, rather incongruously in a line of fabulously-dressed skeletons. Yet fans will also doubtless revel in having this marvellous venue celebrate F1’s youngest champion in the heady atmosphere of the stadium section of Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.Hamilton has experienced it twice, when he sealed the title here in 2017 and 2018, and the seven-time champion’s assessment of Antonelli’s season was as telling as that of his former race engineer.“You never know how anyone’s going to do under pressure until you see them,” he said. “I could assume that he was going to be fine with the weight you have on you. When you have to do all these appearances and all these things, pulled left, right and centre. But he’s taken it in his stride. He’s a relatively old soul in that young body.”Antonelli was withdrawn from his media duties on Thursday, with Mercedes saying he was unwell and needing to recover properly, but the Italian has stated he would like to finish the job in style and be able to relax for the remaining four races. There is no reason to believe he will suffer from any yips, certainly. He has demonstrated no such weakness thus far, even under the most intense pressure, with team principal Wolff sharing a further insight into why the 20-year-old stands ready to make history.“In Austin, he came to my office sat down on the sofa and said: ‘I’m going to enjoy this one. Isn’t it funny? I’m not thinking at all about the championship,’” Wolff recalled. “I said: ‘Stick to that attitude. You have the best job in the world. Don’t forget that.’ He has the right mindset.”The best job in the world and one he has, admirably, embraced with that irrepressible joy. The right mindset indeed. A deserved champion awaiting his coronation. On this form, not for the last time.In first practice in Mexico City, Ferrari once more opened strongly with Charles Leclerc topping the timesheets, six-tenths up on Antonelli in second, with the Italian apparently fully fit after Thursday’s illness. Many of the teams used the session to allow their rookie drivers to rack up track time with 10 taking part. The Danish driver Fredrik Vesti sat in for Russell and was in third, with Hamilton in fourth.In the afternoon session Hamilton lost vital running time when he retired with a loss of power after 30 minutes. His teammate Leclerc was once more quickest, one-tenth up on Lando Norris’s McLaren. Russell and Antonelli were in third and fourth and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen in fifth, three-tenths back, although the Dutchman was carrying some damage after a clash with Liam Lawson that will be investigated by the stewards.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Breeders’ Cup 2026 day one: Haffner wins Juvenile Turf to complete O’Brien double – as it happened | Breeders' Cup | The Guardian
description: European-trained runners completed a second successive clean sweep of the juvenile events on turf at a Keeneland Breeders’ Cup
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: European-trained runners completed a second successive clean sweep of the juvenile events on turf at a Keeneland Breeders’ Cup
Content: 3h ago18.08 EDTEUROPEAN CLEAN SWEEP ON DAY ONE IN KENTUCKYEuropean-trained runners completed a second successive clean sweep of the juvenile events on turf at a Keeneland Breeders’ Cup on Friday evening as Aidan O’Brien’sHaffner,in the Juvenile Turf, followed up earlier wins for George Boughey’sLibertango,in the Juvenile Turf Sprint, and O’Brien’sSun Goddessin the Juvenile Fillies Turf.Billy Loughnane,the new champion jockey on the Flat, got the meeting underway in thrilling style onLibertango, having been confirmed as a late replacement for Flavien Prat in her saddle only around an hour before the race.Prat was declared to rideLibertangoearlier in the week when it seemed that Loughnane would be unable to shed the necessary pounds to weigh out at 8st 7lb.An extended series of sauna sessions got him down to the necessary weight with only a couple of hours to spare, but the effort was worth it as he broughtLibertangowith a strong run in the stretch to win by a length and a quarter.“I can’t put it into words,” Loughnane said afterwards. I never expected to ride the filly at this weight. Thankfully, they have the saunas here so managed to do the weight. I feel great and a big thank you to George Boughey for putting me back on board.”Ryan Moore produced rides of similar coolness and efficiency aboard bothSun GoddessandHaffner,breaking smartly from the stalls to sit close to the lead before striking for home inside the final quarter-mile.The double on the day nudged Aidan O’Brien one clear in the all-time standings with 23 Breeders’ Cup winners, after he was briefly tied at 22 with Bob Baffert after his coltHughestook the Juvenile earlier on the card.ShareUpdated at18.08 EDT

title: Australia set 288 to win on final day after South African centurions turn tide | Australia cricket team | The Guardian
description: Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder hit hundreds for hosts to leave Australia with a last-day chase to win the third Test and the series
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder hit hundreds for hosts to leave Australia with a last-day chase to win the third Test and the series
Content: South Africa's Wiaan Mulder celebrates his century on day four of the third Test to help set Australia a target of 288 at Newlands in Cape Town.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSouth Africa's Wiaan Mulder celebrates his century on day four of the third Test to help set Australia a target of 288 at Newlands in Cape Town.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesAustralia cricket teamAustralia set 288 to win on final day after South African centurions turn tideRyan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder hit hundreds for hostsAustralia face last-day chase to clinch Test and the seriesGeoff LemonFri 30 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt would be unfair to say that Australia let a winning position slip on the fourth day of the third Test at Cape Town, only because that would undersell how Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder prised it away. Australia’s vaunted four bowlers, owners of 1,674 wickets at day’s beginning, could only raise that to 1,678 by day’s end. In the process, a lead of 40 became 287. South Africa had been 40 for four in the first innings at Gqeberha and bounced back to win; they wereeffectively 40 for four in the third innings here, and now have a great chance to do the same.The unlikely basis was Rickelton, a franchise circuiteer who spends most of his year smiting runs or keeping wicket in 20-over blocks. In this series he was monstered in Durban by Josh Hazlewood, out for none and two while pinch-hitting as an opener, then made scant impression down the order with 31 in Gqeberha. He looked like a modern cricketer become anachronism in this ancient form.South Africa all out and set Australia 288 to win decider: third men’s cricket Test, day four – liveRead moreYet, while Rickelton strikes at 150 runs per hundred balls across his T20 career, his first-class rate is one third of that speed. There are strings to his bow that are not dyed royal blue by the global Mumbai Indians conglomerate. That was the particular set of skills he employed here, disavowing the lead of his top order the day before in assuming that a placid surface was made for rollicking shots. Instead, he and fellow white-ball dasher Matthew Breetzke absorbed everything that Australia’s freshly rested bowlers could hurl at them.On a pitch without lateral movement, there was still good bounce for the short ball, and increasingly marked turn for Nathan Lyon out of the footmarks. The pair dealt with both, while Rickelton showed a facility to punctuate defence with a single in most overs, keeping the innings at least rolling in first gear. The first session added 62 runs, the lead 102.View image in fullscreenRyan Rickelton of South Africa takes the applause after reaching his hundred in Cape Town.Photograph: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images/Getty ImagesStill, the lunchtime wicket of Breetzke looked to have turned things Australia’s way, finally impulsive as he pulled to long leg. That ended a streak for Pat Cummins of 372 balls without a wicket, unprecedented in his career, despite some good spells along the way. But Rickelton was now set like cement, and Mulder joined him in that durability, to lunch and beyond.Lyon kept ripping his off-breaks, with an inside edge from Rickelton into Alex Carey’s shin behind the stumps, and umpteen balls that landed safely after deflecting off body or bat, but reward never came. Mulder took the occasional chance attacking spin. Rickelton kept picking off rare bad balls from the quicks, driving down the ground when overpitched, backing himself on the up once the new ball showed no signs of seam. The pair tormented the Australians until well into the final session, Rickelton’s century coming after a slow march through the 90s, the partnership reaching 154 and South Africa’s lead an increasingly daunting 235 on that rapidly wearing pitch, before his departure set off a late burst of activity.
