Much of it involved the livewire Marnus Labuschagne, out of runs but still a red-cordial kindergarten class in the field, getting vast turn with his leg-breaks as Mulder kept sweeping him outside leg stump, where the only risk was a gloved catch.View image in fullscreenAustralia’s Marnus Labuschagne is mobbed by  teammates after a run out.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesYet when Mulder changed tack, repeatedly reverse-sweeping that same line while aiming for the exposed off-side fence, a full toss that would normally disappear over square leg was instead hit to the only fielder in an acre, Inglis at backward point, who spotted Rickelton running and Mulder standing still. Labuschagne at the bowler’s end was quick enough to gather the throw: Rickelton run out for 101.With tired Aussies and 70 minutes to go, things were set up for a Marco Jansen blitz, but he followed the team trend of holing out on the pull, hitting Starc to Lyon for nought. Lyon finally got his first wicket for the day when the opposing off-spinner Simon Harmer shouldered arms on one, big turn doing the trick, then Gerald Coetzee ran himself out for the same score, Labuschagne bobbing up again with a sizzling direct hit from the cordon to the non-striker’s end.Nine down and 251 ahead, South Africa’s lead suddenly looked light. But Mulder fixed that with Kagiso Rabada as support, also taking care of the small personal matter of moving his score from 82 to 115, farming strike for long periods between targeting boundaries. He was finally caught down the ground from a cross-bat shot at Cummins in the last over of the day, trying to hit a fifth six.View image in fullscreenRyan Rickelton looks on as Australia’s Cameron Green and Australia’s Marnus Labuschagne attempt to stop the ball.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesA neatly apportioned match that already had one full innings occupy the entire first day will now have another full innings occupy the fifth. A target of 288 is perfectly balanced for a match that has been so even. At the last, it must tilt one way or the other, and with it the series.Explore more on these topicsAustralia cricket teamSouth Africa cricket teamAustralia sportCricketmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Financial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us all, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: Financial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us all, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: Thomas Clarkson addresses a meeting of the world anti-slavery convention in Exeter Hall, London, June 1840.Illustration: Pictures from History/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThomas Clarkson addresses a meeting of the world anti-slavery convention in Exeter Hall, London, June 1840.Illustration: Pictures from History/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesOpinionSlaveryBritish people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated historyAndy BurnhamFinancial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us allAndy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave tradeFri 30 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 20.54 EDTShareOn 28 October 1787, Thomas Clarkson pushed through the crowds to reach the pulpit of Manchester Cathedral. A campaigner for abolishing slavery, hespoke urgently about the horrors of the slave tradeand the humanity of enslaved people. “He drinks the cup of sorrow,” Clarkson said. “And he drinks it at our hands.”DuringBlack History Month, these are the stories it is important to remember. They show us the complicated truth of our history. Thousands of people in Manchester signed a petition against slavery after Clarkson’s sermon. And yet Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people. There are similar stories up and down the nation. We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives.The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.Our history is intertwined with countries that are now our allies, particularly in the Commonwealth. Next week, I will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests: a beacon of stability, strength and security. Together we can face down shared challenges. We can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration. We can strengthen our respective countries and share our values to build a safer world for us all.But facing a changing world together requires us to stand on firm foundations. To meet those challenges of the future, we need to face up to the past. For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.So we are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.My focus is on building a future where people at home and abroad live in greater peace and prosperity.So we will bring to the Chogm our determination to tackle the issues that affect people across our Commonwealth family and beyond.Today, debt-servicing costs in the poorest and most vulnerable countries are at their highest in more than 25 years. More than 40% of these countries spendmore on interest repayments than on health. I want to launch a new drive on debt, working with our global partners to help those countries repay over a longer time period and with better rates. That is why the chancellor, foreign secretary and I have asked Gordon Brown, who will join us at the Chogm, to help with this work.We will also support the energy transition in the face of the climate crisis. And we will build on the incredible work being done to educate women and girls, give smaller countries a louder voice on the world stage, and end global poverty and inequality.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI want us to build stronger relationships with each other and renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.We stand on the shoulders of those such as Thomas Clarkson and the many ordinary people who spoke out for justice and humanity.In 1862, at the height of the American civil war, Manchester was the cotton capital of the world. In a vote at the Free Trade Hall, the humble cotton workers resolved that they wouldno longer handle slave-picked cotton. Their actions helped end the civil war, prompting Abraham Lincoln to write to them praising their “sublime Christian heroism”.It is so often the case in British history that huge injustices ignored by the powers-that-be are eventually overturned by ordinary people. Those Manchester cotton workers represent that proud British tradition, and I will take inspiration from them as we go forward into our new dialogue.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorse | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: From surgeons to senior civil servants, even the most decent people can make disastrous mistakes. But these gaffes require honesty, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: From surgeons to senior civil servants, even the most decent people can make disastrous mistakes. But these gaffes require honesty, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: ‘There is something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure.’ Liz Truss on stage in February 2025.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreen‘There is something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure.’ Liz Truss on stage in February 2025.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APOpinionMental healthHow do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorseGaby HinsliffFrom surgeons to senior civil servants, even the most decent people can make disastrous mistakes. But these gaffes require honestyFri 30 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTShareGabriel Weston made a mistake at work this summer. It doesn’t define her – she was and is a well-regarded NHS surgeon and author – but it was serious enough, as she explained in an extraordinarily candid series ofInstagramandSubstackposts this month, to prompt an investigation that left her feeling“ashamed and alone and really quite nervous”. Whatever went wrong in the operating theatre was bad enough to be classed a “never event” (something that should never be able to happen if the process is working properly) and triggered a nagging anxiety that she might somehow do it again, unless she figured out where she had unexpectedly gone wrong.It’s a fascinating insight into a process that most people never have the courage to talk about openly. But it also highlights why it’s so hard in practice for doctors and other professionals to acknowledge and learn from mistakes – as every public inquiry into every public scandal ends up recommending, only to repeat it all over again after the next one – rather than close ranks and cover up. Weston says she only spoke up out of frustration with what she saw as her employers’ failure to support her (she had asked to reduce what she considered an overloaded operating list to take some pressure off, which she says has now happened, leaving her full of praise for the hospital’s ultimate response). Judging by the responses to her posts, she’s not alone.I thought of Weston this week when Liz Truss published Bank Job, the second book she has written in two years circling the drain of her career. This one seems if anything even less self-aware, blaming the Bank of England, not herself, for the spectacular failure of her mini-budget (even her old cheerleaders at the Telegraph called itderanged). But it’s also oddly sad. There’s something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure, as if the truth would shatter her. She can’t seem to leave the whole episode alone – can’t withdraw, as Keir Starmer has, into stony silence about his own prematurely curtailed time in Downing Street – yet can’t really face it head-on either.Could 2026 be the year that democracy fought back? | David Van ReybrouckRead moreHow does anyone learn from cataclysmic failure? I don’t mean the frothy, early-career kind that seemed the end of the world at the time, but which you can laugh about now from the security of knowing that eventually everything turned out fine. Those aren’t the kind of failures the state really cares about avoiding. Nor do I mean the kind whose authors somehow manage to fail upwards anyway – or at least onwards, like Truss, into some strange reincarnation on YouTube. The failures that most haunt their authors, but which often hold the most useful lessons for preventing such a thing ever happening again, are often of the “there but for the grace of God go you and I” kind, involving formerly blameless and conscientious people who make one inexplicably dumb mistake, often under pressure or when exhausted.Richard Jacksonwas a high-flying civil servant working on counter-terrorism, who one night accidentally scooped up two classified documents that should never have left the building along with some routine papers he was taking home. Realising his error that night, he fatally compounded it by deciding to sneak the files back before their absence was noticed, only to accidentally leave them on the train – where they were found and handed into a BBC reporter, resulting in a security scandal that cost Jackson his job and left him close to suicide. The advice on coping he shared in a recent episode of BBC Radio 4’s Life Changing series – get dark thoughts out of your head by writing them down or telling someone; keep a note of all the nice things people have ever said to you; don’t let your life be defined by one mistake – seems useful for individuals in the eye of the storm. But so perhaps is what Weston calls a degree of professional “care and acceptance” for good people who have failed, and want help working out why.Shamelessness has a deservedly terrible reputation in public life, and for some mistakes forgiveness can be too much to ask.But it’s shame that prevents thoughtful people learning from failure; shame that drives the cover-up; shame that ruins, and sometimes even ends, lives. People willing to honestly examine their own mistakes for others’ benefit deserve some grace in return. The true shame lies with those refusing to offer it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMental healthOpinionLiz TrussNHSWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: The Traitors suddenly feels tired – time for a politicians version? | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Liz Truss is like a broken record, Harry Kane is for ever Spurs, and the celebs in the castle are getting on my nerves
Author: John Crace
Headline: Liz Truss is like a broken record, Harry Kane is for ever Spurs, and the celebs in the castle are getting on my nerves
Content: Irritating … King Kenny, Maya Jama and Michael Sheen in Thursday night’s episode of The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertView image in fullscreenIrritating … King Kenny, Maya Jama and Michael Sheen in Thursday night’s episode of The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertDigested weekPoliticsDigested week: The Traitors suddenly feels tired – time for a politicians version?John CraceLiz Truss is like a broken record, Harry Kane is for ever Spurs, and the celebs in the castle are getting on my nervesFri 30 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.33 EDTShareMondayYou would have thought someone would have made an intervention by now. To save Liz Truss from the worst excesses and delusions of herself. Most former prime ministers – and there are enough of them by now – make the transition into civilian life with little fuss. More or less. John Major found himself elevated from national joke to statesman after 20 years; Tony Blair took the grandiose step of establishing his very own institute; Boris Johnson took his grumblings to the Daily Mail where he is now more or less ignored; Theresa May opted for obscurity; we have yet to find out Keir Starmer’s next move. Yet Liz Truss seems permanently scarred by her 49 days in office and its abrupt ending. Constantly feeling the need to pick away at the wound that will never heal.She has been abandoned by a Tory party for whom she isnothing but an embarrassmentand now finds herself posting conversations on YouTube with people as deranged as herself for just a handful of viewers. And now she has written a 95-page book that is essentially a distillation of her previous book. Just even worse and a bit more desperate. Havingread the book for a Digested Read, I would suggest you give it a miss. It reads as one extended cry for help. Still insisting that her budget was derailed by the Bank selling gilts the day before – something she had personally signed off – and that the establishment had been out to get her. She is like a broken record. Time for her family and friends to step in.View image in fullscreenDigested photos of the week: ‘Hi. I’m Iggy Pope.’Photograph: Simone Risoluti/ReutersTuesdayThere are some footballers who will be for ever Tottenham. At least for me. There was Jimmy Greaves. He may have played for Chelsea, AC Milan and West Ham too but it is White Hart Lane for which he is most remembered. Likewise Gareth Bale. He won all sorts with Real Madrid but for Spurs fans he will always be one of us. Even if, in retirement, he seems at his happiest when he is playing golf. Then there is Harry Kane. Arguably the greatest of the three. The footballer who seemed to have less raw talent than Greaves and Bale but forged himself into theworld’s best strikerby sheer will and hard work.I was lucky to see almost all of the home games – and many of the away ones – during Kane’s 11-year stay at the club. It would be nice to be able to say I spotted his ability from the off. But I didn’t. I assumed that, like many academy players who were being sent out on loan, he would eventually be shipped out to a lower league club. But when he did get his first-team chance, he scored goals. And kept on scoring them for a decade. A proper team player. As happy making goals for the team as he was knocking them in. Well, almost. A striker measures their seasons in goals. And he acknowledged the fans. When the team had played badly and lost, most of the rest of the players couldn’t wait to leave the pitch. Harry always made sure to thank the fans for their support.Nor was I that sad when he joined Bayern Munich. I thought he had earned the move. He had given us more than enough and deserved the chance to play for a club that regularly won something. This week he wonthe Ballon d’Orand I couldn’t have been happier. Some may have thought it a reward for all the goals he scored for Bayern and England in the last year. I liked to think of it as the culmination of a journey. Come on you Spurs.WednesdayBudget day comes with its own set of rituals. First the photos of the chancellor holding up the red box outside No 11. In the Commons, the budget speech is always preceded by prime minister’s questions. Normally, PMQs are the high spot of the Commons week, but on budget day both the prime minister and the leader of the opposition know that no one is really listening and so they rather just go through the motions. No point in wasting your best lines if no one is going to write them up.If the budget statement is a tough gig for reporters trying to make an instant assessment of its economic impact, it’s a nightmare for the leader of the opposition. She has to make an instant reply with only what’s already been leaked to back it up. So what you normally get is 20 minutes of “it’s all terrible” and “we wouldn’t have done any of it”. It’s only a day later, when economists and politicians have had a chance to go through the numbers line by line, that a proper assessment can be made.View image in fullscreenDigested photos of the week: ‘Thanks for that John. Heaven knows I’m miserable now.’Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesJohn Healey isn’t everyone’s go-to guy as the standard bearer for Andy Burnham’s new brand of optimism. His is the voice of despair, a harbinger of the apocalypse. So it was hard going listening to him rattle off98 not very big measuresdesigned to help with the cost of living through what is forecast to be the toughest decade for the country on record. Healey said he was trying to give everyone some “breathing space”. Very Gen Z. Everyone wants some breathing space these days. But it sounded most that it was thegovernment that needed the breathing space, with the tricky decisions on defence and the welfare bill parked until the next budget. Or the election. Whichever comes sooner.One person who wasn’t in the Commons to hear the budget was Nigel Farage. Heclaimed someone had moved his prayer card. This sounded about as plausible as Burnham claiming he couldn’t make it to PMQs because Lucy Powell had taken his seat. If a party leader needs a seat, one can always be found. At the very least, a junior MP is told to make way. If Nige wasn’t in the Commons, it was because he couldn’t be bothered to turn up.ThursdayIt’s amazing how quickly the unbearable becomes bearable. When we first started to go to the Marsden in Sutton for Jill’s chemo, it all seemed overwhelming and terrifying. Today, as we went back for the latest round, it feels if not comfortable then reassuringly familiar. Jill sometimes sleeps, sometimes reads a book on her Kindle, during the infusions. I sit beside her and watch the proceedings in parliament and write the sketch and diary. Like now. The wifi is better than at home. The Oak Centre, where the treatment takes place, is modern and state-of-the-art. More like what I imagine the BA business class lounge at Heathrow to be. A friend whose husband has Alzheimer’s couldn’t believe just how welcoming the centre was. There’s so much more money being invested in cancer than there is in dementia. The best time for a chemo slot is first thing in the morning. That way you can be sure to get a parking slot – free if you are having treatment – and you can also get a window bay in the centre.For the staff, nothing is ever too much trouble: you never feel as if you are being rushed and they are happy to talk through your fears. Every patient facing their worst nightmare and being held and understood. Made safe. You can always tell where the other patients are in their cycle. There was the Indian woman with the most beautiful hair, hoping the cold cap would do its job. It probably wouldn’t. Then there was the middle-aged bloke who arrived, said hello to the nurses and was asleep in minutes. You could hear the snores from the other end of the room. Best of all is the trolley offering free drinks and sandwiches. It’s staffed by volunteers. My favourite is Sandra who joined the team having been a patient first. Another friend, whose wife died of cancer a few years ago, still volunteers at the hospice where she had palliative care. He makes cocktails for everyone once a week. I call that style.FridayMy bad. Having previously raved about Celebrity Traitors, I feel somewhat embarrassed to say I have changed my mind. Halfway through last Friday’s episode, I realised not just that I was no longer enjoying myself but also that the celebs were actively irritating me. The whole format suddenly felt tired. As if the show had come to the end of its shelf life mid-run. I no longer cared what happened during the missions, murders and banishments. I just wanted someone – anyone – to go as soon as possible. I didn’t want to hear one more celeb saying “I really love you. We’re going to be best friends for life” when the only time they are likely to meet in the future is on a panel show.James Acaster’sround table admission of guiltwas an epic failure of self-awareness. The claim that he had been playing the game as “faithful” traitor was comically absurd. He had lasted that long precisely because he had played a traitor’s game so well. Mind you, I am planning to watch to the end, out of sheer “I’ve started so I will finish” bloody-mindedness. But the producers do need to think of ways of refreshing the look for next year’s version or it won’t be just me who is bored. I still think there is potential for a politicians version. If you’re near Worcester on 26 November, come to my show at Huntingdon Hall. We can try to make it happen.The Guardian’s year in review 2026: On Tuesday 1 December, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan. Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsPoliticsDigested weekcommentShareReuse this content

title: To baldly go: Patrick Stewart was an icon for bald men everywhere | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: The actor was an exemplary bald, unapologetically embracing his hairloss and setting the scalp-based bar for all other men with receding hairlines
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The actor was an exemplary bald, unapologetically embracing his hairloss and setting the scalp-based bar for all other men with receding hairlines
Content: Undeniable sex appeal … Patrick Stewart as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: Insurrection (1998).Photograph: Paramount Pictures/Elliott Marks/AllstarView image in fullscreenUndeniable sex appeal … Patrick Stewart as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: Insurrection (1998).Photograph: Paramount Pictures/Elliott Marks/AllstarPatrick StewartTo baldly go: Patrick Stewart was an icon for bald men everywhereStuart HeritageThe actor was an exemplary bald star, embracing his hair loss and the freedoms it brought. He didn’t go grey or recede – and he didn’t wear a wig like William Shatner as Captain KirkPatrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.29 EDTSharePatrick Stewart managed to be lots of different things at once. He was a towering figure on stage. He was a literal superhero onscreen. And, at times, he wasn’t above sending himself up. It also needs to be said that he was a bald man.And a pioneering one at that. Nowhere was this more clear than during his stint on Star Trek: The Next Generation. Previously, Star Trek had been a kind of space-set action show, where the relentlessly virile Captain Kirk would beam down to new planets to either punch or get off with all the aliens there. But then came its successor, and Kirk was replaced by a nonviolent intellectual called Jean-Luc. Worse still, he didn’t have any hair. What a sign of weakness.View image in fullscreenThe captains … Stewart and Shatner in Star Trek: Generations (1994).Photograph: Paramount/AllstarBut Patrick Stewart made it work. Not only was his cool temperament a nice change of pace from the 1960s take, but his sex appeal was undeniable. Indeed, in 1992 TV Guide readers voted him television’s “most bodacious” man. Stewart received 54% of the vote, putting him ahead of much hairier contenders including Luke Perry and Burt Reynolds.Not that he didn’t have his critics. When Picard’s casting was announced to the world, it is said that a reporter complained to Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry that it didn’t make any sense. After all, the show was set in a future where space travel and teleportation were accepted as the norm, so wouldn’t it stand to reason that humanity would have created a cure for male pattern baldness? According to Stewart, Roddenberry’s response was that, by the 24th century, humanity will have evolved to the point where it no longer cares about baldness.Stewart lost his hair in his teens, and was open about the effect this had on his psyche, telling Rolling Stone that he was so worried about how baldness might affect his love life that he spent more than he could afford on a wig. However, by ditching the hairpiece, Stewart became an icon for the bald.When you lose your hair, you begin casting around for other bald men, because in a small way this helps normalise it. Stewart found himself a magnet for this, telling The New Yorker in 2023, “How many times have I been spoken to in the street by somebody who would pull off his cap, revealing a bald head, and say, ‘You saved my life!’”Again, this is because Stewart was an exemplary bald. So often when men go bald they end up overcompensating by inflating themselves to preemptively ward off negative comments. Look at The Rock, and how much more aggressively he bulked out after he lost his hair. Look at Jeff Bezos, who reacted to baldness by pumping iron and building willy-shaped space rockets. Now compare this to Stewart, who pointed towards a different path of culture and elegance and refinement, embracing his baldness without ever apologising for it.More than anything, though, you just have to look at the reactions to his death to see the real legacy of Patrick Stewart’s baldness. People were generally staggered to learn that he was 86 years old. This is because, as all bald people know, losing your hair ages you, but only temporarily. He was 47 years old when Star Trek: The Next Generation premiered in 1987, but he arguably looked a decade older than that. But then he carried on looking that age for decades afterwards. He didn’t go grey, or recede, or adopt an unflattering dye job, or any of the other things that makes men look old, because he didn’t have any hair. And unlike Captain Kirk, he never worea high-end hairpiece. Patrick Stewart played the long game, and he won. O captain, my captain.Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartcommentShareReuse this content

title: Opening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do it | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address it, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: Andy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address it, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: A pro-EU demonstration outside the Houses of Parliament, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA pro-EU demonstration outside the Houses of Parliament, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOpinionBrexitOpening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do itSimon JenkinsAndy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address itFri 30 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTShareAndy Burnham’sopening debateon whether Britain should rejoin the EU is divisive, painful and politically risky. That is why it should be welcomed. To jeopardise his popularity so soon after coming to office might seem reckless, but the issue is urgent and not going away. Brexit is continuing to damage the nation’s economy. The prime minister’s job is to challenge, if not reform it.The Brexit decade has evoked a bizarre sense of guilt among Britons.Opinion pollsshow nearly 60% regard it as a mistake, with just a third still in favour. Almost a quarter of those who voted for Brexit now regret it. While early forecasts of economic disaster wereproved wrong, the accumulated cost of cutting links with Britain’s biggest trading partner is estimated at6-8% of GDP.This is huge. It must rank as the greatest act of self-harm by a British government in modern times.A year ago Keir Starmer began to ease some of the barriers, with modest deals on youth exchange and meat exports. Burnham wants to take this further, with negotiations resuming in Brussels next month. Yesterday in the Commons he cited damage tothe car industry, while agriculture remains mired in dozens of pages of regulation.Fish rotsin inspection sheds, and cars and passengers queue for hours at borders.Yet if something must be done, the question remains: what? Burnham emphasises that he would not renege on Labour’s 2024 election pledge tohonour the referendumin this parliament. But he certainly wants a revival of the debate and has a personal hope to see Brexit reversed one day. For now he seeks “an honest discussion … an open conversation” on where future negotiations might lead. He murmured the possibility of free movement of people for EU passport holders. The subject’s delicacy was demonstrated as Westminster Brexiters reacted like scalded cats.“Betrayal … catastrophe”, cried Reform UK’s Nigel Farage.A reason for Burnham to proceed cautiously is that the public’s regret overBrexitis not matched by agreement on what should take its place. While 55% of all Britons would support rejoining the EU, that falls to 35% if the condition is surrendering the UK’s previous opt-outs – which would mean joining the euro and participating in the Schengen passport-free travel zone.There could be a middle-ground Brexit model, including a bespoke place for Britain within a wider European economic area. But this in turn might be unacceptable to some existing EU countries. An alternative could include membership of the European Free Trade Association or a customs union.The truth is Britain has always been ambivalent in its attitude to European unions. Ireland and Denmark had in the past reversed anti-EU referendums by negotiating opt-outs with Brussels. David Cameron attempted no such remedy in 2016. He simply resigned.During the post-referendum Commons debates it was clear that many MPs would have favoured a “soft Brexit” option, its form as yet unclear. A responsible parliament at the time might have formed a coalition to pursue such an option. As it was, Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party preferred to exploit Theresa May’s internal divisions and leave the way open for Boris Johnson and his “hard Brexiters”. Manning Westminster’s party barricades took precedence over seeking a sensible compromise with Brussels.Burnham must therefore tread with care. Westminster’s political culture slithers instinctively into conflict mode without thought for the message that this sends to the outside world. Plenty of Europeans remain sceptical of whether Britain truly wants to rejoin the EU, and will resist any demand for extensive opt-outs or concessions. But that is for another day. For now, Labour is committed to honour its referendum manifesto promise.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham is right to open the conversation. But he must first detoxify Brexit and diminish its prominence – and that of the party whose existence depends on it, Reform. For the time being, as there is no question of rejoining the EU, there is no issue of British sovereignty. The negotiations should be boring, over regulations, conventions and protocols. These would inevitably involve compromise – but compromise that ensures both parties come away with something gained.One solution would be to do what was not done after 2016: establish a strong cross-party Commons committee to monitor the November talks and take Burnham’s conversation forward. This should concentrate on reducing barriers to trade and growth, and promoting cultural and security relations with Europe. To put it mildly, Europe needs such concentration, and badly. On that, surely Westminster can agree.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionForeign policyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Could 2026 be the year that democracy fought back? | David Van Reybrouck | The Guardian
description: Elections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark times, says Belgian author and philosopher David Van Reybrouck
Author: David Van Reybrouck
Headline: Elections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark times, says Belgian author and philosopher David Van Reybrouck
Content: Supporters of Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrate in Rio de Janeiro, 25 October 2026.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAView image in fullscreenSupporters of Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrate in Rio de Janeiro, 25 October 2026.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAOpinionSerbiaCould 2026 be the year that democracy fought back?David Van ReybrouckElections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark timesFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTShareIt is undoubtedly too early to declare victory, but the recent electoral defeats ofViktor Orbán,Aleksandar VučićandFlávio Bolsonaromake me wonder: is 2026 turning out to be the year democracy slowly, but surely, fought back?Even inIsrael, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reigning bloc lost its parliamentary majority and saw the spectacular rise of Arab parties. Though the opposition may not be able to form a government yet, it does have the larger parliamentary bloc.The shift began with an astonishing election result in Hungary in April. Against all odds, Orbán, the EU’s most deeply entrenched autocrat, was unseated by challengerPéter Magyar. Over his long years in office, Orbán had done everything possible to consolidate and perpetuate his authoritarian grip on power. The media were in his pocket, the judiciary ate from his hand and academic freedom was systematically curtailed. Yet a broad civic movement coalesced around Magyar’s party and succeeded in ousting him. The banks of the Danube witnessed theirmost exuberant night of celebrationthis century.Joy wasequally palpablelast Sunday night, 300km down the river in Belgrade. There in Serbia, the Student List, a bottom-up alliance of students, academics and angry citizens, unexpectedly sent Vučić packing. Vučić had held a tight grip on power since 2014, first as prime minister, then president, relying on a familiar cocktail of far-right bravado,financial scandalsand contempt for the rule of law: the winning formula of recent years. But there seems to be a limit to what citizens are ready to accept. Vučić’s fate was sealed after the newly constructed roof canopy of theNovi Sad train station collapsed in 2024, killing 16 people and triggering widespread public fury against systemic corruption.Then came the biggest news of all on Monday morning, whenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvadefied expectations to emerge victorious in Brazil’s presidential election. In the first round, Flávio Bolsonaro had been in the lead, and almost every poll predicted he would win the run-off. Many Brazilians braced themselves for an administration at least as radical-right as his father’s. Instead, Lula, the son of poor, illiterate farmers and a former factory worker himself, surprised friend and foe alike by winning the presidency of Latin America’s largest economy for the fourth time.Commentators were quick to point out that Lula’s victory halted a winning streak for rightwing populists across Latin America. That is certainly true, but zooming out reveals a broader pattern. This is not primarily a story of left v right, but rather of democrats v post-democrats. Hungary’s Magyar is by no means a leftist; he is a centre-right leader who was once a member of Orbán’s own party. In Serbia, the Student List washeaded by Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist and university professor with no pronounced ideological profile. While he champions liberal values such as press freedom and the rule of law, his stance on Kosovo aligns with traditional Serbian nationalism: it should not be independent.What Magyar, Srdanović and Lula share – despite significant political differences – is a fundamental belief that the rules of the democratic game must be respected. Elections must be fair, judges and journalists must work independently, and checks and balances exist for a reason.Post-democrats, by contrast, treat laws and international agreements as mere suggestions, a convenient menu of policy options from which they can cherrypick. They use elections to gain power, only to hollow out democratic institutions once they are in office and maximise their private business profits. As corruption is key, they have to remain in power to stay out of jail. Opposing voices must be muzzled and critical media prosecuted. Post-democrats only keep the outer shell of democracy. Bolsonaro Jr took a page fromDonald Trump’s playbook: election results are declared unimpeachable when he wins, andrigged when he loses. Similarly, Netanyahu is now attempting to discredit the Israeli election outcome, by suggesting Qatar interfered on behalf of the Palestinian parties.Post-democrats have been on the rise for years, and it is terrifying. Since 2000, we have witnessed a steady, deliberate dismantling of democratic achievements across every continent. Anyone reading the latest internationalDemocracy Report, produced by the V-Dem Institute, could easily despair. In terms of overall democratic health, it finds that we have effectively regressed to the levels of 1978. Only 7% of the world’s population live in liberal democracies.Yet after years of alarming headlines about global democratic backsliding, the news from Budapest, Belgrade and Brasília offers rays of hope in dark times. So does the massive wave of Gen Z protests this year, from India and the Philippines to Albania, Argentina and Chile. Huge crowds of young people have taken to the streets to challenge autocratic power and corruption in their countries.Could liberal democracy be finding its second wind? Is it actually possible to defeat autocrats and authoritarian regimes after all? Could this mark the beginning of a democratic revival that might extend to the US next week? Most polls suggest that the Democrats stand a strong chance of reclaiming at least the House of Representatives in the upcoming US midterms.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, thedelegitimisation of Arab votersin Israel this week reminds us of the limitations of change via the ballot box. Elections can help us get rid of post-democrats, but in deeply divided societies they are not enough to heal. The individual, silent act of voting must be complemented with collective processes of deliberation.Nonetheless, globally, 2026 may come to rank as the best year for democracy in more than a quarter of a century. Could this be the turning point?What this tells usahead of critical electionsin some of the EU’s largest member states in the year ahead – France, Spain, Germany and Poland – remains anyone’s guess. Looking at the momentum of the AfD in Germany, rightwing populist parties with post-democratic tendencies remain very much alive in Europe. AndVox could be part of a People’s party-led governmentin Spain in a matter of weeks. But Hungary, Serbia and Brazil have delivered a vital reminder: the rise of autocratsand their permanence in power are not immutable laws of nature. Soon enough, post-democracies may start to feel passé.David Van Reybrouck is a Belgian author and philosopher laureate for the Low Countries. He is the author of Against Elections: The Case for Democracy, and the initiator ofDemocracy27Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The hill I will die on: Dumplings are the ultimate proof of our common humanity | Joseph de Weck | The Guardian
description: Across nations and classes, there is one thing we can all agree on – that putting delicious things inside dough is a good idea, says writer Joseph de Weck
Author: Joseph de Weck
Headline: Across nations and classes, there is one thing we can all agree on – that putting delicious things inside dough is a good idea, says writer Joseph de Weck
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onComfort foodThe hill I will die on: Dumplings are the ultimate proof of our common humanityJoseph de WeckAcross nations and classes, there is one thing we can all agree on – that putting delicious things inside dough is a good ideaFri 30 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTShareOn a recent Saturday morning in Paris, I made a life-changing discovery. It came in the frozen aisle of an Asian supermarket: you can buy premade dumpling wrappers. Take a moment to think about the implications of this. Chinese shrimp wontons? Ukrainian potato varenyky? Italian veal ravioli? You’re halfway there before you’ve even chopped an onion (as long as you’re not precious about usingexactlythe right dough for each recipe).Since then, I’ve fallen into a full-blown dumpling rabbit hole, my nights spent on YouTube, watching grandmothers sitting in circles, pinching dough. So many shapes. So many techniques. Team inward pleats or outward?Columbia University Press has just publishedThe Epic History of Macaroni and Cheese: From Ancient Rome to Modern America. But clearly someone should also write The Long Arc of Putting Things in Dough: A Transcultural History. Because what does it say about humanity that all around the globe, at various points in history, people have invented some version ofadelicious thing wrapped in dough?Perhaps we all secretly long to be dumplings; there is certainly something reassuring about being enclosed. The French philosopher Claire Marin calls this a nostalgia for our “lost envelopment” – a longing to return to that primordial experience of being fully embraced in the womb.Indeed, how fortunate is a filling’s existence: held, knowing it is exactly where it belongs. Desired, yet protected. And entirely individual, but never alone; dumplings are herd beings. Plus, they’re cute. So much so thatsquishy mystery dumplingshave become the latest trend toy. The Labubu is so 2025.Perhaps we need to go back to the stone age to understand the worldwide dumpling craze.In her 1986 essayThe Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction, the American novelist Ursula K Le Guin suggested that our narrative of human history may be badly skewed. We picture early humans as men chasing bison. Yet the first human tool may have been a basket, not a spear. Gathering probably provided most of the calories; hunting was more often a hobby to kill time. And the fact that we say “hunter-gatherers” rather than “gatherer-hunters” is probably another vestige of the patriarchy.“It is a human thing to do,” Le Guin writes, “to put something you want, because it’s useful, edible or beautiful, into a bag … and then take it home with you.”Dumplings, those lovely edible containers, take this human instinct and make it culinary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Comedians should not be hot | Amy AnnetteRead moreWhatever the reasons for the dumpling’s global triumph, it fills me with hope. Every time I eat Afghan mantu, Argentinian empanadas or Austrian kasnudeln, I feel that these little envelopes are trying to teach me a small lesson in universalism.Forget the clash of civilisations. Dumplings, whether you like them or not, are the ultimate proof of our common humanity.Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zürich and ParisExplore more on these topicsComfort foodThe hill I will die onChinese food and drinkFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Replacing government grants with revenue streams from taxation will not in itself reduce regional inequalities. But the political implications are radical
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Replacing government grants with revenue streams from taxation will not in itself reduce regional inequalities. But the political implications are radical
Content: John Healey delivers the budget speech in the House of Commons, 28 October 2026.Photograph: parliamentlive.tvView image in fullscreenJohn Healey delivers the budget speech in the House of Commons, 28 October 2026.Photograph: parliamentlive.tvOpinionEconomic policyThe Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal EnglandEditorialReplacing government grants with revenue streams from taxation will not in itself reduce regional inequalities. But the political implications are radicalFri 30 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTShareFollowing Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, waschallengedby the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringingdeclarationof long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action.Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolutionroadmapunveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal.From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.These are structural changes that will transform the relationship between local government and a notoriously overly centralised state. They have so far failed to generate anything like the coverage that accompanied the Conservatives’levelling-upprogramme, which degenerated into a tawdry pork barrel exercise for “red wall” Tory MPs. But it is on this municipal terrain that Mr Burnham’s aspiration to rebalance the country, reduce regional inequality and “roll back” the 80s will be played out.Andy Burnham.Photograph: Sky NewsReplacing government grants with guaranteed income streams will give strategic authorities more certainty over future revenue – against which they will be able to borrow – and the ability to plan flexibly according to locally set priorities. The devil will be in details to be announced in next year’s spending review, in particular regarding mechanisms to ensure poorer areas with a smaller tax base do not lose out. But the roadmap is a first move towards restoring proper agency to local authorities struggling to cope with the disastrous twin legacy of deindustrialisation and austerity.Further steps will need to be taken if, as the prime minister intends, local government is to drive “good growth” that improves general living standards and prospects throughout communities. As the Local Government Associationpointed out, cash-strapped councils on the frontline face a £7bn funding gap by 2028-29, and are in a perennial struggle merely to meet their statutory obligations on social care. Strategic authorities need to be given the capacity to gradually reassume control of priorities insectorssuch as care, housing and the utilities. That will take time and investment at scale in forms of community provision that can offer an alternative to a model in which services have been outsourced and profitsoffshored.Devolution will not of itself reduce inequalities or restore a degraded public realm. But this week’s budget measures began the necessary process of rewiring British politics. Mr Burnham’s core conviction is that radical devolution can redistribute power to those who know their own community best, and allow councils to rebalance the relationship between the public and the private sector. After decades in which the latter has profited hugely from calling nearly all the shots, that is very much the right direction of travel. The starting gun has been fired in a process that can lead to a genuine renaissance of municipal England.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writing | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Richard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessons
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Richard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessons
Content: ‘Prof Dawkins is often too polemical, but most science writing tends to be heavily didactic, with little argument or rhetorical flourish.’Photograph: Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Prof Dawkins is often too polemical, but most science writing tends to be heavily didactic, with little argument or rhetorical flourish.’Photograph: Rex/ShutterstockOpinionEvolutionThe Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writingEditorialRichard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessonsFri 30 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTShareRichard Dawkins’ The Selfish Gene was not predicted to be a success. Its initial print run, published this week in 1976, was just 5,000. It went on to sell millions, and is perhaps the most influential work of pop-science ever. For 50 years, it has been the go-to resource for the layperson seeking to understand evolution.What accounts for its enduring power? Prof Dawkins’ central claim, that “we are survival machines – robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes” was provocative, stripping the messy stuff of human and other life down to a simple law. And yet the book is primarily concerned with proving that complex, selfless behaviour such as altruism in animals can emerge from these basic “selfish” drives, satisfyingly resolving an apparent paradox. Prof Dawkins – a zoologist by training – also succeeded in conjuring entertaining, vividly drawn vignettes of the lives of animals, from lions and ants to hawks and honeybees, to make his points.Nevertheless, 50th anniversary celebrations have been somewhat muted. In anessay in the journal Nature, the historian of science Nathaniel Comfort suggests there is something almost malign about The Selfish Gene’s commitment to a simple kind of determinism.There is certainly that and more to take issue with. Prof Dawkins fought publicly with eminent biologists such as Stephen Jay Gould about whether genes were the primary target of natural selection, rather than the individual organism or group – a legitimate clash between differing theories that was mirrored in the scientific literature. More quietly and damningly, many biologists bemoan the way the book seems to assume every trait is some kind of adaptation – hardly the textbook view, which has long recognised the role of randomness and chance in evolution. It also focuses almost exclusively on animals. And it is hard to read Prof Dawkins fresh, without the knowledge that the later books are repetitive and that his comments outside his field – including on feminism,disabilityand describingIslamas “the greatest force for evil in the world today” in 2013 – don’t suggest a great or sensitive thinker.Perhaps the best way to read The Selfish Gene is alongside its critics. Prof Dawkins’ Oxford tutor Arthur Cain called it a young man’s book, pointedly suggesting that the author would come to regret or recant his most bombastic claims. Prof Dawkins never really did, but his intransigence brought out the best in his critics, from Prof Gould to Richard Lewontin or Hilary and Steven Rose. Read all together, it makes for a full and rollicking picture of modern evolutionary debateIt also remains a model of style. The philosopherJohn Dupré, no fan of Prof Dawkins’ scientific thought, nonetheless calls it a paradigmatic example of successful popular science writing. The book works on this level because it takes a point of view in a live scientific debate, and argues its side with engaging dash and zeal. Prof Dawkins is often too polemical, but most science writing tends to be heavily didactic, with little argument or rhetorical flourish. And it is possible to both inform and persuade: Sean Carroll’s Endless Forms Most Beautiful and Nick Lane’s The Vital Question take a similarly clear, provocative line.The science has moved on, and The Selfish Gene has flaws. But any writer looking to supplant its place in the public imagination with a more capacious vision of evolution must reckon with the reasons for its long-running success. For all its problems, it remains a model of its genre.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: This budget fails to live up to Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Letters: Caitlin Boswell of Tax Justice UK and others on what Aditya Chakrabortty described as a ‘Martin Lewis budget’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Caitlin Boswell of Tax Justice UK and others on what Aditya Chakrabortty described as a ‘Martin Lewis budget’
Content: ‘I know that things are tight, but could the government not have funded a red box with “CR III” painted on it rather than the “ER II” sported by Mr Healey?’Photograph: Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘I know that things are tight, but could the government not have funded a red box with “CR III” painted on it rather than the “ER II” sported by Mr Healey?’Photograph: Sopa Images/ShutterstockBudget 2026LettersThis budget fails to live up to Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoricCaitlin Boswellof Tax Justice UK and others on what Aditya Chakrabortty described as a ‘Martin Lewis budget’Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTShareAditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget (Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham.As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it.So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched. Recouping the massive wealth and profits siphoned off to shady tax havens each year, equalising how the tax system treats income from wealth and work, and building HMRC’s capacity to properly measure and collect tax from the very richest would raise tens of billions to help pay for targeted, meaningful cost of living support and Burnham’s ambitious plans to fix the housing crisis, fund social care and devolve power and wealth to every region.Reforming capital gains tax – aproposalsupported bymembersof his own party – would make things fairer and raise around £19.7bn a year, enough to build90,000 new council homes(the number needed each year to end the housing crisis) and train128,000 new NHS nurses.This government cannot survive much longer on vibes alone, andLabouris already on its last chance. Burnham must use his 10-year plan and spending review to lay out a proper roadmap to genuinely improve lives and transform the country, otherwise he risks being remembered for gherkins, which isn’t much better than Liz Truss’s lettuce.Caitlin BoswellDeputy director, external affairs, Tax Justice UKAditya Chakrabortty is right to say that Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric and romantic notions need to be translated into a bold programme of change. Unless this government tackles income and wealth inequality seriously, people’s anger will unceremoniously sweep it from office at the next election.Hugh FirthNewcastle upon TyneLiving in a rented band B property, my “breathing space” was short-lived on budget day. The £100 energy payment announced by the chancellor will be entirely swallowed up by Northern Energy’s own announcement via email at 5pm the same day: “a temporary fuel surcharge of £17 per delivery will be applied to LPG deliveries as from your next delivery”.Although this is “temporary”, customers are warned that the need to cover the elevated fuel costs is likely to remain for the foreseeable future. I had six deliveries of LPG last year – do the maths.Juliet LunnCockermouth, CumbriaOnce again, tax thresholds are frozen. What a missed opportunity. It would have been so easy to raise the threshold in line with the state pension, and keep them aligned. This simple mechanism would ensure that those with no other income pay no tax, and keep a little more money in the pockets of working people and others on very low incomes. Maybe next year?Jack KenwardSouth Molton, North DevonAlthough abolishing the standing charge is something I agree with, presumably one of the groups that will benefit are second (and third) home owners. This includes approximately177 MPs, Airbnb properties and holiday lets.John Victor DaviesHastings, East SussexI know that things are tight, but could the government not have funded a red box with “CR III” painted on it rather than the “ER II” sported by Mr Healey?Robert BowdenBristolHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Don’t just ban school uniforms from pornography – ban them altogether | Child protection | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to a campaign by teenage girls against the use of uniforms in pornography
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to a campaign by teenage girls against the use of uniforms in pornography
Content: ‘As a not-so-little feminist and former schoolgirl decades ago, it struck me how we just took it for granted that we would be catcalled in our uniforms.’Photograph: PjrTravel/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘As a not-so-little feminist and former schoolgirl decades ago, it struck me how we just took it for granted that we would be catcalled in our uniforms.’Photograph: PjrTravel/AlamyChild protectionLettersDon’t just ban school uniforms from pornography – ban them altogetherReaders respond to a campaign by teenage girls against the use of uniforms in pornographyFri 30 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.11 EDTShareThis is a wonderful campaign by Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow to ban the use of school uniform in pornography (We’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us?, 23 October).Perhaps it could be followed by another to ban school uniforms altogether. The reasons for having them are specious and outdated. There is an idea that it makes class differences invisible. As someone who wore a visibly secondhand and well-worn uniform at school and was the butt of much teasing, I know it does no such thing.There is another idea that they are worn as a badge of honour and indicate pride in being part of a community. On the contrary, some children have to wear home clothes on the way to and from school to avoid being bullied on the bus or the street because of their uniform.Most schools in Europe do not make uniform a part of school life – they should be banned. This would also undermine the pornography industry’s fixation with school uniforms, thus killing two birds with one stone.Susanna DammannLondonView image in fullscreenA video still from Britney Spears singing …Baby One More Time.Photograph: VevoWell done to Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow for their wonderfully written opinion piece and campaign. As a not-so-little feminist and former schoolgirl decades ago, it struck me how we just took it for granted that we would be catcalled in our uniforms. Sunday afternoons enjoying St Trinian’s films on television reinforced this, and it was only Britney Spears’s video for…Baby One More Timethat brought me up short and I thought: “Hold on, why are we sexualising school uniforms and schoolgirls?” And well done to the Guardian for allowing the students the platform to share their impressive campaign.Amanda RaeIlkley, West YorkshireI was – I now understand – groomed at school from the age of 11, and the relationship with my teacher became sexual when I was 15. After I left school, he asked me to wear the top half of my school uniform while we had sex. I will never, ever get the picture of myself like that, in the mirror at the end of his bed, out of my mind.I couldn’t applaud Rose, Mae, Willow and Aylin’s campaign more, and they are right when they say that adults should be taking care of this. I admire their realisation that this is not how things should be. If I had been as aware as they are, my life would have turned out very differently.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Pedestrianisation won’t save Oxford Street | Transport policy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Oliver Schick writes that there is a limit to how much footfall is beneficial. Plus letters from Iain Nelson and Tom Hardy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Oliver Schick writes that there is a limit to how much footfall is beneficial. Plus letters from Iain Nelson and Tom Hardy
Content: Cars, buses, taxis and bicycles can no longer travel along much of Oxford Street, with almost a kilometre of the road now pedestrianised.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCars, buses, taxis and bicycles can no longer travel along much of Oxford Street, with almost a kilometre of the road now pedestrianised.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesTransport policyLettersPedestrianisation won’t save Oxford StreetOliver Schickwrites that there is a limit to how much footfall is beneficial. Plus letters fromIain NelsonandTom HardyFri 30 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.11 EDTShareThe real causes of the problems seen in Oxford Street (The long read, 22 October) are high rents, the chaotic system of business rates and the replacement of many smaller footprints with larger ones; these are the main factors that have made the street less viable. The large flagship shops depend on being surrounded by good-quality small businesses to attract customers.Much of what the mayor ofLondonis doing here is a de facto part-privatisation – stopping up a very important public highway for a large number of users of “unwelcome” modes of transport, to benefit private landowners.Rather than buses being a main culprit here, it is much more likely that the gradual downgrading of bus services along Oxford Street has contributed significantly to its decline.The strategic mistake of routing Crossrail along Oxford Street – long after this plan lost its part-justification (dating from when it was conceived decades ago) of stimulating the West End – has caused the dangerously high footfall levels that have become a main motivation for pedestrianisation.The Crossrail route should have been changed to connect Heathrow and Stratford through centres in south London, but we have to live with it now. There is a natural limit to how much footfall is beneficial for urban centres, and disadvantaging everyone who doesn’t want to get there by underground railway isn’t going to change this.The factors at play that have weakened Oxford Street are not unique to it, and none of them will be affected by these actions from the mayor of London, who is largely powerless to address them without central government taking corrective action.Oliver SchickLondonI like to see Sadiq Khan contributing to the Guardian, but on this occasion I have to quibble with his description of Oxford Street as “our nation’s high street” (We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too, 26 October). I live on the border of Wales, and whether a street in London is pedestrianised or not is entirely irrelevant to me. It’s not my high street and never will be.Iain NelsonSelattyn, ShropshireCredit where credit is due. Contrary to accusations at the time that businesses had suffered,footfall on Oxford Street actually increased by 13.5%as visitors were drawn to the utopia that was Extinction Rebellion’s blockade in April 2019 – a harbinger, in microcosm, of what a greener, less polluted world might look like.Tom HardyLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: One man’s war on the scourge of sodcasting  | Public transport | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article about learning from Japan on curbing ‘loudcasting’ and antisocial behaviour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article about learning from Japan on curbing ‘loudcasting’ and antisocial behaviour
Content: ‘I give sodcasters on the bus a minute or so and then ask them to use headphones or turn off the sound..’Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I give sodcasters on the bus a minute or so and then ask them to use headphones or turn off the sound..’Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/AlamyPublic transportLettersOne man’s war on the scourge of sodcastingReaders respond to an article about learning from Japan on curbing ‘loudcasting’ and antisocial behaviourFri 30 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.11 EDTShareEmily Bratt missed out one way of addressing antisocial behaviour – on buses or elsewhere – which is to address the problem oneself rather than waiting for official enforcement (Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan, 24 October). I give sodcasters on the bus a minute or so and then ask them to use headphones or turn off the sound. It doesn’t always work, but the offenders don’t like it, and the less they like the response they get, the less they will do it.Donald SmithHaddington, East LothianI’m all for banning “loudcasting” – because I’m a retired bus driver and I will not be the one charged with enforcing it. Heaven help the poor sods who will.Jenny EldershawBuxton, DerbyshireIt’s not only in Japan that children are taught to be socially responsible. When my eight-year-old daughter visited her new UK primary school on return from her early school years in ruralZimbabwe, she didn’t understand when the teacher apologised for the state of the classroom because the cleaners were on strike. She also asked: “Which day does our class clean the toilets?”Anne SpargoUpper Colwall, HerefordshireRe Emily Bratt’s suggestion that schoolchildren should help with “caring” for their school, when I was at Dartington Hall – a progressive co-educational boarding school – in the 1960s we did what was called “useful work” before classes. It involved us in the processes of running the school. Among other things, I tidied the library, thus learning the Dewey classification system; was printer’s devil to the bookbinder, Eric McNally, producing play programmes and the school prospectus; spent two terms in my O-level year setting up chemistry lab equipment for A-level classes; and was filing clerk for the careers advice department.Responsibility was a key word at Dartington, it being well understood that freedom is not free – it comes at a price – and that consideration for others and support for the community are essential.Ruth GilbertMarsden, West YorkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Spain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PM | Spain | The Guardian
description: Pedro Sánchez vows to investigate crash that killed 69 people – and rebuild public confidence
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Pedro Sánchez vows to investigate crash that killed 69 people – and rebuild public confidence
Content: Cranes lift one of the wrecked carriages from Wednesday’s crash, in which 69 people died and more than 100 were injured.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCranes lift one of the wrecked carriages from Wednesday’s crash, in which 69 people died and more than 100 were injured.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesSpainSpain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PMPedro Sánchez vows to investigate crash that killed 69 people – and rebuild public confidenceEurope live – latest updatesSam Jonesin Madrid andJakub KrupaFri 30 Oct 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’strain collisionthat killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.Sánchez saidSpainwas “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding his government was committed to finding what had caused the country’s second deadly train collision this year.Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when theycollided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other trainslammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda, in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.10:20Survivors shell-shocked after deadly Spain train crash - The LatestThe crash came nine months after 46people were killedand dozens injured when two trains – again one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz, in Andalucía.“It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system. Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez (L) and the Castilla-La Mancha regional president Emiliano Garcia Page hold a press conference.Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPAShortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, who is under growing pressure to resign, gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but emphasised that such incidents were not uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.The minister added that the crash had occurred after an Adif operator ordered the Renfe train to move off at “normal” speed, rather than following the protocols, which stipulate a top speed of 40kph (25mph) so that drivers can see any dangers ahead in good time. According toa preliminary investigation reportreleased on Thursday, the Renfe train was travelling at between 160kph and 200kph when it hit the Iryo train.The report concluded: “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers.”Puente said the operator in question was a 48-year-old man,with all the relevant up-to-date training and two years of experience in control centres, who had been managing this specific area since February this year. “So, it was a sector he knew well,” the minister added.Transport unions have pushed back at the government, arguing that current workloads are too demanding to handle safely and asking for more personnel.“We believe [the minister] is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” Raquel Ayllón, a spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told the Associated Press. “Human error isn’t incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.”Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP), which is forecast to topple Sánchez’ socialist-led minority coalition government in next month’s snap general election, has repeatedly called for Puente to step down.The PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said his party was holding Puente and Sánchez “politically responsible” for both rail crashes. “Whoever has failed in their duty to run the transport ministry properly must bear the consequences,” he said. “And the person who appointed them – and kept them in their post – even more so.
