If they do not resign, we will remove them at the ballot box.”Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor who now leads the leftwing Frente Amplio coalition that is running in the election, also said Puente needed to go. “We’re not going to engage in the triviality of debating whether that resignation should take place today, tomorrow, or the day after,” she said. “It must happen as soon as possible.”Puente, asked about thepossible effect of the latest crash on the election, said he had given the matter “zero thought”.“I don’t believe anyone would expect me to be thinking about the election campaign at a moment like this,” he told reporters.Explore more on these topicsSpainTrain crashesPedro SánchezRail transportEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro in Brasília on Sunday after his election defeat. He landed in Miami on Wednesday.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro in Brasília on Sunday after his election defeat. He landed in Miami on Wednesday.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersBrazil‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockeryBrazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of armsTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroFri 30 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – todeclare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaperthunderedon Friday.Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday night, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.Perhaps most bizarrely, he claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the 19th-century Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted an outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator,toldthe network GloboNews.The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.View image in fullscreenA woman reads a newspaper with news of the election result on Monday in São Paulo.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,”Malafaia was quoted as sayingby O Globo.Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s winRead moreThe Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.Others warned Bolsonarismo would remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement was now in doubt.Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São PaulocalledLula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, the US president replied: “I won’t get involved.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroJair BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe | Archaeology | The Guardian
description: Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79
Content: Archaeologists found the personal belongings in a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, once one of Pompeii’s busiest streets.Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological ParkView image in fullscreenArchaeologists found the personal belongings in a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, once one of Pompeii’s busiest streets.Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological ParkArchaeologyPerfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobeArchaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79Angela Giuffridain RomeFri 30 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.View image in fullscreenA charm from a crepundia, a type of necklace often worn by children.Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological ParkBut the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.View image in fullscreenBronze weights and a box closure found among the possessions.Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological ParkThe home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its ​facade was first excavated ​in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.View image in fullscreenA bronze oil lamp with a deflector.Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological Park“It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, alarge and sophisticated thermal bathcomplex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.Ahome containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.Explore more on these topicsArchaeologyItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Police watchdog to investigate Met’s handling of Meghan warning letter | Metropolitan police | The Guardian
description: IOPC launches independent investigation after referral by Scotland Yard over 2019 letter about Thomas Markle
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: IOPC launches independent investigation after referral by Scotland Yard over 2019 letter about Thomas Markle
Content: The contents of the 2019 letter are understood to have played a part in the Duchess of Sussex’s estrangement from her father.Photograph: Cyril Zingaro/Keystone/APView image in fullscreenThe contents of the 2019 letter are understood to have played a part in the Duchess of Sussex’s estrangement from her father.Photograph: Cyril Zingaro/Keystone/APMetropolitan policePolice watchdog to investigate Met’s handling of Meghan warning letterIOPC launches independent investigation after referral by Scotland Yard over 2019 letter about Thomas MarkleVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentFri 30 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScotland Yard faces an independent investigation into its failure in 2019 to pass claims alleging wrongdoing by Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex, to law enforcement agencies overseas.The force hadreferred itselfto the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) over its handling of a letter written by Markle’s former wife, Roslyn Loveless. Markle, 82, is now facing claims of child sexual abuse in the Philippines, which he denies, and is under investigation by authorities there.On Friday, the IOPC decided to use its formal powers to launch an investigation into the Met. The police watchdog views the claims in the 2019 letter as potentially alleging serious offending.Its investigation will look at who in the Met made decisions such as not to pass on the claims to police forces in countries where wrongdoing by Markle was alleged, and whether police policies and procedures were followed.An IOPC spokesperson said: “Following a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, we have decided an independent investigation is required into its failure to pass on allegations of serious offending, contained in a letter it received in 2019, to relevant overseas authorities at the time.”The Met had announced on Thursday its voluntary referral to the IOPC about the handling of the 2019 letter. It also referred whether its decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duchess of Sussex could have been a breach of data rules because it contained sensitive information. The IOPC has decided it will not investigate that.The contents of the letter are understood to have played a part in Meghan’s estrangement from her father. The Guardian understands that the long letter made claims about Markle’s activities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.The Met has said it did not investigate because the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas. But for seven years it did not pass on details to the countries affected, and it is only now sending details of the letter to the FBI in the US and law enforcement in the Philippines, where Markle lived until May, as well as Thai counterparts.Markle, now in the US, has admitted paying for sex but denies possessing material that would be illegal. On Saturday, the Philippine interior minister, Jonvic Remulla,told the Guardianthat all signs pointed to Markle being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” and that a full forensic investigation would give a “definitive picture”.Investigators in the Philippines are examining digital images alleged to belong to Markle and alleged to have been found at his former home in the south-east Asian country.Meghan’s half-brother, also called Thomas, reported to Philippine authorities last week the alleged discovery of child sexual abuse images. Footage on Thursday showed Markle Jr present as Philippine officials started gathering material to examine.On Friday the Daily Mail claimed that a garage close to where Markle Sr lived in Mexico, before moving to the Philippines in 2025, contained material the paper characterised as child sexual abuse images.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt said it had reported its alleged find to the FBI.The scale of embarrassment for the Met will depend on whether investigators in the Philippines assess that the allegations relating to child sexual abuse images have any credence.On Thursday, the Met commander Adam Slonecki, who leads its protection command, said the letter had been sent in 2019 to the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre. “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom,” he said.“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”Explore more on these topicsMetropolitan policeIndependent Office for Police ConductMeghan, the Duchess of SussexPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortages
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortages
Content: People gathering in Oleshky before the joint relief evacuation operation taking them on a route through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory.Photograph: Facebook official account of Kyrylo Budano/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenPeople gathering in Oleshky before the joint relief evacuation operation taking them on a route through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory.Photograph: Facebook official account of Kyrylo Budano/AFP/GettyUkraineEvacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of OleshkyHumanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortagesPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentFri 30 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southernUkrainewere evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.Thelocalised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson regionallowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.View image in fullscreenRussian military personnel pass by damaged vehicles during a de-mining operation near Oleshky.Photograph: Russian Defence Ministry/ReutersWhile Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.View image in fullscreenThe convoy carrying more than 500 evacuees from Oleshky.Photograph: ReutersWhile earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.View image in fullscreenPeople in Oleshky have endured months of food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation.Photograph: The Office of the Commissioner for Human Rights in Russia/EPASome say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied OleshkyRead moreKsenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.“They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.View image in fullscreenUkraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets (centre), and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova (left), talk to journalists before the evacuation.Photograph: Office of the Ukrainian Ombudsman/AFP/Getty Images“I’ve been told that ‌it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for ​such a significant duration.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Twice as many plants and animals sold in wildlife trade as previously thought, says report | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: More than 100,000 species are traded globally, whether illegally smuggled, sold as ornaments or in fisheries, timber and fashion industries, study finds
Author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
Headline: More than 100,000 species are traded globally, whether illegally smuggled, sold as ornaments or in fisheries, timber and fashion industries, study finds
Content: Parrots found inside drainage pipes in a raid in Labuha, North Maluku, Indonesia. The trade in wildlife has been ‘completely underestimated’, the report says.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenParrots found inside drainage pipes in a raid in Labuha, North Maluku, Indonesia. The trade in wildlife has been ‘completely underestimated’, the report says.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe age of extinctionWildlifeTwice as many plants and animals sold in wildlife trade as previously thought, says reportMore than 100,000 species are traded globally, whether illegally smuggled, sold as ornaments or in fisheries, timber and fashion industries, study findsSupported byAbout this contentRebecca RatcliffeFri 30 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of plant and animal species in use or sold in the wildlife trade is more than twice as high as previously thought, researchers have discovered.A study,published in Science Advances, warns that there are huge gaps in global assessments of how wildlife is traded, and that past estimates have failed to keep up with changes such as theboom in the online exotic pet trade, where sellers offering to post spider eggs across the world or sneak reptiles on to planes are just a click away.“The dimensions of trade have changed. Without monitoring it in a representative way, we cannot manage it,” said Alice Hughes, a professor at the University of Melbourne and lead author of the study. “At the moment, we are completely underestimating what modern trade looks like – for the pet trade and for the ornamental trade, we are not capturing it. And it poses a major risk to species.”The study comes as the US-based nonprofit, theCenter for Biological Diversity, filed a petition asking the US Fish and Wildlife Service to listthe Javan slit-faced batunder the Endangered Species Act, warning that consumers are buying the bat for decor, placing it at risk of extinction. Taxidermy bats are sought after, particularly by US consumers, who are looking for gothic or spooky decorations for Halloween or Christmas gifts, the centre said.The wildlife trade study identified 107,356 species that are either in use or traded globally – far higher than a previous estimate of about 50,000, which was made by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform onBiodiversityand Ecosystem Services (IPBES).The study draws on more comprehensive datasets, as well as newer research papers that havetracked species sold onlinefor decoration. It shows flaws in our understanding of what species are at risk; for example, the number of butterfly species found to be traded is greater than the IPBES’ entire estimate for all traded terrestrial invertebrates.Molly Brown, programme officer for wildlife use and trade at the International Union forConservationof Nature and a co-author of the paper, said the findingswere a reality check. “The number of species that we are talking about is still an underestimate, and that’s really clear in the paper, because we cannot access and we do not have the type of monitoring data that we really need,” she said.Discussions about the wildlife trade often focus on criminal activities, such as illegal smuggling of ivory orpangolin scales. However, the wildlife trade encompasses sectors such as fisheries and the timber trade as well as fashion and the sale of species as ornaments. This includes activities that may be sustainable, as well as trade that is driving species to extinction.Even assessing the value of the legal trade compared with the illegal trade is challenging. The under-regulation of wildlife trade has created loopholes that allow species, including sought-after exotic pets, to be “laundered into legality”, researchers said.Four years ago, nearly 200 countries agreed to ensure that trade of wild species was “sustainable, safe and legal”, as part of alandmark set of targetsaimed at ending the destruction of nature. Efforts to meet these targets are hampered by a lack of data about what is being sold and where it originated.The main data point for measuring progress on a globally agreed wildlife trade target refers only to fish stocks, which would account for at most 3% of all traded species, said Hughes.View image in fullscreenVenomous tarantulas seized by custom officials in Quezon City in the Philippines.Photograph: Rouelle Umali/Xinhua/AlamyExperts say there needs to be more systematic data collection and sharing. Globally, fisheries are monitored by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, while the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites) monitors and regulates international trade in about 40,000 species to protect them from over exploitation.However, researchers said that this excludes large numbers of potentially vulnerable species, warning the Cites system is too slow moving to keep up with new trends in threats to wildlife. Most countries lack any systematic data outside Cites, the study says. “Sometimes, it is years before things get listed and that means that they can be virtually extinct in the wild by that point,” said Hughes.Species that are newly described are often rare and have a small range, meaning they are especially valuable to trade, and can be quickly wiped out.Chris Shepherd, a conservation advocate at the Centre for Biological Diversity, who was not involved in the study, added that he had observed the wildlife trade for decades and that new species were continually appearing.“The demand for wildlife, especially live wildlife traded for pets, is growing fast, as is the number of species involved,” he said. “This trade is pushing an ever-growing list of species towards extinction, and as such, putting in place mechanisms to better monitor this trade are essential.”Explore more on these topicsWildlifeThe age of extinctionIllegal wildlife tradeAnimalsConservationBiodiversityPlantsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targets | Renewable energy | The Guardian
description: Ex-energy secretary Ed Miliband’s agenda appears undermined as money is diverted from renewables to defence
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Ex-energy secretary Ed Miliband’s agenda appears undermined as money is diverted from renewables to defence
Content: The budget on Wednesday cut subsidies to heat pumps.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe budget on Wednesday cut subsidies to heat pumps.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesRenewable energyHealey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targetsEx-energy secretary Ed Miliband’s agenda appears undermined as money is diverted from renewables to defenceKiran StaceyPolicy editorFri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain is unlikely to hit its targets on green heating after the cuts announced byJohn Healeythis week, experts have warned, as critics of Ed Miliband claim the former energy secretary’s green agenda is being dismantled.The chancellor unveiled more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget this week, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.One casualty of the cuts is the government’sscheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions are being undermined.Some believe the cuts are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor,Miatta Fahnbulleh. However, energy department sources insisted the government’s longer-term changes will incentivise people to move towards cleaner power sources and benefit the overall green agenda.Andrew Sissons, a director at the research charity Nesta, said: “After the cuts announced on Wednesday, it is very difficult to see how we can hit our clean heating targets. It is even possible that aLabourgovernment will be the first to miss the targets it has signed up to in the current carbon budget.”Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHomes across UK to get low- or no-interest loans to fund solar panels and heat pumpsRead moreUnder the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, andwas planningto increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. However, ministers said on Wednesday the scheme’s funding would rise only in line with inflation, meaning the number of installations is likely to stagnate or rise much more slowly than previously planned.“It’s disappointing – so frustrating,” said Ed Matthew, the director of the UK programme at the thinktank E3G. “We are behind a lot of other countries in rolling out heat pumps and we need a sea change in take-up to change that.”Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new worldRead moreThe cuts to heat pump subsidies came alongside about £250m of other cuts to the warm homes plan, £500m worth of cuts to hydrogen schemes, and £200m to funding for carbon capture and storage technology – all projects once championed by Miliband.Healey also announced that renewable projects would only be approved in future if they could be shown to bring costs down and were ready to be connected with the grid. Officials insist the government remains committed to its target of having clean power by 2030, though many experts believe that will be impossible under the new system.One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.”Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean.“This was something that has been discussed in government before – but Miliband always won that argument. Now he’s not in that department any more, it’s happened.”Ovenden added: “Had he not helped to oust Starmer and Reeves, he’d probably be in post still and it wouldn’t have been possible.”But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels.One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.”A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes.“We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”Explore more on these topicsRenewable energyBudget 2026Ed MilibandMiatta FahnbullehJohn HealeyMilitaryEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can see the water going down’: residents on edge as one of England’s worst-hit reservoirs dries up | Drought | The Guardian
description: After UK’s hottest summer on record, Ardingly near Haywards Heath is just 19% full – and next-closest reservoir is unusable due to broken treatment works
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: After UK’s hottest summer on record, Ardingly near Haywards Heath is just 19% full – and next-closest reservoir is unusable due to broken treatment works
Content: The depleted Ardingly reservoir.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe depleted Ardingly reservoir.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianDrought‘You can see the water going down’: residents on edge as one of England’s worst-hit reservoirs dries upAfter UK’s hottest summer on record, Ardingly near Haywards Heath is just 19% full – and next-closest reservoir is unusable due to broken treatment worksPippa NeillEnvironment reporterFri 30 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“You can see the water level at Ardingly going down and down. I don’t remember ever seeing it this low,” says Caroline Allan, a lifetime resident of Haywards Heath, the nearest town to one of England’s most depleted reservoirs.The Ardingly reservoir, managed bySouth East Waterand serving about 95,000 properties in and around Haywards Heath and Uckfield in Sussex, is currently 19% full.View image in fullscreenPippa Neill on the reservoir’s shoreline. In normal conditions, she would be underwater.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianThe day the Guardian visited, the weather was grey and rainy, incongruous with the muddy reservoir bed that should have been submerged under six metres of water.Earlier this month asevere drought was declaredin parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex, with urgent measures being taken to secure public water supplies after the UK experienced itshottest summer on record.Severe drought is the highest level of drought and is declared when evidence shows drought is causing or will soon cause serious harm, and when emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services.“They will probably never lift the hosepipe ban and it just seems so unfair that they’re making the area more and more crowded but they’re not increasing the capacity to store water,” said Allan.View image in fullscreenArdingly reservoir is well below capacity after a dry summer.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianThere has been a steady stream of new housing developments around Haywards Heath, sparkinglocal opposition, with concerns that a growing local population is putting pressure on already strained resources.Water demand is increasing as the population grows and new industrial demands from datacentres and energy infrastructure require more water. Plus, the water available to supply those needs is reducing as the climate crisis worsens, resulting in greater variability and unpredictability of rainfall and greater water demand during hotter, drier summers. There has also been a lack of investment over several decades in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs.Could England and Wales ever run out of water?Read moreMost of Europe has endured back-to-back climate crisis-driven heatwaves this summer. The extreme heat, coupled with little rainfall, means 82% of England and large parts of Wales are still in drought or severe drought.The Environment Agency would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of year and yet supplies at several reservoirs are critically low. This includes Ardingly and Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers and is 14.5% full.View image in fullscreenWimbleball in Exmoor has been declared one of the three lowest reservoirs in the country by the Environment Agency.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenThe low water levels have revealed the old stone Bessom Bridge (centre) in Wimbleball Lake.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAIt is estimated that 120% of average rainfall is needed between now and April for all areas to be considered out of drought. The government’s national drought group was told on Wednesday that despite the “weather whiplash” brought byStorm Austen and Boelo, the recent rain has not changed the drought outlook.Less than six miles away from Ardingly, Southern Water’s Weir Wood reservoir is 80% full because a water treatment works at the site has been out of action since 2018.“It’s crazy that they’ve got Weir Wood next door and they’re not using it. I think that’s madness,” Allan said.Graham Ward, who has lived in Haywards Heath for his whole life, also said it was “crazy” that there was a full neighbouring reservoir that cannot be used.During the drought in 2025, South East Water announced emergency plans to connect the Ardingly and Weir Wood reservoirs together by an overground pipeline. When the rain came and the drought conditions eased, these plans were shelved.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSouthern Water is now seeking to rebuild the treatment works at Weir Wood by 2030, and South East Water is conducting afeasibility studyof a buried pipeline to connect the two reservoirs.But after government guidance tostockpile essential goods, water scarcity has become a pressing concern for local residents. “We’re really not that far away from Weir Wood, and we’ve got Ardingly with hardly any water in it and we’re told to buy water. It’s just crazy,” said Allan.Ward said he has already been storing water for some time in anticipation.View image in fullscreenThe Environment Agency would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of year.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArdingly supplies about 95,000 properties served by South East Water in Haywards Heath, Uckfield and the surrounding areas.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty Images“I am worried, but I also think there should be responsibility on the water companies to get the reservoirs working as they should be. The infrastructure is crumbling and it’s not fit for purpose any more; if we continually have hot summers, this is going to be a problem every year,” he said.Delphine Hazeldon, who has lived in Haywards Heath for more than 20 years, also said she has never seen the Ardingly reservoir so low.“Our relatives in Australia, they’re always asking for updates and they’re horrified. It is a definite worry, we’re approaching 80, but we think well, it’ll be our children and our children’s children facing the problem. The whole thing is a mess.”View image in fullscreenDelphine Hazeldon said she had never seen the reservoir so low.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianA spokesperson at Southern Water said: “Weir Wood reservoir is being rebuilt to ensure long-term water resilience for the North Sussex region, in the face of climate change and population growth. The existing treatment works date from the 1950s and reached the end of its operational life, with significant reliability and water-quality challenges. The site was therefore taken out of supply in 2018.“While a number of options were considered, a complete rebuild was identified as the best long-term solution to provide a reliable and resilient water supply for customers in the area. While we already supply water to South East Water through an existing interconnected network, Ardingly’s current situation would not be resolved if Weir Wood treatment works were operational.”Water minister, Emma Hardy, who chaired a national drought group meeting on Wednesday, said: “Despite the recent rain, the situation remains serious. As we move through autumn and winter, we now face the challenge of having drought and flood simultaneously as the rain struggles to be absorbed by the hardened ground.“Resilience to our changing climate is key and we need to be thinking about next year now. Water companies must continue to take every available measure to secure current supplies while also ensuring that we start the spring in the strongest possible position.”South East Water declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsDroughtSouth East WaterWaterWater industryWest SussexEnglandClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Local devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell Burnham | Devolution | The Guardian
description: John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not Westminster
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not Westminster
Content: Andy Burnham and Scotland's first minister, John Swinney, in Glasgow on Friday.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Scotland's first minister, John Swinney, in Glasgow on Friday.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/PADevolutionLocal devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell BurnhamJohn Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not WestminsterPeter Walker,Bethan McKernanandAndrew SparrowFri 30 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScotland and Wales’s first ministers have toldAndy Burnhamthat decisions on local devolution rest solely with their parliaments, in response to the prime minister’s push to extend English-style regional powers across the UK.After Burnham held discussions in Glasgow with John Swinney andRhun ap Iorwerthabout localised employment and reindustrialisation powers, Downing Street characterised the talks as constructive.However, the defence secretary,Wes Streeting, caused friction before the summit by criticising Swinney’s government for hoarding powers it acquired from Westminster rather than devolving them further.Westminster’s time is coming to an end, say first ministers of UK’s Celtic nationsRead moreStreeting told BBC Scotland: “One of the critiques we have … is that for the Scottish government, devolution is often about transferring power, responsibility, resources from Westminster to Holyrood and the challenge Andy Burnham is setting out is: ‘What about devolving more power also from Holyrood to local government acrossScotland?’”Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, had also been due at the talks, but did not attend after a political row between Sinn Féin and the DUP. Burnham said it was “disappointing” she was not there.The prime minister said he hoped to have all four UK nations moving at the same pace on devolution, particularly on efforts outlined in Wednesday’s budget to give mayors in England more powers over tax revenues.“There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind,” Burnham said. “I don’t want to seeWalesleft behind, but also, crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.”View image in fullscreenThe Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, speaks to the media in Glasgow on Friday.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/ReutersAp Iorwerth said he had pushed Burnham on his wish to have more powers for his government.He added: “I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd.”Swinney’s comments after the summit took a similar line, saying he would “work constructively and collaboratively” in devolving more powers to his government, while adding that Burnham had assured him “that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour”.Despite the emollient tone, tensions remain. Shortly before the summit, ap Iorwerth said Burnham’s first budget, which theWelsh governmentsaid amounted to a real-terms funding cut for the country, showed the prime minister was “not serious about Wales”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlaid Cymru, which won May’s Senedd elections, putting nationalists in office in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, has already formally asked Burnham to give Wales the same devolved powers as Scotland.The SNP-led government is frequently irritated by comments such as those by Streeting, characterised by one Scottish official as “lecturing us on devolution”.Separately, Lee Waters, who was a minister in the Labour-led Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until the elections in May, told the Guardian that Burnham, who was the Greater Manchester mayor before becoming prime minister, should not try to impose an English-style mayoral model on Wales, as “we are not comparing like with like”.He said: “The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas.“Transposing an English mayoral worldview on to a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.“Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government.”Explore more on these topicsDevolutionJohn SwinneyRhun ap IorwerthWalesWelsh politicsWelsh governmentScottish politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andreas Malm condemns UK travel ban as ‘drift into authoritarianism’ | Palestine Action | The Guardian
description: Swedish climate academic says he has been ‘kept in the dark’ over Home Office decision to revoke his travel authorisation
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Swedish climate academic says he has been ‘kept in the dark’ over Home Office decision to revoke his travel authorisation
Content: Malm was due to speak alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action, at an event in London. He now plans to appear via video link.Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenMalm was due to speak alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action, at an event in London. He now plans to appear via video link.Photograph: Album/AlamyPalestine ActionAndreas Malm condemns UK travel ban as ‘drift into authoritarianism’Swedish climate academic says he has been ‘kept in the dark’ over Home Office decision to revoke his travel authorisationMatthew WeaverFri 30 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm has condemned a travel ban imposed on him by the UK government as a “drift into authoritarianism” amid criticism of the move.Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked.He said he had only been told that his presence in the UK was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”,as the Guardian revealed.Speaking to Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, he speculated that the only plausible rationale for the ban was hisadvertised appearance at a conferencenext Wednesday alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action.He said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”He added: “What I am going through here is just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world. And that’s a very sad thing.”Malm confirmed to the Guardian that he would speak via video link at the event organised by Tribune magazine.In his BBC interview, he denied supporting or helping to financePalestine Action. But Malm, who has long campaigned for Palestinian rights, added: “You might be able to guess my opinions and sympathies.”TheHome Officesaid it could not discuss individual cases. However, a source said: “Decisions to refuse or cancel an ETA on the grounds that presence in the UK may not be conducive to public good are based solely on an assessment of the potential risk an individual may pose to UK society.”Malm said: “I don’t have any concrete evidence for what this is all about. I’m left in the dark. I have asked for clarification, explanation. I haven’t received any.”Malm was challenged on Today over whether his description of the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 as an “act of liberation” could be the reason for the ban.He replied: “It could be. But my views about what happened on 7 October and in Palestine have been in the public realm for a long time. I was most recently in the UK in May.”Malm added: “I’ve done nothing in public that is associated with Palestine Action. I have not publicly supported them or promoted them in any way.”Malm said he was invited to speak alongside Ammori to discuss the war in Iran.“So, what they’re preventing here is for us to have a discussion about the drivers of the imperial aggression in the Middle East,” he said.“The only link to Palestine Action is her [Ammori] as a person. If you continue with these guilt-by-association links, then presumably if I am a threat to the public good in the UK by dint of talking to her, then someone who talks to me presumably is also a threat to the public good. Where does that end?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe travel ban has been widely criticised. The author Sally Rooney said it was a “sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm”.In apost on X,the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said: “This all feels very much Starmer’s Labour government 2.0. An extraordinary attack on free speech from Andy Burnham.”The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who last yearoffered to stand down from his Norwich South seatto allow Andy Burnham the chance to return to parliament, said: “When any government starts barring academics for their political views, alarm bells should be ringing.“If ministers have evidence Andreas Malm is dangerous, produce it. Otherwise, this looks like political censorship dressed up as public safety. That’s a dangerous road for any democracy.”Ammorisaid in a post on X: “Banning academic and author Andreas Malm from entering Britain to stop him from speaking alongside myself, a Palestine Action co-founder, is another disgusting attack on free speech as a result of the draconian ban. The ban must be overturned.”Neal Lawson, the director of the thinktank Compass,tweeted: “This makes me ashamed to be British and ashamed of an @UKLabour government that enacts illiberal attempts to stifle legitimate voices.”The former shadow chancellor John McDonnellwrote: “You would have thought there was someone in government to appreciate the irony of effectively censoring someone who wanted to come here to discuss censorship. Home Office policy-making has degenerated into dangerous farce.”How to Blow Up a Pipeline, which inspired a film of the same name, argues that sabotage and destroying property are morally and strategically justified forms of activism.Explore more on these topicsPalestine ActionFreedom of speechHome OfficeLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Man who ran over cyclist and dragged him under car for a mile convicted of murder | Greater Manchester | The Guardian
description: Simon Richardson knew headteacher Michael Mullins was under his 4×4 as he kept driving in Manchester, jury heard
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Simon Richardson knew headteacher Michael Mullins was under his 4×4 as he kept driving in Manchester, jury heard
Content: Richardson in his Volvo after the fatal collision in April.Photograph: CPS/PAView image in fullscreenRichardson in his Volvo after the fatal collision in April.Photograph: CPS/PAGreater ManchesterMan who ran over cyclist and dragged him under car for a mile convicted of murderSimon Richardson knew headteacher Michael Mullins was under his 4×4 as he kept driving in Manchester, jury heardMark BrownNorth of England correspondentFri 30 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA motorist who drove through give-way markings, collided with a cyclist and then dragged him, trapped under his car, for more than a mile has been found guilty of murder.Simon Richardson, 35, crashed into headteacher Michael Mullins, 56, who was cycling home from work at Stretford grammar school, Greater Manchester, on the evening of 20 April. Mullins hit the bonnet and windscreen of Richardson’s Volvo XC90 and then went under the car, becoming entangled in the suspension.Richardson continued to drive for more than a mile, knowing that the trapped cyclist was just inches under his feet, a trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court heard.View image in fullscreenFamily photograph of Michael Mullins.Photograph: Greater Manchester police/PAMembers of Mullins’ family were in tears after the guilty verdict was delivered on Friday. The trial judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, discharged jurors from taking jury service again for 10 years and told them: “This was, I know, an upsetting case and there was evidence which you may have found distressing.”Richardson had denied knowing the father-of-two was under his car but the prosecutor Phil Barnes KC said the defendant knew “and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway”.“For a split second after the collision, for a brief moment, he possibly thought about doing the right thing and getting out and taking ownership of what he had just done and help the man he had just run down.“But Simon Richardson did not get out. He did not do the right thing. He chose to drive away. The obvious reason is because he wanted to escape the consequences of what he had just done.”Richardson’s front-seat passenger, his cousin Gabrielle Debotte, told the trial they both heard “moaning” from outside as he drove away from the collision scene. Giving evidence for the prosecution, she said Richardson went on to say: “He’s under the car.”The collision happened in the village of Warburton. The court heard Richardson drove to a secluded farm track in Lymm, 1.3 miles away, in an attempt to dislodge Mullins.After he stopped, Richardson twice tried to pull Mullins out, before returning to the car and driving sharply and deliberately from side to side before mounting a grass verge, the court heard. Mullins was finally released but was then driven over again as Richardson reversed and drove away.A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood from the collision spot and discovered Mullins alone and barely breathing on the grass verge, the court heard. Emergency services attended but were unable to save Mullins, from Northwich, Cheshire, who died from multiple injuries.Richardson was arrested the next day after a police vehicle pursuit. He denied murder as he claimed he did not realise Mullins was underneath his car and said he did not get out of his vehicle to try to free him.In a statement, the family of Mullins said: “He was devoted to his family and our lives will never be the same. A gap has been left in our hearts and within his role as a headteacher of Stretford grammar school.”In his closing speech to jurors on Tuesday, Jaime Hamilton KC, defending, said: “You are likely to hold Simon Richardson in contempt. That contempt may well manifest itself in a loathing of Simon Richardson and, in fairness, you are probably right to. Because it is right that we acknowledge it was the actions of Simon Richardson that led to the death of Michael Mullins.“Not only is he responsible for the death of Michael Mullins, he acted in the most selfish of ways with one thought in his mind – himself. But that does not make him guilty of the homicide offences on this indictment.”Jurors went out to consider their verdict on Wednesday and returned to find Richardson guilty on Friday. The judge said she would sentence him on Monday.Explore more on these topicsGreater ManchesterManchesterCrimeCyclingEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Public sector an ‘afterthought’ to North Sea oil jobs, says Unison leader | Trade unions | The Guardian
description: Andrea Egan calls for same political focus on teachers, care sector and NHS and says Jackdaw decision ‘a serious misstep’
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: Andrea Egan calls for same political focus on teachers, care sector and NHS and says Jackdaw decision ‘a serious misstep’
Content: Ambulance workers and paramedics on the picket line at Northallerton ambulance station in 2023.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenAmbulance workers and paramedics on the picket line at Northallerton ambulance station in 2023.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverTrade unionsPublic sector an ‘afterthought’ to North Sea oil jobs, says Unison leaderAndrea Egan calls for same political focus on teachers, care sector and NHS and says Jackdaw decision ‘a serious misstep’Matthew TaylorFri 30 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leader of the UK’s biggest trade union has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas.Andrea Egan, the general secretary ofUnison, said too often public sector workers were treated as an “afterthought” by the government compared with the “massive political focus” on protecting jobs in the North Sea.“There’s no question it is vital for oil and gas workers to be guaranteed secure, well-paid jobs in the industries of the future,” Egan said. “But public service workers, in contrast, often seem like an afterthought for ministers. What about the thousands of jobs cut in recent years across local government, the NHS and education? Care workers, nurses, teaching assistants.”North Sea oil and gas has been in the headlines again in recent weeks after the government gave thego ahead to the Jackdaw gasfieldfollowing huge pressure from the fossil fuel industry and rightwing politicians – in the UK and abroad.Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaignersRead moreThe decision causedanger among climate campaigners and scientists, as well as many Labour supporters, who argue that extracting more fossil fuels will further escalate the crisis and do nothing to reduce bills, significantly improve energy security or halt the long-term decline in jobs in the sector. A final government decision on themore controversial Rosebankoilfield is expected before the end of the year.After Wednesday’s budget, which factored in the project’s approval in its forecast, the Guardianrevealedsome Labour MPs were lobbying Andy Burnham and John Healey not to overrule the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, if she decided to block Rosebank.Egan said approving Jackdaw was “a serious misstep from the government” and sent the wrong signal about the UK’s climate commitments. She said ministers should instead focus on creating secure, well-paid jobs in the renewable sector for oil and gas workers and give similar support to the millions of employees in the public sector, which has also been hit by severe cuts in recent years.“It’s time for the government to get its priorities straight: invest in clean energy, invest in the public services that communities rely on – to the benefit of us all.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cutsRead moreThere is a split among the UK’s main trade unions on allowing fossil fuel companies to drill in the North Sea. Unite and GMB, which represent many oil and gas workers, back more licences, while Unison and the National Education Union oppose more drilling as part of a wider drive to create long term sustainable jobs and tackle the climate crisis.One concern among unions is that jobs in the rapidly growing renewables sector are often not unionised and therefore not as secure or well paid as in those in the oil and gas sector.However, last week Unison announced a new recognition deal with the UK’s largest energy company,Octopus Energy, known as a progressive organisation with a focus on renewable energy.The GMB unionhad been attempting to gain recognition at Octopusbut the company said Unison “stood out for its commitment to the energy transition”.Egan said it was an important step to securing good, secure jobs in the renewable sector. “Unison is proud to be leading the way as the clean energy union. We urgently need more well-paid, unionised jobs and to transition away from fossil fuels at pace. This agreement is a step in the right direction on both counts.”Explore more on these topicsTrade unionsClimate crisisUnisonGreen jobsFossil fuelsRenewable energyGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christa Pike makes first public comments since failed execution: ‘There is pain in my mind and in my soul’ | Christa Pike | The Guardian
description: Pike is facing death penalty for 1995 murder of classmate, despite surviving a botched execution last month
Author: Ed Pilkington
Headline: Pike is facing death penalty for 1995 murder of classmate, despite surviving a botched execution last month
Content: Christa Pike enters a Knox county criminal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on 4 December 2007.Photograph: J Miles Cary/ReutersView image in fullscreenChrista Pike enters a Knox county criminal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on 4 December 2007.Photograph: J Miles Cary/ReutersChrista PikeChrista Pike makes first public comments since failed execution: ‘There is pain in my mind and in my soul’Pike is facing death penalty for 1995 murder of classmate, despite surviving a botched execution last monthEd PilkingtonFri 30 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChrista Pike has marked a month since her failed execution by Tennessee and released a statement in which she laments the “incompetence” that has led to this moment, adding that despite ongoing healing she remains in constant physical pain and mental anguish.In comments released by her legal team on Friday, the prisoner said that there had not been a moment since she was injected with a massive dose of the sedative pentobarbital that she had not been in pain. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” she said.Though she does not mention the state authorities who tried to kill her a month ago by injecting a full 5g of pentobarbital into her arms, she does make a pointed criticism clearly targeted at them. “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” she said.Pike was strapped to a gurney in the Tennessee execution chamber on 30 September, facing death for the 1995 murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. Members of the execution team spent almost an hour trying to establish an intravenous line through which to pump the sedative, but the procedure was botched and theprisoner survived.Medical expertstold the Guardianthey were shocked by the apparent level of incompetence displayed in the execution chamber, after a blow-by-blow account of events was released by Pike’s lawyer, who was present in the room.Pike is being held in the infirmary at the Debra Johnson rehabilitation center in Nashville, where she was returned after 10 days of intensive hospital treatment. She is being kept largely in solitary confinement, she said, “away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me”.Such isolation was its own form of pain, she said, given that she spent the first 28 years on death row in solitary confinement.The events of 30 September have roiled Tennessee and sent shock waves across the US. The Republican governor of the state, Bill Lee, hasordered a pauseon further executions until an outside review is conducted.It is not clear what Tennessee intends to do with Pike. Earlier this week,Lee said he expectedher death sentence to remain the same unless the courts determine otherwise.Pike, dictating her statement to her lawyers, said that she had been prepared to die that night. “I had made my peace.”Since she awoke, “alone in a hospital confused and in pain”, she has been searching for meaning about what happened to her. “I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”She said in her slow road to recovery she drew sustenance from the “extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is humbling.”She thanked the first responders, doctors and nurses who cared for her in hospital, as well as her attorneys and those who “fought for me, stood beside me and refused to give up on me”.She added: “I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone.”Explore more on these topicsChrista PikeTennesseeUS crimeCapital punishmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Democratic lawmakers demand ICE data on detainee miscarriages | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Demand comes after Guardian investigation found ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: Demand comes after Guardian investigation found ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026
Content: Joyce Beatty, Brittany Pettersen, and Robin Kelly are asking ICE to explain what, if any, steps are being taken to recover the missing data.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoyce Beatty, Brittany Pettersen, and Robin Kelly are asking ICE to explain what, if any, steps are being taken to recover the missing data.Composite: Getty ImagesICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Democratic lawmakers demand ICE data on detainee miscarriagesDemand comes after Guardian investigation found ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026Maanvi SinghFri 30 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS lawmakers are urgently demanding thatImmigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)disclose how many pregnant immigrants have experienced miscarriages, stillbirths and pregnancy-related hospitalizations while in the its custody, after the agency admitted it lost count last year.US representatives sent the request followinga recent Guardian investigationrevealing that theTrump administrationis detaining a record number of pregnant women and teens, and at the same has lost track of how many suffered miscarriages.Revealed: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant womenRead moreIn a letter sent this month to ICE’s acting director, David Venturella, Democratic representatives Brittany Pettersen, Joyce Beatty and Robin Kelly also asked the immigration enforcement agency to explain what – if any – steps have been taken to recover any missing data about these cases.Government documents obtained by the Guardian found that ICE had placed more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year. The agency recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents found, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.Detained pregnant women said that they were struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. Medical experts told the Guardian that lapses in care both during pregnancy and during and after miscarriage could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies.In their letter, the representatives also cite a 2021 directive instructing ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist” – and ask the agency to clarify on what grounds it is detaining pregnant immigrants. The directive also requires ICE to closely monitor and document the health of all pregnant people in its custody, and continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained.“ICE’s inability to follow agency directives, provide adequate medical care and maintain accurate records of pregnancy-related medical outcomes is unacceptable,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter, which was cosigned by 64 other representatives.In an interview, Pettersen said it was “deeply concerning” that ICE had failed to account for a full year of pregnancy outcomes. “I’m just devastated for the people who have gone through this, who’ve lost pregnancies unnecessarily, who have been left without the medical care that they need after miscarrying,” she said. “It’s hard to imagine how we are ever going to right these wrongs.”In internal agency documents, ICE said it had no data on miscarriages because the agency changed medical billing providers in October. The agency’s medical claims processing has been delayed for months. Immigration attorneys and former government officials told said it was odd, but plausible, that ICE was keeping track of miscarriages solely via its medical billing provider.In response to follow-up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in the ICE internal documents – the agency does not have data on miscarriages between October 2025 through June 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe DHS did not confirm to the Guardian whether it had received the letter from Congress members. “Claims that any pregnant detainees are receiving subprime care are FALSE,” an agency spokesperson said.In their letter, lawmakers asked ICE’s acting director to detail when “ICE leadership first became aware of concerns regarding miscarriage reporting and deficiencies in agency tracking systems”. They gave the agency until 6 November to respond.Prior to the Guardian’s reporting, the agency had never acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data.The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention, and the health outcomes for this population.Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)DemocratsMiscarriageUS immigrationWomen's healthHouse of RepresentativesUS CongressnewsShareReuse this content

title: Basketweavers get in a twist over Alexander Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband | Movies | The Guardian
description: Why is he not made of willow? Why is he plaited and not woven? World’s basket makers have plenty of questions
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Why is he not made of willow? Why is he plaited and not woven? World’s basket makers have plenty of questions
Content: Alexander Skarsgård next to his ‘wicker’ alter ego at the premiere of Wicker in Los Angeles.Photograph: Jim Ruymen/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAlexander Skarsgård next to his ‘wicker’ alter ego at the premiere of Wicker in Los Angeles.Photograph: Jim Ruymen/UPI/ShutterstockMoviesBasketweavers get in a twist over Alexander Skarsgård’s Wicker HusbandWhy is he not made of willow? Why is he plaited and not woven? World’s basket makers have plenty of questionsChloe Mac DonnellFri 30 Oct 2026 08.24 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHollywood heart-throbs are known for their good looks and charisma. But in a classic plot twist, the latest big-screen dreamboat causing viewers to get hot and bothered isn’t even human.Alexander Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband character inthe romcom Wickerhas sent the internet into a frenzy.“Never looking at my patio furniture the same again,” says one Instagram comment. Ikea captioned a picture of its wicker furniture with the term “husband material”.The basketweaving community, however, is getting worked up for very different reasons. The fact the Wicker Husband isn’t made of willow, and he appears to be plaited rather than woven, has angered some makers.View image in fullscreenAlexander Skarsgård as the Wicker Husband and Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman.Photograph: Black Bear/PADeborah Needleman, former editor of the New York Times’s T magazine turned basket maker, was one of the first to question it. Writing onInstagram, she said: “I’m excited that the basketweaving community now has our own hot, woven leading man, but I’ve also got issues. Why is a dude woven in an English fishing village not made of willow – or even rush?!” More than 100 fellow basket makers have since weighed in.The Oxford English dictionary defines wicker as “thin sticks of wood twisted together to make baskets, furniture etc”.Eleanor Morgan, trade adviser to the Worshipful Company of Basketmakers in London, says that while willow has commonly been used to denote wicker, it is less popular today. “Historically wicker could have meant any pliant twig or osier,” she says.Joe Dunckley, a prosthetic designer at Wētā workshop, the special effects studio in New Zealand that created the upper body of the Wicker Husband, says it was a “big challenge” to create a costume for a character that is sentient but made of wicker. “Most prosthetic materials are soft to mimic skin. But he’s not flesh and bone.”To get the wicker effect, Dunckley and his team of 80 specialists created 50 interlocking body pieces for Skarsgård to wear. Using a rubber-like thermoplastic elastomer, they were able to 3D print a bespoke weave coded by the studio that was then attached to a spandex suit.
