During the 18-month process they also created 10 facial appliances.View image in fullscreenAn artisan creates a limb of the Wicker Husband at the Wētā workshop in New Zealand.Photograph: PR HandoutDunckley says willow wasn’t a viable option for what they needed the suit to be able to do. “It is a similar reason to why, in film, we don’t make armour out of actual steel or use real swords. This is a fantasy film.”Lewis Prosser, a basket maker from Cardiff, says every maker is thinking about how they would have approached the task. “It certainly isn’t the way I would have done it, but that doesn’t mean that it is bad,” he says.Prosser says his understanding of wicker is that it is “an object that is woven but one that is specifically not textile”, adding that “some will disagree with me”. Some basket makers, including Needleman, argue that wicker refers to a type of weave rather than a material.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor Prosser, who creates wicker costumes using techniques traditionally found in Wales and the south-west of England, there are three main ways to make a basket. Coiling, where threads of plant materials are wound together in a spiral, braiding, or stake and stand basketry whereby vertical rods are woven through horizontal strands. “What we would traditionally call ‘wicker items’ would usually have that latter aspect,” Prosser says. The Wicker Husband does not.Although the actor Olivia Colman and her fellow villagers in the film speak in a range of British dialects, the film is not set in England. Dunckley suggests the basket maker character played by Peter Dinklage has travelled the world, learning skills from other makers.View image in fullscreenLead weaver Jasmin van Lith at the Wētā workshop.Photograph: PR HandoutProsser says that if the film had been set in a specific location, it would be more authentic for the costume to reflect the plants that grow there. In the UK, willow would be apt, whereas in Spain, Esparto grass would be fitting.Dunckley and his team worked using a 3D cast of Skarsgård to ensure the “audience would be able to recognise Alexander in basket form”. Key to this is what Dunckley calls the “Skarsgård smoulder”, which they captured by ensuring the weave could furrow at the brow. His hair, beard and lashes were made from muka, fibres from New Zealand flax.Describing the interest and criticism from the weaving community as “really cool”, Dunckley says: “I don’t blame anyone. True artists of the craft have dedicated years to it. I would expect them to look at a fantasy version of their art form and see failings in it.”For the willow purists, Morgan says “there is no lack of osier-related eye candy” in the film, pointing to a plethora of basket scenes. Prosser says he is thrilled the film has drawn attention to basket making, especially as someskills and traditional techniques are now endangered. TikTok is rife with wicker costume making guides, including nipple tutorials which Skarsgård has said was the “best part” of his suit. He gave his own pair to theTV host Graham Nortondescribing them as “extraordinary craftsmanship”.Explore more on these topicsFilmCraftAlexander SkarsgårdTextile artVisual effects (VFX)newsShareReuse this content

title: FBI arrests North Carolina man for allegedly posting classified information on social media | North Carolina | The Guardian
description: Authorities say army contractor James Thomas Ashbacher shared top-secret data online and stole night-vision goggles
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Authorities say army contractor James Thomas Ashbacher shared top-secret data online and stole night-vision goggles
Content: James Thomas Ashbacher was a government contractor working at Fort Bragg.Photograph: Chris Seward/APView image in fullscreenJames Thomas Ashbacher was a government contractor working at Fort Bragg.Photograph: Chris Seward/APNorth CarolinaFBI arrests North Carolina man for allegedly posting classified information on social mediaAuthorities say army contractor James Thomas Ashbacher shared top-secret data online and stole night-vision gogglesMarina DunbarFri 30 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheFBIhas arrested a formerNorth Carolinagovernment contractor for allegedly leaking classified national defense information on social media.James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, was taken into custody after charges that he shared top-secret safety data online, unlawfully stored national defense materials at his residence and stole night-vision equipment from the US army special operations command.He faces federal counts of unauthorized transmission of national defense information, unlawful retention of defense records and theft of government property, prosecutors said.Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing womanRead moreAccording to apress releasefrom the justice department, Ashbacher “photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site.”The statement further alleges that, in a private direct message, Ashbacher had urged a social media user to take down several uploaded materials, explaining that he was “trying to do some damage control”.Federal agents conducting a subsequent search of his home discovered a classified military award nomination containing sensitive national defense information – as well as a specialized night-vision goggle system that had previously been reported missing from an army special operations command unit.Ashbacher worked for a contractor providing security and emergency management services to the US army at North Carolina’s Fort Bragg, where he held a top secret clearance with sensitive compartmented information (SCI) access.His arrest came nearly two years after a federal judgesentenceda Massachusetts air national guard member to 15 years in prison in connection with his pleading guilty to leaking highly classified military documents about Russia’s war in Ukraine.Jack Teixeira admitted that he illegally collected those secrets and shared them with other users on the social media platform Discord.Ashbacher’s case is being investigated by theFBICharlotte’s field office in coordination with the US Department of the Army’s criminal investigation division.Explore more on these topicsNorth CarolinaFBIUS militaryUS crimeShareReuse this content

title: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports | Technology | The Guardian
description: Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough
Content: Futures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on 30 October 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenFutures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on 30 October 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersTechnologyTech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reportsBig tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enoughBlake Montgomeryand agenciesFri 30 Oct 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies droveUS marketsdown by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged theNasdaqcomposite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq ⁠100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough.The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. ⁠The index has fallen ⁠more than 5.8% so far in ​October as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms,Alphabetand Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure.Intel tumbled nearly 30% and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell far short of analysts’ expectations.Amazon fell 1.8% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. The company also disclosed that it had spent more this year than anticipated.A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12%, wiping $500bn from its market capitalization, to its worst day on record after telling investors that it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring because of similar, mammoth investments in AI.Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make AI investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI datacenters have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.A drop of 3.1% forNvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward.Such losses overshadowed an otherwise mixed day for the rest of Wall Street, with the S&P 500 roughly evenly split between gainers and losers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExpectations are high broadly for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)Datacenters – USStock marketsUS marketsNasdaqMarket turmoilnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK house prices grow at slowest pace in two years as mortgage rates rise | Housing market | The Guardian
description: Average price for property stands at £273,566 in October, flat on previous month, says Nationwide
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Average price for property stands at £273,566 in October, flat on previous month, says Nationwide
Content: Nationwide says property prices are likely to fall further, with surveyors reporting that new buyer inquiries remain weak.Photograph: scenicireland.com/Christopher Hill Photographic/AlamyView image in fullscreenNationwide says property prices are likely to fall further, with surveyors reporting that new buyer inquiries remain weak.Photograph: scenicireland.com/Christopher Hill Photographic/AlamyHousing marketUK house prices grow at slowest pace in two years as mortgage rates riseAverage price for property stands at £273,566 in October, flat on previous month, says NationwideBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaFri 30 Oct 2026 05.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK house prices grew by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two years, as higher mortgage rates put off potential buyers.The average price for a property in the UK stood at £273,566 in October, flat on the previous month and down from 0.8% in the year to September, according to the lenderNationwide.The slowdown in the market comes as buyers face higher borrowing costs. This month the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hit the 6% barrierfor the first time in three years.What you need to know about Your First Home scheme for first-time buyersRead moreThe average stood at 5.99% on Thursday, according to the financial information provider Moneyfacts, while the average two-year rate was not far behind at 5.97%.There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week the monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.Robert Gardner, the chief economist at Nationwide, said the Middle East conflict had fed concerns around inflation, driving up expectations of higher interest rates.Property prices are likely to fall further, he said. “Surveyors report that new buyer inquiries remain weak.“Consumer sentiment dipped noticeably in October, with households becoming less confident about the outlook for the general economy as well as their own financial situation in the year ahead.”Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, added that the impact of rising mortgage costs “eclipses any support measure announced in this week’s budget”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis week the chancellor, John Healey, confirmed the government’s new £4.7bnYour First Homescheme, which is designed to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have access to the “bank of mum and dad”.Bill added: “The absence of major shocks from the chancellor may produce a modest relief bounce in coming months. However, asking prices will need to reflect the much tougher financial landscape that buyers face.”Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said the government’s new scheme could provide a “modest boost” to the market but that prices were likely to remain subdued next year.Explore more on these topicsHousing marketHouse pricesPropertyReal estateNationwideBanks and building societiesMortgagesnewsShareReuse this content

title: BP profits hit ‘obscene’ 18-year high as Iran war drives up oil refining margins | BP | The Guardian
description: Oil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Oil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’
Content: ‘We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market,’ said BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market,’ said BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersBPBP profits hit ‘obscene’ 18-year high as Iran war drives up oil refining marginsOil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’Jillian Ambrose,Damien GayleandLauren AlmeidaFri 30 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 04.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBP’s quarterly profits have been labelled “obscene” after they hit an 18-year high of $8.46bn (£6.3bn), as the war in the Middle East drove up oil and gas prices.The energy company hailed a “banner quarter” on Friday, with its underlying ​replacement ⁠cost profit – a key measure of its income – almost quadrupling in the three months to the end of September, from $2.2bn in the same period ​a year ​ago. The jump meant BP’s quarterly profits hit their highest levelsince the $8.9bn recorded in 2008.BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told Bloomberg TV: “It really was a banner quarter for the refining business. We had very strong margins from the BP-operated refineries, we also had very strong underlying performance. We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market.”However, climate crisis campaigners said it was outrageous that BP was profiting so handsomely on commodities causing serious damage to the environment.It is just over a week until diplomats will meet in Antalya, Turkey, for the Cop31 UN climate summit. Recent climate-linked disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal will be at the forefront of many delegates’ minds. There are likely to be tensions with fossil fuel producing countries, which have sought to stymie calls for a transition to clean energy.BP’s strong results also come as motorists in the UK face high fuel prices, with diesel now at 198.79p a litre, according to estimates from the RAC. The cost of petrol has also risen, with an average price of 172.92p a litre, compared with 132.83p in late February, before the latest conflict in the Middle East began.Jonathan Noronha-Gant, of the campaign group Global Witness, said it was “obscene that polluters are continuing to cash in on the fallout of the war in Iran, making more bumper profits from spiralling oil prices while innocent civilians suffer.“These massive profits come as ordinary people across Europe are struggling with the rising cost of living, with many struggling to afford to heat their homes as winter arrives,” he said.Danny Gross, of Friends of the Earth, said: “As millions of households brace themselves for a cold winter, huddling under blankets and clutching hot-water bottles as they struggle to pay their bills, BP is raking in huge profits while doubling down on gas and oil production and slashing investment in renewables.”Although the link between fossil fuels and climate breakdown has been known for decades, scientists directly linked carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel companies to dozens of deadly heatwavesfor the first time a year ago. Yet more heatwaves swept across Europe this summer, with separate research suggesting theyled to a record 50,000 excess deaths.As people in cities sweltered, infernos tore through forests and brush in parched rural areas.France experienced its largest area burned on recordand fires blazed in usually cooler regions, such as the Cairngorms in Scotland.In the Pacific, a superchargedEl Niñois brewing, with water temperatures reaching more than 3C higher than usual. The weather phenomenon is likely to be the most extreme of its kind in at least 1,000 years, dumping vast amounts of extra heat into an atmosphere already warmed by climate breakdown.“The climate crisis is not an abstract future threat,” said Clémence Dubois, head of global campaigns at350.org. “People are facing deadly heat, destroyed livelihoods and growing insecurity now. Governments are being forced to find money to protect their populations, while fossil fuel companies are forecast to make extraordinary profits.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRecord oil company profits come as the UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is weighing up whether to allow drilling in the North Sea’sRosebankoilfield, after approving a licence for the less controversialJackdawgasfield earlier in October.BP’s quarterly earnings were bolstered by higher profits from the oil refining business as the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined fuels such as diesel and gasoline soared, earning almost $47 for each barrel produced.Although global oil prices have remained below the peaks recorded during the 2022 energy crisis, the pump prices for fuels, including diesel, have risen to all-time highs across the UK, Europe and the US in recent months because of severe disruptions to refineries in the Gulf region and across Russia.BP’s earnings windfall announcement came after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergiesreported their strongest profits since 2022, also thanks in large part to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel.BP earnings windfall announcement came after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergiesreported their strongest profits since 2022, also thanks in large part to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel.Explore more on these topicsBPOil and gas companiesEnergy industryOilCommoditiesGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie Wicker | Movies | The Guardian
description: She plays a depressed fisherwoman. He plays a man made of wicker who is solely dedicated to her pleasure. How did the actors feel about this strange, emotional connection – and what did Colman draw from her own marriage?
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: She plays a depressed fisherwoman. He plays a man made of wicker who is solely dedicated to her pleasure. How did the actors feel about this strange, emotional connection – and what did Colman draw from her own marriage?
Content: The look of love … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard in Wicker.Photograph: Courtesy of Black BearView image in fullscreenThe look of love … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard in Wicker.Photograph: Courtesy of Black BearMoviesInterview‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie WickerRyan GilbeyShe plays a depressed fisherwoman. He plays a man made of wicker who is solely dedicated to her pleasure. How did the actors feel about this strange, emotional connection – and what did Colman draw from her own marriage?Fri 30 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 05.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnother year, another raunchy comedy-drama in which Alexander Skarsgård is the answer to a social outcast’s erotic dreams. “I fucking lovedPillionso much!” says Olivia Colman, reliably sweary straight out of the gate, as she brings up last year’s British indie hit starring Skarsgård as a leather-clad dom with a timid traffic warden as his submissive. “And when they kissed at the end …Aww.” The 52-year-old Oscar-winner for The Favourite gives a mock-sniffle and a little shake of her frizzy grey locks, then pretends to dab her eyes.Seated beside her in a London hotel room and wearing a bright orange “I’m With Stupid” T-shirt, Skarsgård tilts his head appreciatively. In Pillion, it was Harry Melling who had the privilege of being ravaged by the 50-year-old Swedish actor. Now it is Colman’s turn in Wicker, an earthy adult fairytale filmed in Budapest and set in a medieval village populated almost exclusively by British comic actors who converse in language both archaically formal (“Happy to transact with you”) and bluntly colloquial (“I’d better fuck off”). Among them is Phil Daniels as a leering butcher and Richard E Grant as a doctor who is even more inept at his job than Grant was as a Celebrity Traitor.View image in fullscreenMan behind the mask … Colman and Skårsgard on set.Photograph: Courtesy of Black BearColman plays the Fisherwoman, ridiculed by the other villagers for her pong and her general absence of allure. In the spirit of mocking the dominant patriarchal conventions, where men put metal collars on their wives when they get married, she asks the Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) to fashion her a husband. A month later, she has a groom made entirely of wicker and dedicated solely to her pleasure and happiness. If the movie works, says Alex Huston Fischer, who wrote and directed Wicker with his wife, Eleanor Wilson, “you are essentially connecting emotionally to a basket”.This is where Skarsgård comes in. His performance as the Wicker Husband was augmented by Weta Workshop, the New Zealand special-effects outfit behind the Lord of the Rings series. “I had a full bodysuit, a mask glued to my face, then added prosthetics for lips and eyelashes,” the actor says. “Oh, and hair made from flax. Highly flammable.” He tried out different accents but that felt “too removed from myself, what with the mask and everything else”. Colman gives an amused snort: “Might as well have got someone else in,” she says. Her co-star responds by puffing out his chest: “Hey, people pay big bucks to see Alexander Skarsgård on screen!”In truth, he is humbler than all that. “Alex gets very awkward with compliments,” says Colman, then turns to him: “Well,tough. I don’t think there are many people who could have got quite so much across while acting within such restrictions. It’s a mark of how good you are. Sorry!” Is it fair to call his performance minimalist? “From my point of view, it was maximalist,” he says. “Because of the mask, I had to exaggerate everything and it felt like I was being hammy. Subtleties wouldn’t register. Underneath that beautifully crafted suit, I was like: ‘Aaah!’, ‘Grrr!’” His guttural sounds are accompanied by facial expressions which suggest a beginner’s guide to semaphore acting.View image in fullscreenElizabeth Debicki as the ‘spiteful Emma’ and Colman in Wicker.Photograph: Courtesy of Black BearSkarsgård’s performance and the cross-hatched weave effect are magically textured. The impact of the creaking sound design should not be underestimated either, especially once the newlyweds get down to conjugal business. As one Letterboxd user put it: “Whoever chose the erection sound effect … you’re a genius and I love you.”It turns out I’m not the only one amused by Wicker’s Letterboxd reviews. “As a director, you should never read the comments,” says Fischer. “But these ones are so entertaining.” Users have offered alternative titles (John Wicker, The Shape of Wicker, Fifty Shades of Hay), double entendres (“All my eggs are going in his basket”) and the witty suggestion that Etsy could become the new Hinge. One astute comment likened Elizabeth Debicki’s character, a jealous neighbour who tries to sabotage the Fisherwoman’s happiness, to the spiteful Emma, played by Mercedes McCambridge, in the classic western Johnny Guitar.In any discussion of Wicker, the word “horny” is never far away. “We even included it when we pitched the movie,” says Fischer. “There’s something so human about it,” says Wilson. “We are these fleshy bodies with desires that are embarrassing and messy. It seemed like a great place for comedy.” Fischer notes that Colman’s goggle-eyed reactions were vital: “For someone to be surprised by incredible sex is very funny to us. Especially when it’s Olivia. She’s so good.”View image in fullscreenBasket case … Peter Dinklage in Wicker.Colman returns the compliment. “You get sent a lot of scripts that you feel you’ve seen before. But when I read this, I was like an octopus. I changed colour and went: ‘Oooh!’” A deft impression of a cephalopod follows, arms undulating. The Fisherwoman is the only female character with her own name, Colman points out, rather than being known as, say, The Bakerwoman or The Innkeeper’s Wife. “And she’s the only woman with agency. She’s perfectly happy with her life. It’s when pushed that she says, ‘I’m going to fuck this up and make a mockery of your beloved convention of marriage.’ Then she gets this kind, beautiful creature, and suddenly the world is even more joyous.”Wicker is based on Ursula Wills’ short story The Wicker Husband, which has already been adapted as a stage musical combining actors and puppetry.Reviewing that version in 2020, the Guardian theatre critic Arifa Akbar saw it as a story about “insider parochialism, the demonising of outsiders and the tyranny of conformity” with “echoes of Brexit Britain”. All pertinent, the directors agree now. “Those things were in our heads when we were writing,” says Fischer. “Elizabeth’s character is trying to protect herself and the village from what she sees as this foreign element that is there to destroy them.”Dev Patel was originally set to play Colman’s basket-case beau until a scheduling clash forced him to pull out. Never having quite shed his Slumdog Millionaire innocence, Patel seems a more natural choice for the part than Skarsgård, who even prior to Pillion was drawn to stone-cold alphas: a tech bro (Succession), a violent husband (Big Little Lies), a coke-snorting cop (War on Everyone). Even he admits that he is cast against type in Wicker. “I tend to play characters who are messed up or internally conflicted. That duality is something I’ve done a lot and still enjoy. That wasn’t there for this character: he has a purity to him that was different to what I’ve done in the past. It was about making him relatable and interesting without that inner struggle. So that was a bit of a departure, and slightly intimidating.” Wilson argues, though, that Skarsgård has “qualities that are very Wicker Husband: he has a stoicism, and such presence. We needed that. It’s the sweetness that is the big surprise.”The Fisherwoman’s newfound fulfilment and her husband’s inherent goodness eventually have a destabilising effect on the other villagers, who realise how impoverished their own lives are by comparison. Trouble follows. Had the honeymoon period between the couple continued, however, would it not have got irritating eventually? Don’t relationships need a little creative friction to remain interesting? “Oh, I don’t know,” says Colman, thoroughly unconvinced. “I quite like a friction-free life. I don’t think I’d cope with a fighty relationship. I prefer to work things out gently.”View image in fullscreenRichard E Grant as the inept town doctor in Wicker.Photograph: Courtesy of Black BearHer thoughts turn to her own marriage to writer and producer Ed Sinclair, with whom she has three children. “We’ve been together for 32 years and married for 25,” she says. They have also worked together several times, including on Wicker, which they co-produced. While their domestic life is harmonious, there have nevertheless been “moments with the odd little look” in a professional context. She gives an example of one such look. The narrowed eyes, the abrupt withdrawal of warmth: no one would want to be on the receiving end of that. All the cosy Olivia Colman-ness has drained away in an instant.“But we’ve never had big fights,” she says, back in chirpy mode again. “Very early on, when we first started working together, there was a suggestion from him of an acting note.” Hearing this, Skarsgård lets out a wicked laugh, instantly spotting a taboo. “Strong side eye,” he says. She continues: “Or sometimes when I’ve needed to do a taped audition, I’d say: ‘Can you tape this for me?’ And he’d ask, ‘Have you thought of trying it like this … ?’” There’s that look again. “Then he’d say, ‘OK, point taken!’”Where does she think Wicker ends up vis-a-vis marriage? “I’d say it’s pro equal relationships. It’s perfectly possible to do it nicely. If you’re planning to share your life with someone, be considerate. Ask yourself: Have I been a good partner this week?” She draws a tick in the air with her finger. “Check!”Wicker is out now in the US, on 30 October in the UK and 5 November in Australia.Explore more on these topicsFilmOlivia ColmanScience fiction and fantasy filmsRomance filmsComedy filmsFilm adaptationsComedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror movies | Movies | The Guardian
description: For Halloween, Guardian writers have picked the most efficiently terrifying films outside of the horror genre from How to Have Sex to The Hunchback of Notre Dame
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: For Halloween, Guardian writers have picked the most efficiently terrifying films outside of the horror genre from How to Have Sex to The Hunchback of Notre Dame
Content: Mia McKenna-Bruce in How to Have Sex.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenMia McKenna-Bruce in How to Have Sex.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMovies‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror moviesFor Halloween, Guardian writers have picked the most efficiently terrifying films outside of the horror genre from How to Have Sex to The Hunchback of Notre DameMinor spoilers aheadRadheyan Simonpillai,Morgan Jerkins,Alaina Demopoulos,Veronica Esposito,Andrew Lawrence,Juan A Ramírez,Jesse Hassenger,Shrai Popat,Rafaela Bassili,Benjamin Lee,Adrian HortonandAndrew PulverFri 30 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBurningView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pine House Film/AllstarHiding in plain sight throughout Lee Chang-dong’s deliciously enigmatic Burning, in which a spirited young woman (Jeon Jong-seo) disappears, and a wealthy playboy (Steven Yeun) gives serial killer vibes, is a disaffected male rage. That’s perhaps the most commonplace horror of our times, whether on the internet or politics, and you feel the tremors of it steadily breaking the surface in Yoo Ah-in’s performance. He plays Jong-su, an aspiring writer, quietly frustrated with his lot in life. Jong-su works odd jobs and tends to his incarcerated father’s dilapidated farm, growing more desperate to grasp some sense of control over the world around him, which is where the scary part comes in. Lee is the master dramatist who with Burning tilts violently into thriller territory, navigating elements from Taxi Driver, The Vanishing and Michael Haneke’s Caché, using the language of horror movies to conjure up a creeping anxiety and dread that erupts into pure existential fear.Radheyan Simonpillai‘Extreme heebie-jeebies’: writers on their scariest movies of all timeRead moreBurning is available to watch on Mubi and Tubi in the US, to rent digitally in the UK, and on Netflix in AustraliaThe Hunchback of Notre DameView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Walt DisneyThe scariest non-horror movie for me is Disney’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame. The scene where Quasimodo is bound to a pillory where the townspeople throw food and jeer at him because of his appearance and disability will for ever be seared into my brain since I first watched it as a six-year-old child. To this day, I still believe that I was far too young to witness that particular depth of human cruelty even though it’s very real. Not to mention that the story deals with xenophobia and bigotry towards the Romany people and sexual predation from a religious leader that takes the basic idea of good versus evil to a whole new level. The Hunchback of Notre Dame reminds me that you don’t need jumpscares and gore to frighten someone. Sometimes, the real monsters are human beings with a bit of social standing over someone else due to money, beauty, authority or all of the above.Morgan JerkinsThe Hunchback of Notre Dame is available on Disney+The SniperView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyAn insane loner motivated by his all-consuming misogyny perches beside his bedroom window, methodically shooting women on the street below. He writes of his compulsion to kill in a series of letters to police and begs the authorities to hurry up and catch him. This grimly prescient noir from 1952 feels all too familiar for modern viewers who are numb to stories of gun violence and incel culture. It’s a disturbingly acute portrait of urban alienation and the destructive nature of obsession, released more than two decades before Taxi Driver epitomized those themes. Equally haunting is The Sniper’s backstory. Director Edward Dmytryk was one of the blacklisted Hollywood Ten who refused to testify in front of the House Un-American Activities Committee. He later reversed course after a six-month prison sentence, ghoulishly ratting on his contemporaries and ending countless careers.Alaina DemopoulosThe Sniper is available on YouTube in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and Australia2001: A Space OdysseyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mgm/Stanley Kubrick Productions/Kobal/ShutterstockIn Stanley Kubrick’s magisterial 2001, human creativity is such a mysterious and foreboding thing that it isn’t even couched as of this world – rather, an eerie alien monolith gives it to the primates who later evolve to be human beings. The film will for ever be remembered for its visionary jump cut from a bone spinning in slow motion – tossed triumphantly into the air by a primate in a fit of conquering rage – to an orbiting space satellite carrying nuclear weapons: in one deft motion Kubrick encapsulates the history of creativity as a carrier of our liberation, but also our destructive potential. From there, what unfolds is a carefully choreographed dance of death between humanity’s ability to responsibly discharge its ever-growing technological powers and the devices that become more and more dangerous to our survival as a species. Although Kubrick ends the movie on a note of hope and transcendence, what sticks with me more is the existential terror that one of our greatest strengths as beings will ultimately lead to our collapse. In an age of extremes where we are regularly reminded of the many technologically fueled threats to global civilization, it’s hard not to feel that fear. In 2001, astronaut-protagonist Dave Bowman manages to save himself – and thus take the next leap in human evolution – by simply disconnecting the runaway AI known as HAL 9000, but in our world we’ve already passed the point where that would have been possible.Veronica EspositoHidden horrors: our writers on the scariest movies you (probably) haven’t seenRead more2001: A Space Odyssey is available on HBO MaxHoward the DuckView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Cinetext/Universal/AllstarThere’s so much I loved about growing up in the 80s: the funny pages, the power ballads, going for a drive, malls of genuine value – entertainment and otherwise. But one thing I didnotlove and still don’t was the era’s obsession with animatronic realism, of stuffed animals come disturbingly to life. And by far the worst offender was Howard the Duck. Here was a human adult-sized mallard foisted from his alien nest on to the unwitting citizens of Cleveland, Ohio, looking for all the world like a Donald Duck mascot who had fallen into a vat of primordial ooze (with those golf ball eyes screamingHelp!).That Howard also happens to be a martial arts-wielding feminist with an appreciation for hair bands never endeared him to me more than the Dark Overlord who’s also summoned from deep space to … fuck with him? With us? (His true goals still remain somewhat unclear.) My nine-year-old mind was not prepared to see him in bed with Lea Thompson, and rarely does aHalloweengo by when some part of me isn’t bracing for a surprise reunion with this quack at a backwoods haunted house. You simply cannot release a movie like this two years after Child’s Play and expect people not to mistake it for a horror. I wonder if the comics company that spawned this duck ever recovered …Andrew LawrenceHoward the Duck is available to rent digitally in the US, on YouTube in the UK and to rent digitally in AustraliaHow to Have SexView image in fullscreenPhotograph: MUBIRemember the backseat scene in Bo Burnham’s excellent Eighth Grade, where a horny teen tries to seduce its young lead through a coercive game of truth or dare until her guilelessness catches up to his intentions? How to Have Sex is that unbearable, all-too-recognizable dread blown up to 91 minutes. In an extraordinary breakout performance, Mia McKenna-Bruce plays a 16-year-old on holiday in Greece with two more developed girlfriends. As they flirt with boys and party endlessly, she realizes that keeping up with a shot count might not equal sexual maturity. What’s brilliant about writer-director Molly Manning Walker’s debut is that the worst rarely ever happens: the girls can stumble home down a dark alley and make it back all right, but the threat of the worst-case scenario suffuses every single frame. It’s a queasy, unforgettable viewing experience, activating both parental and innocent impulses as we hope for the best for McKenna-Bruce’s fully realized heroine.Juan A RamirezHow to Have Sex is available on Netflix and Mubi in the US, on Mubi in the UK and on SBS on Demand in Australia8mmView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Columbia Pictures/Sportsphoto/AllstarThe horror movie my friends and I were supposed to see that day was The Rage: Carrie 2, a little-seen sequel to the 1976 masterpiece. We did see it – I’d even call it mildly underrated! – and it was indeed a horror film, albeit not the scariest one. But the movie that sent us off into the night so rattled that my buddy briefly drove down the wrong direction of a one-way street was what we casually ducked into afterward: 8mm, a thriller starringNicolas Cage. Cage was the draw there, so I didn’t think much either way about the subject matter, which was snuff films; Cage plays a private investigator hired to find out if such a film, starring a teenage runaway, is real. I understand why critics at the time mostly shrugged the Joel Schumacher movie off as exploitative, histrionic and even cheesy, but screenwriter Andrew Kevin Walker knows his way around bringing rococo horrors into a stylized version of the real world (he also wrote Seven), sneaking horror into more quasi-respectable genres. The movie’s detective-thriller trappings are probably what ultimately made its more over-the-top elements, including multiple gruesome deaths, an extended confrontation between Cage and a creep played by James Gandolfini, and Cage tracking down a mysterious snuff-film performer called Machine, so viscerally upsetting. My two buddies and I left shellshocked. I like to pretend that I haven’t revisited 8mm since its 1999 release because I’d be embarrassed by how affected I was by such shlock, but the truth is, I’m still a little afraid of the damn thing.Jesse Hassenger‘Genuinely disturbing’: Guardian writers on their scariest horror villainsRead more8mm is available to rent digitally in the US, the UK and AustraliaAwakeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyThere are many reasons why Awake – the melodramatic thriller in which Hayden Christensen plays a wealthy finance bro who undergoes a heart transplant but remains conscious for the entire operation – continues to scare me the more I think about it. First, the idea of anesthesia failing is terrifying enough. But being paralyzed and unable to communicate that it’s not working? That feels unnecessary. Then there are the film’s many competing plot points. Christensen’s billionaire protagonist, Clay (a name I’ve yet to encounter in nearly a decade in the US), is apparently saint-like. While awake on the operating table, he gleans that his friend and cardiac surgeon (Terrence Howard) is in cahoots with his new wife (Jessica Alba) to kill him. The film is largely confined to a New York hospital, which sounds like a compelling chamber drama? Well, you’d be wrong. Because there apparently isn’t enough anxiety in Joby Harold’s directorial debut, we also get Clay’s hallucinations, including memories of his abusive father. It becomes a race against time for Clay’s mother (Lena Olin), another benevolent billionaire, to stop the plot. Somehow, it only gets more unbelievable. Still, Awake is weirdly exhilarating. Everyone commits fully to the madness, acting with a capital A.Shrai PopatAwake is available on Tubi in the US, to rent digitally in the UK and on Netflix in AustraliaDark WatersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Focus Features/AllstarTodd Haynes’s 2019 legal drama, Dark Waters, tells a familiar American story: a principled lawyer goes up against a massive, unscrupulous corporation and loses. But there is a lot in this film, which was based on Nathaniel Rich’s 2016 New York Timesprofileof former corporate defense lawyer Robert Bilott, to make this duel terrifying. Throughout his career, Haynes has looked at how external forces contaminate the domestic sphere, and here, it’s no different: the obsessive spiral that sweeps Mark Ruffalo’s Bilott is nearly as scary as the complete indifference with which DuPont, the chemical corporation responsible for knowingly poisoning West Virginians with “forever chemicals”, regards human life. One image in the film haunts me more than others: Bilott kneels among stacks of paper that tower over him as menacingly as Nosferatu’s shadow. It’s a terror of scale – all that work won’t kill Bilott, but it will whittle him down to a wisp. To DuPont, crushing Bilott is as simple as swatting a fly. Once you see the horror, you can’t unsee it.Rafaela BassiliDark Waters is available to rent digitally in the US and the UK and on SBS on Demand in Australia‘I squeamishly refuse to rewatch’: Guardian writers on their scariest movie endingsRead moreThe HuntView image in fullscreenPhotograph: courtesy/REX ShutterstockThere’s something uniquely, nightmarishly terrifying about trying to defend yourself against a false accusation. It’s what makes documentaries about particularly egregious examples of injustice not just enraging but seriously scary – how mechanically efficient the system can be when it’s focused on destroying you, often as the result of something as random as bad luck. In Thomas Vinterberg’s almost unbearably clammy drama The Hunt, a claim is made and believed and it’s cleverly one we’re never kept in the dark about. We know instantly that Mads Mikkelsen’s kindly kindergarten teacher didn’t sexually abuse the young daughter of a friend who, through a confused blur of emotions, makes a comment that is seen as proof of something devastating. With every small decision then made by those around her, some initially understandable and some maddeningly ill-advised, a tight-knit community turns on someone they had previously embraced. It’s horrifying to watch for so many reasons, exposing just how incredibly fragile the trust and acceptance of others can be and how so many are happy to rely on grim preconceptions about men who work with children. What’s chilling is how unstoppable the spiral can often seem and, in a disquieting final scene, how unfathomable it can be to move on from even if the crime has been disproved. In The Hunt, a pitchfork is far scarier than a knife.Benjamin LeeThe Hunt is available on Tubi in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and AustraliaZodiacView image in fullscreenPhotograph: AJ Pics/AlamyThere are many reasons why Zodiac, David Fincher’s 2007 film on the infamous serial killer, is considered one of the best detective movies of all time: its precise detail, its masterclass escalation of suspense, its immersive and unsettling mood. But the legacy of Zodiac, to me, isn’t Jake Gyllenhaal’s obsessive spiral, or the vexatious unsolved cryptograms, or even Guillermo del Toro’sviral tweet threadon the movie’s perfection. It is the unnerving re-enactment, about 20 minutes in, of a black-clad man striding in broad daylight toward a picnicking couple. At first he appears to be just another park visitor; only after a few paces can you see that he is masked, marked by an ominous symbol and carrying a gun. Fincher mostly keeps the camera trained on the female victim’s face, as her initial curiosity morphs to concern, then fear, then terror. That shift – when she knows something is off, but can’t yet tell it’s dire – pops into my mind when, say, a stranger approaches on an empty sidewalk, or when I am alone in a park. My dread has yet to ever be substantiated, but that scene is a pathway to panic: sometimes, as in this actual 1969 murder, your fear was right.Adrian Horton‘Fear is contagious’: why horror shows are taking over the New York stageRead moreZodiac is available on YouTube and Paramount+ in the US, on Netflix and Amazon Prime in the UK, and on Netflix in AustraliaRequiem for a DreamView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ronald GrantAs a committed avoider of actual horror movies, my most scary experiences at the cinema tend to sneak up on me when I’m not really expecting them. Both the original Vanishing and Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin contained scenes that temporarily put the fear of God into me, but I think for cumulative dread and general misery, Darren Aronofsky’s mighty adaptation of Hubert Selby Jr’s junkie novel stands supreme. As its title indicates, Requiem is a nightmare inversion of the American dream: after attempting to go into business with a “pound of pure”, the three youthful protagonists, played by Jared Leto, Marlon Wayans and Jennifer Connelly in manifestly career-high performances, end up having an arm amputated, being battered by prison guards and being forced into gruesome sex work, respectively. In this film, heroin is the equivalent of the creepy killer doll, or hulking monster no one else can see; it’s the silent, remorseless slayer THAT CAN’T BE STOPPED. And that’s not even counting the fourth protag, Ellen Burstyn’s gameshow wannabe, so hopped up on speed-laced diet pills that she goes into amphetamine psychosis. This isn’t a tale of terror, as such, but their collective descent into abject misery is as profoundly disturbing an experience as cinema has ever recorded.Andrew PulverRequiem for a Dream is available on Peacock and Tubi in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmHalloween2001: A Space OdysseyDavid FincherDarren AronofskyMads MikkelsenThomas VinterbergfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Oh to Believe in Another World review – William Kentridge’s amazing animated ballet of black comic pain | Movies | The Guardian
description: William Kentridge’s cine-musical creation, made to accompany Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony, is a marvel of puppetry, dance and humour, exploring humanity, grief and idealism
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: William Kentridge’s cine-musical creation, made to accompany Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony, is a marvel of puppetry, dance and humour, exploring humanity, grief and idealism
Content: Defiance … an image of Oh to Believe in Another World, taken at a performance in London in April 2025, accompanied by the Philharmonia Orchestra and conductor Marin Alsop.Photograph: Pete WoodheadView image in fullscreenDefiance … an image of Oh to Believe in Another World, taken at a performance in London in April 2025, accompanied by the Philharmonia Orchestra and conductor Marin Alsop.Photograph: Pete WoodheadMoviesReviewOh to Believe in Another World review – William Kentridge’s amazing animated ballet of black comic painKentridge’s cine-musical creation, made to accompany Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony, is a marvel of puppetry, dance and humour, exploring humanity, grief and idealismPeter BradshawFri 30 Oct 2026 05.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBaku international arts festival in Azerbaijanis showcasing an amazing cine-musical creation, perhaps the most amazing animation I have ever seen. Oh to Believe in Another World is an hour-long collage animation with live-action choreography by the 71-year-old South Africanartist and film-maker William Kentridge. It is shown with the live orchestral accompaniment of Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony, and this event is partly in honour of the 120th anniversary of Shostakovich’s birth this year, and partly to honour Shostakovich’s reportedly unrequited love (and lifelong friendship) for his student, Azerbaijani pianist and composer Elmira Nazirova.The 10th symphony was inspired by Stalin and premiered shortly after his death, so it seems probable that Shostakovich had been at work on it for some time before this, long enough beforehand for at least some of the composition to have been conceived without any sense of Stalin’s death. Could part of it perhaps have been originally intended as an obediently dramatic tribute to Stalin? Yet the music arguably combines fear, awe, revulsion, and a hysterical reaction to the mad energy of Stalin’s genocidal tyranny, a darkly ambiguous respect for the great dictator whose victory in 1945 was a mainstay of the postwar dispensation; perhaps there is also a feeling in the music’s swirl that a great and terrible era has passed away, and with it a kind of grief at all that had been sacrificed to it.For this, Kentridge creates models and masks of famous and notorious Soviet figures, including Stalin, Lenin, Trotsky and the poet Mayakovsky whose work provides the title and the intertitles, with maxims like: “We’ll chase humanity into happiness with an iron fist.” These masks are variously blurred and scribbled, some blank with the faces just outlined, like constructivist cutouts. Lenin is severe; Stalin has a half smile, Mayakovsky is haunted; Trotsky looks oddly pained and outraged. Some of these faces are small and attached to models, some lifesize and attached to actual human dancers. The humans and the models both become 2-D cartoon-grotesque figures, their stern or noble facial portrait expressions at odds with their absurd rickety flatness, their faces are like posters or placards. Their bodies below caper through a bizarre landscape: adansemacabreof history and tragedy. The models are green-screened into meticulously and brilliantly created model interiors; we enter their tiny world and it becomes lifesize, as fascinating asthe dollhouse dioramas in the Thorne Rooms at the Art Institute of Chicagothat captivated Orson Welles. The little models become the same height as full-size humans, a hyperreal effect.We see a dusty old Soviet museum … a wrecked auditorium where a newsreel movie is still playing … an eerily empty swimming pool, where Lenin appears on a high diving board. Then in the first movement, the Moderato, there are photographs of faces: faces of people destined to be eliminated by the state. We see the title, presented in the way as the succeeding intertitles: and we can sense something tragic or heroic about believing in anything at all. Shostakovich himself emerges as another of these puppet cutouts, sinuously conducting his own work. In the second movement, the Allegro, the tempo accelerates and the movie has something of Vertov’s Man With a Movie Camera. In the third movement, the Allegretto, we see Nazirova, Shostakovich’s love from Azerbaijan, dancing. But it is in this movement that Stalin, his poster-face at all times bearing the mild half-smile, takes out a gun and starts shooting. The fourth movement, Andante, Allegro, shows us the masks coming off and Kentridge’s own giant hand intruding into the frame.My colleague Jonathan Joneshas written about Kentridge’s filmbut what I hadn’t anticipated was how funny it is: the simple, preposterous effect of seeing Stalin’s great big monumental face on top of a dancer’s body, and seeing that face remain unchanged despite the exertions below, staring resolutely ahead at the far horizon of history. It is hilarious, a little like Terry Gilliam’s animations for Monty Python. But is it supposed to be funny? Chaplin showed that the way to defy Hitler was to laugh at him. Kentridge (and Kentridge’s Shostakovich) are doing something similar with Stalin but not exactly the same. It is a ballet of black comic pain.I have experienced many live-orchestral cinema events for silent movies: movies for which an ambitious new orchestral score has been composed. Many of these have been wonderful events, but on every occasion I have been aware of how the music can never quite match up to what’s on the screen, and to some extent washes diffusely over the action. But Oh to Believe in Another World is something else. It is precisely the other way around. The film has been created for the music. To believe in another world, a better world; that is the yearning exclamation at the heart of the music. The October revolution was pursued by those who wanted to believe in another world and lived to see one come into being. But under the Stalinist tyranny, they were yearning for another world as well, a world to overturn this one. The music mourns that lost idealism and mourns that another kind of idealism is necessary.TheBaku international arts festival is in Baku, Azerbaijan, until 8 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmWilliam KentridgeDmitri ShostakovichRussiaEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: From Possible Love to Ali G: Who Iz I?: the seven best films to watch on TV this week | Television | The Guardian
description: Lee Chang-dong’s edgy drama asks uncomfortable questions about class and exploitation. Plus, love him of loathe him – Ali G is back
Author: Simon Wardell
Headline: Lee Chang-dong’s edgy drama asks uncomfortable questions about class and exploitation. Plus, love him of loathe him – Ali G is back
Content: Table talk … In-sung, Cho Yeo-jeong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu in Possible Love.Photograph: Joo Jae-bum/NetflixView image in fullscreenTable talk … In-sung, Cho Yeo-jeong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu in Possible Love.Photograph: Joo Jae-bum/NetflixThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekTelevisionFrom Possible Love to Ali G: Who Iz I?: the seven best films to watch on TV this weekLee Chang-dong’s edgy drama asks uncomfortable questions about class and exploitation. Plus, love him or loathe him – Ali G is back after 20 yearsSimon WardellFri 30 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekPossible LoveIn Korean director Lee Chang-dong’s involving, edgy drama, documentary-maker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) is attempting to make a film about factory workers sacked after a strike was violently broken by the state. She is particularly intrigued by the sullen, possibly traumatised Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu). He is resistant but Ye-ji develops a bond with his enthusiastic wife, Jeon Do-yeon’s Mi-ok. As the parties get to know each other, with the addition of Ye-ji’s wealthy spouse Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), uncomfortable questions of class and exploitation swirl around them. Just as in his last film, 2018’s Burning, Chang-dong has a sharp eye for what’s hidden behind everyday lives.Friday 6 November,NetflixAli G: Who Iz I?View image in fullscreenIs it cos I is back? … Sacha Baron Cohen in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyHot-footing it from cinemas, Sacha Baron Cohen’s satirical documentary dusts off his deluded 90s Staines wideboy rapper for a series of pranks taking aim, mostly, at American Maga and anti-woke folk and their zeal to protect the border from immigrants. Morgana Robinson co-stars as the very pregnant “me Julie”, with Ali G heading to the US on the promise of a new show to fund impending fatherhood. Your enjoyment of all this will depend on your taste for gross-out gags and political provocation, and a character whose time has arguably passed.Out now, Prime VideoBoorman and the DevilView image in fullscreenCareer crossroads … John Boorman features in Boorman and the Devil.Photograph: PR IMAGEIf you’ve ever read one of his books, you’ll know the great British film-maker John Boorman (Point Blank, Deliverance) is a wonderful raconteur. And in David Kittredge’s deep-dive documentary, he’s great value as he recalls his time directing Exorcist II: The Heretic, a disastrous, glorious mess of a horror sequel that almost killed his career – and him. Stars Linda Blair and Louise Fletcher add further context to a cautionary tale that includes a drunken Richard Burton, locust wrangling and Boorman falling prey to a sand-based fever.SWSaturday 31 October, 8pm, Sky DocumentariesThe FogView image in fullscreenMurky … Hal Holbrock, Janet Leigh, Jamie Lee Curtis and Ty Mitchell in The Fog.Photograph: Embassy Pictures/AllstarMuch of the plot of John Carpenter’s classic 1980 horror yarn will be familiar to viewers of recent Apple TV homage Widow’s Bay. A California coastal community is assailed by ghostly forces from the sea hidden in a mysterious fog – the result of a 19th-century curse – and nobody is safe; not Adrienne Barbeau’s local radio DJ Stevie, nor hitchhiker Elizabeth (Jamie Lee Curtis) nor fisher Nick (Tom Atkins). Carpenter’s mastery of low-budget film-making is evident here: he does so much with a bit of dry ice, a few backlit figures and his own ominous electronic score.Saturday 31 October, 9pm, Sky Artsskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFanny and AlexanderView image in fullscreenJoy and pain … Bertil Guve (left) and Pernilla Allwin (second right) / in Fanny and Alexander.Photograph: ScreenProd/Photononstop/AlamyIngmar Bergman delved fruitfully into his own childhood for this resonant three-hour period drama (cut down from the even better five-hour TV original). The titular children are part of a large, well-off Swedish family who own a theatre in their town. Their emotional, magical life is brilliantly evoked in sumptuous Christmas celebrations, but the kids’ joy is short-lived when their mother is widowed, then marries a cold, cruel bishop who prioritises “purity and austerity”. An intoxicating masterpiece.Saturday 31 October, 9.20pm, BBC FourTalk to MeView image in fullscreenPossessed … Sophie Wilde in Talk to Me.Photograph: APPrior to their teeth-clenchingly brilliant Bring Her Back last year, Australian twins Danny and Michael Philippou had already explored the grisly scope of grief in this nail-biting 2022 horror. A group of teenagers are introduced to a party game that involves holding a severed hand – which may have been a medium’s – and summoning a dead person, which you invite to (briefly) possess you. But when Mia (Sophie Wilde), who lost her mother a year ago, agrees to let her best friend’s kid brother Riley (Joe Bird) try it out, things go bloodily wrong. Great, ghostly goings-on from an up-and-coming duo.Saturday 31 October, 10pm, Film4The Nature of LoveView image in fullscreenClass division … Magalie Lépine Blondeau and Pierre-Yves Cardinal star in The Nature of Love.Photograph: Immina Films et Fred GervaisOpposites may attract but, Monia Chokri’s romantic drama asks, can love overcome the differences in the long term? Canadian philosophy lecturer Sophia (Magalie Lépine Blondeau) falls in lust at first sight with lumberjack-shirted builder Sylvain (Pierre-Yves Cardinal), to the extent of breaking up her marriage. As she socialises with his working-class family and he attends a dinner party with her intellectual friends, there’s plenty of fish-out-of-water comedy to be had, but Chokri is careful not to condescend or satirise either side of the social divide.Tuesday 3 November, 11.35pm, Film4Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Black Doves to Stick: the seven best shows to stream this week | Television | The Guardian
description: Keira Knightley returns for more chaos and thrills with guns in an espionage drama. Plus, Owen Wilson is back as charming washed-up golf pro Pryce Cahill
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Keira Knightley returns for more chaos and thrills with guns in an espionage drama. Plus, Owen Wilson is back as charming washed-up golf pro Pryce Cahill
Content: Best shot … Ambika Mod and Keira Knightley star in Black Doves.Photograph: Matthew Towers/Courtesy of Matthew Towers/NetflixView image in fullscreenBest shot … Ambika Mod and Keira Knightley star in Black Doves.Photograph: Matthew Towers/Courtesy of Matthew Towers/NetflixThe seven best shows to stream this weekTelevisionBlack Doves to Stick: the seven best shows to stream this weekKeira Knightley returns for more chaos and thrills with guns in an espionage drama. Plus, Owen Wilson is back as charming washed-up golf pro Pryce CahillPhil HarrisonFri 30 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekBlack DovesHelen Webb (Keira Knightley) is now the prime minister’s wife. Will that temper her treachery? Not a bit of it. This hugely entertaining espionage thriller returns with Helen cracking a safe (and adding to her spectacular body count) at an official engagement. The Black Doves spy ring is now in chaos after a key disappearance and, worse still, Sam (Ben Whishaw) has become a loose cannon, forced to take on hit jobs without much due diligence. Soon, absolutely everyone is somehow on a direct collision course. It’s a glorious mess of motive, morality and murder, and the superb cast – which now includes Ambika Mod and Babou Ceesay – are clearly having a ball. So will you.Netflix, from Thursday 5 NovemberSCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard OfView image in fullscreenJust a second … Catherine O’Hara and Andrea Martin in SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of.Photograph: Netflix“I have watched those things 122 times,” says Tom Hanks, “and I still laugh.” For the uninitiated, Second City TV was an oddball Canadian sketch comedy that ran between 1976 and 1984. It was defiantly lo-fi and made on a shoestring, but also unapologetically itself. And it launched the careers of soon-to-be superstars including John Candy, Catherine O’Hara and Eugene Levy. The documentary is every bit as endearing as the show was – it’s evident that this scrappy enterprise changed the life of almost everyone who encountered it.Netflix, out nowStickView image in fullscreenTo a tee … Owen Wilson is Pryce Cahill in Stick.Photograph: Jessica Brooks/Jessica Brooks/Apple TVOwen Wilson’s charming performance as ageing golf pro Pryce Cahill elevates this comedy drama above the current glut of feelgood sports stories. The key is Wilson’s vulnerability which, for all the laughs, gives the show high stakes and an edge of melancholy. As season two begins, Pryce senses that his brilliant protege Santi (Pete Dager) is starting to outgrow him. The professional tour beckons and big-time agents are sniffing around. But Pryce is enjoying something of a late bloom himself – could he still be a contender in his own right? Clearly, it’s a dream he won’t be able to resist chasing.Apple TV, from Wednesday 4 NovemberAll’s FairView image in fullscreenPlotters … Kim Kardashian, Sarah Paulson and Naomi Watts star in All’s Fair.Photograph: Ser Baffo/DisneyThe first season of this Ryan Murphy monstrosity was the recipient of a rare but richly deserved zero-star review from the Guardian. However, these days there’s no such thing as bad publicity: All’s Fair is back and it is leaning into its witlessly camp grotesquery. “Vengeance is a savage game,” Glenn Close’s Dina Standish warns in the opener. Is she addressing a fellow character or the world’s TV reviewers? Arguably both. What unfolds involves hit jobs, a Carrie spoof and Kim Kardashian still trying to act. Vengeance complete.Disney+, from Wednesday 4 Novemberskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe GreatestView image in fullscreenPunchy … Muhammad Ali’s life is examined in The Greatest.Photograph: Brooke Palmer/PrimeThe life of Muhammad Ali is exhaustively documented but, even so, this eight-part drama (made with the cooperation of Ali’s estate) is a worthy addition. The story begins at the 1960 Olympics when the former Cassius Clay won gold and kicked open the door to wealth and fame. But, from family tensions to the US culture wars in which he became a central figure, his path was never smooth. The political dimensions of Ali’s life are never overplayed but always insistently drawn, the fight scenes are thrilling and Jaalen Best plays Ali with a steely calmness.Netflix, from Wednesday 4 NovemberThe AssassinView image in fullscreenShooting star … Keeley Hawes is retired gun-for-hire Julie in The Assassin.Photograph: Mark Cassar/AmazonThe most riveting mother-and-son relationship on TV is back: this thriller starring Keeley Hawes as grumpy, semi-retired assassin Julie is still preposterous fun. Julie and her son Edward (Freddie Highmore) are estranged again but, for all Edward’s diffidence, trouble keeps finding him. When his wife, Kayla (Shalom Brune-Franklin), is kidnapped on their honeymoon and he gets an inkling that the police might have been involved, he has no choice but to ask for Julie’s help. Julie and Edward’s comically toxic anti-chemistry remains a weird delight to watch.Prime Video, from Friday 6 NovemberAwkwafina: The Unlikely CookView image in fullscreenPerfect recipe … Nora Lum in Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook.Photograph: Christina Belle/Courtesy of AppleWhen we first meet comic and actor Nora “Awkwafina” Lum, she’s making instant ramen with spam. A call to her horrified grandmother confirms that this isn’t exactly traditional Chinese cuisine. But Nora is on a mission: her family were behind a much-loved (but now closed) restaurant that she’d like to revive. But can she learn to cook? While the various scenarios sometimes feel contrived, this breezy series is at its best when Lum considers her family’s experiences in the context of an immigrant community in America trying to establish themselves.Apple TV, from Friday 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionThe seven best shows to stream this weekTV streamingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racket | Music | The Guardian
description: The Rotterdam band are a riot of sound, look and attitude led by Eva Kah, who is as much a living artwork as she is a phenomenal live performer
Author: Richard Foster
Headline: The Rotterdam band are a riot of sound, look and attitude led by Eva Kah, who is as much a living artwork as she is a phenomenal live performer
Content: ‘In your face’ … Eva Kah of Bombstrap.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘In your face’ … Eva Kah of Bombstrap.Photograph: PRAdd to playlistMusicThe week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racketThe Rotterdam band are a riot of sound, look and attitude led by Eva Kah, who is as much a living artwork as she is a phenomenal live performerRichard FosterFri 30 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromRotterdam, the NetherlandsRecommended if you likeGnod, Discharge, GwarUp nextDebut album Big Enemy out now via Tartarus, playing Le Guess Who festivalRotterdam’sBombstrapare a riotous and theatrical fusion of sound, look and attitude. An embodied version of John Milton’s Pandæmonium with the amp turned up to 11, the band revel in hardcore alternative living, internet wormholes, art-school pretensions and a gungy form of hardcore. Based in and drawing succour from one of the most famous squatted centres in the city, Het Poortgebouw, Bombstrap are a noisy counterblast to the increasing and overwhelmingly witless “circuses-and-bread” gentrification of Rotterdam.Visual artist and singer Eva Kah is a living artwork and phenomenal live performer, whose in-your-face act illuminates those grey areas between righteous anger, nihilistic energy and teeth-grating bad taste. Kah’s vocals ape the warning screams and ululations a crone would make over the grave of Achilles. A natural extension of the look, obviously.Some of the uncompromising attitudes heard in debut album Big Enemy also betray their links to Manchester’s punk and squat scenes; previous members of the extendedGnodfamily have played with them. But the sound is a shifting, amorphous one, permanently up for grabs in the listener’s interpretation. The gravelly mix of chopped-up rhythms and raw, high-decibel punk guitars could even hark back to ancient prog-punk gonzoids such as the Pink Fairies. They are one of the last cries of homegrown, communal, anarcho hippy-punkdom and have all the social and sonic baggage that that entails. There is no career path in sight.Richard FosterThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenDeep and dramatic … Clementine Douglas.Photograph: Lily AjaibClementine Douglas​ – So PreciousSelf-penned, and gorgeously self-produced with a ribbon of synth melody pirouetting from the bottom of the mix, this is deep and dramatic vocal house from the British singer normally found belting alongside Calvin Harris, Dom Dolla et al.​DJ Heartstring – 3am/4am (ft Monk, 3ndles5 & Crazymike)The German dance duo get their countryman Monk to flow over their breakbeat euphoria, while there are shades of Real Lies’ nocturnal social realism to 3ndles5’s spoken English-language verse.Josh Johnson – Jazz Chord PossessionJazz saxophonist Johnson is sideman to Jeff Parker and producer to Meshell Ndegeocello and Flea. His own latest single has two sweetly swaying melodic motifs set against each other, plus analogue synth burbling out back.​Isaac Kniveton​ – Love GrooveLike a colourful plastic playground with its edges melting in the sun, there’s a bright psychedelia to the way the British producer’s Kompakt-style techno-pop unfolds, peppy and woozy all at once.Anamanaguchi – Sucker PunchThe New Yorkers pair crunching, muscular chords with delicate electronic detailing, building up a dense bank of shoegaze that’s illuminated from within by a thousand points of neon light.​Metoronori – Lights of the BayDreampop is an overused phrase, but it’s appropriate for the otherworldly beauty and wrongfooting shifts in the Japanese singer-producer’s new album, Forgot Reef Number: this track has a music-box prettiness.Waterbaby – CreekWe loved her albumMemory Be a Bladeearlier this year, and the Stockholm singer-songwriter is back with this waltzing lullaby, full of her trademark blend of wounded emotion and stoic endurance.Ben Beaumont-ThomasSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistNetherlandsEuropeSquattingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Radie Peat: No Human Tongue Can Tell review – Lankum singer’s solo debut is the year’s best folk album | Folk music | The Guardian
description: Collecting traditional songs of female struggle and strength, the Irish singer invests them with staggering power
Author: Jude Rogers
Headline: Collecting traditional songs of female struggle and strength, the Irish singer invests them with staggering power
Content: ‘No nonsense, startling and moving’ … Radie Peat.Photograph: Dave SmithView image in fullscreen‘No nonsense, startling and moving’ … Radie Peat.Photograph: Dave SmithFolk album of the monthFolk musicReviewRadie Peat: No Human Tongue Can Tell review – Lankum singer’s solo debut is the year’s best folk album(Rough Trade)Collecting traditional songs of female struggle and strength, the Irish singer invests them with staggering powerJude RogersFri 30 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLankum singer Radie Peat’s extraordinary debut album begins without frills or ornament: just her voice, stark and low, each breath like air vibrating through the metal reeds of a harmonium. Singing Hares on the Mountain to the tune Shirley Collins arranged for 1964’s Folk Roots, New Routes, Peat accompanies herself subtly on Fender Rhodes piano before adding layers of Mellotron and Wurlitzer. Her simple, quiet approach is consistently startling and profoundly moving.View image in fullscreenRadie Peat: No Human Tongue Can Tell album coverNo Human Tongue Can Tell collects songs of female struggle, suffering, strength and endurance, although Peat only realised this, she writes in her liner notes, after limiting her choices by her “own mind and abilities” and “personal preferences”. Epic statements clearly aren’t her bag; her gut-deep connection with songs she’s sung live for years clearly matters more, with many delivered in new versions, pulsing with urgency.Willow Garden, performed in a major-key chorus by Lankum in 2017, becomes a reverb-heavy, haunting elegy, with Peat’s handling of the lyric “poor little girl” buckling with sadness. She paints the woman “hanging out the wash” vividly against rolling guitar arpeggios in Same Old Man, and summons oceans of yearning in the frightening Still I Love Him, a song found by fellow contemporary Irish singer John Francis Flynn, in which a woman savagely beaten by her husband remains emotionally bound to him.Just as arresting is Peat’s take on Dark Horse on the Wind, Liam Weldon’s 1966 lament for the lost dream of the Irish republic, written on the brink of the Troubles. “Now the warriors spring from the earth / To maim and kill their own,” Peat sings against a solid drone. John “Spud” Murphy’s production brilliantly brings out earthy, granular details, from the sucking-in of air through Peat’s concertina bellows on Cailín Deas to the disruptive thwack of Eleanor Myler’s drums. How staggering for traditional songs to taste so like fresh blood: stunning, brutal and unforgettable.Also out this monthArriving alongside a self-penned anthology,Bróna McVittie’s Supernatural (Company of Corkbots) is an ambitious collection of fairy songs for Samhain, with a prevailing sound that feels like a soft-folk successor to William Orbit’s work for Madonna during the Frozen era. Lithuanian singer Jausmė, Ukrainian bandura player Anastasiya Voytyuk and Spanish flamenco guitarist Antonia Jiménez also make gorgeous contributions.Bird in the Belly’s Only Dogs As Friends (GF*M) is another solid set of strange folk from Laura Ward and Ben Webb, lit up by warm, radio-friendly arrangements. Highlights include the rousing Go Along Bobby and the shivery Lambs. South African guitaristGuy Buttery’s Improvisations from a Rural Church: Volume 1 brings the swarmandal (an Indian zither) and the shakuhachi (Japanese bamboo flute) into a succession of ambient folk explorations around a pump organ in the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands. Listen out for bats, birds, rats, passing tractors and stormy weather adding tension and texture.Explore more on these topicsFolk musicFolk album of the monthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kali Malone: Burning Song review – drone composer wields Bach’s organ to breathtaking effect | Experimental music | The Guardian
description: The US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpiece
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpiece
Content: Acute attention … Kali Malone.Photograph: © Kingsley IfillView image in fullscreenAcute attention … Kali Malone.Photograph: © Kingsley IfillExperimental musicReviewKali Malone: Burning Song review – drone composer wields Bach’s organ to breathtaking effect(Ideologic Organ)The US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpieceLaura SnapesFri 30 Oct 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn drone world, Burning Song is Kali Malone’s pop record.
