These pieces are significantly shorter than the lengthy ones that made the US composer’s name, and she takes a newfound emotional approach to composition, forsaking the contrapuntal canon form.View image in fullscreenKali Malone: Burning SongIn some arcane land, this probably constitutes unforgivable selling out. In more rational circles, the result is still 40 minutes of beautiful, plaintive tonality, with Lucy Railton on cello and Stephen O’Malley of Sunn O))) (also Malone’s husband) on bowed acoustic guitar. Malone plays the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche, where the composer was cantor for his last 27 years. Rather than a saint, it’s him who is buried under the altar. “That made it feel like a church for music,” Malone toldBlackbird Spyplane.‘I want an indescribable feeling’: composer Kali Malone on her search for the sublimeRead moreIf Malone’s longer pieces are music to get lost in, the compact forms and liberated mood shifts of Burning Song command acute attention. The trio play in synchronicity, their crackle and breath and scrape simmering intensely. They start Grieving Figure with a sustained note that sounds like a distant ship’s horn, then brightens like blazing final moments of a fierce sunset. Bells on a Branch starts sounding like a swarm of bees and ends utterly parched; Railton’s cello circles ominously amid the drama of Crawling Ashore.As for emotion, it’s no Max Richter-style lunge for the cheap seats. The heavy opening notes of Map the Path are solemn yet startlingly direct for Malone, feeling for the first time as if she’s lifting her fingers from the keys and shaking the listener by the shoulders.Explore more on these topicsExperimental musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Philippa Gregory: ‘I read 100 of the 18th century’s most popular novels – the perfect author’s apprenticeship’ | Philippa Gregory | The Guardian
description: The British novelist on discovering Molly Keane, coming to Dickens late, and the books that taught her the importance of writing about history
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The British novelist on discovering Molly Keane, coming to Dickens late, and the books that taught her the importance of writing about history
Content: ‘Great writing gives any experience a significance’ … Philippa Gregory.Photograph: Chris LeahView image in fullscreen‘Great writing gives any experience a significance’ … Philippa Gregory.Photograph: Chris LeahThe books of my lifePhilippa GregoryPhilippa Gregory: ‘I read 100 of the 18th century’s most popular novels – the perfect author’s apprenticeship’The British novelist on discovering Molly Keane, coming to Dickens late, and the books that taught her the importance of writing about historyPhilippa GregoryFri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryMy mother always read me a bedtime story, but by around age three, I was not looking at the pictures but reading the text. After that, I read to myself, and would read four books a week from the library.My favourite book growing upAs a child I read Elizabeth Goudge’s The Little White Horse, and the combination of history and gothic fantasy was very powerful for me. It’s realistic and charming and frightening without being nightmarish. It started my love of historical fiction, and has since become a family favourite for my own children.The book that changed me as a teenagerThey all did, I was a voracious reader. I really enjoyed Rudyard Kipling, and later went on to historical fiction, especially Georgette Heyer. I read all of Jane Austen’s novels early on and learned to love her economy of style and precision. She still seems to me the finest writer in the English language.The writer who changed my mindEP Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class is a radical account of the emergence of a working-class consciousness and was a revelation to me when I first read it as a young woman. It made me understand the real importance of writing history, and the passion that a great historian can bring to the subject. It’s become a model for me in my own work – showing that you can find and write a hidden history.The book that made me want to be a writerFor my PhD thesis I read more than 100 of the most popular novels in the 18th century. Don Quixote, Clarissa, Gulliver’s Travels, Moll Flanders and many more. It was the perfect author’s apprenticeship. Not only did I read the novels, I analysed them all, which meant I learned about structure, characterisation and tempo. But more importantly, I learned about the craft of novel writing at the very time novels were being invented.Thebook I came back toI didn’t enjoyCharles Dickensuntil later in life. Now, I think he is one of the great writers of the big book. One of my favourites of his is Dombey and Son. The huge sentimentalism around a beautiful frail child is combined with a story about a merciless social climber. It’s a great and unpredictable read.The book I rereadGreat writing gives any experience a significance, and a good novel can take us into another place and time. I read and reread Iris Murdoch’s The Sea, the Sea, whenever I need comfort. It’s a book that is far away from my own concerns and yet entirely about the human struggle to own the person you love, when you know that cannot be achieved, to free yourself from your own vanity and greed, to recognise those who are your deep companions and friends. At the same time it’s a deeply engaging story about a gossipy, vain theatre director in his retirement home at the sea.The book I discovered later in lifeI discovered Molly Keane, a between-the‑wars Anglo-Irish novelist, recently. At first sight she tells delicious stories of the eccentric Anglo-Irish wealthy elite, but every novel is highly aware of the injustice that underpins that society. One of my favourites is Good Behaviour, about a pair of adorable siblings who live for hunting in an enormous estate and care for nothing but each other, their horses and dogs, and their father, who they call “The Sir”. It’s a wonderful picture of a society that has completely disappeared, and a fictional creation of huge charm.Royal Witch by Philippa Gregory is published by HarperCollins. title: The best recent translated fiction – review roundup | Books | The Guardian
description: Minihorror by Barbi Marković; Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch; Hafni Says by Helle Helle; Googling for Soul by Hamid Ismailov
Author: John Self
Headline: Minihorror by Barbi Marković; Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch; Hafni Says by Helle Helle; Googling for Soul by Hamid Ismailov
Content: Antic energy … Barbi Marković.Photograph: /Apollonia T. BitzanView image in fullscreenAntic energy … Barbi Marković.Photograph: /Apollonia T. BitzanTranslated fiction roundupBooksReviewThe best recent translated fiction – review roundupMinihorror by Barbi Marković; Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch; Hafni Says by Helle Helle; Googling for Soul by Hamid IsmailovJohn SelfFri 30 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinihorrorby Barbi Marković, translated by Jen Calleja (Faber, £14.99)This eccentric and fantastical collection of very short stories is bursting with weird life. Mini and Miki (the Disney mouse names in Serbian) are a sometime boyfriend and girlfriend living in Austria. They visit Mini’s family, who gather round a pit and make her climb down into it (when she told Miki “they’re dragging me down”, he thought it was a metaphor). They visit Miki’s family, where a dog Mini draws on a card comes alive and attacks her. Things swing from hopeful – “they’re having fun like a couple in an advert” – to dismal: a hair dye goes wrong and “Mini looks like a 13-year-old dog”. Minihorror combines a Bernhardian comic gloom (“in summary, everything’s tainted, and existence is a particular hardship”) with antic energy. “Miki isn’t sure what to think about life. Is it good? Is it bad?” It’s everything, just like this book.Paradise Burnsby Pol Guasch, translated by Mara Faye Lethem (Peninsula, £12.99)“Stories, if you give them an order, aren’t stories but lies.” Catalan author Guasch makes the point vividly in this novel which flits briskly from present to past and from narrator to narrator. It’s set in a changed climate – “One only knows it’s winter now by the shrunken days and long nights” – where young men join a firefighting service and fight “wildfire simulations of blazes that could not be put out”. The central characters are friends Rita and Líton, but Líton is dead when the book begins – “twenty-four short years, a life as fleeting as a shooting comet” – so the story goes backward, to find out why. The jumpy narrative ranges from Rita’s childhood diary, to three “crafty old biddies” in the neighbourhood, to Líton and his lover René. But inside the hectic structure is a tribute to the value of friendship, and how a friend “has to be the net beneath the tightrope that is life”.Hafni Saysby Helle Helle, translated by Martin Aitken (Akoya, £12.99)Hafni, at 48, is leaving her husband – literally, by taking a road trip through Denmark. “Many’s the time he’d cycle off and I’d be standing at the kitchen window wishing the wind would take him.” Now it’s her turn to go. Alongside details of life away from home – washing her pants in the sink, opening beer bottles with a metal comb – she reflects on how liberating it is to be free of a sense of obligation. The rules she has lived by can be abandoned, if not forgotten. “No more phrases like ‘you shouldn’t have’.” She meets new people – such as a dying woman who sees it as her duty to keep everyone around her cheerful – and wobbles between hope and fear. But ultimately this is a subtle, affecting story of what happens when a woman stuck in her life says, “I don’t want to be me. I want to change who I am.”View image in fullscreenGoogling for Soulby Hamid Ismailov, translated by Shelley Fairweather-Vega, Dani Ismailov, Irina Buss-Zolotareva and Andrew Bromfield (Glagoslav, £17.99)This sequence of stories about Uzbeks, often exiled in Russia, is full of rampant action, blunt comedy and real horror. In the title story, a man believes his life is echoing the events of Andrey Platonov’s story Soul, and also believes that Hamid Ismailov, the author of this book, has been arrested on terrorism charges. (In reality, Ismailov was forced to flee Uzbekistan in 1992.) Other stories include a man driven to penury by the escapades of a nephew he’s never met before; two in-laws thrown together by fate; and a girl with a precious doll (her story seems more subdued than the others until her drunk father chases her with a knife). Ismailov’s characters have a lively line in insults: “You have the complexion of a fart,” says a father telling his son to eat better. “It’s as if the world had rejected seriousness,” says one character – but Ismailov’s blend of seriousness and sparkle is a seductive combination.Explore more on these topicsBooksTranslated fiction roundupFiction in translationHorror booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Attention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo review – a slippery liar’s tale | Books | The Guardian
description: Shortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Shortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answers
Content: Brilliant and breathless … Aea Varfis-van Warmelo.Photograph: Naomi Joanne DelormeView image in fullscreenBrilliant and breathless … Aea Varfis-van Warmelo.Photograph: Naomi Joanne DelormeBook of the dayBooksReviewAttention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo review – a slippery liar’s taleShortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answersAimée WalshFri 30 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 04.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Goldsmiths prize-shortlisted debut from British-Greek author Aea Varfis-van Warmelo opens with a confession: “I have never told this story before.” The narrator, who bears the author’s name, goes on to tell the reader that she is a liar. From Humbert Humbert’s self-justifying account of abuse in Lolita to the devastating misinterpretation at the heart of Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the trope of the unreliable narrator exposes the dangerous gap between the stories we tell and the truths they obscure. In Attention Seeking Behaviour, the reader is asked to examine their own capacity for trust.A young woman aspires to be a writer – yet she has paused her postgraduate degree in poetry. She works unfulfilling jobs that demand little from her and has a lot of sex, which she describes as offering her “solitude”. She does all this while lying compulsively. She lies for fun, to flirt, to steal, for sympathy. She lies out of a desire to hurt others, but also to preserve her own privacy. Lying is, as the narrator claims, universal, though success at lying is not. She regards fraudsters and scammers with derision: they are “divorced from reality” and give her “second hand embarrassment”. In her eyes, her own lies are somehow purer.Grief and trauma pulse beneath the story, as the narrator is haunted by the dead bodies she sees in parks and floating in canals. She says she has called emergency services, but her account is slippery: the harder we try to grasp it, the more it slips through our fingers. Can we believe a word she says?double quotation markThe reader may find their own response to the narrator’s story as unsettling as the story itselfAttention Seeking Behaviour draws the reader through personal confession and a gripping narrative of misadventures while dating, but the novel loses some of its momentum in its discussions of deceit. An essay on Paul Ekman’s Facial Action Coding System for classifying facial movements to determine deception disrupts the narrative drive. When this bleeds into the narrative, her boyfriend says: “No more. Please.” These sections interrupt the flow and lack the immediacy achieved elsewhere.In the book’s second part, questions of credibility become more acute. Acting on behalf of a journalist, the narrator copies files at a legal firm relating to a rape case in which a lecturer is accused of assaulting his student. The victim bares her soul, giving first her phone over to the police, then her laptop. Eventually, after police question her for signs of deception, she withdraws her participation in the investigation. The case is closed.Complainants often anticipate the difficulties of a police investigation. Their testimony is the evidence, their body a crime scene. The narrator says: “We are ambiently aware of what is believable – of what people think is true, whether or not it is real.” Victims of sexual violence are judged in courts and beyond, for what they wore on the night in question, for what they did or did not do in the aftermath. Here lies the book’s genius: it turns the question of reliability back on the reader, exposing the expectations we place on women. Must an account of rape be consistent, coherent or complete to be worthy of belief? Should a woman’s past, including what she has said and done, have any bearing on whether she is believed? The reader may find their own response to the narrator’s story as unsettling as the story itself. The narrator cannot name the trauma that happened with her ex-boyfriend Isaac. Instead, she unravels it “like a police report”, recounting what she said (nothing) and what she felt (numb). The book asks, unflinchingly, do you believe her?Brilliant and breathless, Attention Seeking Behaviour brings no easy resolutions to questions of memory, truth and justice. Yet, as the narrator tells us again and again, all she wants is to be believed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one | Games | The Guardian
description: Voicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a father
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: Voicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a father
Content: Draga, protagonist of Black Tides Draga's Wake, played by Dominik DiamondPhotograph: Strange Creature Factory LtdView image in fullscreenDraga, protagonist of Black Tides Draga's Wake, played by Dominik DiamondPhotograph: Strange Creature Factory LtdGamesAfter 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in oneDominik DiamondVoicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a fatherFri 30 Oct 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTShare“I listen to you on the radio and I keep hearing your voice in my head!”Not a typical opening to a creative partnership, but that is how Greg Strangis introduced himself to me 16 months ago, when he asked me to come to his garage in the middle of nowhere and have a look at a game he was making called Black Tides Draga’s Wake.If this sounds dodgy, remember that when I was 21 years old, a posh bloke asked me to come to a random church in the East End of London and talk saucy in front of him and a couple of other posh blokes. This turned out to be my audition for GamesMaster.So, I go to Greg’s garage. He has a giant yet well groomed beard, eyes that flash with intensity underneath one of those Peaky Blinders caps and talks faster than other humans. He’s basically a hipster Rasputin. He is also a character artist who has worked for Rockstar, Naughty Dog and Guillermo del Toro. He ticks all the genius boxes for me.And then I see the actual game. It is gorgeously dark and twisted: a survival horror game set on a decaying 1900s steamship after a heist gone wrong. The titular Draga is a big, tough-as-hell sailor with a dark past, infected by an ancient god that grows within him.View image in fullscreenGorgeously dark and twisted … Black Tides Draga’s Wake.Photograph: Strange Creature Factory Ltd.It sounds exciting, it sounds original, it sounds terrifying. And he wants me to be in it.But it sounds nothing like me. I am not a sailor. I am not big and tough as hell, and the only ancient god I have ever been infected with is gout. (Trust me, the pain is biblical.)I am going to have to …act.I did study drama at university, but this was the University of Bristol in the early 90s, so it was less about high kicking on stage to Oklahoma or learning Shakespearean monologues and more about poring over some obscure Russian play where potatoes are a metaphor for gender politics, written by a bloke who once gave Gorky a lift.I never told Greg this at the time, but when I see my first attempts at voice acting play out in the game, I don’t like it. I see this amazing badass character smashing disgustingly huge monsters with my tinny tones coming out of him. So I lower my voice ever so slightly and stop trying to act so much. And it works! Helpfully, Greg’s direction always makes me feel comfortable and encouraged.Every time I turn up for a session I am inspired by the work done by the team, who are in different corners of the world, doing this in their spare time. I see their message threads with all kinds of ideas, pictures and animations. It reminds me of the bedroom programming culture of the ZX Spectrum, fuelled by the unshakeable belief in an idea and a passion for gaming. In an age where huge publishers are decimating studios all over the world, it is a reminder of how vibrant game-making can still be.View image in fullscreenExistential crisis … Dominik as a survival horror action hero.Photograph: Dominik DiamondI don’t want to be the weak link in this chain. I don’t want my performance to be something that takes a prospective publisher out of the moment. I learn to love pushing and pulling the words in different directions. The biggest challenge is improvising fight noises that Greg and the team can add in wherever and whenever they want. During the game this is supposed to seem natural, but in reality it is a Scottish dad in his 50s making the kinds of noises he hasn’t made since his honeymoon. In a garage. In the middle of rural Nova Scotia. With another guy telling him he has to be more aggressive.It’s unbearably weird when I play the game. I feel distraught when I die, because itisme. I feel equally bad when I see other people playing the game, leading to uncomfortable new thoughts about video game characters’ lack of free will. It’s all a bit of an existential crisis.But then I play clips for my kids without telling them I am in it. I see their faces break out into wide grins as they realise it’s their grumpy old Scottish dad playing a survival horror action hero. It’s one of my favourite ever moments as a parent.It has also made me appreciate voice acting in games, something that didn’t register with me before, because for me it always felt like thecharactertalking – which is testament to the quality of voice acting and directing in games. Or at least games since the original Resident Evil. I now truly appreciate performances like Nolan North as Nathan Drake, Ashley Johnson in The Last of Us, and every single actor who says any of the words in Expedition 33.The announcement trailer for Black Tides Draga’s Wake dropped a month ago. It got 200,000 views in the first couple of days. Greg is in discussions with assorted publishers. I still have to pinch myself that after playing games for 50 years, I am finally going to be in one.Explore more on these topicsGamescommentShareReuse this content

title: Big hair with the pre-Raphaelites, 17 Orkney stand-outs and night frights in Derry – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: William Morris and the gang collaborate in Cambridge, artists celebrate at Stromness harbour and Halloween haunts Derry
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: William Morris and the gang collaborate in Cambridge, artists celebrate at Stromness harbour and Halloween haunts Derry
Content: The Bridesmaid by John Everett Millais, 1851.Photograph: Fitzwilliam Museum, University of CambridgeView image in fullscreenThe Bridesmaid by John Everett Millais, 1851.Photograph: Fitzwilliam Museum, University of CambridgeArt Weekly newsletterArt and designBig hair with the pre-Raphaelites, 17 Orkney stand-outs and night frights in Derry – the week in artWilliam Morris and the gang collaborate in Cambridge, artists celebrate at Stromness harbour and Halloween haunts Derry –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 30 Oct 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekA Call to ArtIf you feel you need to see another exhibition about William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites, get yourself to Cambridge for this exploration of late Victorian art and politics.Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge, until 3 MayAlso showingThe Night JournalAisling O’Beirn, Wilhelmina Peace and more meditate on the night: what does it mean when the world goes dark? One for Halloween maybe.CCA Derry until 19 DecemberRobert RauschenbergA special display from the Artist Rooms collection of the great magician of found stuff, with an emphasis on his later work – was it a falling off, or seriously underrated?Tate Modern, LondonMóti CollectiveA collective of no fewer than 17 artists and designers who work in Orkney celebrates their 10th anniversary in a gallery evocatively placed on Stromness harbour.Pier Arts Centre, Stromness, until 24 DecemberWilhelminaBarns-GrahamThe Cornish landscape becomes a bony but ethereal abstraction in this modernist painter’s work.Tate St Ives until 3 MayImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lotus L KangThis image may share the unpretentious quiddity ofGiorgio Morandi’s bottle paintingsand the prismatic lucidity ofRodric O’Conor’s, but it is not an everyday still life. At the Venice Biennale, Lotus L Kang arranged 49 bottles of spirits in front of film reels of tidal mudflats and visualisations of birdsong, to reflect the Buddhist belief that a soul spends 49 days between death and rebirth. The images are now part of Kang’s shortlisted entry for the prestigiousDeutsche Börse photography prize.What we learnedThe Bayeux tapestry has become a pop culture hitAs the prestigious Deutsche Börse photography prize marks its 30th anniversary, this year’s nominees considered surveillance and sabotageAn excellent survey of LS Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopiaThe Iranian photographer Hoda Afshar’s work is beautiful – and shockingFans swarmed San Francisco for a BTS star’s art exhibitionskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMasterpiece of the weekAutumn Evening by Henri-Joseph Harpignies, 1894View image in fullscreenPhotograph: National Gallery, LondonThis painting is a reminder that art isn’t really a progression from old to new, a wave of movements displacing the past, but a great big fascinating mess, with artists at any one time working in many styles, including archaic ones. For this calming, eerily beautiful view of rusty-leaved birches against a bronzed evening sky was painted in the 1890s when Cézanne, Munch and Toulouse-Lautrec were building modernism – but Harpignies has absolutely no interest in that. This painting is not even touched by impressionism, which had started in the 1870s. Instead it is completely loyal to the artistic ideas of the painter’s youth. Born in 1819, Harpignies was a diehard classicist steeped in the light of Italy that he saw on his travels. This landscape has the same charm as finding a totally archaic bistro in a remote French village and eating its coq au vin as the sun goes down.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get intouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ceilidh: A New Musical review – a joyous, riotous celebration of Scottish culture gets the audience on its feet | Musicals | The Guardian
description: Scott Gilmour and Claire McKenzie’s audience participation musical gets toes tapping and bodies spinning – even if its story lacks a little depth
Author: Emma John
Headline: Scott Gilmour and Claire McKenzie’s audience participation musical gets toes tapping and bodies spinning – even if its story lacks a little depth
Content: Heartwarming … Ceilidh: A New Musical at Shoreditch town hall, London.Photograph: Luke DysonView image in fullscreenHeartwarming … Ceilidh: A New Musical at Shoreditch town hall, London.Photograph: Luke DysonMusicalsReviewCeilidh: A New Musical review – a joyous, riotous celebration of Scottish culture gets the audience on its feetShoreditch town hall, LondonScott Gilmour and Claire McKenzie’s audience participation musical gets toes tapping and bodies spinning – even if its story lacks a little depthEmma JohnFri 30 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s only one thing you need to know before you dance in a ceilidh, we’re told at the start of this show: “In 2,000 years, no one has ever looked good doing it.” But who notices, or cares, when they’re spinning dizzyingly in a joyful mass of bodies? Certainly not the audience at Shoreditch town hall, as they took to the floor in Scott Gilmour and Claire McKenzie’s interactive new musical.Staged in the round, with ample space for stripping the willow, Ceilidh is directed by Sam Pinkleton, whose Tony-winning Oh, Mary!proved what he can do with anarchic energy. It began its UK tour at the Pitlochry festival theatre after a short run in the US and feels like an authentic community event. Before curtain-up, actor-musicians mill sociably with the punters on the dancefloor, and by the time the bodhrán rhythms kick off in earnest, every toe is tapping in anticipation.View image in fullscreenAnarchic energy … Ceilidh: A New Musical at Shoreditch town hall, London.Photograph: Luke DysonWhich is important because, as our caller Ramsay – played by Gilmour himself – explains, we’re all invited to join in the dances, which punctuate the story of his father, Leo (David Rankine), and his blossoming romance with English rose Uena (Kirsty Findlay). Gilmour and McKenzie’s book and lyrics are full of Scottish wit, delivered with a bracing bluntness (Star Penders’ hilarious Granny Maclavaney is a woman who can “eat an entire shepherd’s pie in 90 seconds”). There’s a glorious meet-cute in a Glasgow chippie, and Laura Lovemore is a grinding, pouting riot as Uena’s best friend, to whose wedding we become de facto guests.‘Ceilidh renaissance’ lures gen Z offline in search of real-life joyRead moreThese vignettes are overlaid with a full bingo card of Scottish traditions, from piping in the haggis to the bells of Hogmanay. The fragility of memory is a key theme – one barnstorming number traces the comically hazy passing down of dance moves through the generations – alongside a message of inclusivity that’s heartwarmingly, if unsubtly, conveyed. As an inveterate joiner-inner, I loved the experience; I also wondered whether those who chose simply to observe would feel well enough served by a narrative that never quite allows the characters enough time or depth.AtShoreditch town hall, London, until 13 November, then touring until 7 March 2027Explore more on these topicsMusicalsTheatreImmersive theatreLondon listingsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: LSO/Pappano review – Kendall’s engaging new work has a tea kettle, tremolo and slam-dunks of timpani | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The British composer’s ‘i have discovered the secret of death’ was beguiling and compelling, the centrepiece of a programme that saw Pappano and the London Symphony Orchestra firing on all cylinders
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: The British composer’s ‘i have discovered the secret of death’ was beguiling and compelling, the centrepiece of a programme that saw Pappano and the London Symphony Orchestra firing on all cylinders
Content: Communicating with disturbing clarity … Fleur Barron and Hannah Kendall at the composer’s world premiere at the Barbican on 29 October.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenCommunicating with disturbing clarity … Fleur Barron and Hannah Kendall at the composer’s world premiere at the Barbican on 29 October.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewLSO/Pappano review – Kendall’s engaging new work has a tea kettle, tremolo and slam-dunks of timpaniBarbican, LondonThe British composer’s ‘i have discovered the secret of death’ was beguiling and compelling, the centrepiece of a programme that saw Pappano and the London Symphony Orchestra firing on all cylindersFlora WillsonFri 30 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStage resets between musical works are a standard feature of orchestral concerts: pianos are moved around, additional players file on or off. But I’ve never before seen a tea kettle brought on and placed ceremoniously at the front of the stage, as occurred ahead of the world premiere ofHannah Kendall’s LSO commission I have discovered the secret of death. But thenKendall’s music is vibrantly unconventional, often incorporating noise-makers from beyond classical music’s usual lineup.Her latest work was exceptionally engaging, the beguiling textures of its opening – scratches and whistles, jingles and nervous twitches of piano tremolo – periodically interrupted by violent slam-dunks of timpani, double bass pizzicato, low brass. Later there were music boxes (a hallmark of Kendall’s scoring) and the narrow whine of woodwind reeds detached from instruments.Mezzo-sopranoFleur Barronwas amplified but positioned less as a soloist, more as another line within the orchestra as she sang through her hands, a harmonica and that whistling tea kettle. Her diction was crystalline, her tone urgently compelling, but only certain words and phrases – by Guyanese poet and activistMartin Carter– were audible through these physical barriers. Kendall’s long programme note explained the significance of kettles in the history of slavery as a means of resistance. But what communicated with disturbing clarity through her music alone was struggle: to speak and even to breathe.The rest of the programme could hardly have been more different. Under Antonio Pappano, Liadov’s maximalist miniature The Enchanted Lake was all glistening surface – as exquisitely saccharine as if Wagner’s Tristan had procreated with a candyfloss machine. After the interval,Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No 5 was served as a vast dollop of heart-on-sleeve romanticism. The fine print was mostly present and correct: passages of rustic oompah in the first movement, a deliciously tender horn solo in the second, witty phrasing in the waltz of the third. But for long stretches, Pappano had the LSO firing on all cylinders, Tchaikovsky’s countermelodies and rhythmic chugging as prominent as any big tune, the climaxes turned up to brash. It certainly wasn’t subtle – but when as polished as this, the primary-colours approach is also a lot of fun.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicLondon Symphony OrchestraAntonio PappanoExperimental musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Carmen review – Costa-Jackson’s smouldering heroine blazes brightly  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Ginger Costa-Jackson is an elemental and powerful Carmen in this revival of Damiano Michieletto’s 2024 staging that relocates the drama to Franco’s Spain
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Ginger Costa-Jackson is an elemental and powerful Carmen in this revival of Damiano Michieletto’s 2024 staging that relocates the drama to Franco’s Spain
Content: Emotional and thrilling … Ginger Costa-Jackson and Russell Thomas in Carmen.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenEmotional and thrilling … Ginger Costa-Jackson and Russell Thomas in Carmen.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicOperaReviewCarmen review – Costa-Jackson’s smouldering heroine blazes brightlyRoyal Opera House, LondonGinger Costa-Jackson is an elemental and powerful Carmen in this revival of Damiano Michieletto’s 2024 staging that relocates the drama to Franco’s SpainClive PagetFri 30 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDamiano Michieletto’s Carmen has plenty going for it. The Italian director’scolourful 2024 staging,revived here for the second time already, is an effective update of a work where sexual violence can feel normalised if not handled with care. Here, it’s a subtle combination of emotional immaturity, relentless heat and habitual boredom that eventually blows the lid off the pressure cooker.With the action relocated to Franco’s Spain, the oppressive police presence and reactive societal lawlessness ring true, even if Michieletto glosses over the era’s darker elements. In a remote rural community, Carmen and her smuggler associates may be merely kicking against the pricks, but their antiestablishment chutzpah wins hearts and minds from the get-go. None of them are actually freedom fighters, but we root for them as if they were.View image in fullscreenHer fate is on the cards … CarmenPhotograph: Mihaela BodlovicIsolated within a barren Mediterranean landscape, Paolo Fantin’s confining, Hopper-esque buildings heighten the claustrophobic mood. Alessandro Carletti’s torrid lighting does the rest. Carla Teti’s gaudy 70s costumes seem a little stagy – such brightly clad smugglers would be shot on sight – but the vibe is, on the whole, authentic. Within this Latin nowheresville, Carmen, the only local with a bit of get-up-and-go, almost wills the unfolding tragedy – a change, after all, is as good as a rest.The production has its faults. Don José’s mother popping up as a symbol of fate is overused and over literal (and why can only Carmen see her?). Worse, though, is the cutesy parade of children during the entr’actes, which ruins some of Bizet’s most charming music, while their comedic presence is increasingly at odds with the onstage brutality. But then Michieletto seems keener on pointing to a certain picaresque quality to be found in Prosper Mérimée’s original novella.It’s a complex staging and Dan Dooner’s revival is a bit rough around the edges. The blocking occasionally feels purposeless, but the chorus, and especially the children, sing well, and Sesto Quatrini’s lively conducting grows bolder as the evening progresses.At the heart of this production isGinger Costa-Jackson’s elemental Carmen, an emotional powder keg, smouldering, smoking and frequently raging against her destiny. Her mounting frustration rarely disturbs the voice, however, which is dark and velvety with a battering ram lower register. Russell Thomas produces a thrilling stream of sound as Don José, rising to an electrifying final scene. Earlier, though, the spark between them sputters, not helped by his having to sing The Flower Song to a brick wall.Adriana González’s phrasing and dynamics lend vocal appeal to Michieletto’s mousey, myopic Micaëla, and Alexander Vinogradov brings swagger and style to the neon-suited toreador. The night, though, belongs to Costa-Jackson, a Carmen who blazes as brightly as any, before inevitably going down in flames.Carmen is at the Royal Opera House, London until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicRoyal Opera HousereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ignorance towards immigration is horrible. It’s not British’: Skepta on his long-awaited return – and his anger at the racist right | Skepta | The Guardian
description: Thirty-three months after it was announced, the grime legend’s new album is coming out. He explains how skinheads, fatherhood and rap history came to bear on its socially conscious contents
Author: Dan Hancox
Headline: Thirty-three months after it was announced, the grime legend’s new album is coming out. He explains how skinheads, fatherhood and rap history came to bear on its socially conscious contents
Content: ‘I’m growing and I’m learning’ … Skepta.Photograph: Jordan HemingwayView image in fullscreen‘I’m growing and I’m learning’ … Skepta.Photograph: Jordan HemingwaySkeptaInterview‘Ignorance towards immigration is horrible. It’s not British’: Skepta on his long-awaited return – and his anger at the racist rightDan HancoxThirty-three months after it was announced, the grime legend’s new album is coming out. He explains how skinheads, fatherhood and rap history came to bear on its socially conscious contentsFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ican’t be perfect,”Skeptasays, pulling a black Arc’tyrex beanie down over a furrowed brow with both hands. “But I can be conscious.” The self-proclaimed king of grime has always been a serious person, wary of fools and time-wasters. Focus is important to him, perhaps becausehe’s often multitasking: balancing his music career, his fashion label Mains, film-making and acting (his debut short, Tribal Mark, came out in 2024), his Big Smoke festival and a house music project, Más Tiempo.He coordinates them all from the scruffy but functional studio in London’s West End where we meet. At one point, he picks up a Rubik’s Cube from the cluttered coffee table, and, over the course of five minutes of conversation, solves it. “This album has been winding me up,” he admits, referring to The Fork and Knife, which is out next week, 33 months after it was first announced. “But I think I’ve actually made something here that is what the people want from me.”Now 44, Skepta isn’t just grappling with the rap elder’s struggle of how to stay relevant in middle age, but also the impact his words carry, and his responsibility to say and do the right thing. He seems newly attached to the idea of being a “conscious” rapper, and more mindful than ever of his past missteps. The mums of his children’s friends are going to hear what he’s spitting about on the radio while they’re all doing the school run, he says – there’s no room for loose talk any more.“Don’t get me wrong,” he says. “I’m human. I’ve made ignorant songs, I’ve made ‘turn up’ [ie party] songs, there’s still that side of me. I’m still Joseph from Tottenham. But I’m growing and I’m learning.”In person, Skepta is wary about not being seen as preachy, a stance bolstered by his experience of talking about politics to his two young children. “They don’t like getting into the isms and schisms,” he says. “That’s some adult shit to them.”The task for the new album, then, is to “deliver these conscious messages, but still have a vibe”, he says. “I’m like, damn Skep, you’ve used your voice for grime, but what’s happened over time is your voice has become something that people believe in and follow – so what are you gonna use your voice for now?”He chose his recent single Innocent Smile, featuring a guest spot from Suggs and hectic breakbeats from Chase and Status, to answer that question. “Don’t ask what happened to my innocent smile,” he spits. “Ain’t no love for an immigrant child.” In the first verse alone he references lyrics by Oasis, J Hus and Mobb Deep, criticises MPs’ scapegoating of immigrants, and celebrates his parents’ resilience, and the journey they made “from Nigeria to Meridian” – Meridian Walk, the Tottenham estate he grew up on.View image in fullscreenFrom Nigeria to Meridian … Skepta.Photograph: Jordan HemingwayThe choice of Suggs for this grandstanding defence of multicultural Britain is no accident. Skepta pulls his collar aside to show me the two-tone neck tattoo he got 14 years ago. “I’ve always loved that movement,” he says. “That was the time when my dad came to the UK, and he was a DJ, so he was always playing ska tunes in the house. I’d see skinheads in my house when I was younger. My dad would come home with his friends from work and start playing his vinyl, and my mum would have her white friends round, Auntie Elaine and Auntie Susannah.”Skepta sees multiculturalism not as an abstract idea, but as something that’s “second nature to me”. It is, he says, at the root of what he does – ska couldn’t have come from anywhere else but the UK’s unique cultural mix, and nor could grime. “A British outlook is a universal one,” he says. “All our kids are mixes of different cultures. Even my parents: my mum’s Igbo, my dad’s Yoruba, and in Nigeria, they’re not supposed to mix, they’ve had wars together. But they came to England, met each other, fell in love and had me. This whole ignorance towards immigration at the moment is horrible. It’s not British. We know who it is when we open the door to the Uber: it’s just people here trying to work.”Skepta’s ongoing reckoning with his personal responsibility is why it has taken him seven years to make his sixth album, and it’s the source of his pride in it, he says. The Fork and Knife, his first full solo record since 2019’s Ignorance Is Bliss, was announced on 1 January 2024, and now it’s complete, it’s not a full-on conscious manifesto but features a fuller sound enhanced by the wisdom of age.Its 15 tracks range from the smooth Chippie, a zouk-flavoured R&B collaboration with French-Malian star Aya Nakamura, to Belly, a fierce eight minutes of grime packed with guest verses from a younger generation of MCs:north-west Londoner Kiboin particular shines through. The new stars are given the opening verses, and, in a clever nod to their roles as elder statesmen, the closing verses by Boy Better Know members JME, Frisco and Skepta himself balance new lyrics with classic old-school punchlines.For two decades, Skepta’s rap style has prioritised sounding clear and direct on the mic over sound effects, gimmicks or skippy flows, but the decades’ battle scars have leant his distinctive voice the authority of experience. The rap swagger is still there on The Fork and Knife, but the sheer bravado of his earlier material (his 2007 debut was called Greatest Hits) has been tempered with epiphanies and reflection. Perhaps the clearest window into his state of mind is the poignant Revenge, a memoir of his mid-career missteps, his subsequent redemption and his resilience after 20 years in music. “It was 2008 when I lost my way … I fucked up the greatest run,” he spits, referring to a time when his reputation as king of the grime underground was clouded by a string of ill-advised mainstream dalliances.Skepta is the rare artist who acknowledges his mistakes head-on: his infamous pornographic music video for 2011 single All Over the House, the playground transphobia of 2009’sDisguise, wearing Gucci and Louis Vuitton in a way that wasnot him, doing the Rolex Sweepwith Timmy Mallet. As a result, these gaffes have become understood as part of his redemption arc – the awards, magazine covers and sold-out shows that have flooded his way since 2016’s Mercury-winning Konnichiwa and its hit singles That’s Not Me and Shutdown.View image in fullscreenSkepta wins the 2016 Mercury prize for his album Konnichiwa.Photograph: Nils Jorgensen/ShutterstockHe apologised again in January 2024, when the artwork for the new album’s first single, Gas Me Up (Diligent), showed a group of men with shaved heads, one of whom had “GAS ME UP” (slang for “hype me up”) tattooed on his skull. There was consternation over its – inadvertent – evocation of the Holocaust; Skepta had intended to draw on the same interest in 1980s British youth culture as the Suggs collaboration. At the time, Skepta vowed “to be more mindful going forward”.Today, he says the issue left him frustrated. He was trying to celebrate the unity found through youth culture that existed in his childhood, in spite of the racism in wider society; his dad would DJ at east London parties “where Black people and skinheads used to link up”. While he acknowledges the misinterpretation, his message hasn’t changed at all: “We’re still definitely British, definitely multicultural, definitely two-tone. This is an important part of my British story.”Also in 2024, he apologised for the contract he signed with Puma in 2022. The sports brand has been on the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions campaign’s boycott list for their sponsorship of the Israel Football Association (IFA). Challenged by fans on social media,Skepta notedthat Puma would soon be severing their ties with the IFA, and said that in hindsight he wished he had stayed independent. “I’ve realised it’s a lot more than reading the small print,” he wrote at the time. “[You’ve] gotta do your due diligence … I am forever a student.”“I’m from Nigeria, innit,” he replies when I ask about the Puma spat. “I’ve spoken about injustices in Nigeria all my career; we see injustices in Sudan, Congo, Palestine, everywhere. And I’m not at the point where I’m doing it for money – I don’t think I’veeverdone it for money.”During the album’s long gestation, Skepta has been thinking a lot about rap’s history, as well as his own. “People like Run-DMC, Public Enemy and Tupac made their rap at a point when Black people were looked at as degenerate, and they made it sophisticated, they had messages,” he says. “But over the years, we’ve been paid – and bought – to start talking about twerking and drugs and foolishness.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSkepta’s engagement with public criticism is perhaps one reason he has more than once managed to recoup lost credibility, and moved forwards where so many of his peers have fallen by the wayside. The other is his unusual self-belief and persistence. It is 19 years since I first interviewed Skepta. On that occasion I arranged the interview by messaging him on MySpace – a few years into underground stardom, he still didn’t have a manager, a PR or a record label – and spoke to him at 2am after he played a small gig in east London. It was 2007, and after a few years of frantic energy, almost everyone had given up on grime. That night, Skepta told me he had had major label prospects, and a collaboration with Mike Skinner, dangled and then withdrawn again.View image in fullscreen‘The journey we’ve been on’ … at this year’s Reading Festival.Photograph: Simone Joyner/Getty ImagesThe Black British club scene was moving rapidly on to funky house, dubstep was beginning to take the international language of “wub-wub” bass to global dancefloors, andDizzee Rascal had just met Calvin Harris. The received wisdom went that the arcane style and bright flame of grime was quickly burning out.Implausibly, pigheadedly, Skepta disagreed. “I believe that we don’t have to change grime to make anyone buy it,” he told me then. “People are running away from grime thinking it’s not working, but they’re sellouts, man. That’s why Boy Better Know is easily going to be the best thing in grime.”Nineteen years later, this August, he played to vast, raucous crowds on the main stages of the Reading and Leeds festivals. I tell him that the same festival I’d attended as a teenager in the 90s was so guitar-heavy that it would have had at most two rap acts on the bill each year. He smiles. “That’s the journey we’ve been on.”Even back in 2007, when Skepta was one of the last men standing in a flailing grime scene being shut out by the British music industry and shut down by the Metropolitan police’s notorious risk-assessmentForm 696, he told me he wanted to write and perform for as wide an audience as possible. In the mid-2020s,pulling in primetime audiences at Glastonbury, that hasn’t changed.View image in fullscreenFamily man … with his daughter River at London Fashion Week in 2023.Photograph: David Fisher/Shutterstock“I love the way rock bands can write,” he says. “I love the way they can write songs that are almost like nursery rhymes, but they’re so impactful, and they mean so much.” He references the unlikely trio of Jamiroquai, the Bee Gees and Oasis. “My aim every time I go into the studio is to make songs that are as big as Wonderwall. I even think about things that Shakespeare wrote that we still use now. It’s always been my mission to make classics.”He recalls touring Europe playing clubs in the late 2000s with dubstep DJs Plastician, Mala, Benga and Skream, when something clicked. At a show in Prague, Skepta found that the London slang and references that were getting acclaim back home weren’t “really hitting. It wasn’t making sense.” It was time to write for an audience beyond the world he grew up in. “If you want to be a world rapper, you need to think of words that the world can say with you, and rap in a way that the world can sing with you,” he says. “Maybe I’ll get Liam Gallagher to come in on the next album and play some maracas.”The fact this is a plausible option is not lost on an MC who grew up in Tottenham. “I’ll never forget the junior that used to sit on the wall in Meridian, swinging his legs,” he says, as if reminding himself as much as anyone else. “I won’t do him dirty.”‘Cantona’s a Kwengletarian!’ Inside the maximalist, magical mentality of rising London Irish rapper KiboRead moreNot long ago Skepta moved out of London for a quieter life, and recently took his son back to the estate where he grew up. “Going to Tottenham brings up a lot of trauma,” he says. “If I ever go to Tottenham, it’s generally to process some trauma.” He wanted his son to understand his dad’s humble origins and the distance between their childhoods: what it means to have a garden, a nice house, financial stability, the humble immigrant dream.What was his son’s response, I ask. “He didn’t give a fuck,” says Skepta immediately, and laughs harder than he has all afternoon. “He’s only four! He’s looking at me like, ‘Dad, can we go and get ice-cream?’” It’s been a long road from there to here, says Skepta. “But I knew it was only a matter of time until people were singing along with me.”The Fork and the Knife is released by Big Smoke/Epic on 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsSkeptaGrimeRapHip-hopMercury prize 2016Black British cultureBritish identity and societyinterviewsShareReuse this content
