title: Susan Saint James obituary | US television | The Guardian
description: US TV star known for the sitcom Kate & Allie and for starring opposite Rock Hudson in McMillan & Wife
Author: Anthony Hayward
Headline: US TV star known for the sitcom Kate & Allie and for starring opposite Rock Hudson in McMillan & Wife
Content: Susan Saint James with Rock Hudson as McMillan & Wife. Their screen relationship was a hit with global audiences.Photograph: ABC/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSusan Saint James with Rock Hudson as McMillan & Wife. Their screen relationship was a hit with global audiences.Photograph: ABC/Everett/ShutterstockUS televisionObituarySusan Saint James obituaryUS TV star known for the sitcom Kate & Allie and for starring opposite Rock Hudson in McMillan & WifeAnthony HaywardFri 30 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSusan Saint James, who has died of pancreatic cancer aged 80, was a major star onUS televisionfor two decades, shooting to worldwide fame alongside Rock Hudson in the police drama McMillan & Wife and playing one of two divorced single mums in the female “odd couple” sitcom Kate & Allie.Saint James was cast as McMillan’s wife, Sally, after being spotted in a 1970 episode of another crime series, McCloud, playing a police officer on the trail of a serial killer. The role of Stewart McMillan, or “Mac”, a debonair San Francisco police commissioner, was Hudson’s first in a TV series after more than two decades as a movie heart-throb in Hollywood’s so-called golden age, alongside sex symbols such asGina LollobrigidaandDoris Day. The husky-voiced Saint James more than held her own in the show, in which she starred for five years from 1971.View image in fullscreenSaint James, left, as Kate, and Jane Curtin as Allie in the 1980s sitcom Kate & Allie, about two divorced single mothers who move in together.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockThe programme’s winning twist is that the apparently scatter-brained Sally is more shrewd than she appears, and often steps in to help her husband, as well as uncovering new crimes. The couple’s social invitations to dinner parties and charity events invariably lead them to discover robbery or murder, too, while at other times Sally herself is targeted by criminals, kidnapped more than once and, predictably, rescued by her loving husband.The screen relationship made McMillan & Wife a hit with global audiences – and its demise came when Saint James left after five series following a contractual dispute. Sally was killed off in a plane crash and the programme returned titled simply McMillan, surviving for only one more series.Saint James switched to comedy for Kate & Allie (1984-89). She played Kate McArdle alongside Jane Curtin as Allie Lowell, two divorcees and former high-school buddies with three children between them who move into a Greenwich Village apartment together to ease their financial and emotional burdens. The two actors had previously played suburban housewives in the 1980 film comedy How to Beat the High Cost of Living and Saint James herself had already gone through two failed marriages.The producers of the show made clear that there was no sexual relationship – the pair’s separate bedrooms with single beds were highly visible.“This is not a statement saying, ‘Girls, leave the guys and go live with your best friend,’” said Saint James. “Kate and Allie didn’t plan this. It’s just the best solution they could think of, and their friendship sustains them.”Like McMillan & Wife, Kate & Allie thrived through the on-screen relationship between the characters, while the sitcom saw the friends go on to start their own catering business as their children grow up.When it ended, Saint James mostly retired from acting – returning to the screen just a handful of times – to bring up her own children and concentrate on voluntary work withSpecial Olympics, an organisation providing opportunities for children and adults with learning disabilities. She also co-owned the soft-rock radio station WZBG based in Litchfield, Connecticut, from its launch in 1992 until its sale in 2024.View image in fullscreenSaint James in the 1977 film Outlaw Blues, co-starring Peter Fonda.Photograph: Warner Bros/Kobal/ShutterstockBorn in Los Angeles, she was the daughter of Constance (nee Geiger), a teacher, and Charles Miller, a toolmaker with a newsreel and movie camera manufacturer. The family moved to Rockford, Illinois, when Charles became president of the model kits and hobby products company Testor.After boarding at a Catholic school, the Woodlands Academy of the Sacred Heart, in Lake Forest, Illinois, Susan had plans to study at Connecticut College, but ditched them when a Life magazine photographer at her brother’s wedding told her she would make a professional model. Moving to New York, she landed a contract with a leading agency.She then spent 18 months modelling in Paris, where she was also a stagehand at L’Olympia music hall, work that included assisting the French singer-actorCharles Aznavour, who encouraged her to act.On returning to the US in 1966, she took acting classes, changed her name to Susan Saint James and, aged 19, signed a seven-year contract with Universal Studios.She walked straight into a part in a TV pilot, Fame Is the Name of the Game (1966), playing Peggy, an editorial assistant, alongside Tony Franciosa as an investigative reporter. It ran as a series titled The Name of the Game (1968-71) and won Saint James a Primetime Emmy award in 1969 (followed by two more nominations). She earned further Emmy nominations for McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie.In between those programmes, she acted in run-of-the-mill TV movies while enjoying film roles asPeter Fonda’s girlfriend in Outlaw Blues (1977) and, with her dark hair dyed blond, the love interest of Dracula (George Hamilton) in the hit 1979 vampire spoof Love at First Bite. (“Even industry people didn’t recognise me as the blond model, though I shared top billing,” she said.)View image in fullscreenGeorge Hamilton and Saint James in the spoof vampire film Love at First Bite, 1979.Photograph: American International Pictures/Everett/ShutterstockShe was also seen as a war correspondent in a 1980 episode of the sitcom M*A*S*H, and had a brief relationship with the musician Stephen Stills of Crosby Stills & Nash.In later years Saint James occasionally appeared on television in series such as Law & Order: Special Victims Unit (in 2006), Suits (in 2011) and Upload (2020-22).Her first two marriages, to the scriptwriter Richard Neubert (1967-68) and Tom Lucas, a make-up artist (1971-77), ended in divorce. In 1981, she married Dick Ebersol, a television executive. Their son Teddy died in 2004.Ebersol and their other sons, Charlie and Willie, survive her, along with Sunshine and Harmony, the children from her second marriage, a sister, Mercedes, and seven grandchildren.Susan Saint James (Susan Jane Miller), actor, born 14 August 1946; died 26 October 2026Explore more on these topicsUS televisionTelevisionobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Everyone is thin and we’re not allowed to say so: the toxic legacy of body positivity | Life and style | The Guardian
description: In the late 2010s, a movement argued that no one body type is superior than another. Now in the GLP-1 age, people are still pursuing thinness - and just not talking about it
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: In the late 2010s, a movement argued that no one body type is superior than another. Now in the GLP-1 age, people are still pursuing thinness - and just not talking about it
Content: Body positivity has all but vanished within mainstream visual culture.Photograph:  Jill Connelly /Bloomberg via GettyView image in fullscreenBody positivity has all but vanished within mainstream visual culture.Photograph:  Jill Connelly /Bloomberg via GettyLife and styleEveryone is thin and we’re not allowed to say so: the toxic legacy of body positivityIn the late 2010s, a movement argued that no one body type is superior than another. Now in the GLP-1 age, people are still pursuing thinness - and just not talking about itHannah MarriottFri 30 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVogue World Milano was held beneath the vaulted glass domes of Italy’soldest shopping arcade, featuring Gigi Hadid in archival Valentino couture and robots dancing on the catwalk while Miuccia Prada scowled at them. A splashy event staged in the midst of a month of fashion shows in New York, London, Milan and Paris, in which97.5%of models were a US size four or under, what ticked people off most was the presence of trillion-dollar pharma company Eli Lilly on the list of sponsors.Eating disorder advocates spoke out against the association between an aspirational fashion show and the manufacturer of the weight-loss drugs Zepbound and Mounjaro.Fans of doublespeak, however, would have found much to enjoy in the language an Eli Lilly spokesperson usedto defend the partnership, sayingit collaborates with “cultural platforms like Vogue … because that is where conversations about bodies and health take place. Lilly is working to shift the conversation about weight from aesthetics to health and to challenge the stigma people with obesity face every day.”View image in fullscreenThe runway during Vogue World: Milano 2026 at Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II on September 22, 2026 in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images for VogueSo to summarise, Eli Lilly is partnering with Vogue – a byword for fashion, glamour and thinness for more than a century – in order to shift the conversationawayfrom aesthetics.But Eli Lilly is not alone in serving word salad in this bewildering moment.We are living through a strange time in the language around bodies. Body positivity – a movement which peaked in the late 2010s, and argued that no one body type is morally, sexually or aesthetically superior to any other – has all but vanished within mainstream visual culture. At the same time, much of its social training lingers.During the body positivity movement’s peak, of the late 2010s, many of us learned to try to think differently about bodies – our own, and other people’s. All bodies are beautiful, we were told, first by activists, then by brands which used those ideas to sell deodorant. At the same time, phrases such as “fat shaming” and “body shaming” went viral as high-profile women revealed the pain wrought by relentless objectification by industry gatekeepers, trolls, fans and the media in the previous decade. We learned, too, that casual body chat could be actively damaging for people suffering from eating disorders. Diet chat became taboo. Self-acceptance, not skinniness, was the prize, we learned – or, at least, we tried to.double quotation markSelf-acceptance feels like a relic from the pre-Covid eraWe are now in a very different moment, with ideals shaped by a very different set of cultural and economic forces. Self-improvement strategies are pushed at us near-constantly. Social media feeds are thick with thin fitness influencers, GLP-1 before and afters, and injector-influencers advising us how we can jab our way to our best ever faces. A million GLP-1, Botox and plastic surgery adverts stare down at us from billboards and in doctor’s offices. The dominant narrative suggests we can have near-perfect control over our bodies, if we just have the time, taste and budget. Self-acceptance feels like a relic from the pre-Covid era.View image in fullscreenA body equality campaign for Old Navy displayed in New York City.Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images for Old NavyStill, in many circles, it remains socially frowned on to talk about weight loss as an aesthetic goal – even as weight loss could scarcely be more high profile, with many GLP-1 drug adverts citing average pounds lost, and telehealth companies targeting slim people who want tolose the “last 10lb” on social media.It remains taboo to overtly venerate thinness – particularly within the sanctioned spaces of media interviews or marketing for large corporations – or even to admit to noticing thinness in other people, yet slimness has never been more culturally rewarded. It’s hard to ignore the reality that so many high-profile people, now, from actors playing cops on TV, to Instagram chefs to musicians selling us beauty products, appear to be shrinking. What we’re left with is a world in which skinny bodies are lionized in fashion, culture and daily life, but to either admit a desire to conform, or express concern about it, feels socially verboten.What body positivity wasBody positivity has radical roots, said Tigress Osborn, chair of the National Association to Advance Fat Acceptance (NAAFA). The phrase has been used by eating disorder therapists, and “especially fat liberation and fat activists”, she said, since at least the 1990s. Osborn views the phrase in tandem with other “body liberation” movements, includingHealthat Every Size, which argues that higher bodyweight should not be pathologised, and also “bodily autonomy”, not only in terms of sexual freedom or reproduction, but meaning “you own yourself and you get to do what you want” with your body.Its mainstream adoption began with plus-sized people, who posted pictures, on Tumblr and Instagram, along with captions of self-love and self-acceptance along with the hashtag #BoPo. Gradually, those ideas went viral.I thought we’d entered the age of body positivity. Then came ‘shrinking girl summer’ – is everyone getting smaller except me?Read moreWhat followed was heralded as a golden age of body inclusivity. In 2015, the model Tess Holliday was billed as “the world’s first size 22 supermodel” on the cover of People magazine. The rise of celebrities who didn’t fit the usual skinny celebrity mould like Meghan Trainor, with her 2014 body positivity anthem All About that Bass, and plus-sized superstar Lizzo, who rapped joyfully about “getting thicker” became part of a cultural narrative. Mainstream brands soon jumped on board, with campaigns urging body positivity through the purchase ofself-tanandleggings. Luxury fashion tentatively followed suit, with US Vogue featuring a plus-sized model, Ashley Graham, on its cover for the first time in 2017, though the composition of the shot – wedged between straight-sized models, so that the contours of her body were not visible – raised immediate questions about the authenticity of this apparent milestone. Though, by the time Lizzo covered US Vogue in 2020, as the first Black plus-sized woman to do so, presented in a full-body shot wearing tomato red Valentino chiffon, the movement’s impact on the highest echelons of fashion felt more certain.The way body positivity was embraced by the fashion industry could sometimes feel hollow. Osborn describes peak body positivity as: “you go, girl!” She said that it was still “radical to declare that you love yourself in a world that is constantly telling you that you should hate yourself” but said the industry’s focus was only on the “personal and individual” and not about trying to “change or dismantle systems”.Others said it glorified obesity. One plus-sized influencer, Gabriella Lascano, said thatthe cultural movement ignored health concernsand encouraged her to put her own wellbeing at risk. (The CDClinks obesity to an increased risk of many serious diseases and conditions, thoughfitness is a better indicator of health than BMIand it is amisconceptionthat better health always means a smaller body.)What most people agreed on was that its adoption by companies wishing to sell products often felt inauthentic.In mainstream consumer spaces, brands from Dove to Aerie to Lane Bryant were using body positivity slogans, and more diverse models and influencer-ambassadors, to try to sell products.The more mainstream things got, said former body-positivity activistMatthew Diaz, the more the same beauty standards it was supposedly railing against came into play. Those being “lifted up”, he said, were only “slightly outside what would be considered acceptable by the norm, but by no means representative of the biggest swaths of the community”.View image in fullscreenAn advert for Lane Bryant’s plus-sized lingerie line, Cacique.Photograph: Thomas Iannaccone/WWD/Penske Media/Getty ImagesAs a consequence, Diaz grew to question the term itself which, he said, “still focuses a lot on appearances, but just allows for more diversification”. He is now a “body neutrality advocate” a concept which, “decentres your appearance. The issue isn’t that my body isn’t right. The issue is that I am deriving all of my value from it.”Within luxury fashion, body positivity did have a limited impact. In the late 1990s and 2000s, plus-sized models were virtually nonexistent on luxury catwalks. Extreme catwalk skinniness, on the other hand, was so ubiquitous that it prompted frequent public outcries, andindustry initiatives were establishedto protect models, particularly after two modelsdied from complications of anorexia in 2006.During the body-positivity era, according to online publication the Fashion Spot, which tracked catwalk diversity between 2015 and 2022, there was a trend towards diversity: only six plus-sized models walked in the fall 2016 season, but there were 50 in fall 2020, and arecord 103, or 2.34% of all castings, in fall 2022. Since then, though, according to Vogue Business, which uses slightly different metrics and began tracking shows in 2023, size diversity has decreased. Ninety-five per cent of looks were shown on straight-sizemodels (US sizes 0-4) in 2023 and 2024. That has risen to 97% in the two years since.Many household name brands didn’t do body positivity at all (one academic studyfound that Calvin Klein, Versace and Chanel did not use a single plus-sized model between 2013 and 2018.) Even so – from a very low bar – the presence of even a couple of plus-sized models in, say, every third or fourth fashion week show felt like progress.double quotation markWe’re living in a twilight zone where you can’t comment on something that’s clearly unhealthy without sounding meanAnastasia VartanianBehind the scenes, though, inclusivity wasn’t really part of the business model, saidMichaela Stark, an artist, model and couturier who worked in fashion at the peak of body positivity. Brands often didn’t actually make clothes in plus sizes, even when they modelled them on plus-sized models (as was the case with Paloma Elsesser’s 2022 I-D cover, on which she later commented: “I am not just going to wear a stretchy dress. I’m wearing the Miu Miu” – when Miu Miu did not make clothes in her size in reality.)For hundreds of years, said Stark, “every single micro level of fashion has catered to creating clothes for an ultra-thin body. Brands would have to invest a whole lot of money and expertise into reinventing that.” That didn’t happen.She would sometimes help cast diverse models for brands, and the process could be painful. At one shoot for a magazine in Paris, a creative director asked her to cast models as though from a shopping list, she said: “It was like: one Black, one Asian, one old, one fat. You’re not casting these people because of who they are. You’re just trying to tick every box,” she said. She modelled herself and remembers a stylist telling her: “You look like a squished sausage!” Her own artistic work – she creates corsets which accentuate rolls of flesh – was branded as “body positivity” which did not sit right with her, “not because I don’t strongly believe in the ethos, but because, in the peak, you could feel people doing it for cultural validation”.The impacts of body positivity, even at its peak, remain contested.Severalstudiesfound viewing body positive imagerybeneficial for individuals’mood and body satisfaction in the short term; others claim otherwise. But it was this inauthenticity that put off the next generation of young fashion fans, said Anastasia Vartanian, who writes as @FatAnnaWintour– a name wittily capturing the tension she felt as a curvy, teenage Tumblr fashion obsessive. They found the worthiness “cringy”, she says, and overcorrected. Among young people now, “it’s almost now cool to be problematic,” she says. As the Y2K trend infiltrated young people’s wardrobes, she started noticing “a lot of worship of old 2000s runways” online, featuring pictures of very thin models posted with captions along the lines of: “bring back real models!” and “fashion’s not the same any more!”Vartanian said what has happened since “is really wild. It’s unsettling how a lot of people in the public eye are so very thin. And it feels as though we’re living in a twilight zone where you can’t comment on something that’s clearly unhealthy without sounding mean. But some people are using the language of body positivity, even body neutrality, towards what is clearly anorexia, and I’m finding that such a headfuck.”An unnamable thing called thinnessWhat body positivity has changed, and profoundly, islanguage.In the 00s it was commonplace for objectively slender celebrities to be labelled “porky” in the tabloids, acceptable for Victoria Beckham to be weighed on live TV, for Karl Lagerfeld to say “no one wants to see curvy women” or blame “the hole in social security” on “all the diseases caught by people who are too fat” (Lagerfeld lost 90lb himself in the early 2000s. Perhaps he was hungry.)It was normalized, too, for Victoria’s Secret models to detail their grueling preshow routines. In 2011, for example, model Adriana Lima said shedid not eat solid food for nine daysbefore walking the catwalk in her undies. And who could blame her? Because, during this time, famous women were constantly told they were too fat by producers and impresarios. It was so normalised that when, in 2004, Simon Cowell told a 19-year-old X Factor auditionee she wastoo overweight to be a pop star, Sharon Osbourne – the good cop in this scenario – invited her to the next round by saying, with a kind smile: “Mrs, go on a diet.”double quotation markIf you want to lose weight with these drugs that’s your business. But you shouldn’t be sociopolitically coerced into itTigress OsbornMuch of the pushback against this kind of talk came from high-profile women themselves, who spoke out against the scrutiny they had faced for decades. Ashley Graham, for one, wrote a viral essay declaring: “The cycle of body-shaming needs to end.I’m over it.” Jessica Simpson, Keira Knightley, Hayley Atwell, Jennifer Lawrence all made similar comments. In a receptive, peak #MeToo era, the tide turned.Then came Ozempic. Even body-positivity icons including Trainor and Lizzo lost weight with semaglutides. Oprah, whose yo-yo diets and weight struggles had been watched like a soap opera for decades by the public, spent most of 2023 talking about her GLP-1 weight loss experiences while promoting a book she co-authored, Enough: Your Weight, Your Health, and What It’s Like to Be Free.Fans expressed disappointment as these women became icons for something else entirely: the idea that, deep down, we had all wanted to be thin anyway. As ever, individual women were taken to task, and were understandably annoyed about it. AsAdele said: “It’s not my job to validate how people feel about their bodies – I feel bad that it’s made people feel horrible about themselves but it’s not my job. I’m trying to sort my own life out.”The average GLP-1 weight loss is 10-20% within one year, meaning many plus-sized people who take GLP-1s remain plus-sized afterwards, Lizzo included. Yet the narrative about fatness has shifted profoundly.View image in fullscreenA person walks down the steps past an ad showing Megan Fox in a campaign for telehealth company Ro at the Times Square subway station in New York City.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesNow, talking about weight loss for aesthetics remains taboo – but talking about weight and health is a different story. For people in larger bodies, whom others believe would be healthier if slimmer, “it emboldens literally everyone,” said Osborn. “People get to tell themselves that they’re being kind to you by telling you that you should be using it.” This pressure, she feels, is at odds with bodily autonomy: “If you want to lose weight with these drugs that’s your business. But you shouldn’t be sociopolitically coerced into it.”Weight goes unsaidIn June 2021, at the same time the first GLP-1, Wegovy, was approved for weight loss, social media was shifting profoundly. TikTok was booming; it became the world’smost-downloaded appin 2022. The workings of its algorithm, though notoriously opaque, were very different from what had come before. It’s For You page apparently served content based on demographics and engagement, rather than prioritizing content from accounts users had chosen to follow.This seemed to skew thin: studies found that TikTok perpetuated “toxic diet culture” and promoted the misconception that “weight is the most important measure of a person’s health”. Instagram’s feed changed accordingly. The idea that our better selves could “curate our feed” – a frequent refrain in the body positivity era, when campaigners urged us to follow accounts representing a variety of different bodies – no longer felt possible.Many women reported feeds flooded with GLP-1 content, fitness chat and plastic surgery before-and-afters. Eating disorders had mushroomed during Covid and, for some, this contributed to very serious mental health issues. In 2025,TikTok announcedthat it had banned a hashtag – #SkinnyTok – which promoted disordered eating. But much worrying content still remains, and is very easily accessed. Amanda Raffoul, a University of Toronto assistant professor, explains that “the particular unique danger of the modern age of social media is the algorithmic funneling”, because content is pushed “to people who might not have been seeking it out in the first place”. The apps are doing better, she said, in banning “blatantly pro-eating disorder” content. But there is so much “grey area content that platforms are either not succeeding, or maybe don’t care to do a good job in eliminating, because it reaches larger audiences and is more profit-generating”.Is it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answerRead moreImages of certain celebrities have fuelled week-long churn cycles, as when Ariana Grande appeared looking desperately thin in her Petal music video. The debates about whether it was OK to comment about her appearance fuelled the story for days. And there isn’t a right answer, said Raffoul, adding that even those working to combat eating disorders struggle. If you were worried about a person in your real life circle, she said, the advice would be straightforward: “you ask them about how they’re feeling. But we can’t ask a celebrity, ‘Hey, girl, how you doing?’ And those people have social capital.” Picking apart an individual is counterproductive, but also: “what message are we relaying if we say nothing?”There is no right answer, so debates abound, which appears to be how the algorithm likes it.And still, for all of the noise in the comments, in the legitimized spaces of school gates and red carpet interviews and offices, the idea that we might want to be skinny is only ever uttered in a whisper.Fitness does a lot of heavy lifting. As one nutritionist, Hadlee Garrison, put it in arecently posted video liked by 40,000 people, titled “Girl from 2006 meets girl from 2026”, we have developed a new lexicon. Influencers talk about macros, not calories. Looking snatched or toned, not looking skinny. Our feeds are full of advice on eating more protein, achieving calorie deficits, but never diets.View image in fullscreenAthletes and influencers participate in a fitness session hosted by Liquid IV at 1 Hotel San Francisco on 7 February 2026 in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Presley Ann/Getty Images for TikTokAs 2026 girl explains, she never weighs herself. “The scale is such a flawed metric,” she said. “I do a body-composition scan. It tells your fat percentage, visceral fat, lean mass, water weight, metabolic age.”This week’s Victoria Secret show demonstrated the shift. Preparation, in 2026, is not about avoiding food, said Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. It’s “a mindset more than anything” it’s about “feeling strong and fit, as opposed to thinking about a number on the scales or on a measuring tape”. Yes, there is strength training, rest, hydration and protein, lymphatic drainage, cold plunges and facials, but “nothing is off the table for me ever with my diet”.And so word salad abounds.Fashion magazines that would never openly applaud skinniness run galleries titled: “Abs Are the Best Beauty Flex at the 2026 Grammys”. Influencer-injectors claim they would never comment on, for example, Susan Dell’s face – before unpicking “why this look can happen and what you can do if you feel like it’s happening to you”, and asking, amusingly, while pointing at a picture of Dell’s face: “now, what are the key features that stand out that look human?”Demi Moore, who looks about 25 in her 60s, stars in People magazine’s World’s Most Beautiful People issue, while saying her appearance “doesn’t define my value or who I am”, then promotes Lancome’s Absolue Longevity MD range which, she said, is “moving away from this idea that we’re fighting something through anti-ageing”. The product’s aim, rather, is to “reverse the skin’s visible biological age at every life stage”, which sounds quite similar.What we are left with is doublespeak – as the rhetoric popularised in the body positivity era is skewed to fit a very different purpose – or silence, as friends shrink before our eyes and we don’t say a word, or celebrities become stick-thin and it feels unsisterly to notice. In many real-life circles, weight becomes the great unsaid, an issue that is too grave to look at directly. Only in the anonymity of the comment section, are bodies truly discussed – ad nauseam and for hours.Recently, though, when the Practical Magic 2 star Joey King responded to speculation that she had had a facelift at 26 – after the internet described her as “snatched” on the Met Gala red carpet – she revealed her actual pregame tactics. A36-hour fast– “No food, nothing but water … I don’t promote that,” she said – and lymphatic drainage. There was remarkably little pushback or handwringing about that online – rather it was presented in some headlines using the body-positivity era language of her “shutting down” facelift rumours. Perhaps, finally, there was nothing to argue about. At least she was being honest.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleWeight-loss drugsHealthDiets and dietingModelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dripping with style: what fashion insiders wear in the rain – plus we pick the best raincoats and accessories | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Top tips on how to stay dry and stylish from those who know. Plus this autumn’s best rain gear, from practical jackets to puddle-proof boots
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Top tips on how to stay dry and stylish from those who know. Plus this autumn’s best rain gear, from practical jackets to puddle-proof boots
Content: Photographs: Martina Lang/The Guardian. Hat, £25,Didriksons. Jacket, £198,Lululemon. Styling: Melanie Wilkinson. Set design: Lee Flude. Model: Roberta at Milk. Hair and makeup: Sophie Higginson using Sam McKnight and Kama AyurvedaView image in fullscreenPhotographs: Martina Lang/The Guardian. Hat, £25,Didriksons. Jacket, £198,Lululemon. Styling: Melanie Wilkinson. Set design: Lee Flude. Model: Roberta at Milk. Hair and makeup: Sophie Higginson using Sam McKnight and Kama AyurvedaGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FashionDripping with style: what fashion insiders wear in the rain – plus we pick the best raincoats and accessoriesTop tips on how to stay dryandstylish from those who know how. Plus this autumn’s best rain gear, from practical jackets to puddle-proof bootsInterviews byEllie Violet BramleyFri 30 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenJess Cartner-MorleyAssociate fashion editor for the GuardianThere is a way to look chic in a downpour. Outside fancy hotels or swanky fashion parties they have men (not being sexist, it just is always men) whose job it is to greet you with an enormous umbrella as you step out of your Uber and provide shelter until you are safely inside. This is both effective and aesthetically pleasing.Alas, not a practical everyday strategy. Look, I have thought about this a lot, because I have the kind of pathetic fine hair that is plastered forlornly to my head after 30 seconds in drizzle. Still, we want to be rain-ready without looking aggressively practical. A 50% chance of rain is not the apocalypse. And it’s a hard no to the umbrella alone: good ones are cumbersome; the flimsy kind that fit in a handbag are profoundly depressing – and either way those spikes are borderline sociopathic.View image in fullscreenBarbour Carville jacket;M&S Chelsea bootsBut hoods make coats look so juvenile! My solution is a hood that detaches, and bellow pockets so that the hood can be folded up within one of these except when it’s actually raining. I have a trusty old Barbour – similar to its currentCarville style. Set an alarm on Vinted. You may want to be quite snappy about it: Claudia is wearing a v similar Barbour on Celebrity Traitors this season (theMarron), which means everyone will be after one.Also, a sturdy boot. I choose a low block heel over a flat, because it keeps your jeans hem out of puddles, and a cleated sole rather than a flat one, for grip and durability. A pull-on M&SChelsea bootworks with tights and skirts as well as with trousers.If all else fails, stand outside Claridge’s looking helpless.Aja BarberWriter and sustainability consultantI’m very unfussy and I don’t like my rainy-day aesthetic to look too different from my non-rainy-day aesthetic. But when it’s raining cats and dogs, I use myPonch poncho– it’s recycled and colourful; rather joyful for a poncho. Or I’ll use my umbrella – I likethe rainbow one from Roka. I enjoy an umbrella because you can share it and huddle together with a friend or a lover, laughing hysterically as you try not to get wet.View image in fullscreenPonch poncho;Roka rainbow umbrellaI often don’t bother with waterproof footwear, but again, if it’s really bad I go for the J Crew rubber Chelsea boot that I’ve had for decades (before I swore offallfast fashion). I tend to wear a lot ofEgg baggy short trousers,but I mostly buy them secondhand because they’re expensive new.Sometimes a downpour is unavoidable. When I moved to the UK, I decided no more blowouts and straighteners. That way I’m never upset. I recommend becoming low maintenance to anyone and everyone.View image in fullscreenRain jacket, £80,Tretorn. Dress, £89,Boden. Socks, £14, by My Accessories London, fromAsos. Wellies, £150,Wellipets. Dog rain coat, £49.95,Barbour. Canine model: PercyView image in fullscreenLuke TurnerAuthor and editorWhat I wear to keep dry depends on where I am. If I’m on a proper walk in the countryside, I’ll wear my Berghaus waterproof Cornice jacket, which I’ve had for about 20 years (they still sellan updated version). It keeps me bone-dry and has good breathability, but it is pretty ugly.In a city, I’ll wear my old rubberised-cotton black railway jacket from my favourite shop,Levisons. I love mine – it’s very solid and keeps me dry, but it is a bit like a portable sauna. I also have acompromise Barbour jacket, which I’ll wear if I’m going for a little walk in the forest. But prices have gone up a lot since I bought mine two years ago.I don’t really bother with waterproof trousers. I do have apair, also from Berghaus, but I always forget or don’t bother to put them on. It just starts raining and you think: “Sod it.”View image in fullscreenBerghaus waterproof jacket;Scarpa walking bootsI don’t worry too much about getting my head wet in the rain – it’s a good feeling, so even if I’m wearing my cagoule, I generally walk along with my hood off. And I honestly think umbrellas should be banned in city centres.My feet are a different story. If I’m in the forest in winter I have a pair ofgood quality Le Chameau wellies.The amount of wellies I used to get through because they break … but these are amazing and have lasted ages. Otherwise, I wearleather walking boots from Scarpa. I always wear them to music festivals, because they’re so comfortable that I can yomp around in them for days. For rainy days in the city, I doDr Martens 16-hole boots in soft leather. I’ve worn them since I was a teenage Suede fan. They’re so comfy – I’ve got bad knees, so the bouncy soles really help.I like to think about shape when it comes to keeping stylish in the rain. I like 60s and 70s outdoor wear, in oranges and yellow, or muted olive greens.Rag Parade/Jojo’s General Store in Sheffield always seems to have the nicest pieces. The way that those things are cut is really nice compared with the super-scientifically designed garments of today.View image in fullscreenCaryn FranklinFashion and identity commentatorI like simplicity when it comes to rainy-day dressing. I have awaterproof backpack by Rains, which I wear over a plain black coat. On my bottom half I like calf-length skirts; long trousers always gather water at the back and then the moisture creeps up the leg. Sometimes I’ll wear jeans rolled up or I pull in the strings of my khaki fatigues to look a bit, to my mind, Clockwork Orange.On my feet, I wear vegan leather high-ankle boots with elastic sides from ethical footwear company Po-Zu, which is sadly now closed, althoughMatt & Nat has a good match– think rounded-toe Chelsea boots. The great thing about vegan leather is that it’s totally waterproof. And I like a thick, knee-length sock to protect against the cold. I buyblack thermal knee-high ones from M&S.If things are really bad – dog-walking paths in Suffolk can get very watery – I’ll wear a pair of waterproof trousers with an old military showerproof coat I bought secondhand (Etsy is good for army surplus). I tuck my trousers in myknee-high Frostline wellingtons by Grubs. The upper leg is made from neoprene and they are soft underfoot, like slippers.View image in fullscreenGrubs insulated wellies;Rains rolltop rucksackKey for me in any wet weather situation is keeping my hair dry and under control. It’s long and grey and can turn into frizzy candyfloss in the rain, or even if there’s drizzly moisture in the air. One answer is to wear it back, which I do a lot. To control it, and minimise water and humidity damage, I use a Kiehl’s diluted texturising clay from the crown to the ponytail band, which keeps everything flat to my scalp. It’s now discontinued, butSalt Grooming’s Compound Clayis a good option and it’s paraben-free. The key is that it’s off-white in colour and that is good for my grey hair. I dilute it with water and smooth it over my hair. Then I plait the rest.Another defence mechanism is my magic umbrella from Knirps.Sadly, it no longer makes the kind I have, which folds into a sturdy holder in my bag if it looks like rain, and can be put straight back in the holder – that way, I haven’t lost any umbrellas for a long time.ButAnatolehas one that’s made fromrecycled plastic bottles – it’s 100% rPET, has a wooden handle, a sustainable canopy and is only 17.5cm long.View image in fullscreenPoncho, £55,Tretorn. Umbrella, £39,Original Duckhead. Trousers, £39.90,Uniqlo. Ankle Wellies, £90,Merry PeopleView image in fullscreenDal ChodhaWriter, editor andpathway leader at Central Saint MartinsI like to wear as few layers as possible – one or two, max – whether it’s raining or not. Just because it’s raining, it doesn’t mean that I change the fabrics I like to wear. That means I wouldn’t necessarily have anything that’s technically proficient in keeping me dry, but I did recently buy acotton cape from a London-based brand called Sono. It’s based – I think – on an old 80s German cycling cagoule. It’s a rectangle of fabric with a hole in the middle and a hood, then two belt loops at the sides that keep it closer to your body. I don’t shop for clothes often, so when I add something to my wardrobe, it’s with the understanding that it’s going to be there a long time. If it’s cold and raining I will simply wear my cape with a jumper wrapped around my neck as a scarf.I can get away with not wearing something more sturdy because I live in a city. You get splashed and then you dry off, especially if wearing natural fabrics.View image in fullscreenTekla Canvas beach bag;Vivobiome ‘barefoot’ footwearOn my feet, if it’s hot and it’s raining I will still wear sandals, but they’rerubber, from Vivobarefoot. When it’srainingraining, I wear a soft shoe, like asneakerballerinafrom a brand I love called Abra. And a few years ago I did buya version of an Ugg boot, also from Abra– they’re waterproof, and slopping about in the rain in those feels heavenly.I hate umbrellas. I’ve tried all manner but I loathe carrying them, so I prefer to let the rain ruin what mistakes God already made.The one thing I do worry about is my bag. If you’ve got a semi-nice bag, or a leather bag, protect it from the rain. On a rainy day I’d go for a nylon or canvas bag instead –Tekla does a good onethat is very thick, andTopologie does some nice nylon alternatives.Also, not to be pretentious, but in some ways the jolt of being wet is a weirdly human experience. I’m a bit likeDrew Barrymore when it rains.15 of the best rainy-day clothes and accessoriesView image in fullscreenWomen’s jacket£115 at the North Face£115 at Ellis BrighamView image in fullscreenCrossbody bag£60 at Stubble and CoView image in fullscreenMen’s clogs£95 at HunterView image in fullscreenUmbrella£45 at London UndercoverView image in fullscreenTote bag£22 at RainkissView image in fullscreenWomen’s raincoat£110 at Seasalt Cornwall£110 at NextView image in fullscreenMen’s trousers£169 at RainsView image in fullscreenWellies£60 at Joules£60 at NextView image in fullscreenMen’s windbreaker£320 at StutterheimView image in fullscreenWomen’s trousers€70 (about £58.63) at Ilse Jacobsen£59.23 at Made in ParadisView image in fullscreenBarbour ankle wellies£70 at Schuh£70 at FlannelsView image in fullscreenWaterproof cap£35 at Sealskinz£30 at AmazonView image in fullscreenBarbour x APC hat£59 at Stuarts London£59.95 at BarbourView image in fullscreenBackpack rain cover£50 at HaglofsView image in fullscreenMen’s jacket£69.90 at UniqloExplore more on these topicsFashionWinter coatsBootsWomen's coats and jacketsMen's coats and jacketsMen's trousersWomen's trousersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Ayllu’s sakura no hana – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: An elegant and slightly flamboyant Japanese-Peruvian fusion with delicate, floral notes and a fruity finish
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An elegant and slightly flamboyant Japanese-Peruvian fusion with delicate, floral notes and a fruity finish
Content: Ayllu’s sakura no hana.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenAyllu’s sakura no hana.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Ayllu’s sakura no hana – recipeAn elegant and slightly flamboyant Japanese-Peruvian fusion with delicate, floral notes and a fruity finishShak NematulloevFri 30 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInspired by our restaurant’s Japanese-Peruvian roots, and to mark the 1-2 November Day of the Dead celebrations, this drink combines white rum and sake with a dash of bitters and a red-wine float: the result is a light, layered cocktail with delicate, floral notes, juicy berry fruit and just enough theatre to impress without being hard to make.Sakura no hanaServes150ml white rum– we use Bacardi25ml sake10ml standard 1:1 sugar syrup2 dashes bitters– we use Angostura15ml red wine, ideally malbec, to float on top1 edible flower(we use a cherry blossom when it’s in season), to garnish (optional)Fill an old fashioned glass with ice, then add all the liquids except the wine and stir to combine. Slowly pour in the malbec, so it sits as a separate layer on top of everything else, garnish with the edible flower, if using, and serve.Shak Nematulloev, bar manager,Ayllu, London W2Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodJapanese food and drinkWinerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s miso-toffee apple hand pies – recipe | Bonfire Night | The Guardian
description: Warm your hands on these sweet little pastries – perfect Bonfire Night fodder!
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: Warm your hands on these sweet little pastries – perfect Bonfire Night fodder!
Content: Helen Goh’s toffee apple hand pies.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s toffee apple hand pies.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotBonfire NightHelen Goh’s miso-toffee apple hand pies – recipeWarm your hands on these sweet little envelopes of gently spiced, toffee-glossed apples wrapped in puff pastry. Perfect Bonfire Night fodderHelen GohFri 30 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese plump and rustic little parcels are perfect for Bonfire Night: warming, portable and, wrapped in a napkin and held in one hand, easy to eat outdoors. Filled with gently spiced, toffee-glossed apples, they are deliberately more homely hand pies than anything overly neat or patisserie-like. The small amount of miso in the filling deepens the toffee flavour and rounds out the sweetness, without making it taste too savoury or funky.Miso-toffee apple hand piesPrep10 minMacerate30 minCook1 hr 15 min, plus chilling and coolingMakes8800g apples, ideally a mixture of granny smith and pink lady (about 3 of each), peeled, cored and cut into 1½-2cm pieces (650g net)80g light brown sugar2tbsp apple cider vinegar1 tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ground nutmeg¼ tsp fine sea salt, plus a generous pinch for the egg wash50g unsalted butter20g white miso1 tsp vanilla extract1 small egg50g plain flour2320g packs shop-bought puff pastry1tbsp demerara sugarPut the apple pieces in a large bowl with the brown sugar, vinegar, cinnamon, nutmeg and salt, and toss to combine. Leave to macerate at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, tossing occasionally.Strain the apples, reserving the liquid; you should have about 100ml. Melt the butter in a large, wide frying pan on a medium-high heat. Add the strained apples and cook, tossing occasionally, for four to five minutes, until they begin to soften. Pour in the reserved liquid and cook for a further three to four minutes, until the liquid reduces and a glossy caramel forms around the apples. Stir in the miso and vanilla until evenly incorporated, then take off the heat. Spread the filling over a tray or large plate, so it can cool quickly, then refrigerate until completely cold.To assemble, lightly beat the egg with a generous pinch of salt and put the flour in a small dish. Unroll one sheet of pastry, leaving it on the baking paper it comes with, and cut into four equal rectangles. Keep the second sheet refrigerated while you assemble the first four pies.Spoon about 60g filling on one half of each pastry rectangle, leaving a 1½cm border around three outer edges surrounding the filling, then brush these borders lightly with egg, keeping the egg wash just inside the cut edges (brushing it over the sides can seal the pastry layers and prevent them from rising properly). Fold the uncovered half of pastry over the filling and gently press the three edges together. Dip the tines of a fork in the flour, then use this to crimp all around the edges to seal.Slide the four pies on their baking paper bases on to an oven tray and refrigerate while you repeat with the second pastry sheet and the rest of the filling on a second tray. Refrigerate both trays for 20-30 minutes, until the pies are cold and firm.Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Brush the tops of the pies with the remaining egg wash and sprinkle with demerara sugar. Using the tip of a small, sharp knife, cut three slashes in the top of each pie, so the steam can escape, then bake for about 30 minutes, swapping the trays around halfway through cooking if necessary, until puffed and deeply golden. Leave the pies on the trays for 10 minutes, then transfer to a rack. Serve warm or at room temperature.Explore more on these topicsBonfire NightThe sweet spotFoodBakingSnacksPastryFruitHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Gherkins galore! 17 delicious ways to enjoy pickles – from frickles to pickletinis | Food | The Guardian
description: One of the UK budget’s big surprises? A discount on gherkins. And while they’ll always be good on a burger, there are many more unusual ways to indulge, from fried cheese treats to savoury ice-cream
Author: Leah Harper
Headline: One of the UK budget’s big surprises? A discount on gherkins. And while they’ll always be good on a burger, there are many more unusual ways to indulge, from fried cheese treats to savoury ice-cream
Content: A fine pickle … fried pickles with spicy dipping sauce.Photograph: LauriPatterson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fine pickle … fried pickles with spicy dipping sauce.Photograph: LauriPatterson/Getty ImagesFoodGherkins galore! 17 delicious ways to enjoy pickles – from frickles to pickletinisOne of the UK budget’s big surprises? A discount on gherkins. And while they’ll always be good on a burger, there are many more unusual ways to indulge, from fried cheese treats to savoury ice-creamLeah HarperFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn John Healey’s first budget as chancellor this week, he announced that he will remove import tariffs on more than 100 products – including, crucially, gherkins. Baked beans and boiled sweets, too, butgherkins stole the limelight, perhaps due to gen Z’s long-heldobsession with all things pickled, including cucumbers.But for those who think of a gherkin as either something to be chomped straight from the jar or swiftly removed from a Big Mac, do not worry: there are, in fact, plenty of ways to get more bang for your newly discounted gherkin buck.If you’re unsure about gherkins in general, let me ease you in with a gateway dish:the frickle, AKA a fried pickle. Deep frying almost any foodstuff will make it taste better and pickles – as gherkins are commonly known in the US – are no exception. Remember to pat dry your gherkins, which typically come swimming in their own brine. Then it’s simply a case of making a batter, dredging, frying and trying not to get grease all over your chin.View image in fullscreenPickle your fancy … deep-fried pickles at a barbecue restaurant in Kentucky.Photograph: Yarvin Market Journeys/AlamyFrickles are usually paired with a creamy dipping sauce such as aioli or ranch dressing – but why not go double gherkin and make your own tartare?Nigel Slater’s classic tartare sauceuses gherkins to cut through greasiness, allowing us “to continue eating”. You don’t have to ask me twice.Alternatively, there’s alsogherkin ketchup: Tom Kerridge’s recipepromises that “your guests will think you’re a pickling genius” – despite the fact that you are essentially serving up pureed gherkins.Now that you’re a gherkin convert, time to try something a little more adventurous. Sophie Wyburd’s recipe forbaked camembert with spicy pickle dressingis a tangy twist on a classic comfort food, adding gherkins to the more traditional dressing components of oil, rosemary and chilli. Plus, I would challenge anyone to turn down the “croissant crouton” dippers, which she serves in place of the usual crusty bread.Cosy indulgence not the vibe? Why not freeze your gherkins to make something altogether fresher. Recipe developer Emily Bonner blitzes her frosty pickles to create a kind of savoury granita, thenuses it to top a burrata.View image in fullscreenAdded zip … Nashville-style chicken burger with pickles.Photograph: Nazar Abbas/GettyThe cheese and gherkin pairings don’t end there: Nicola Lamb combines gherkins with cheddar for herflaky cheese and pickle scones, whileMatt Tebbutt adds them to a gruyère and salami toastie, intended to accompany french onion soup – although I’d venture it’s tasty eaten alone, too. Is the viral TikTok “chickle” snack – yes, that’s gherkins wrapped in fried cheese – an upgrade on the frickle? I couldn’t possibly say.Hamish Ruia and Max Desoutter – AKA the Flavour Fellas – use a grated gherkin and dill mixture to turn the traditional Spanish dishpan con tomateinto “pan con pickle”. And, while at first glanceAlexa Weibel’s fried chicken sandwichmay appear to simply use gherkins as a garnish, she also uses the brine to marinate the meat as well as chopped gherkins to “add zip” to her coleslaw.If this is all sounding a little bready, how about Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’s super-tangypotato and egg salad with gherkins and capers– orTamsin Burnett-Hall’s dill pickle macaroni salad. They’re both described as a side dish, but perhaps now is the time to make them the main event?View image in fullscreenDill or no dill … Tom Hunt’s gherkin brine ice-cream.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianOK, let’s get weird: can I interest you in apickletini? Sure, it’s like an appletini, except … yes, I’m afraid it’s gherkins. Brine and garnish – plus vodka and vermouth; classier than apickleback– whiskey “chased” with a shot of pickle juice – if not necessarily more enjoyable. Alternatively, there’sDua Lipa’s spicy diet coke: the singer mixes pickle and jalapeno “juice” with the carbonated soft drink, before topping with a couple of slices of each. That pickletini’s not sounding so bad now, huh?Tom Hunt describes hispickled cucumber and vodka ice-creamas “one for the true gherkin fanatic” – but you’ve come this far, so I can only assume you’d be willing to give it a go. He suggests you “serve in cones and top with a gherkin” – but to my mind that rather ruins the fun of asking guests to guess the flavour.If you do want to be upfront about it, you might as well servechocolate-covered mini gherkins– optional toppings include sea salt, chilli flakes and freeze-dried raspberries, none of which do much to disguise the fact that these are, in effect, gherkins dipped in Dairy Milk. The recipe describes them as “quirky canapés … or party conversation starters” – which I imagine is certainly true. Pair with marmalade or garlic to really make the most of those post-budget bargainsExplore more on these topicsFoodPickling, fermenting and preservingSauces and graviesCocktailsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK government’s obesity plan ‘doomed to fail’, MPs warn | Obesity | The Guardian
description: Cross-party committee says ‘moonshot’ vow to end obesity epidemic in a decade will fail without personal leadership from PM
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Cross-party committee says ‘moonshot’ vow to end obesity epidemic in a decade will fail without personal leadership from PM
Content: Obesity should be tackled by a ‘joined-up, cross-government action plan’, the MPs said.Photograph: Rawpixel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenObesity should be tackled by a ‘joined-up, cross-government action plan’, the MPs said.Photograph: Rawpixel/Getty ImagesObesityUK government’s obesity plan ‘doomed to fail’, MPs warnCross-party committee says ‘moonshot’ vow to end obesity epidemic in a decade will fail without personal leadership from PMPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentFri 30 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government’s promise to reverse rising obesity rates in the next decade is “doomed to fail” without a major rethink and a new plan led directly by the prime minister, a cross-party committee of MPs has concluded.The health and social care select committee said in a report that there are no signs the so-called “moonshot ambition on obesity”, set outin the 10-year health planfor England, will achieve anything significant.More than a year after the promise to “end the obesity epidemic” within a decade was made, even the most basic questions – such as how progress will be measured and how a cross-departmental plan would work – remain unanswered, the MPs said.The report said: “While the ambition to ‘end the obesity epidemic’ is a laudable one, we currently have no faith in the government’s commitment to this aim or ability to achieve it and predict that, unless they urgently reassess their approach, they are doomed to fail.“The government will fail to tackle a challenge of this scale unless action is led from the top and delivery of the moonshot is made a clear, personal priority of the prime minister.”It called for the creation of a dedicated cabinet committee on the obesity plan, chaired by the prime minister, to drive action and “to send a message that this government takes obesity seriously”.According to themost recent official statistics, 30% of adults in England are living with obesity, with 66% either overweight or living with obesity. Close to a third of children are now estimated to be overweight or living with obesity. Obesity rates for adults and children have increased significantly since the 1990s and, while the trends have levelled off, there are no signs of a fall.One of the major failings of the current strategy, the report said, is a lack of proper distinction between efforts to prevent future obesity, for example by cracking down on unhealthy foods, and those to support and treat people who already have obesity.“Conflating these two things is in part responsible for the muddled thinking and lack of progress from successive governments to date,” the MPs said.Any effective plan must be based on a clear definition of what the ambition to reduce obesity rates means in practical terms, along with interim progress markers that would allow MPs to hold ministers to account, they said.The MPs also called for a “joined-up, cross-government action plan”, taking in the departments responsible, their planned actions and how these will be funded, covering prevention and treatment for adults and children.Ministers should come to parliament within the next three months to set out the plan, the report said.Leadership from No 10 was vital, said Layla Moran, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the committee. She added an effective plan “will mean standing up to the food industry on numerous points – regulating the constant presence of adverts and promotions for unhealthy food and drink that wallpaper our lives, simpler labelling on products, targets for supermarkets to sell more healthy foods and restricting fast food outside schools”.She said: “This issue transcends government departments, and experience tells us that if the prime minister isn’t calling the shots on such a huge societal issue, the loose ends won’t join up and the moonshot will crash land.“We urge him to take up this ambition and be the driver of change. In turn, theNHS, public health and the economy will reap the long-term benefits.”A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Obesity is one of the biggest challenges facing our health service, and this government is taking bold action to help drive the shift from sickness to prevention and give every child the best start in life.“We have already restricted junk food advertising on television before 9pm and online, banned volume-price promotions on less healthy food and drink products, and given councils stronger powers to block new hot food takeaways near schools.“Alongside our focus on prevention, we are supporting those already living with obesity by expanding access to weight management support, including NHS weight-loss drugs for those with the greatest clinical need.”Explore more on these topicsObesityHealth policyHealthNHSnewsShareReuse this content
