title: DIY socks, messy collars and cummerbunds: nine wardrobe updates from the catwalks | Fashion | The Guardian
description: High fashion looks without a big budget? Follow our frugal guide to pinch the biggest autumn/ winter ‘26 catwalk trends for free.
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: High fashion looks without a big budget? Follow our frugal guide to pinch the biggest autumn/ winter ‘26 catwalk trends for free.
Content: Top collar … Bottega Veneta’s one-in-one-out shirt style.Photograph: BottegaView image in fullscreenTop collar … Bottega Veneta’s one-in-one-out shirt style.Photograph: BottegaFashion Statement newsletterFashionDIY socks, messy collars and cummerbunds: nine wardrobe updates from the catwalksHigh fashion looks without a big budget? Follow our frugal guide to pinch the biggest autumn/winter ‘26 catwalk trends for freeDon’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereChloe Mac DonnellFri 30 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDark mornings, darker evenings and the end of Celebrity Traitors. It’s easy to feel a bit meh at this time of year. However, without sounding too TikTok life coach, just as you are encouraged to winter-proof your morning routine (light a breakfast candle, make your favourite cup of tea) to start your day on a brighter note, the same approach could be applied to your wardrobe. An outfit you look forward to wearing to the office or an accessory update that can make a long-term favourite piece feel new again, can help put some much-needed pep in your step. That’s even when the forecast reads five days of rain in a row.The autumn/winter 2026 collections shown on the catwalks way back in February (yes time works funny in fashion) have finally hit shop floors, and high-street brands have been quick to pay homage. But there are plenty of styling tips and tricks you can borrow for free. Here are nine to get you started …***In-N-OutIn good news for those who struggle to make decisions, this season, collars come half tucked, half untucked this season. See Bottega Veneta (above), where shirt collars popped over knits and coats and Jil Sander where they half emerged over blazers. Yes, it will be annoying when someone tries to tell you your collar is only partly popped.Sewing skillsView image in fullscreenAccept imitations … these floral socks modeled by Bella Hadid cost £860 but can be easily copied with a needle and thread.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesLove the Prada floral socks? Nearly fainted when you saw the£860 price tag? You’re not alone. DIY instead with a packet ofsatin ribbon rose budsand your favourite knee-highs. Haven’t picked up a needle and thread since textiles class? Don’t worry, a crash lesson on YouTube and some sheer determination will get you through it.Tuck and goView image in fullscreenTucking great … Chloe’s catwalk was filled with trousers disappearing into boots.Photograph: ChloéAt Chloé, creative director Chemena Kamali tucked everything from jeans to leather trousers into over-the-knee boots in contrasting colours. Over at Celine and Bottega Veneta, tailored trousers were loosely stuffed into ankle boots. It’s one way to worry less about hems and puddles.Coming up rosesView image in fullscreenPin pony club … Simone Rocha’s rosette-inspired look.Photograph: Victor Virgile/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesStill have a pile of rosettes from your sports day victories or pony club days? Pin them to a blazer or silky top a la Simone Rocha. For extra impact, try clustering them together. Top tip? Avoid sky blue unless you want to be mistaken for a Tory candidate on the election trail.Reverse itView image in fullscreenBack yourself … Givenchy’s backwards shirt.Photograph: Indigital.TVWe all know how useful a white shirt is, and now, thanks to Givenchy, there’s even more mileage to it. Follow the lead of creative director, Sarah Burton, and style yours backwards. Very useful if you happen to spill tomato soup down the front of it too.Nighttime necklaces pivot to daywearskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCharm offensive … Celine’s oversized necklace.Photograph: CelineA jingly jangly necklace isn’t just for party season. At Celine, oversized versions were styled over formal coats and blazers. For affordable costume jewellery, secondhand sites and charity shops are a good bet.Don’t skip the glovesView image in fullscreenEasy and impactful … the effect of coloured gloves as shown in Ralph Lauren’s Polo collection.Photograph: Ralph LaurenYes, by day 15 of rain, wind and cold, you will get bored of wearing your winter coat. Slow down this process by adding a pair of colourful gloves to your look. At Polo Ralph Lauren, emerald greens and marigold yellow brightened up charcoal coats and denim jackets, while leather opera gloves in cacao and teal popped up at Balenciaga. It’s similar to thegreat red sock trendof 2023. Easy yet surprisingly impactful.Cinch and goView image in fullscreenWaist away … the cummerbund as envisioned by Valentino.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images for ValentinoMake your next secondhand search a cummerbund. The menswear black-tie accessory has now been reimagined by fashion brands including Kallmeyer, Dries van Noten and Valentino, the latter whose cinched top and dresses with contrasting coloured waist sashes. We’ve also seen formal cummerbunds wrapped around trench coats and striped ruby shirts which adds an unexpected edge.Downplay a personality skirtView image in fullscreenLow-key loud … Tory Burch’s shiny patent skirt paired with a classic orange jumper.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesUnless your daily screen time is a single digit, you will be well aware that a personality skirt is gearing up to be big in fashion. Think a leather midi skirt. An embellished pencil skirt. Or in the case of Tory Burch above, high-shine patent. This all sounds quite scary for real life, but follow Burch’s lead and pair it with something boring on top, such as a cotton sweatshirt or a cashmere jumper. For extra laid-back energy, roll up the sleeves. Main character who?To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Expect goosebumps!’: to celebrate Halloween, readers choose the spookiest places in the UK | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: From a ghostly hill fort on the South Downs to a haunted farmhouse in remote Northern Ireland, you guide us to some frightfully scary places
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From a ghostly hill fort on the South Downs to a haunted farmhouse in remote Northern Ireland, you guide us to some frightfully scary places
Content: ‘Wonderfully spooky’ Dunnottar Castle.Photograph: Charlotte Graham/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Wonderfully spooky’ Dunnottar Castle.Photograph: Charlotte Graham/ShutterstockReaders' travel tipsUnited Kingdom holidays‘Expect goosebumps!’: to celebrate Halloween, readers choose the spookiest places in the UKFrom a ghostly hill fort on the South Downs to a haunted farmhouse in remote Northern Ireland, you guide us to some frightfully scary placesTell us about an escape in the wilds of Scotland– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 30 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 04.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinning tip: an eerie clifftop castle near AberdeenDunnottar Castle, perched on cliffs above the crashing North Sea, is one of Scotland’s eeriest places. The most haunting part is the Whigs Vault, where more than 160 prisoners were confined in dreadful conditions in 1685. Standing in that dark chamber, it’s impossible not to imagine their fear and suffering. With my Fraser ancestry, the castle’s history feels especially poignant. The names of multiple Frasers are recorded, their details written on the wall. The wind whistles through the stonework, the waves thunder below, and there’s a sense that the past hasn’t quite left. It’s beautiful, tragic and wonderfully spooky, especially beneath Aberdeenshire’s brooding grey skies.RosieA Neolithic burial chamber in PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenPentre Ifan.Photograph: Louise France/AlamyMy dad and I reachedPentre Ifanon a November evening, just before dark. The burial chamber defies explanation: 16 tons of weathered capstone, barely touching three sharp stone points, as though something unseen was holding it up. There was a low hum from somewhere; I hoped it was the wind spilling over the Preseli hills. As the daylight crept away, the chamber beneath grew darker than the settling dusk around us. My dad, who has an explanation for everything, stood silent. I think we walked back to the car a little faster than we had come.TomHaunted by criminals in SomersetView image in fullscreenShepton Mallet prison.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianMy recommendation isShepton Mallet prison, or “the Mallet” as it used to be called, back when it was used as a military prison. It opened in 1625, and you can still crawl through a wall into an original cell. The prison has three Victorian blocks and umpteen stories of past prisoners, including the Kray twins. You can have a daytime tour, or a night-time ghost tour, where you’ll hear stories of spooks and ghouls witnessed by many visitors and staff over the years. You can even stay the night in a real, cold, grim prison cell. The staff are friendly and all great characters, I can’t recommend it enough!CharlieHollowed out tower in West YorkshireView image in fullscreenSt Thomas à Becket church, Heptonstall.Photograph: Philip Silverman/AlamyPerched high above Hebden Bridge in the historic hilltop village of Heptonstall lies the roofless shell of St Thomas à Becket church. Raked into ruin by a storm in 1847, this 13th-century structure was left to decay alongside its19th-century successor, creating a rare site where two parish churches share a single churchyard. Gaunt, towering arches frame open skies, and the hollowed-out stone tower feels like the Tower tarot card made real. Expect goosebumps!Finbarre SnareyA pub night you won’t forget in StaffordshireView image in fullscreenThe Four Crosses Inn.Photograph: Alex Telfer/The ObserverTheFour Crosses Innis the most haunted pub in England – and I should know: it was in my mother’s family for many generations! I grew up hearing about all the ghostly goings on. It was also one of the oldest pubs (it’s onlyopen for toursnow), and family lore has it Dr Johnson stayed there. On the edge of creepy Cannock Chase moor in Staffordshire, the scene of many murders, it has dank cellars and creaking attics for you to get really scared in.RobPoltergeist stories in County FermanaghView image in fullscreenFivemiletown, Northern Ireland.Photograph: Bonzo/AlamyCooneen Ghost House, near Fivemiletown, is one of Northern Ireland’s eeriest places. The abandoned farmhouse is private, but it can be glimpsed from the road, which somehow makes its old poltergeist stories feel even more unsettling. NearbyCrocknagrally Forestis perfect for a cold-weather ramble to make a day of it, especially on a misty winter afternoon when the tracks are wonderfully secluded and it all feels very remote and spooky. The kind of walk where folklore seems woven into the landscape: dark trees, lonely roads and an old haunted house just out of reach. There are loads of stories around this place that locals will share.Christina Haweskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRomantic tragedy on Llŷn peninsulaView image in fullscreenAbandoned works at the Cae’r Nant quarry above Nant Gwrtheyrn.Photograph: Peter Martin Rhind/AlamyThe once abandoned quarrying village ofNant Gwrtheyrn, on Llŷn peninsula, lies at the foot of Yr Eifl, down a terrifyingly steep and winding road. On a misty autumn day, with the crashing waves below you and the unsettling presence of a wild goat peering down at you from the cliffs above, it can be truly eerie. The woods in the valley are home to the tale ofRhys and Meinir– a traditional prenuptial game of hide and seek gone awry, with the skeletal remains of a bride-to-be revealed by a bolt of lightning. The site is free to visit.SionedCrashing waves and call of rooks in AberdeenshireView image in fullscreenSlains Castle.Photograph: AlamyOn a cold grey daySlains Castleon the east coast of Scotland, north of Aberdeen, certainly has a spooky air. Although rumours about the castle inspiring Bram Stoker when writing Dracula are apparently untrue, the castle ruins bring to mind bats pouring out of windows and unsavoury aristocrats lurking around corners. It is precariously located on cliffs above the North Sea and the crashing waves and calls of rooks and jackdaws provide an evocatively eerie soundtrack to your visit.Joel RawlingsUnexplained screams on the South DownsView image in fullscreenChanctonbury Ring.Photograph: Veronique Stone/AlamyChanctonbury Ring is an iron age hill fort ringed by beech trees, on the South Downs in West Sussex. Folklore claims that by walking or running around the ring seven times you’ll see the devil. Writer Robert Macfarlane certainly had an unnerving experience there while camping, as recounted in his 2012 bookThe Old Ways: A Journey on Foot, when awakened in the dead of night by terrifying human-sounding screams high above him in the tree canopy, which seemed to divide and converge before swooping down upon him. Accessible only on foot, who dares follow in Macfarlane’s footsteps to check out the myth?Kirsty McHattieGothic atmosphere in WhitbyView image in fullscreenWhitby Abbey.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyMy favourite spooky spot isWhitby Abbey, perched high above the Yorkshire coast. Its ruined arches and weathered stone look dramatic in daylight, but imagine them at dusk, with mist drifting in from the North Sea and the wind moving through the empty windows. Whitby’s narrow streets and harbour add another layer of atmosphere, especially when the lamps come on and the town grows quiet. It is easy to see why Bram Stoker found inspiration here for Dracula. I would love to explore the abbey as the light fades, then wander down towards the harbour, listening to the waves and letting my imagination do the rest. The best spooky places are where history, landscape and legend meet – and Whitby has all three. Its magic endures.EmilioExplore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysReaders' travel tipsHalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I live in the house from the 80s horror movie Poltergeist | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I was a fan of the film, so when it came on the market, I snapped it up. Now I allow other fans to come and stay in this piece of Hollywood history
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: I was a fan of the film, so when it came on the market, I snapped it up. Now I allow other fans to come and stay in this piece of Hollywood history
Content: Rachel Powers: ‘I added playful touches – a TV that plays only static.’Photograph: Bradley Meinz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Powers: ‘I added playful touches – a TV that plays only static.’Photograph: Bradley Meinz/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I live in the house from the 80s horror movie PoltergeistI was a fan of the film, so when it came on the market, I snapped it up. Now I allow other fans to come and stay in this piece of Hollywood historyRachel PowersFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfirst saw Poltergeist at the movie theatre with my mom and sisters, back when it came out in 1982. I remember being scared, especially during the part when the toy clown drags little Robbie Freeling under the bed. At that age, the idea of a family experiencing something terrifying in the kind of everyday suburban house I was familiar with made a big impression. Later, it became a ritual of mine to put the movie on every Halloween.I grew up in the Chicago area, but moved to California in the early 90s to go to art college. My sister moved there, too – to Simi Valley, not far from the house used as the Freeling family’s home in the movie. I’d drive past it when I visited her. A couple of years ago, I had a gut instinct that it would soon go up for sale. Sure enough, just weeks later I was sitting with my sister in her back yard when she looked up from her phone and said, “Hey! The Poltergeist house went on the market!”As it happened, I’d been looking for a new home for me and my three daughters, so I booked a viewing. The house was being sold by the same people who’d owned it when it appeared in the movie. Walking in for the first time was the most bizarre experience – it still had honey-coloured retro furniture everywhere, and I got the trippy impression that I’d travelled back to the 80s.Experience: a brain surgeon dropped part of my skull on the floorRead moreThere were multiple offers, so when mine was accepted I was very excited. I spent the first night at the house with just my dog, Emmy, who kept barking like crazy all night long. Even when I managed to fall asleep, I’d wake up with pictures from the movie running through my head. Part of me felt very uneasy – what did I just purchase?The sale had attracted a lot of press attention, which made me realise I’d entered into a different realm of home ownership. Families would stop and take selfies outside, and Poltergeist fans from all over the world started emailing me their memories of watching the movie. It occurred to me I could give some of them the opportunity to experience the house for themselves by allowing them to visit or rent it for an overnight stay.View image in fullscreen‘My dog kept barking like crazy’: Rachel Powers outside her home.Photograph: Bradley Meinz/The GuardianWithout attempting to recreate the movie set, I started adding playful touches for these occasional visitors, sometimes with help from fans who had found particular items seen onscreen. I had to have a TV that played only static when switched on, as a nod to the one in the film, and ensured guests had access to my own video cassette copy of Poltergeist, along with a stack of other 80s movies. My daughters are not fans of the movie, and were unimpressed when I also added a 1980s Atari console.double quotation markGuests reported seeing flickering lights, or hearing mysterious voices when they picked up the landline receiverWhenever fans stayed in the house, I’d take the girls camping, or we’d go to my sister’s. I loved hearing the creative ways our visitors spent their time here – recreating the scene where a steak comes to life on a kitchen counter, or filming each other sliding along the floor as if being pushed by invisible hands. Many arrived with their own clown doll.Some guests reported seeing flickering lights, or hearing mysterious voices when they picked up the landline receiver. The house still has old copper phone lines, so there’s probably a perfectly ordinary explanation, though perhaps it’s more fun not to know.But everyone agrees the house is a welcoming one – certainly more so than in the movie. The tree that comes alive outside the bedroom window was taken away after filming, and the muddy hole full of skeletons that the mother Diane Freeling falls into is now a finished swimming pool.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI still get many requests from fans wanting to stay here, especially this time of year. We haven’t taken any recent bookings, though Oliver Robins, who played Robbie Freeling, has dropped in a couple of times. Last Halloween he came and we handed out candy together in front of the house. He wore red jammies, just as he did as an eight-year-old boy in the movie.When we first moved in, I didn’t necessarily picture this as my for ever home, but I think that’s changing. Even my kids now say, “Mom, you can never let go of this house!” It’s a unique piece of film history, and to be able to live in it is an honour.As told to Chris BroughtonDo you have an experience to share? title: Forget water features – a tiny pond will bring wildlife to your garden | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: You might think ponds are complicated things with liners, but you can make one from a washing-up bowl
Author: Alice Vincent
Headline: You might think ponds are complicated things with liners, but you can make one from a washing-up bowl
Content: Even an old bucket will do.Photograph: Nigel Francis/AlamyView image in fullscreenEven an old bucket will do.Photograph: Nigel Francis/AlamyGardening adviceForget water features – a tiny pond will bring wildlife to your gardenYou might think ponds are complicated things with liners, but you can make one from a washing-up bowlAlice VincentFri 30 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you remember the 90s, when everyone was obsessed with “water features”, mostly thanks to Charlie Dimmock? A simpler time. Perhaps I’m hanging out with the wrong garden designers, but I rarely hear much talk of water features now. For years, Chelsea flower show gardens have featured subtle Cor-Ten steel-clad trickles or elegant mirrored ponds. There have been a fair few naturalistic streams (such as ARewilding Britain Landscapeby Lulu Urquhart and Adam Hunt, with beaver-gnawed twigs, which controversially won best in show in 2022), but scant fountains or burbling rocks. Water features are out, I guess. Ponds are in.My mum built one the other day. Hers is smaller than a piece of A3, lined with rocks and terracotta seedling pots, with two metal ducks stuck around the edge in a boggy bit of her compact urban garden. You might hear “pond” and think complicated things involving liner and algae, but you could make one from a washing-up bowl – and there are plenty of benefits to doing so.double quotation markMicro ponds are ideal for those with small children and/or small gardens. I’ve had one in an old bucket for yearsPonds are brilliant for wildlife. They can play host to insects including dragonflies and damselflies, and lure frogs and newts, which makes them a delicious buffet for birds, bats and those increasingly rare hedgehogs. I made one because I wanted something to eat slugs. It’s just a helpful part of the garden ecosystem to encourage.Smaller – or “micro” – ponds are ideal for those with small children and/or small gardens. I’ve had one in an old galvanised bucket for the past five years. You get bonus points for reusing something, and this is where I once again mention plastic storage boxes. Essentially, you just need a container that doesn’t leak water. And if it does leak water, you can use a pond liner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionContainer gardens are pots of fun – and autumn is the ideal time to give them a makeoverRead moreWhether you sink your pond into the ground or have it sitting on top is up to you. Make sure it gets some light, but if it’s in full sun you’ll end up with a lot of algae. Cover the bottom with large rocks, bits of old brick, upturned plant pots – hard solid things that won’t move for smaller wildlife to perch on, arranged in a way that helps them get in and out of the pond.Once you’ve filled up your pond with rainwater, you can plant. I’ve been really surprised by the resilience and variety of aquatic plants in my micropond, which has been largely left to its own devices. My receipts suggest I cheated and bought theContainer Planting Scheme D for Shadefrom Waterside Nursery, which delivered four plants in mesh baskets ready to pop in. Five years on and the yerba mansa offers delicate creamy flowers against the slender club rush.Pond life: easier than you think. Just don’t go calling it a water feature.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg | Mining | The Guardian
description: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective
Content: Wemmer Pan Road, near Rosettenville in Johannesburg, has been occupied by illegal gold miners. Photograph: James Oatway/The GuardianThere is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffectiveByRachel Savagein Durban DeepFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.In late September, dozens ofzama zamas– the name given to illegal miners inSouth Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.View image in fullscreenCora Bailey, who founded the charity Claw, has encountered illegal miners since 1991.Photograph: James Oatway/The GuardianPolice told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden thezama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspectedzama zamasacross the country in the previous week.However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that atenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn,was being exported illegally.Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025,93 bodieswerepulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm,sparking a gold rushthat led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peakedin the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.View image in fullscreenMiners working illegally near the defunct Durban Deep goldmine.Photograph: James Oatway/The GuardianIn 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had producedmore than a third of the gold ever minedglobally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name toan Elton John song.The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.View image in fullscreenThe remains of the Durban Deep goldmine, which is now an illegal mining flashpoint.Photograph: James Oatway/The GuardianZama zamashave stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault ofzama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that hadcompletely collapsed.The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.View image in fullscreenA drone view of a section of Wemmer Pan Road, which was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs.Photograph: James Oatway/The GuardianHowever, when it comes to sinkholes, experts sayzama zamasare being scapegoated.Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined byzama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time byzama zamasis completely fallacious.”View image in fullscreenA drone view of a collapsed section of Wemmer Pan Road near Rosettenville in Johannesburg. Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, says the biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining.Photograph: James Oatway/The GuardianZama zamasare also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including aSeptember mass shootingin Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”Explore more on these topicsMining (Business)Mining (Environment)South AfricaGoldAfricaCommoditiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF
Content: Nusseibeh said she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE to be ‘mindful of the obligations of independence’ the UN role would entail.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersView image in fullscreenNusseibeh said she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE to be ‘mindful of the obligations of independence’ the UN role would entail.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersUnited NationsSudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top jobCritics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSFCarlos Mureithiin NairobiFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMembers of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that theUnited Arab Emiratesis fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had“hallmarks of genocide”.Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn ofAfrica, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisationSudanAction Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that theUnited Nationsis not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch,saidNusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”Additional reporting by Kaamil AhmedExplore more on these topicsUnited NationsUnited Arab EmiratesSudanAfricaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries | European Union | The Guardian
description: Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’
Content: Antonio Costa, the European Council president, with Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister and, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in Montreal.Photograph: Graham Hughes/EPAView image in fullscreenAntonio Costa, the European Council president, with Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister and, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in Montreal.Photograph: Graham Hughes/EPAEuropean UnionCanada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countriesAlliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’Leyland Ceccoin TorontoFri 30 Oct 2026 15.42 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada andEuropehave announced a new alliance of like-minded nations toserve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president,Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.As they concluded their two-day summit,Canadaagreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever betweenEuropean Unionand a non-European country”.Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionCanadaAmericasEuropeMark CarneyUrsula von der LeyennewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro in Brasília on Sunday after his election defeat. He landed in Miami on Wednesday.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro in Brasília on Sunday after his election defeat. He landed in Miami on Wednesday.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersBrazil‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockeryBrazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of armsTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroFri 30 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – todeclare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaperthunderedon Friday.Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday night, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.Perhaps most bizarrely, he claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the 19th-century Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted an outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator,toldthe network GloboNews.The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.View image in fullscreenA woman reads a newspaper with news of the election result on Monday in São Paulo.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,”Malafaia was quoted as sayingby O Globo.Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s winRead moreThe Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.Others warned Bolsonarismo would remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement was now in doubt.Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São PaulocalledLula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, the US president replied: “I won’t get involved.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroJair BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Turkey has been hit by powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expected
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Turkey has been hit by powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expected
Content: Heavy rainfall in the Dalaman district of Muğla, south-west Turkey, caused serious flooding.Photograph: Durmus Genc/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHeavy rainfall in the Dalaman district of Muğla, south-west Turkey, caused serious flooding.Photograph: Durmus Genc/Anadolu/Getty ImagesWeather trackerExtreme weatherSevere rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western TurkeyTurkey has been hit by powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expectedOllie Lewis for MetDeskFri 30 Oct 2026 06.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe andTurkeyover the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and centralIndiaas it does so.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows Typhoon In-fa in the Pacific Ocean on Thursday.Photograph: CSU/Cira & JMA/Jaxa/ReutersHeading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150mph (240km/h), with winds gusting over 185mph (296km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered byTyphoon Champiearlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which havealready been batteredby four super typhoons this year alone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of westernMexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherWeather trackerTornadoesFloodingEurope weatherAmericasAsia PacificGreecenewsShareReuse this content

title: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme | North Korea | The Guardian
description: Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income
Content: At university, some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenAt university, some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.Photograph: APNorth KoreaAnalysisHow crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programmeDan SabbaghDefence and security editorCryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency incomeFri 30 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTShareNorth Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn)Binancecryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’Read moreAUN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.View image in fullscreenStolen funds are used to fund North Korea’s military, including its nuclear weapons programme.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesCiaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and theproduction and trafficking of crystal methfor export in the 2000s.The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?Read moreThe irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film starsJennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid lessthan their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.The attack,by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.Explore more on these topicsNorth KoreaHackingCryptocurrenciesAsia PacificBinanceCybercrimeInternetanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities | China | The Guardian
description: Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts
Content: Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.Photograph: Ng Han Guan/APView image in fullscreenPolice had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.Photograph: Ng Han Guan/APChinaBeijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authoritiesForums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say expertsAmy HawkinsSenior China correspondentFri 30 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues.Film festivalsin particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, wasclosed down in 2014after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independentChinese film festival that was due to be held in New Yorkwas cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre,were cancelledbecause of police harassment.Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.Explore more on these topicsChinaLGBTQ+ rightsAsia PacificHuman rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials | China | The Guardian
description: The unprecedented number of empty seats at the political meeting – a symbol of expulsions – indicates the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: The unprecedented number of empty seats at the political meeting – a symbol of expulsions – indicates the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
Content: Members of the Politburo Standing Committee including Xi Jinping at the fifth plenum. Beijing has purged a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP).Photograph: Li Xiang/Xinhua/APView image in fullscreenMembers of the Politburo Standing Committee including Xi Jinping at the fifth plenum. Beijing has purged a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP).Photograph: Li Xiang/Xinhua/APChinaChina expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officialsThe unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi JinpingAmy Hawkinsin BeijingThu 29 Oct 2026 22.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded amajor political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leadersRead moreThe confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent yearsthe campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.View image in fullscreenZhang Shengming, top, sits behind Chinese leader Xi Jinping during the opening session of the fifth plenum in Beijing.Photograph: Andy Wong/APXi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.Explore more on these topicsChinaXi JinpingAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: El Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea a ‘national crisis’ as rivers dry up and local farms fail | Papua New Guinea | The Guardian
description: As many as eight million people have been affected by the cascading issues of food shortages, electricity loss and health clinic closures
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: As many as eight million people have been affected by the cascading issues of food shortages, electricity loss and health clinic closures
Content: Farmers like Laity, from PNG’s Eastern Highlands province, have watched crops wither due to weather affected by El Niño.Photograph: Kate Newsome/CARE PNGView image in fullscreenFarmers like Laity, from PNG’s Eastern Highlands province, have watched crops wither due to weather affected by El Niño.Photograph: Kate Newsome/CARE PNGPapua New GuineaEl Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea a ‘national crisis’ as rivers dry up and local farms failAs many as 8 million people have been affected by food shortages, electricity blackouts and health clinic closuresGraham Readfearnand Rebecca Bush in Port MorsebyThu 29 Oct 2026 21.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 21.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExtreme drought driven by an historic El Niño is affecting as many as 8 million people inPapua New Guinea, causing a cascade of issues from shortages of food and water, to electricity scarcity and schooling disruption.A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industryRead moreAn influential coalition that includes churches, trade unions and business groups has said the Pacific nation is in the midst of a “national crisis”, but there appears to be “no coordinated plan to protect vulnerable communities from the worsening impacts of El Niño.”Residents and community leaders have told the Guardian that rivers and creeks have dried up and family food gardens – a vital source of food and income for many – have shrivelled. Schools and health facilities are being forced to close early because they lack sufficient water to provide basic services.Emilly Meren, humanitarian projects manager at CARE International in PNG, said in rural highland areas families were rationing food to one meal a day – while food insecurity was leading to localised disputes between families.“For women and girls, they are expected to do more to support their families,” she said, yet they were “the last to eat because they have to serve others first”.“They have to travel three to four hours to source water and food and are exposed to a heightened risk of harassment. We are hearing stories of transactional sex happening in the community – exchanging sex for money or for food.”View image in fullscreenA failed tomato crop and a field of plantains burned in an unplanned fire in PNG’s Eastern Highlands.Photograph: Kate Newsome/CARE PNGTheEl Niño climate patternis gaining strength in the tropical Pacific with forecasts suggesting it will bethe strongest ever recordedwith its impacts worsened by global heating.Some parts of PNG have had less thana quarter of their usual rainfall since August.The PNG National Weather Service declared theonset of El Niñoin June but Kasis Inape, the service’s assistant director, said at that point, much of the country was already in drought and about 8 million people had been affected.Inape said PNG was one of the wettest places in the world with rain fed by warm tropical waters, but the El Niño had seen those waters shift east “and we’re starved of rain”.“Because we’re a rain-fed country, a lot of our people are subsistence farmers and they depend just on rainfall to survive and to feed themselves,” he said.PNG’s wet season is between November and April and Inape said while some short term relief was forecasted, there were concerns El Niño would shorten the season.View image in fullscreenWomen ready for work with a day’s drinking water carried from a village well nearly a kilometre away.Photograph: Kate Newsome/CARE PNG“The place is so dry – just two months of rain is not enough to allow crops to grow and water levels to be comfortable,” Inape said.In Morobe province’s Bulolo district, smaller rivers have dried up leaving families without access to water for drinking, cooking and washing.Resident Theophil Zarack said many schools and health centres were operating for only half a day, with some clinics no longer accepting inpatients due to a lack of available water.Martha Zureno, a resident in Leklu village, said: “All our rivers have dried up, including the one behind my house. Now, my children and I have to walk for miles every afternoon to fetch water for cooking and drinking from the other side.“We have a well that we dug ourselves, but we only use that water for washing. All the crops in our gardens have dried up and died, and we cannot grow anything now.”Zureno said that most of the local residents depend on panning for gold to earn an income, but without water, “even that has become increasingly difficult”.Meanwhile, a destructive hailstorm in parts of Enga province earlier this month – not blamed directly on El Niño – buried sweet potatoes under ice, exacerbating the food scarcity issue, according to George Iki, president of the Sambe Unity Development Association.View image in fullscreenIn drought-stricken areas of PNG, residents have learned new preservation techniques to shore up food supplies.Photograph: Kate Newsome/CARE PNGIn the capital Port Moresby, PNG Power has begun planned electricity blackouts after falling dam levels cut hydropower generation and said disruptions could continue for up to 10 months. The company was working to manage dam releases to protect the city’s water supply.Peter Aitsi, a prominent PNG business figure and co-chair of the Community Coalition Against Corruption, said the government needed to carry out “proper assessments” of the unfurling impacts, particularly on rural communities.Last month the group called the drought situation a “national crisis”, but according to Aitsi, urban centres have been mostly shielded from the impacts. That could change, however, with electricity blackouts and a shortage of fresh food from drought-stricken areas, he said.Aitsi said the capital had been covered in a smoke haze in the past week from fires elsewhere on the island, and in Indonesia to the west, thatscientists say have been fuelled by El Niño.Prime minister James Marape has directed provincial and district authorities to prepare for a prolonged dry season, saying his government was examining financial arrangements to support disaster responses.“Cabinet is looking at tailoring provisions of our financial instructions to make sure that districts and provinces are assisted to respond to disasters as they happen where appropriate,” Marape said.Explore more on these topicsPapua New GuineaDroughtEl Niño southern oscillationPacific islandsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case | Australian law | The Guardian
description: Scraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey says
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Scraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey says
Content: The attorney general, Michelle Rowland (pictured), says the government is committed to supporting creatives even as concern mounts over a possible weakening of Australian copyright laws.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenThe attorney general, Michelle Rowland (pictured), says the government is committed to supporting creatives even as concern mounts over a possible weakening of Australian copyright laws.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPAustralian lawExperts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights caseScraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey saysGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerFri 30 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAltering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide.The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point asthe movie The Castle, the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI.“We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian
