Australia.Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”.In a rush to lure AI companies, the Australian government risks undoing a creative ecosystem that has taken decades to build | Dan GuthrieRead moreLabor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, haspromised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropicsuggested an “opt-out” modelwhich would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection.A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”.“If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member ofthe federal parliamentary committee on AI.“How we support property rights is core to this.”A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes.Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues.“The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here.Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish celebrities beat AI companies lobbying to get free use of their work. They have a warning for AustraliaRead moreCadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues.Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders.Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”.“It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.”Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals.He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners.“The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said.Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community.“The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said.Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern.“That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders.“The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.”Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks.“There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know whatwillhappen,” Cadell said.“I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian lawAI (artificial intelligence)Australian politicsAustralian musicAustralian booksAustralian filmAustralian televisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Erin Patterson to die in prison after losing bid to overturn mushroom murder convictions | Erin Patterson mushroom trial | The Guardian
description: Victorian court of appeal rules Patterson should be jailed for life with no parole over deadly beef wellington lunch that killed three people
Author: Nino Bucci
Headline: Victorian court of appeal rules Patterson should be jailed for life with no parole over deadly beef wellington lunch that killed three people
Content: Erin Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment for the murders of Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson and the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, after a deadly mushroom-laced lunch at her home in rural Australia.Photograph: James Ross/APView image in fullscreenErin Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment for the murders of Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson and the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, after a deadly mushroom-laced lunch at her home in rural Australia.Photograph: James Ross/APErin Patterson mushroom trialErin Patterson to die in prison after losing bid to overturn mushroom murder convictionsVictorian court of appeal rules Patterson should be jailed for life with no parole over deadly beef wellington lunch that killed three peopleErin Patterson mushroom murders appeal – live updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNino BucciJustice and courts reporterFri 30 Oct 2026 01.31 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleErin Patterson has lost her bid to overturn her convictions and been resentenced to life behind bars with no chance of release, as Victoria’s highest court handed down its decision on two appeals regarding hertriple murder case.The court of appeal ruled on the two appeals on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.Erin Patterson appeal live updates: Victorian woman loses bid to overturn triple-murder convictions over deadly mushroom-laced mealRead morePatterson, 52, did not attend the 15-minute court hearing in person, and showed no emotion on the video feed as McLeish outlined why her appeal had failed, and how the director of public prosecutions had succeeded in seeking a longer sentence.Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailShe was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.McLeish said the court had granted leave to appeal on the first two grounds of Patterson’s appeal, but dismissed the appeal, and dismissed the five other grounds raised by her lawyers.He said the court granted the DPP appeal against the sentence, however, as it was clear the original sentence did not properly reflect the seriousness of her offending.1:21Erin Patterson appeal: judges reject mushroom murderer’s bid to overturn sentencing - videoMcLeish said Patterson sustained an intent to murder all four people for three weeks, from the time they were invited to the lunch, during the meal, and during the “protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted”.The offending was “carefully planned and deliberate”, he said, and involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” including claims that she had cancer, denying she had foraged mushrooms, and lying about the source of the mushrooms.“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest possible terms,” McLeish said.When the judges left court, Patterson also stood, took a book from beside her, and walked off-screen.In the courtroom, family members hugged and were emotional, and detectives involved in the case looked elated. Nobody commented outside court.A visual guide to people involved in the storyPatterson now must apply to the high court for leave to appeal, should she wish to continue fighting her conviction or new sentence.She is one of only a handful of Victorian offenders sentenced to life without parole, and one of the only women in Australian history to be given the sentence.Written reasons for the decision were provided to media later on Friday.In them, the court said while the first ground of the DPP’s appeal – that trial judge erred in finding that there was a substantial chance Patterson would be in solitary confinement for much of her sentence – had failed, it was clear the second ground, that the sentence was manifestly inadequate, should succeed.The court found they were “heinous crimes” and “we are driven to conclude that a non-parole period of 33 years fails to reflect the calculated criminality of the applicant in committing three murders and attempting a fourth”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust to members of the applicant’s extended family,” the court found.“The taking of three lives (and the attempt on another) in these circumstances called in our view for much stronger denunciation.”In relation to Patterson’s appeal, the court described many of the grounds as having no substance, being without merit, or even fanciful.In relation to the ground that the sequestering of the jury in the same hotel as the police informant and members of the prosecution amounted to a substantial miscarriage of justice, the court found that it “was plainly unfortunate that [the] situation arose”. It said it was “highly undesirable” and “the judge would not have countenanced this arrangement if approval for it had been sought in advance”.But the justices said there was no evidence any wrongdoing had occurred.“The accommodation arrangements offered fertile grounds for speculation but no objective basis for the fair-minded person to reasonably apprehend that the jury might not have discharged its function of rendering a verdict according to law. “In relation to ground two – that undue weight was placed on evidence given by a telecommunications expert that raised the possibility she visited two sites where death cap mushrooms had been reported – the court found the probative value of the evidence was not outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice to Patterson.In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.Richard Edney, for Patterson, had said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial.1:24Erin Patterson: Australia’s mushroom murderer sentenced to life in prison – video“What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August.During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.Explore more on these topicsErin Patterson mushroom trialVictorianewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Sydney childcare worker Ashley Paul Griffith hit with 202 more abuse charges | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: NSW police say charges include child rape and relate to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five at a Sydney childcare centre
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: NSW police say charges include child rape and relate to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five at a Sydney childcare centre
Content: A court sketch of Ashley Paul Griffith in 2024. The convicted paedophile is facing hundreds more charges since being extradited to NSW.Photograph: AAPView image in fullscreenA court sketch of Ashley Paul Griffith in 2024. The convicted paedophile is facing hundreds more charges since being extradited to NSW.Photograph: AAPNew South WalesFormer Sydney childcare worker Ashley Paul Griffith hit with 202 more abuse chargesNSW police say charges include child rape and relate to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five at a Sydney childcare centreGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressFri 30 Oct 2026 01.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 22.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Australia’s most notorious paedophiles is facing hundreds more child abuse charges, including for the alleged rape of children as young as one.Days after being extradited from Queensland toNew South Wales, Ashley Paul Griffith was hit with 202 charges dating from between 2014 and 2017, with police labelling the allegations “deeply disturbing”.TheQueenslandman was working at a childcare centre in Sydney’s inner west at the time of the alleged offending, which included dozens of alleged rapes against children between one and five.Griffith, 48, was jailed for life in Queensland in November 2024 after he pleaded guilty to more than 300 child sexual offences against nearly 70 victims.The fresh charges from NSW include 68 counts of rape of a child aged less than 10 and 42 counts of aggravated rape of a child aged less than 10 who was under his authority.Other charges include 69 counts of aggravated indecent assault and 23 charges of producing child abuse material.Police said the charges pertained to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHe was charged while being held in Silverwater Correctional Complex in Sydney.NSW Det Supt Linda Howlett said charging Griffith with further alleged offending could help potential victims.“There’s no other word for it, it’s actually horrific,” she said in relation to the allegations.The child abuse squad commander thanked witnesses, alleged victims and detectives for their work in preparing the challenging but “airtight” case.Police are extending every assistance to those involved, Howlett said.Griffith did not apply for bail in a brief court appearance on Friday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe NSW police assistant commissioner Brett Greentree said the lengthy investigation included collaboration with police across the nation.“The allegations before the court are deeply disturbing and involve some of the most vulnerable members of our community,” he said.“Every child deserves to be safe and protected from harm. NSW Police is committed to ensuring those who exploit positions of trust to offend against children are identified, investigated and brought before the courts.”Griffith arrived in NSW on Wednesday.In Queensland, he admitted to assaulting and filming young girls over the course of years while working at childcare centres.His transfer was approved by a Brisbane magistrate earlier in the month, where the alleged victims’ supporters yelled insults at the rapist as he stood in the dock for the decision.In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids helplineon 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsNew South WalesQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortages
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortages
Content: People gathering in Oleshky before the joint relief evacuation operation taking them on a route through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory.Photograph: Facebook official account of Kyrylo Budano/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenPeople gathering in Oleshky before the joint relief evacuation operation taking them on a route through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory.Photograph: Facebook official account of Kyrylo Budano/AFP/GettyUkraineEvacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of OleshkyHumanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortagesPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentFri 30 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southernUkrainewere evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.Thelocalised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson regionallowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.View image in fullscreenRussian military personnel pass by damaged vehicles during a de-mining operation near Oleshky.Photograph: Russian Defence Ministry/ReutersWhile Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.View image in fullscreenThe convoy carrying more than 500 evacuees from Oleshky.Photograph: ReutersWhile earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.View image in fullscreenPeople in Oleshky have endured months of food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation.Photograph: The Office of the Commissioner for Human Rights in Russia/EPASome say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied OleshkyRead moreKsenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.“They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.View image in fullscreenUkraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets (centre), and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova (left), talk to journalists before the evacuation.Photograph: Office of the Ukrainian Ombudsman/AFP/Getty Images“I’ve been told that ‌it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for ​such a significant duration.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian society being ‘systematically crushed’ says Novaya Gazeta as newspaper announces closure | Russia | The Guardian
description: Independent outlet, whose former editor Dmitry Muratov won Nobel prize, cites intolerable pressure from authorities Europe live – latest updates
Author: Shaun Walker
Headline: Independent outlet, whose former editor Dmitry Muratov won Nobel prize, cites intolerable pressure from authorities Europe live – latest updates
Content: A woman reading a copy of Novaya Gazeta's European edition in Riga, Latvia, in May 2022.Photograph: Toms Kalniņš/EPAView image in fullscreenA woman reading a copy of Novaya Gazeta's European edition in Riga, Latvia, in May 2022.Photograph: Toms Kalniņš/EPARussiaRussian society being ‘systematically crushed’ says Novaya Gazeta as newspaper announces closureIndependent outlet, whose former editor Dmitry Muratov won Nobel prize, cites intolerable pressure from authoritiesShaun WalkerFri 30 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNovaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent media outlets, has announced it will permanently close next month. The newspaper, whose former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratovwon the Nobel peace prize in 2021, cited intolerable pressure, including being stripped of its newsroom, its donation platforms and its legal right to publish.“This is not just our own story; it is the story of a country and a society that are being systematically crushed,” wrote its editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, on the newspaper’s website.Launched in the 1990s and for many years partly funded by the late Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya made its name through dogged, long-form reporting on corruption, rights abuses and social issues. Over the years, six of its journalists have been assassinated, including Anna Politkovskaya, who was gunned down in the stairwell of her Moscow apartment block in 2006.While Novaya always swam against a tide of repression, thefull-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022made independent reporting almost impossible and decimated the Russian media landscape. Novaya was one of the last critical voices still operating from inside the country.“For nearly five years of ***, we managed to keep working while being completely encircled by the security services. Now it’s over. We have found ourselves in a ‘kill zone’,” wrote Sokolov. The stars were used in place of the word “war”, as under Russian law, journalists must refer to the war in Ukraine as a “special military operation” or face consequences.View image in fullscreenSergei Sokolov, the Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief.Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty ImagesThe newspaper’s first response to the invasion was to put out a special bilingual Russian-Ukrainian edition in the days after Vladimir Putin launched the invasion. It described the war as “madness” on its front page. Soon after, the Kremlin implemented draconian new censorship laws, which forced media outlets to publish only the Russian official narrative about the conflict.“We said it’s not journalism and we’re not going to do that,” said Nadezhda Prusenkova, the head of Novaya’s press service. The newspaper published blank white spaces instead of euphemisms and false information, to provide a visible reminder of the censorship laws.By the end of March 2022, Novaya decided to stop publishing its print edition altogether, but the threats and pressure only increased. In April that year, Muratovwas doused with red paint while on a train, an attack that damaged his eyesight and thatUS officials saywas carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence agencies. In September that year, the newspaper’s official licence was taken away and soon after their website was blocked in Russia.Novaya’s journalists, long used to operating in a hostile environment, found ways to circumvent the bans. Many left Russia, and a number of exiled former employees set up Novaya GazetaEurope, a legally distinct outlet. Muratov and a core team stayed behind and continued to publish a series of magazines with a print run of 999 copies, taking advantage of a law that means magazines with under 1,000 copies do not require an official licence. Novaya’s website continued running, too, although the Russian state hit the outlet with various new legal threats.“The fact Novaya kept working for this four and a half years after everything that happened was a miracle, but it was not just a miracle, it was also the daily choice of people who continued to go to work even when it was very scary,” said Elena Kostyuchenko, a former Novaya journalist who spent 17 years at the newspaper. “Today I feel very inspired by my colleagues, but also very painful and sad for them, and for all of us.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion​Pragmatic or pointless? Europe’s rift over whether to pick up the phone to PutinRead moreIn recent months, Prusenkova said the pressure had become intolerable. In April, the journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”. He is under house arrest awaiting trial and last month Sokolov’s home was searched as part of the case.This month, the newspaper’s landlords informed Novaya staff that they must vacate their longstanding office premises in central Moscow by 9 November. The newsroom has been the hub of the newspaper for decades and houses a memorial museum to Politkovskaya in the former office of the murdered journalist. Prusenkova said the exhibits would be taken down and put into storage, for now.On top of the eviction notice, all the outlet’s donation platforms have been shut down, leaving the paper without any source of funding. The court case, combined with the eviction and the lack of funds, gave the newspaper no choice but to close, said staff.“Sometimes it happens that your enemies win. At this moment in time, it seems like they have won, and we have no options left,” said Prusenkova. But she said it was probable Novaya’s journalists would try to find some way to continue their work. “After all, we don’t know how to do anything else,” she said.Explore more on these topicsRussiaPress freedomNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesEuropeJournalist safetyInvestigative journalismnewsShareReuse this content

title: People of 27 nationalities may be among those killed or injured in Spain train crash, Sánchez says – as it happened | Spain | The Guardian
description: Some 69 people have been confirmed dead but the toll may rise further, with at least 70 people reported missing
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Some 69 people have been confirmed dead but the toll may rise further, with at least 70 people reported missing
Content: 10.24 EDTSpain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PMSam Jonesin MadridSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’sdeadly train collisionthat killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez (L) and Castilla-La-Mancha regional president Emiliano García-Page hold a press conference.Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPASánchez saidthe Spanish state was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims– who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding that his government was committed to finding what had caused Spain’s second deadly train collision this year.Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when theycollided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the otherslammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.Huge cranes lift one of the wrecked carriages of a train crash between a Renfe AVE train and an Iryo train, two days after the deadly accident in Urda, in the province of Toledo.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesThe crash came nine months after 46people were killedand dozens injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.“It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain– which has such a powerful high-speed rail system –to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,”the prime minister said on Friday.“Therefore,our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutionsto further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system.Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”Shortly after Sánchez spoke,Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente – who is under growing pressure to resign – gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down,promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.Transport minister Óscar Puente during a press conference at the ministry's headquarters in Madrid, Spain.Photograph: Atilano Garcia/SOPA Images/Shutterstock“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can.If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif.He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but stressed that such incidents were not at all uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers ultimately reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.Spain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PMRead moreShare

title: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe | Archaeology | The Guardian
description: Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79
Content: Archaeologists found the personal belongings in a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, once one of Pompeii’s busiest streets.Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological ParkView image in fullscreenArchaeologists found the personal belongings in a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, once one of Pompeii’s busiest streets.Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological ParkArchaeologyPerfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobeArchaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79Angela Giuffridain RomeFri 30 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.View image in fullscreenA charm from a crepundia, a type of necklace often worn by children.Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological ParkBut the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.View image in fullscreenBronze weights and a box closure found among the possessions.Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological ParkThe home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its ​facade was first excavated ​in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.View image in fullscreenA bronze oil lamp with a deflector.Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological Park“It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, alarge and sophisticated thermal bathcomplex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.Ahome containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.Explore more on these topicsArchaeologyItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cost of living protests  to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Halloween | Europe | The Guardian
description: Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing
Content: A worker shutters the windows of the luxury jewellery brand Tiffany & Co in Berlin on Friday, the day before the protests.Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA worker shutters the windows of the luxury jewellery brand Tiffany & Co in Berlin on Friday, the day before the protests.Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropeCost of living protests  to spread to Germany and reignite in France on HalloweenActivists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housingEurope live – latest updatesDeborah Colein Berlin andJon Henleyin ParisFri 30 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStreet protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread toGermanyand reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.Weeks of,at times violent, student demonstrationshave rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country.In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return tomandatory military service.View image in fullscreenStudents and activists block access to the Andreas-Gymnasium in Berlin this month in protest against compulsory military service and education cuts.Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/ShutterstockAlexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those inFrancemust be prevented at all costs.”But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.View image in fullscreenA Gen Z regelt poster in Leipzig announcing a protest on Saturday at Augustusplatz.Photograph: Maria Castro/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAbout 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.Large rallies have also been called in Cologne, Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.The team behind Gen Z regelt has used social media and its website to call on participants to exercise restraint: “Our protest is peaceful, without exception. Violence goes against everything we stand for. Only through peaceful means can we achieve something together.”By Friday,more than 160,000 people had registered on the websitesaying they planned to attend the protests.View image in fullscreenStudents block the entrance to the Otto Suhr Institute of the Free University of Berlin this week under a banner saying: ‘Stop war research!’.Photograph: Volodymyr Sindieiev/Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe federal pupils’ conference, a youth political lobbying group, has distanced itself from Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the initiative’s “unclear” organisational structure made the events unpredictable.It plans to hold a separate protest in Berlin on 20 November that will include teachers and other youth movements focused on themarked decline in German school performance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn France, the interior minister, Laurent ⁠Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalisedgilets jaunes[yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities ‌across France,” he said.The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.View image in fullscreenProtesters holding a French flag amid clashes during demonstrations in Paris last Saturday.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersMeasures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.It is unclear what will happen in Paris. Two separate marches planned by unions andgilets jaunesthrough the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. Both sets of organisers are challenging the decision to exclude them from the centre.The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a firstwave of mass protest on 17 October.Unions and thegilets jaunesmovement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide ​strike called for 5 November.Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.Explore more on these topicsEuropeGermanyFranceProtestCost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report | Middle East and north Africa | The Guardian
description: IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’
Content: A fire near Dubai international airport in March after a ‘drone-related incident’ set a fuel tank alight.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fire near Dubai international airport in March after a ‘drone-related incident’ set a fuel tank alight.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesMiddle East and north AfricaGulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says reportIISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’Patrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 30 Oct 2026 08.49 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at theUnited Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.View image in fullscreenFlights were suspended at Dubai’s international airport in March after the attack.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes thatthe US-Iran warhas shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFriday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?Read moreThe study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.Explore more on these topicsMiddle East and north AfricaUS-Israel war on IranIranUS foreign policyUS defence spendingUnited Arab EmiratesDrones (military)newsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Oxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil Shamsan
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Oxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil Shamsan
Content: Yemenis fill jerrycans with water at a distribution point in Taiz this month. Water shipments are being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city, the governor said.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYemenis fill jerrycans with water at a distribution point in Taiz this month. Water shipments are being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city, the governor said.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesYemenHouthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city saysOxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil ShamsanPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 30 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHouthisare trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.The city’s daily minimum water needs are estimated at about 35,000 cubic metres, he said, but no more than 1,000 cubic metres was being allowed to reach it each day and that water shipments were being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city.View image in fullscreenA padlock on a water tap connected to a storage tank in the city.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesWith food stocks depleted and the price of wheat soaring, he said “citizens are heading back to the stone age”. Restaurants had closed due to the lack of fuel.Shamsan said that as many as 1,800 people were in need of dialysis treatment but were unable to access supplies, that 120 health centres had been suspended and schools had closed, affecting hundreds of thousands of children.He said 64 people had been killed, including civilians, from August to 20 October 2026 and a further 173 injured. More than 6,400 newly displaced families, each averaging seven members, had come to the city to flee the fighting.“We are not talking about living, just surviving,” he said.His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”View image in fullscreenFuel shortages are threatening neonatal intensive care units in Taiz, where 120 health centres have been suspended.Photograph: Hamza Mustafa/Anadolu/Getty ImagesShamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.People in occupied territories were being required to show loyalty to the Zaydi religion and to sign forms affirming they had joined the Houthis. “They are not starting a war but an revolution in identity,” Shamsan said, adding that scores of children from each village were being forcibly ordered without their parents’ consent to join the frontlines in Saada and elsewhere.Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.View image in fullscreenRubbish is piling up in the city’s streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.Photograph: Hamza Mustafa/Anadolu/Getty ImagesShamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricaInternally displaced peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties? | Israel | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political moment
Author: Libby Brooks
Headline: In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political moment
Content: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition looks to be coming to an end.Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPrime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition looks to be coming to an end.Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesFirst Edition newsletterIsraelFriday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political momentLibby BrooksFri 30 Oct 2026 02.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 02.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presentsIsraelwith a significant dilemma.Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result.But the country that is desperate for change remains bitterly divided. After a campaign mired in racism, during which Israel’s far-right demonised the Palestinian population as the enemy within, Netanyahu has gone further since Tuesday’s vote, claiming that Palestinian-led parties have “stolen the election”, despite Israeli authorities insisting there is no evidence of election fraud.As coalition talks commence, I spoke to our chief Middle East correspondentEmma Graham-Harrisonin Tel Aviv, about false narratives and the stark choice facing the country. But first, the headlines.Five big storiesUK politics| John Healeyhas backed awayfrom cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.Patrick Stewart| The acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi,died at his homein Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, his longtime spokesperson said.Environment| One of the mostambitious nature recovery projectsever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland.Europe| Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 peoplewho died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.US news| The Trump administrationhas opened a criminal investigationin California over claims that thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in the state, and has begun subpoenaing election officials.In depth: There is no evidence of election fraudView image in fullscreenMansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, is committed to working with Jewish Israeli opposition parties.Photograph: Mahmoud Illean/APWith the final results released early on Friday local time, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, compared with 48 for the grouping led by rival Eisenkot. Palestinian parties won 19 seats, a record high. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.With neither bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israeli president Isaac Herzog is expected to invite the party most likely to be able to form a government to start coalition negotiations, and has already urged politicians to have an “open mind” before talks begin. The country potentially faces weeks of rancour and uncertainty.Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, told Israeli media on Thursday that he was meeting Eisenkot and others for initial talks. If the opposition can’t agree some kind of coalition, or even secure Palestinian support for a minority government, Netanyahu may have a lifeline. He is already pushing for a right-wing governing coalition, and would probably welcome new elections or a lengthy period of uncertainty during which he will stay on as caretaker prime minister.And yet throughout the campaign, voters’ discontent with Netanyahu was evident.That didn’t mean a shift to the left: young Israelis are more rightwing than older generations, as Emmawrote about here. The national conversation ahead of the election was dominated by security at home and abroad. Although he was in charge on 7 October 2023, when Hamas attacks resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, the prime minister tried to shift blame on to the security services.His opponents pledged a state commission of inquiry into the events of 7 October, and spoke to voters’ concerns about the social toll of three years of multi-front wars, and anger about the draft exemption for ultra-orthodox young men when other Israelis are spending hundreds of days on reserve duty.Netanyahu’s false narrativeThroughout the campaign, Netanyahu and his far-right allies have framed Palestinian voters – who make up about 20% of the population – as a direct threat to ​the state, with Netanyahu repeating the slogan “the right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew.“It’s both tragic and depressing,” Emma tells me, “attempting to paint Palestinians as untrustworthy citizens with dual loyalties, a racist trope that also appears in antisemitic attacks.”This tactic extended to election day, when voters received a robocall purporting to come from the prime minister falsely claiming that Palestinian party leaders had been caught with envelopes full of cash. Netanyahu and his allies repeatedly made claims about high turnout in Palestinian areas, in a bid to get his own voters out.Then on Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming, again without providing evidence, they had “stolen the election,” calling for the central elections committee and Shin Bet internal security agency to investigate foreign interference in the vote. These claims were amplified by far-right Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who called for the arrest of Arab Israeli leaders.He was swiftly accused ofusing smear tacticsto cling to power. Eisenkot warned that Likud and Netanyahu “have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election”. President Herzog stepped in with a rebuke to the prime minister and said “we must avoid tarnishing an entire community”. Meanwhile, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson rejected “ridiculous and dangerous” accusations his country had interfered in Tuesday’s election.It bears repeating: Israeli police and the central elections committee have said there is no evidence of election fraud.The Palestinian-led parties who could be kingmakersThere was a surge in support for Arab parties after Palestinian citizens came out in historic numbers to vote.Many had boycotted previous elections “on the grounds that participating endorses a discriminatory system or because they felt their representatives had little leverage”, Emma explains. But this year, the mood changed: “They’re watching ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, a genocidal war in Gaza, and are under huge pressure inside Israel from an openly racist government, which has allowed organised crime to soar, ramped up home demolitions, and targeted political speech. They felt that, if Netanyahu managed to get another mandate with his far right allies including [extremist security minister] Ben-Gvir, this would only accelerate.”The Joint List – which represents a number of mainly leftist Israeli Arab-led parties – is led by Yousef Jabareen. He has previously said the Joint ​List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s ‌military operation in Gaza and southern Lebanon, but has left open the possibility of bolstering a minority government through confidence votes.The other main Palestinian party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, and includes a Jewish former chief of police as number two on their slate, a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis but also their desire to tackle organised crime, which is a big issue for the Palestinian population.Ra’am joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time a Palestinian party entered an Israeli coalition, but their pact collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.Thebig dilemmaA surveytaken as polls closed on Tuesday showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu.While Eisenkot has not ruled out cooperating with Palestinians because of their race, he has effectively barred them from a future coalition by laying out conditions for any partner which are politically impossible for them to accept.Still, Emma notes an inconsistency: Palestinian citizens play a key role in Israeli life, with outsized representation in professions from medics to security guards, including much of the team at Eisenkot’s election night HQ. “You would think some of these parties might ask, if you trust Palestinian citizens to secure your campaign events why don’t you trust them to be part of your government?”Emma points to a rarely referenced precedent from three decades ago, whenYitzhak Rabinrelied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict. Might such a compromise be possible now?“This whole campaign has been based on Israeli voters urgently wanting change, because Netanyahu has led them to the brink of disaster. And now they have voted, this is an existential moment,” she said“You have a parliamentary majority to bring about that change. Is your racism ultimately more important to you? What matters more: the desire to exclude Palestinians or the desire to get rid of Netanyahu?”What else we’ve been readingView image in fullscreen‘It was like a youth club’ … Boogie Times Records in Romford.Photograph: Danny DonnellyTim Burrows’deep diveon how Romford might actually be the birthplace ofjunglewas surprising and gave me a sense of nostalgia for a time that I wasn’t really part of.Poppy Noor, newsletters teamThelatest instalmentof our US politics film series,Anywherebut Washington, really captures the vibe in Texas where all eyes are on a hotly contested midterm Senate race.MichaelAdrian Chiles onthe cryptic signoutside hislocal pubwas a lesson in when not to brag. I now know far more about pub tubes, mould and yeast than I ever cared to know.PoppyAndy Beckett’s odeto theBritish Librarycomes as some of its silent, free-to-access reading rooms face a #coworking space fate. Fun fact, I once fell asleep for a whole hour inside one …MichaelReaders’ reactionstothe budgetwas a real take on the different ways people in the country live.Poppyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSportView image in fullscreenTara Elimbi Gilbert is embraced by her PSG teammates after scoring a late equaliser.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/UEFA/Getty ImagesWomen’s Champion League| Paris Saint-Germain’s Tara Elimbi Gilbert had a late equaliser moments after Khadija Shaw scored a penaltyas Manchester City drew their third leaguephase game in a row.Cricket|England beat Sri Lankain the One Day International by 55 runs but still do not progress to the final on Sunday.Football|Everton beat Newcastle 3-1with goals by James Garner, Hayden Hackney and Thierno Barry to set up a Carabao Cup quarter-final with Fleetwood Town.Something for the weekendOur critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right nowView image in fullscreenTrue love … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård as her wicker husband in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PAFilmWicker (in cinemas now)| ★★★☆☆Olivia Colman stars as a depressed and bullied fisher in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker.Read Peter Bradshaw’s full review.TVNocturne (Apple TV) | ★★★★☆Stephen Graham plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars. With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for Halloween.Read Lucy Mangan’s full review.MusicThe Big Moon: Forever | ★★★★☆After front person Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincing.Read Dave Simpson’s full review.BookAre You With Me Now? by Hanif KureishiAfter his catastrophic accident, the rebel writer’s musings on everything from sex chatbots to film stars have become gloriously unleashed.Read Melissa Denes’s full review.The front pagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Guardian“Netanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to power”, is theGuardian’s front page today.TheTimesleads with “Defence to benefit from off-the-book spending”, theTelegraphwrites “Prepare for decade of pain, warn IFS”, and thei Paperleads on “No welfare cuts before election – as Britons face ‘worst decade’ for pay growth”, while theMailhas “Humiliation for Healey”.TheFTsays “Alphabet shares battered as cash burn deepens investor fears over AI returns”.Metrowrites “Manosphere ‘as bad as smoking’” and theSunsplashes “Fright of the round table”.The LatestPhotograph: The GuardianShock and anger in Spain after deadly train crashSpain has begun three days of mourning after at least 69 people were killed and more than 100 were injured in a crash between two high-speed trains. The town of Urda has become the site of a major operation, as emergency services continue to search through the wreckage and relatives wait for news of their loved ones. There is growing public anger over the incident, which is the second fatal train collision in Spain in less than a year. Lucy Houghspeaks to the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent, Sam Jones.Cartoon of the day | Ben JenningsView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenAn electric ferry in New York.Photograph: Climate CentralMoving away from diesel-powered ferries to electric vessels has not been an easy task. Batteries are heavy, which means more power is needed to propel electric boats forward through significant resistance. But more companies are finding solutions to the problem and creating workable vessels that reduce emissions.One such company is Vessev, whoseelectric ferriesrely on underwater wings called hydrofoils that lift the boat above the water. This dramatically reduces drag by up to 66%, making their boats more energy-efficient. Swedish company Candela are designing boats, they claim, which can reduce energy use by 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.Sign up herefor a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.Quick crosswordCryptic crosswordWordiplyExplore more on these topicsIsraelFirst Edition newsletterMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahunewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Man accused of sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband says he thought it was ‘their kink’ | UK news | The Guardian
description: Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been drugged
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been drugged
Content: From left, top: Connor Sanderson Doyle, 32, and Norman Macksoni, 48; bottom, from left: Mohammed Hassan, 38, and Richard Wilkins, 62.Composite: PAView image in fullscreenFrom left, top: Connor Sanderson Doyle, 32, and Norman Macksoni, 48; bottom, from left: Mohammed Hassan, 38, and Richard Wilkins, 62.Composite: PAUK newsMan accused of sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband says he thought it was ‘their kink’Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been druggedSteven MorrisFri 30 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMen accused of sexually assaulting a woman whose then husband drugged her for years and allowed her to be abused have described being invited to the couple’s home via online adverts and a swinging website.One of those accused of assaulting Joanne Young, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, as she lay restrained and blindfolded said he was a young man “trying out things” and had no idea she was drugged.A second said there was a large “cuckold community” of men who watched their wives having sex, claiming his encounter was “just a sex meet” and she seemed “fine”.Philip Young, 50, has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and sexually abusing his former wife, 49, at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, over a number of years. The prosecution has said he advertised his wife online and “loaned” her out to other men.Four other men are on trial at Winchester crown court, including Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, who denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016.In police interviews read out to the jury, Sanderson-Doyle said he contacted Philip Young via Craigslist after seeing an ad in its adult section for a woman tied and blindfolded. He said he thought he had met a couple “trying to live out whatever their kink is”.He said he went to the Youngs’ house on his motorcycle. He asked if he should take his shoes off when he arrived, but kept his balaclava on throughout. He saw there were toys in the house so assumed the couple had children.Sanderson-Doyle, then 21, said he found Joanne Young “tied up and blindfolded” as she had been pictured in the online ad. She did not say anything but seemed awake.The defendant said that at one point he heard her say “No” but he thought she wanted him to do something different rather than stop completely.Sanderson-Doyle told police he started to get a “vibe she wasn’t enjoying it or was not comfortable” and left soon afterwards.He continued: “I thought I had her consent. I didn’t know she was drugged,” adding: “I was just a young guy trying out things.” He called the encounter a “non event”.A second man, Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. He told police he worked as an MC and went by the username “dark stranger” on the swingers’ site where he made contact with Philip Young.He said the site was “about couples living out fantasies” and there was a thriving “cuckold community”. Macksoni told police he had never had sex without consent and Joanne Young was “totally coherent”. He said: “It was just a sex meet and then I left.”The defendant told officers he did not wear a condom and added: “He specifically said she didn’t like them.”Also on trial are Richard Wilkins, 62, of Toothill, Wiltshire, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, of Swindon, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand trial: accusers have ‘nothing to gain’ and were not led by media, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: In closing speech, prosecutor says six women had ‘bravely’ come forward after realising they were not alone
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: In closing speech, prosecutor says six women had ‘bravely’ come forward after realising they were not alone
Content: The women were ‘haunted’ by their encounters with Russell Brand, the prosecutor said.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe women were ‘haunted’ by their encounters with Russell Brand, the prosecutor said.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsRussell Brand trial: accusers have ‘nothing to gain’ and were not led by media, court toldIn closing speech, prosecutor says six women had ‘bravely’ come forward after realising they were not aloneEmine SinmazFri 30 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix women who have been “haunted” by their encounters with Russell Brand came forward to give evidence against him with nothing to gain and no appetite for fame, a court has heard.The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said the women, who do not know one another, had not been compelled to make police complaints by the “magic force” of media reporting on Brand’s alleged misconduct.In her closing speech, she told jurors at Southwark crown court that the women had “vivid recollections” and had “bravely” come forward to the tell “the truth” after realising they were not alone.Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999.
