He denies all the charges.Karmy-Jones denied that a 2023 Dispatches documentary about Brand had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.She said the complainants had described a similar pattern of behaviour, saying: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not looked out for some form of publicity, who have not taken part in a documentary, not made claims for compensation.“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago.”She said the women described how Brand’s “demeanour changed” before he assaulted them. “Listen to their accounts,” the prosecutor told the jury. “Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change. A pivot. His eyes changed, he snapped from charming to frightening and nasty.“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting. In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim.”She said the women had given the court “specific details” about Brand’s conduct. “What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago.“The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years,” she said.The prosecutor also accused Brand of using “gaslighting” to “good effect” by asking some of his accusers for their telephone numbers or emails after the alleged assaults.She said women were a “disposable commodity” to Brand and later added: “He was a defendant who was rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever her wished, whenever he pleased.”Karmy-Jones described the account of the youngest witness, a fan then in her early 20s who accused the TV personality of anally raping her at his London townhouse after meeting her at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.He cared only about his “birthright orgasm” and ignored her pleas for him to stop, the prosecutor said, adding that she was “just another number to add to his 5,000 notches which he was marking up”.The court heard Brand had a “flavour of disdain” towards the allegations, which the prosecution suggested was “a reflection” of his “whole approach to the female species at that time”.“Women as a whole were disposable, they didn’t matter to him. He didn’t even need to know their names. They were just a means to an end.“As he said in a 2017 interview, they were the amusements in what he described as his playground of orgasms,” Karmy-Jones continued.Earlier on Friday the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, gave legal directions to the jury in which he pointed out that they would have “rival arguments” to consider.Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.His barrister, Ian Winter KC, is due to deliver his closing speech on Monday.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Local devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell Burnham | Devolution | The Guardian
description: John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not Westminster
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not Westminster
Content: Andy Burnham and Scotland's first minister, John Swinney, in Glasgow on Friday.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Scotland's first minister, John Swinney, in Glasgow on Friday.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/PADevolutionLocal devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell BurnhamJohn Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not WestminsterPeter Walker,Bethan McKernanandAndrew SparrowFri 30 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScotland and Wales’s first ministers have toldAndy Burnhamthat decisions on local devolution rest solely with their parliaments, in response to the prime minister’s push to extend English-style regional powers across the UK.After Burnham held discussions in Glasgow with John Swinney andRhun ap Iorwerthabout localised employment and reindustrialisation powers, Downing Street characterised the talks as constructive.However, the defence secretary,Wes Streeting, caused friction before the summit by criticising Swinney’s government for hoarding powers it acquired from Westminster rather than devolving them further.Westminster’s time is coming to an end, say first ministers of UK’s Celtic nationsRead moreStreeting told BBC Scotland: “One of the critiques we have … is that for the Scottish government, devolution is often about transferring power, responsibility, resources from Westminster to Holyrood and the challenge Andy Burnham is setting out is: ‘What about devolving more power also from Holyrood to local government acrossScotland?’”Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, had also been due at the talks, but did not attend after a political row between Sinn Féin and the DUP. Burnham said it was “disappointing” she was not there.The prime minister said he hoped to have all four UK nations moving at the same pace on devolution, particularly on efforts outlined in Wednesday’s budget to give mayors in England more powers over tax revenues.“There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind,” Burnham said. “I don’t want to seeWalesleft behind, but also, crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.”View image in fullscreenThe Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, speaks to the media in Glasgow on Friday.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/ReutersAp Iorwerth said he had pushed Burnham on his wish to have more powers for his government.He added: “I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd.”Swinney’s comments after the summit took a similar line, saying he would “work constructively and collaboratively” in devolving more powers to his government, while adding that Burnham had assured him “that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour”.Despite the emollient tone, tensions remain. Shortly before the summit, ap Iorwerth said Burnham’s first budget, which theWelsh governmentsaid amounted to a real-terms funding cut for the country, showed the prime minister was “not serious about Wales”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlaid Cymru, which won May’s Senedd elections, putting nationalists in office in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, has already formally asked Burnham to give Wales the same devolved powers as Scotland.The SNP-led government is frequently irritated by comments such as those by Streeting, characterised by one Scottish official as “lecturing us on devolution”.Separately, Lee Waters, who was a minister in the Labour-led Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until the elections in May, told the Guardian that Burnham, who was the Greater Manchester mayor before becoming prime minister, should not try to impose an English-style mayoral model on Wales, as “we are not comparing like with like”.He said: “The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas.“Transposing an English mayoral worldview on to a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.“Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government.”Explore more on these topicsDevolutionJohn SwinneyRhun ap IorwerthWalesWelsh politicsWelsh governmentScottish politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police watchdog to investigate Met’s handling of Meghan warning letter | Metropolitan police | The Guardian
description: IOPC launches independent investigation after referral by Scotland Yard over 2019 letter about Thomas Markle
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: IOPC launches independent investigation after referral by Scotland Yard over 2019 letter about Thomas Markle
Content: The contents of the 2019 letter are understood to have played a part in the Duchess of Sussex’s estrangement from her father.Photograph: Cyril Zingaro/Keystone/APView image in fullscreenThe contents of the 2019 letter are understood to have played a part in the Duchess of Sussex’s estrangement from her father.Photograph: Cyril Zingaro/Keystone/APMetropolitan policePolice watchdog to investigate Met’s handling of Meghan warning letterIOPC launches independent investigation after referral by Scotland Yard over 2019 letter about Thomas MarkleVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentFri 30 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScotland Yard faces an independent investigation into its failure in 2019 to pass claims alleging wrongdoing by Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex, to law enforcement agencies overseas.The force hadreferred itselfto the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) over its handling of a letter written by Markle’s former wife, Roslyn Loveless. Markle, 82, is now facing claims of child sexual abuse in the Philippines, which he denies, and is under investigation by authorities there.On Friday, the IOPC decided to use its formal powers to launch an investigation into the Met. The police watchdog views the claims in the 2019 letter as potentially alleging serious offending.Its investigation will look at who in the Met made decisions such as not to pass on the claims to police forces in countries where wrongdoing by Markle was alleged, and whether police policies and procedures were followed.An IOPC spokesperson said: “Following a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, we have decided an independent investigation is required into its failure to pass on allegations of serious offending, contained in a letter it received in 2019, to relevant overseas authorities at the time.”The Met had announced on Thursday its voluntary referral to the IOPC about the handling of the 2019 letter. It also referred whether its decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duchess of Sussex could have been a breach of data rules because it contained sensitive information. The IOPC has decided it will not investigate that.The contents of the letter are understood to have played a part in Meghan’s estrangement from her father. The Guardian understands that the long letter made claims about Markle’s activities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.The Met has said it did not investigate because the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas. But for seven years it did not pass on details to the countries affected, and it is only now sending details of the letter to the FBI in the US and law enforcement in the Philippines, where Markle lived until May, as well as Thai counterparts.Markle, now in the US, has admitted paying for sex but denies possessing material that would be illegal. On Saturday, the Philippine interior minister, Jonvic Remulla,told the Guardianthat all signs pointed to Markle being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” and that a full forensic investigation would give a “definitive picture”.Investigators in the Philippines are examining digital images alleged to belong to Markle and alleged to have been found at his former home in the south-east Asian country.Meghan’s half-brother, also called Thomas, reported to Philippine authorities last week the alleged discovery of child sexual abuse images. Footage on Thursday showed Markle Jr present as Philippine officials started gathering material to examine.On Friday the Daily Mail claimed that a garage close to where Markle Sr lived in Mexico, before moving to the Philippines in 2025, contained material the paper characterised as child sexual abuse images.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt said it had reported its alleged find to the FBI.The scale of embarrassment for the Met will depend on whether investigators in the Philippines assess that the allegations relating to child sexual abuse images have any credence.On Thursday, the Met commander Adam Slonecki, who leads its protection command, said the letter had been sent in 2019 to the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre. “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom,” he said.“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”Explore more on these topicsMetropolitan policeIndependent Office for Police ConductMeghan, the Duchess of SussexPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: BP profits hit ‘obscene’ 18-year high as Iran war drives up oil refining margins | BP | The Guardian
description: Oil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Oil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’
Content: ‘We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market,’ said BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market,’ said BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersBPBP profits hit ‘obscene’ 18-year high as Iran war drives up oil refining marginsOil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’Jillian Ambrose,Damien GayleandLauren AlmeidaFri 30 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 04.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBP’s quarterly profits have been labelled “obscene” after they hit an 18-year high of $8.46bn (£6.3bn), as the war in the Middle East drove up oil and gas prices.The energy company hailed a “banner quarter” on Friday, with its underlying ​replacement ⁠cost profit – a key measure of its income – almost quadrupling in the three months to the end of September, from $2.2bn in the same period ​a year ​ago. The jump meant BP’s quarterly profits hit their highest levelsince the $8.9bn recorded in 2008.BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told Bloomberg TV: “It really was a banner quarter for the refining business. We had very strong margins from the BP-operated refineries, we also had very strong underlying performance. We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market.”However, climate crisis campaigners said it was outrageous that BP was profiting so handsomely on commodities causing serious damage to the environment.It is just over a week until diplomats will meet in Antalya, Turkey, for the Cop31 UN climate summit. Recent climate-linked disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal will be at the forefront of many delegates’ minds. There are likely to be tensions with fossil fuel producing countries, which have sought to stymie calls for a transition to clean energy.BP’s strong results also come as motorists in the UK face high fuel prices, with diesel now at 198.79p a litre, according to estimates from the RAC. The cost of petrol has also risen, with an average price of 172.92p a litre, compared with 132.83p in late February, before the latest conflict in the Middle East began.Jonathan Noronha-Gant, of the campaign group Global Witness, said it was “obscene that polluters are continuing to cash in on the fallout of the war in Iran, making more bumper profits from spiralling oil prices while innocent civilians suffer.“These massive profits come as ordinary people across Europe are struggling with the rising cost of living, with many struggling to afford to heat their homes as winter arrives,” he said.Danny Gross, of Friends of the Earth, said: “As millions of households brace themselves for a cold winter, huddling under blankets and clutching hot-water bottles as they struggle to pay their bills, BP is raking in huge profits while doubling down on gas and oil production and slashing investment in renewables.”Although the link between fossil fuels and climate breakdown has been known for decades, scientists directly linked carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel companies to dozens of deadly heatwavesfor the first time a year ago. Yet more heatwaves swept across Europe this summer, with separate research suggesting theyled to a record 50,000 excess deaths.As people in cities sweltered, infernos tore through forests and brush in parched rural areas.France experienced its largest area burned on recordand fires blazed in usually cooler regions, such as the Cairngorms in Scotland.In the Pacific, a superchargedEl Niñois brewing, with water temperatures reaching more than 3C higher than usual. The weather phenomenon is likely to be the most extreme of its kind in at least 1,000 years, dumping vast amounts of extra heat into an atmosphere already warmed by climate breakdown.“The climate crisis is not an abstract future threat,” said Clémence Dubois, head of global campaigns at350.org. “People are facing deadly heat, destroyed livelihoods and growing insecurity now. Governments are being forced to find money to protect their populations, while fossil fuel companies are forecast to make extraordinary profits.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRecord oil company profits come as the UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is weighing up whether to allow drilling in the North Sea’sRosebankoilfield, after approving a licence for the less controversialJackdawgasfield earlier in October.BP’s quarterly earnings were bolstered by higher profits from the oil refining business as the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined fuels such as diesel and gasoline soared, earning almost $47 for each barrel produced.Although global oil prices have remained below the peaks recorded during the 2022 energy crisis, the pump prices for fuels, including diesel, have risen to all-time highs across the UK, Europe and the US in recent months because of severe disruptions to refineries in the Gulf region and across Russia.BP’s earnings windfall announcement came after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergiesreported their strongest profits since 2022, also thanks in large part to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel.BP earnings windfall announcement came after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergiesreported their strongest profits since 2022, also thanks in large part to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel.Explore more on these topicsBPOil and gas companiesEnergy industryOilCommoditiesGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Retired Michigan teacher released from Russian prison believed he would never be freed | US news | The Guardian
description: Stephen Hubbard said that only when he was being taken from Moscow to St Petersburg did he believe he was ‘going somewhere’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stephen Hubbard said that only when he was being taken from Moscow to St Petersburg did he believe he was ‘going somewhere’
Content: Stephen Hubbard listens to Donald Trump speak in the Oval Office in Washington DC, on 30 October 2026.Photograph: Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStephen Hubbard listens to Donald Trump speak in the Oval Office in Washington DC, on 30 October 2026.Photograph: Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty ImagesUS newsRetired Michigan teacher released from Russian prison believed he would never be freedStephen Hubbard said that only when he was being taken from Moscow to St Petersburg did he believe he was ‘going somewhere’Guardian staff and agenciesFri 30 Oct 2026 19.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his first comments since recently beingreleasedfrom a Russian prison, a retired Michigan teacher said he only believed he would be freed when he got new clothes.Stephen Hubbard, 74, remarked on Friday that he had heard many times previously that he would be released – but never really trusted what he was told, adopting a philosophy of “seeing is believing” and “actions speak louder than words”.“Only when they started giving me new clothes and leading me to the exit of the prison,” Hubbard said in his first public remarks since his 21 October release, which came during a visit at the White House withDonald Trump, “I went out and I saw the car, and I was accompanied by a couple of Russians, then I believed, finally believed, on the drive from Moscow to St Petersburg, ‘I’m really going somewhere.’”Hubbard had been behind bars for more than four years on charges that he fought as a mercenary inUkraine, whichRussiainvaded in February 2022. His legal team has denied the Russian accusations and said he was not involved in any military activity.Trump has previously said that he had asked Russian leaderVladimir Putinto free Hubbard – and that the US did not have to release anyone in return.“He was somebody I wanted to get back,” the US president said as he hosted Hubbard on Friday in the Oval Office.The White House allowed a limited pool of journalists into Trump’s meeting with Hubbard, allowing primarily news photographers and a television crew.Many in the international community perceived Hubbard’s release to be Russia’s latest maneuver to bring Trump closer to Putin’s position on the war inUkraine. It also offered Trump a diplomatic victory ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, when his Republican party is expected to lose seats in Congress.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS newsUS politicsDonald TrumpRussiaUkraineMichigannewsShareReuse this content

title: Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan Sullivan | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Mary Peltola denies knowledge as party accused of recruiting spoiler candidate with same name as sitting Republican
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Mary Peltola denies knowledge as party accused of recruiting spoiler candidate with same name as sitting Republican
Content: Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for US Senate, in Kodiak, Alaska, in September.Photograph: Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for US Senate, in Kodiak, Alaska, in September.Photograph: Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan SullivanMary Peltola denies knowledge as party accused of recruiting spoiler candidate with same name as sitting RepublicanAlaska Senate race: what to know about Democrats’ alleged ballot-stacking effortLucy Campbell,Robert Mackeyand agenciesFri 30 Oct 2026 19.13 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Democrats to confuse voters by recruiting a spoiler candidate on the ballot forUS Senatewho shares a name with the Republican incumbent, senator Dan Sullivan.Speaking ata news conferencein Anchorage on Friday, US attorney Michael Heyman citedreporting by the New York Timeswhich suggested that the Senate campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola and nationalDemocratshad, in his words, “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”.Both Dan Sullivans – one a Republican senator and the other a retired schoolteacher with no prior political experience – qualified for the ballot.“We are taking that extremely seriously,” Heyman said.“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets toAlaska,” he added. “As we speak, law enforcement around the country are taking investigative steps with respect to a criminal investigation on these matters.”In a separate filing, the Department of Justice asked a federal judge to order state elections officials to isolate ballots ranking Dan J Sullivan to investigate potential voter “confusion” with the incumbent Dan Sullivan.E. Bryan Wilson, an assistant US attorney in Alaska, in a filing, said the government “seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary”.The justice department on Friday also asked a federal judge to issue a preliminary ⁠injunction ​that would ‌block ‌Alaska from ‌certifying its Senate election result if the incumbent senator loses to Peltola due to the presence of Daniel J Sullivan on the ballot.Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into. It is highly unusual for federal prosecutors to confirm the existence of an open criminal investigation, much less discuss it publicly.“The civil lawsuit is publicly faced, and is focused on preserving the ballots,” Heyman said, referring to a Department of Justice suit filed last week.A day earlier, Peltola denied any prior knowledge of the alleged effort, telling supporters in Juneau, Alaska’s capital: “I am not interested in tricking voters.”“I just want to clear the air,” the Democratic Senate candidate said on Thursday at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about.”Peltola is running against Dan Sullivan, the two-term US senator. A person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after the New York Timesreportedthat Peltola’s campaignappeared to be involvedin recruiting Dan J Sullivan Jr as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.The race is considered one of the most important contests of next week’s midterm elections, and will be key to determining control of the Senate. Alaska is one of a handful of states with Senate races this year thatDemocratsare targeting as they try to win back a majority in the chamber, where they hold 47 seats to the Republican party’s 53, and recent polls have shown Peltola in the lead.More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke to the Associated Press. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.Republicans have condemned the presence in the race of two candidates named Dan Sullivan, calling the newcomer a ploy by Democrats to cost the incumbent re-election by splitting the GOP candidate’s supporters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBefore the August primary, election authorities in the state attempted to disqualify the other Dan Sullivan, but the state supreme courtruledthat he could appear on the ballot. Together with Sullivan and Peltola, the challenger was one of thetop four vote-gettersin the non-partisan primary.On the general election ballot, the senator will be listed as “Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the challenger “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.”Since the New York Times published its report, Mike Dunleavy, Alaska’s Republican governor, separately announcedplans to launch a criminal investigation, saying the story revealed “disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates – including one with the same name as an incumbent US senator – to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes”.“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the report “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.Donald Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate if she won the election.“Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”Later, as he rallied for Darline Graham, a Republican senator, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted”.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026AlaskaUS politicsElection interferenceUS voting rightsUS SenatenewsShareReuse this content

title: Democratic lawmakers demand ICE data on detainee miscarriages | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Demand comes after Guardian investigation found ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: Demand comes after Guardian investigation found ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026
Content: Joyce Beatty, Brittany Pettersen, and Robin Kelly are asking ICE to explain what, if any, steps are being taken to recover the missing data.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoyce Beatty, Brittany Pettersen, and Robin Kelly are asking ICE to explain what, if any, steps are being taken to recover the missing data.Composite: Getty ImagesICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Democratic lawmakers demand ICE data on detainee miscarriagesDemand comes after Guardian investigation found ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026Maanvi SinghFri 30 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS lawmakers are urgently demanding thatImmigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)disclose how many pregnant immigrants have experienced miscarriages, stillbirths and pregnancy-related hospitalizations while in the its custody, after the agency admitted it lost count last year.US representatives sent the request followinga recent Guardian investigationrevealing that theTrump administrationis detaining a record number of pregnant women and teens, and at the same has lost track of how many suffered miscarriages.Revealed: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant womenRead moreIn a letter sent this month to ICE’s acting director, David Venturella, Democratic representatives Brittany Pettersen, Joyce Beatty and Robin Kelly also asked the immigration enforcement agency to explain what – if any – steps have been taken to recover any missing data about these cases.Government documents obtained by the Guardian found that ICE had placed more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year. The agency recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents found, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.Detained pregnant women said that they were struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. Medical experts told the Guardian that lapses in care both during pregnancy and during and after miscarriage could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies.In their letter, the representatives also cite a 2021 directive instructing ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist” – and ask the agency to clarify on what grounds it is detaining pregnant immigrants. The directive also requires ICE to closely monitor and document the health of all pregnant people in its custody, and continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained.“ICE’s inability to follow agency directives, provide adequate medical care and maintain accurate records of pregnancy-related medical outcomes is unacceptable,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter, which was cosigned by 64 other representatives.In an interview, Pettersen said it was “deeply concerning” that ICE had failed to account for a full year of pregnancy outcomes. “I’m just devastated for the people who have gone through this, who’ve lost pregnancies unnecessarily, who have been left without the medical care that they need after miscarrying,” she said. “It’s hard to imagine how we are ever going to right these wrongs.”In internal agency documents, ICE said it had no data on miscarriages because the agency changed medical billing providers in October. The agency’s medical claims processing has been delayed for months. Immigration attorneys and former government officials told said it was odd, but plausible, that ICE was keeping track of miscarriages solely via its medical billing provider.In response to follow-up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in the ICE internal documents – the agency does not have data on miscarriages between October 2025 through June 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe DHS did not confirm to the Guardian whether it had received the letter from Congress members. “Claims that any pregnant detainees are receiving subprime care are FALSE,” an agency spokesperson said.In their letter, lawmakers asked ICE’s acting director to detail when “ICE leadership first became aware of concerns regarding miscarriage reporting and deficiencies in agency tracking systems”. They gave the agency until 6 November to respond.Prior to the Guardian’s reporting, the agency had never acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data.The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention, and the health outcomes for this population.Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)DemocratsMiscarriageUS immigrationWomen's healthHouse of RepresentativesUS CongressnewsShareReuse this content

title: Teen boy from Ghana chased and fatally shot on way to school in New York City | New York | The Guardian
description: Javits Frimpong, 15, was being bullied at school before he was shot and killed in the Bronx on Thursday, his father says
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Javits Frimpong, 15, was being bullied at school before he was shot and killed in the Bronx on Thursday, his father says
Content: Javits FrimpongPhotograph: GoFundmeView image in fullscreenJavits FrimpongPhotograph: GoFundmeNew YorkTeen boy from Ghana chased and fatally shot on way to school in New York CityJavits Frimpong, 15, was being bullied at school before he was shot and killed in the Bronx on Thursday, his father saysUwa Ede-OsifoFri 30 Oct 2026 18.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 18.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA teenage boy fromGhanawas chased down and fatally shot Thursday morning on his way to school in the Bronx.TheNew YorkCity police department (NYPD) received a report on Thursday morning about a shooting near Corona Park in the Bronx, a police spokesperson said on Friday. At about 9.24am, responding officers found Javits Frimpong, 15, with a gunshot wound to his stomach.Javits was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Police have not made any arrests and an investigation is ongoing as authorities search for three teenage boys in connection to the shooting.Surveillance footagereportedlycaptured Javits running, as a person wearing all black trailed behind. Another angle of video footageappearedto show masked individuals in dark clothing fleeing the site of the shooting.The deadly attack has rocked the Bronx’s Claremont neighborhood and the city’s west African community.“I lost him,” the teenager’s father, Thomas Frimpong,toldreporters on Thursday. “I don’t know what to do now.”The fatal shooting came as Javits marked one year of being in New York after arriving from Ghana, Frimpong said. Frimpong described his son as “clever” and “quiet”. Javits was being bullied at the DreamYard preparatory school, according to Frimpong.Frimpong said the high school’s principal, who could not be reached for comment by phone or email, informed him recently that two students were suspended for harassing Javits, he said.AnNYPDspokesperson declined to comment Friday on whether the reports of bullying were related to the attack.Ghana’s minister of foreign affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, condemned the attack in a Friday statement. “We will pursue justice and we will make sure that those who did this do not get away with it.”“Just one year ago, Javits arrived in the United States from Ghana to reunite with his father and begin a new chapter of his life. Like so many Ghanaian immigrant families, his family came together in America with hopes of greater opportunity, security, and a promising future,” the Ghana diaspora public affairs collective, a US-based non-profit, also said in a Friday statement.“That future has now been violently taken away.”Explore more on these topicsNew YorkUS crimeNYPDBullyingYoung peopleGun crimeGhananewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida prosecutors drop felony charge against Rick Ross in domestic violence case | Florida | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her
Content: Rick Ross at the BET Awards 2026 held at Peacock Theater on 28 June 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRick Ross at the BET Awards 2026 held at Peacock Theater on 28 June 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty ImagesFloridaFlorida prosecutors drop felony charge against Rick Ross in domestic violence caseMiami-Dade officials drop charge of battery by strangulation against rapper due to ‘insufficient evidence’Associated PressFri 30 Oct 2026 14.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFloridaprosecutors on Thursday dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross nearly a month after he wasarrestedin Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her, court records said.The Miami-Dade state attorney’s office filed paperwork on Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence”. Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence.Ross, 50, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his attorney said on Friday that his client would continue to defend himself against the allegations.Rick Ross arrested on domestic battery and strangulation chargesRead moreRoss surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on 1 October, two days after the woman filed a report with police, officials said. He was freed on bail several hours later.According to an arrest report, a woman told Miami Beach detectives that she had been living with Ross when he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times on 28 August. She said Ross also choked her with the collar of her shirt and slammed her into a wall. The woman said she was eventually able to leave the home and returned later – after Ross left – to collect her belongings.Ross previously pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2017 after he was accused of forcing a man into a guesthouse at his suburban Atlanta mansion in 2015 and beating him with a handgun, according to Georgia court records. Under a Georgia first-time offender program, the court issued an order exonerating Ross of guilt on that felony count.Ross is a longtime southFloridaresident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single Hustlin’.The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as the southern rap headquarters. Hustlin’ was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America and sparked a bidding war for Ross.He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed byJay-Z.Ross’s debut album, Port of Miami, also went platinum, debuting at No 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s Trilla and 2009’s Deeper ThanRap. He has been nominated for nine Grammy awards.In 2008, he founded the Maybach Music Group label, boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.His most recent album, Set In Stone, was released in July.Explore more on these topicsFloridaUS crimeMiamiHip-hopRapnewsShareReuse this content

title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’ | Binance | The Guardian
description: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses
Content: North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn from a different exchange last year.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenNorth Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn from a different exchange last year.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersBinanceNorth Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so farQ&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?Dan MilmoandKalyeena MakortoffFri 30 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifyingNorth Koreaas the likely culprit.Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars.Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the$1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.Trump says he doesn’t know who crypto tycoon is despite having pardoned himRead moreTRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack.Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets.The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who wasjailed for four months in 2024after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.Donald Trump pardoned himin 2025.The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”View image in fullscreenBinance was founded by Changpeng Zhao.Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMarkets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.”Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m.The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic.View image in fullscreenRichard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance: ‘Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg/GettyWorld Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers.Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.Share your experienceShare your experiencePlease share your response in the form below, anonymously if you prefer. We will contact you before we publish any of your submission.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhere do you live?Tell us a bit about yourself (e.g. age, background, what you do)OptionalIf you've been directly affected by the Binance hack, we'd like to hear about it herePlease include as much detail as possible.How did you hear about the hack? How has communication been so far?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.Has your confidence in crypto altered in any way?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.Do you have concerns?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.If you are happy to, please upload a photo of yourself hereOptionalPlease note, the maximum file size is5.7 MB.Choose fileCan we publish your response?Yes, entirelyYes, but contact me firstYes, but please keep me anonymousNo, this is information onlyPhone numberOptionalYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.You can add more information hereOptionalIf you include other people's names please ask them first.Would you be interested in speaking to our audio and/or video teams?Audio onlyVideo onlyAudio and videoNo, I'm not interestedBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreA spokesperson for the FCA said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.”The Bank of England is also monitoring the hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment.Coinbase, another major cryptocurrency exchange, said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarilyhalted trading after a security incidentinvolving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsBinanceCryptocurrenciesHackingNorth KoreaBitcoinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Government corruption a top issue for US midterm voters, exclusive poll finds | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Harris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday Americans
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Harris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday Americans
Content: A polling station in Atlanta, where early voting has been taking place. In the poll, corruption was the next top issue for voters after the cost of living.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenA polling station in Atlanta, where early voting has been taking place. In the poll, corruption was the next top issue for voters after the cost of living.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS midterm elections 2026Government corruption a top issue for US midterm voters, exclusive poll findsHarris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday AmericansLauren Arataniin New YorkFri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 09.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGovernment corruption has emerged as a top issue in the upcoming US midterm elections, with an overwhelming majority of Americans saying US government officials use their public office for personal financial gain, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem, according to the survey.Three-quarters (76%) of voters said that elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people. Voters were more likely to say that government corruption (65%) is more concerning than corporate power (29%). Just under 10% said that neither concerns them.The rising cost of living is still expected to drive the election, with 36% of voters saying it is the single most important issue to how they plan to vote in the midterms. But in a slate of other issues including immigration, housing costs, abortion, crime and safety and AI, corruption was the next top issue.A bar chart showing the responses from The Harris Poll. This survey question asked what the top issues are for voters. At 36%, cost of living came up as a top issue with the next four as: Government corruption (12%); Immigration (9%); Healthcare (7%); and Taxes (5%).The results come after nearly two years of Donald Trump’s second term, where the president has both figuratively and literally reshaped Washington.The president demolished the historic East Wing of the White House to make way for a $400mballroom– $335m of which he said is coming from private donors, including companies such as Apple and Nvidia. The federal government isdownmore than 420,000 workers after Elon Musk was given the power to introduce huge jobs cuts after donating nearly $300m to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Meanwhile, Trump’s sons are running the family’s lucrative cryptocurrency business that hasmade Trump $1bnsince returning to the White House. And Trump himself accepted a $400mprivate jetas a gift from the Qatari royal family.These actions have not gone unnoticed. Voters in the Harris poll were twice as likely to say thatRepublicanshave a bigger corruption problem than Democrats. Forty per cent of voters, including 29% of Republicans, said the GOP has a bigger corruption problem. A third (32%) of voters said that both parties have the problem equally, while 21% said that Democrats have the bigger problem.Independents, whose votes will be key in swing races across the country, were much more likely to say that Republicans have more of a corruption problem, with 34% saying that Republicans have the bigger issue and 13% pointing toDemocrats. Most Independents (42%) said that both parties share the problem equally.The economy as experienced by everyday Americans has been vastly different from the portrait painted by Wall Street. The stock market has beensoaringon the back of never-ending AI spending. In early October, both the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq stock indices hit record highs.The gains have been a boon for a relatively small group of Americans. Americans in the top 1% of wealth own half of the stock market while the bottom 50% own just over 1% of the market.Armed with more funds than ever, America’s wealthiest people have been driving even more donations into elections. After the supreme court’s 2010 Citizens United case removed limits on campaign contributions, each election year has brought in new records of cash. The midterms have already cost $11.2bn in ads, according toNBC News, the most ever for a midterm cycle.A chunk of these donations are coming from the ultra-rich. Just 40 donors have already contributed $2.5bn to races this year, according to theBrennan Center for Justice. Last week, billionaire Michael Bloombergannouncedhe was contributing $80m in last-minute funding for Democratic candidates, while Donald Trump said his political action committee was contributing a total of $400m to Republicans.This bar chart shows responses on which party has a bigger problem with financial corruption. Republicans top this chart at 40% with Democrats at 21% and both equally at 32%.For everyday Americans, this flood of cash has changed the motivations of elected officials, who many believe will ultimately prioritize themselves and their donors over their constituents. A majority of voters (78%) in the Harris poll agreed that “elected officials care more about enriching themselves than helping people like me”.“Government corruption has shot up to become the second most important issue in the midterms after cost of living. Americans are triggered by leaders they now see as both responsible for and profiting off their growing economic hardship,” said John Gerzema, CEO of Harris Poll.Regardless of who ends up controlling Congress after the midterms, voters across the political spectrum are expecting solutions to address the ongoing affordability crisis that is affecting their lives.Out of a slate of policies to address the cost of living, a third (32%) of voters said that there should be limits on the influence of companies and lobbyists on government decisions. The second most popular policy was removing tariffs (29%), followed by limiting how much companies raise prices on goods (24%).This chart shows what actions should politicians take to address high prices. Ranked as the first choice is “limit the influence of companies and lobbyists on government decisions.” This is 32% of respondents. The second highest is “remove tariffs on imported goods” at 29%.On Tuesday, voters in California will decide on a ballot measure that could place a one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires in the state. Tech billionaires have beenspendingan estimated $1m a day, altogether more than $340m, to fight the measure. Half (50%) of voters in the new poll, including 56% of independents, said that billionaires do not pay their fair share of taxes. Just 28% of Republicans said the same.Some in corporate America are catching on to the discontent. Last week, the United Airlines CEO, Scott Kirby, said in an interview that he supports a national wealth tax, a comment that got himbacklashfrom some Republicans.“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 22 October to 24 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 2,065 US adults, among whom 1,481 are likely to vote in the 2026 midterm elections.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US economyDemocratsRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports | Technology | The Guardian
description: Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough
Content: Futures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on 30 October 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenFutures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on 30 October 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersTechnologyTech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reportsBig tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enoughBlake Montgomeryand agenciesFri 30 Oct 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies droveUS marketsdown by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged theNasdaqcomposite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq ⁠100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough.The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. ⁠The index has fallen ⁠more than 5.8% so far in ​October as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms,Alphabetand Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure.Intel tumbled nearly 30% and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell far short of analysts’ expectations.Amazon fell 1.8% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. The company also disclosed that it had spent more this year than anticipated.A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12%, wiping $500bn from its market capitalization, to its worst day on record after telling investors that it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring because of similar, mammoth investments in AI.Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make AI investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI datacenters have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.A drop of 3.1% forNvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward.Such losses overshadowed an otherwise mixed day for the rest of Wall Street, with the S&P 500 roughly evenly split between gainers and losers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExpectations are high broadly for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)Datacenters – USStock marketsUS marketsNasdaqMarket turmoilnewsShareReuse this content

title: How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe? | Binance | The Guardian
description: The incident at Binance could be the biggest theft of any kind in history. We answer some key questions
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: The incident at Binance could be the biggest theft of any kind in history. We answer some key questions
Content: More than $2.5bn of the $6.3bn taken was withdrawn in one transaction alone.Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/RexView image in fullscreenMore than $2.5bn of the $6.3bn taken was withdrawn in one transaction alone.Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/RexBinanceExplainerHow big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?The incident at Binance could be the biggest theft of any kind in history. We answer some key questionsNorth Korean group blamed for $6.3bn crypto heistTell us: have you been affected?Dan MilmoandKalyeena MakortoffFri 30 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a $6.3bn heist that, according to experts, is likely to be thework of North Korea.This is not the first time a crypto market has been targeted by hackers, and the rogue state has a track record of this type of theft. Here we answer some key questions about what’s happened:Just how big a deal is this?It could be the biggest heist of any kind in history, according to Elliptic, a consultancy specialising in crypto-related crime. The incident, which took place late on Thursday, is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto hack, the $1.5bn onetargeting the Bybit exchange last year. Elliptic says there does not appear to be anything comparable in the pre-crypto era.“This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” says Tom Robinson, the consultancy’s chief scientist. “Before Bybit, that record was held by Saddam Hussein, who took $1bn from the central bank of Iraq in Baghdad on the eve of the 2003 Iraq war. The Binance theft is more than six times larger.”So what exactly is cryptocurrency?This digital asset operates online, outside the traditional financial system. There is no physical version of the most popular form of crypto – bitcoin – or its peers, such as Ethereum, Ripple and Dogecoin.A cryptocurrency such as bitcoin runs on a combination of encryption, which is the sort of technology that keeps your WhatsApp messages safe, and peer-to-peer networks that allow computers to connect without a central server (think of the music-sharing sites like Napster at the turn of the century).In short, the owner of a bitcoin (or part of a bitcoin; you can buy them in fractions) has access to a private key – like a long password – which is needed to access the funds. These transactions are all stored and displayed on a publicly available ledger, like a school register, known as a blockchain. You typically store your private keys in a “crypto wallet”.There are varying estimates for how many cryptocurrencies there are but Coingecko, which monitors the market, claims there are more than 22,000 coins. The entire market is worth about $2.7tn, so it is not a surprise that hackers and rogue states looking for funds are interested in a corner of the global finance industry that has so much money, is largely unregulated and is vulnerable to digital thieves.And what is a cryptoexchange?A cryptoexchange is where you buy, sell and trade digital assets such as bitcoin. They host your crypto wallets, which are typically “cold”, meaning they are not connected online and can be kept safer from hackers. A smaller amount sits in “hot” wallets which are linked to the internet so they can be used for quick withdrawals, making them of greater interest to hackers. Binance is the world’s largest of these exchanges in terms of the number of trades it carries out every day – at a value of about $95bn daily.How was Binance hacked?It does not appear that private keys were hacked. Instead, a Binance engineer’s laptop was infiltrated, which in turn allowed the attackers to drain “hot” wallets. Binance later added that there were “additional points of breach” in its systems as well as the laptop.“Hackers rarely crack the cryptographic keys themselves,” says Robinson. “They instead target people with access to those wallets. Binance says the attack involved a compromised engineer’s laptop, along with other points of breach. This gave the attacker a way into Binance’s internal systems. From there, they made Binance’s own systems sign transactions that sent the funds to the attacker.”More than $2.5bn of the $6.3bn was taken in one transaction alone.“Crypto exchanges are safer than they used to be, but not immune to attacks such as this,” says Robinson. “This hack shows that even the biggest exchange can be breached through one employee’s laptop. What matters most for customers is whether the exchange can cover the loss. Binance says it will repay everyone from its own funds.”How do the hackers get hold of their haul?They will have to “cash out” the crypto and turn it into legitimate money, known as fiat currency. Chainalysis, a crypto research firm, has said the attackers used “never seen before” laundering patterns to exfiltrate the affected assets. Phil Larratt, a senior director at the consultancy, says the thieves will now try to convert the crypto into fiat money in a process that “takes weeks and months, if not years”.“The process is patient and sophisticated,” he says.Laundering methods used by crypto hackers include visiting less scrupulous exchanges, using swapping services that exchange one type of crypto asset for another, and accessing brokers who will convert crypto to cash in exchange for a cut of the proceeds.Do we know who did it?This attack has been attributed to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor, a name assigned to it by the US government. The communist state, short of cash and hamstrung by sanctions, has a strong track record of crypto hacking. TraderTraitor emerged from Lazarus, a group working from North Korea’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, a military intelligence agency.Last year TraderTraitor was blamed for the $1.5bn theft from the Dubai-based Bybit. Elliptic and two other crypto analysis firms have attributed the attack to North Korea. Elliptic said some of the funds taken from Binance have already been traced to wallet addresses used in a cryptoexchange hack last month that is also thought to have been carried out by operatives from the rogue state.Rafe Pilling, the senior director of threat intelligence at the cybersecurity firm Sophos, says North Korea had previously hacked conventional financial targets such as the Bangladesh Central Bank andeven cash machines.But crypto delivers bigger potential rewards, he says. “Crypto is less well regulated, easier to move, easier to launder and that makes it a more enticing target for North Korea. And as a result you have groups like TraderTraitor that are specialising in attacking crypto firms and getting away with huge payments.”Are my crypto investments safe?Any guarantees will be coming from Binance itself, rather than any regulatory or government-backed safety nets. The exchangesaid in a post on Xthat it would “cover all losses” and “user funds are safe”. It also said it had frozen about half the funds targeted in the hack, stopping the thieves from making off with that tranche of cryptocurrency.In Australia, you can claim a capital loss on your tax return if you can offer proof that a crypto asset was lost or stolen. However, most customers won’t have any legal protections.Crypto users are not covered by formal deposit protections in countries such as the US, UK or Australia if things go wrong, including if an exchange is hacked or ever goes bankrupt.Customers of regulated banks are guaranteed capped refunds – up to £120,000 per customer per bank in the UK, and $250,000 in the US – but only if the lender goes out of business. It will not pay out claims if there is a hack but the bank keeps operating.Explore more on these topicsBinanceCryptocurrenciesE-commerceInternetNorth KoreaBankingFinancial sectorexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Arteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memories | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but the Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of the club’s greatest nights
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but the Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of the club’s greatest nights
Content: Mikel Arteta takes Arsenal to Liverpool, having never won there in the league as the Gunners’ manager.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta takes Arsenal to Liverpool, having never won there in the league as the Gunners’ manager.Composite: Guardian DesignArsenalArteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memoriesArsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of club’s greatest nightsEd AaronsFri 30 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta used a Spanish word to describe what it felt like to be helpless at Anfield while playing for Everton in 2011:bajar. “It’s when a cyclist is going up and looks amazing, then in one kilometre he goes ‘boom’ and he’s struggling again,” he said in Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary. “The game was going well and then suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around. The game is passing all over me and I cannot react. I only had that feeling in my career once, and it was at Anfield.”Given Arteta’s record at Liverpool, Sunday’s showdown with his childhood friend Andoni Iraola – five days after Arsenal weredumped out of the Carabao Cup by Fleetwood– could be expected to fill him with dread. Arteta finally tasted victory there as a player with Arsenalin September 2012, after five failed attempts in the Merseyside derby, but ended up spending the night in hospital with concussion after colliding with Jordan Henderson in an incident he has described as “the biggest fear of my life”.Fantastic Fleetwood seal shootout success in Carabao Cup shock against ArsenalRead moreArteta was part of the Arsenal side thatwon at Anfield again six months laterthanks to goals from the new signings Lukas Podolski and Santi Cazorla. That was the last time the club triumphed there in the Premier League. They have not won at Anfield for 13 league matches, equalling the club’s worst run at Liverpool. Arsenal’s one victory at Liverpool in the interim came in the League Cup on penalties in 2020 on Arteta’s second visit as a manager.The Spaniard tried to prepare his players for a trip to Anfield in November 2021 by playing You’ll Never Walk Alone over the training ground speakers butthat ended in a 4-0 defeat. He was criticised after last season’s loss in late August, when DominikSzoboszlai’s late free-kickended a sequence of three Arsenal draws at Liverpool, for a perceived failure to take off the handbrake, having started Mikel Merino as his No 10. Gary Neville went as far as to say Arsenal lacked “the mentality to go and win big matches at big away grounds”, an assertion that will have hurt Arteta but does have credence: they have not beaten Manchester City in the Premier League at the Etihad since 2015 under Arsène Wenger.Arteta will be keen to disprove such perceptions, especially after Arsenal struggled so badly against a team 84 places below them in the pyramid in a stadium that holds fewer than 6,000 people. The strikers Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres surprisingly started in tandem at Fleetwood, presumably in an attempt to lighten the load on Martin Ødegaard, although both look badly out of form. Bukayo Saka isout with a thigh injury, there are concerns over Noni Madueke’s ankle and Arsenal’sfailed appeal over Max Dowman’s red cardrules out the teenager for three matches.View image in fullscreen26 May 1989: the Arsenal manager George Graham hugs Alan Smith after they won 2-0 at Anfield, clinching the league title in the most dramatic circumstances.Photograph: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty ImagesWith that in mind, Arteta’s best chance of beatingLiverpoolis probably by taking the cautious approach that has served him so well and was the cornerstone of last season’s Premier League title triumph. He can take inspiration from one of the most famous nights in Arsenal’s history 37 years ago when George Graham’s side arrived at Anfield needing a 2-0 victory to be champions.“I told my players to keep things tight in the first half – it was imperative we did not concede,” said Graham in an interview to mark the 20th anniversary of that dramatic finale to the 1988-89 season, when Michael Thomas scored in stoppage time to end Arsenal’s 18-year wait for the title. “The papers were saying we’d have to attack from the off, but I was adamant that was wrong. If Liverpool had scored an early goal it would have been over. But they did very little attacking and played into our hands.”Before the 1989 game, Arsenal’s players ran to all four corners of the ground to hand flowers to Liverpool fans as a show of sympathy after the Hillsborough disaster the previous month – an idea proposed by their longstanding director Ken Friar, who died this month.Graham and Arteta were 44 when they won their first league titles and the similarities do not end there. The former Scotland midfielder, who scored almost 80 goals for Arsenal and helped them win the Double in 1971, was known for his emphasis on defending as a manager and “1-0 to the Arsenal” became synonymous with Graham, especially towards the end of his reign.
