Anything that kind of restricts positive and good investment obviously worries [me] but there is a need for rules and we’re 100% fine with that. We are super-transparent. We can reassure the fans that we are financially viable, sustainable, and we’ve made serious investments over the last two years to be profitable and successful in the future.”PosTeamPGDPts1Chelsea Women717192Man City Women711193London City Lionesses711164Man Utd Women7-2115Tottenham Hotspur Women7310Another question facing the club, particularly given their league position, is whether they would be eligible to compete in the Women’s Champions League, given Kang also owns the record eight-time European champions OL Lyonnes in France. Semmens says in reference to Uefa’s multi-club ownership rules: “One hundred per cent, it can be resolved. We will continue to argue the case that you should be able to [invest into multiple clubs] to see the women’s game accelerated.“It’s not about exchanging players like the men’s game. It’s not about one club dominating and the other being a feeder club. It’s a different model but we fully understand and respect the rules. Therefore, we will set ourselves up in a way where we’re allowed to and can compete in Europe together. There are clear rules, clear precedents in the men’s game and clear things you can do to allow both teams to flourish. We’re fully aware of that and we’ll comply with the rules.”London City are three points off Chelsea and Manchester City, and Semmens says the aim is to “build a squad that is consistently in the top three”. He is looking forward to Sunday. “This is probably the No 1 game in the women’s game in the world this weekend,” he says. “That’s what we want to be: on the map.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballLondon City LionessesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s a new chapter to write’: Le Bris upbeat as Sunderland eye Coventry reunion | Sunderland | The Guardian
description: European football has stretched resources but the manager insists busy schedule is not something to complain about
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: European football has stretched resources but the manager insists busy schedule is not something to complain about
Content: ‘This will be an exciting one with our intention to be us, show up with our identity, our pillars,’ said Régis Le Bris of facing Coventry on Saturday.Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘This will be an exciting one with our intention to be us, show up with our identity, our pillars,’ said Régis Le Bris of facing Coventry on Saturday.Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSunderland‘There’s a new chapter to write’: Le Bris upbeat as Sunderland eye Coventry reunionEuropean football has stretched resources but the manager insists busy schedule is not something to complain aboutLouise TaylorFri 30 Oct 2026 10.56 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty seconds of stoppage time remained when Enzo Le Fée picked up the ball and kissed it before taking a corner. As intended, the Frenchman’s perfect, right-footed delivery dropped into the corridor of uncertainty that leaves goalkeepers torn between leaving their line or standing firm.It also dipped at the right moment for Dan Ballard to power a header in off the crossbar. Extra time in the 2025 Championship playoff semi-final second leg was almost over andSunderlandhad secured a 1-1 draw that consigned Coventry to a 3-2 aggregate defeat.As an outpouring of the loudest, most raucous emotion imaginable left the Stadium of Light feeling as if it was literally shaking, Régis Le Bris momentarily looked bewildered. By the time joyous comprehension began spreading across the Sunderland manager’s face, Frank Lampard was already a study in misery. Sunderland were on their way to Wembley, leaving Coventry in the Championship for another year.Ballard’s 122nd-minute goal shatters Coventry and puts Sunderland in playoff finalRead moreLe Bris always believed that, at heart, football managers must be storytellers, and, suddenly, he had created the most compelling narrative of his career.His players bought into his vision to such an extent that,having beaten Sheffield United in the playoff final, they finished seventh in the Premier League last season, qualifying for the Europa League.Everything went so well it appeared almost a fantasy but now this magic carpet ride looks in peril of ending. Much hinges on whether Sunderland can secure only their second league win of the season at Lampard’s 19th-placed, finally promoted, Coventry on Saturday.“There’s always a new story and a new chapter to write,” said Le Bris. “This game will be an exciting one with our intention to be us, show up with our identity, our pillars, our foundations and, after that, the game will be the game. Coventry have won twice in thePremier Leagueso they are competitive. The Premier League is a new chapter for them but they are still efficient.”Perhaps overstretched by the demands of European football, Sunderland have proved alarmingly inefficient at times this season. So much so that Nordi Mukiele, the former Paris Saint-Germain defender, recently accused his teammates of turning “arrogant”.Clear the air dressing-room talks ensued and Le Bris seemed much happier after lastSunday’s 0-0 home draw with Leeds. “We saw Sunderland on the pitch today,” said the 50-year-old. “We showed we want to embrace the challenge. We were ourselves.”A manager arguably let down by this summer’s recruitment refuses to fret about a demanding itinerary that, givenWednesday night’s 3-2 Carabao Cup win against Brentford, has just become even more congested.“You won’t hear me complaining about this new journey, the busy schedule,” said Le Bris. “This is exactly where we want to be, with the opportunity to play regularly in Europe, to be competing in the Premier League and the domestic cups too.“It’s demanding, but it creates the conditions to get better, to evolve and to be more proactive.”If his attempts to introduce a more attacking style this season have produced mixed results, Sunderland’s manager has been hampered by the club’s failure to sign a long-coveted right winger, and a Premier League-ready striker capable of competing with Wilson Isidor as Brian Brobbey’s understudy. Recent injuries to Brobbey and Isidor have exposed a glaring lack of cover in this department.While Florent Ghisolfi, Sunderland’s director of football, presided over some brilliantly radical recruitment immediately after promotion, backroom churn at the Stadium of Light has seen two previously key transfer market experts leave in the past year.The formerly influential sporting director, Kristjaan Speakman, departed amicably once it became apparent there was too much overlap with Ghisolfi’s role. Stuart Harvey, the head of player recruitment, also left by “mutual consent”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘Sunderland’s story is important and something we’ve analysed,’ Frank Lampard said in August. ‘To see how they played last season gives us inspiration.’Photograph: Ryan Browne/ShutterstockNow the technical director at Stoke, Harvey was very highly regarded, with his intelligent use of data said to have played a significant part as he and Speakman helped lift Sunderland from League One to the top tier.Ghisolfi, recruited from Roma, has an exceptional European contacts book and remains much admired. Yet in the case of Kevin Danso, a Tottenham loanee defender who will sign permanently next summer, his decision to prioritise height and power this summer has possibly proved questionable. Although an excellent character off the pitch, Danso has made some worrying individual errors as Sunderland have struggled in the absence of the hamstrung Ballard.Paradoxically, the team’s one relatively diminutive summer signing – the £30m former Lyon winger Malick Fofana – has struggled to make an impact on the left. That said, a much-improved Carabao Cup performance against Brentford hinted of better things to come from the 21-year-old Belgium international.The richly talented Le Fée remains integral to Le Bris’s plans, but constructing the right framework to bring out the best in a playmaker reportedly close to a senior France call-up has proved tricky at times.It does not help that Granit Xhaka has not quite been his usual imperious self this season. Maybe at 34, age is catching up with the defensive midfielder, and perhaps Switzerland’s World Cup journey took his toll on the international captain? Certainly Xhaka’s recent suspension from the Switzerland squad after his admission ofpurchasing a fake Covid vaccination certificatehas been an unwelcome distraction.Le Bris, now working with a new set-piece coach, could do with having Xhaka back to his best at Coventry, and is also hoping Mukiele recovers from a minor throat injury to start.There is a certain irony that, in August, Lampard described the Wearsiders as a post-promotion role model. “Sunderland’s story is important and something we’ve analysed,” he said. “To see how they played last season gives us inspiration.“But now it is up to us to write that story for ourselves.”Explore more on these topicsSunderlandCoventry CityPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Red Roses put defeats behind them by crushing USA to extend 35-year streak | Women's rugby union | The Guardian
description: England bounced back after two defeats with a comprehensive 55-12 win over USA
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: England bounced back after two defeats with a comprehensive 55-12 win over USA
Content: Claudia Moloney-MacDonald was in fine form on her return to the side.Photograph: Caean Couto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenClaudia Moloney-MacDonald was in fine form on her return to the side.Photograph: Caean Couto/Getty ImagesWomen's rugby unionRed Roses put defeats behind them by crushing USA to extend 35-year streakUSA 12-55 EnglandClaudia Moloney-MacDonald runs in four triesSarah RendellFri 30 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 21.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland have seen a lot of records crumble around them in this WXV Global Series but the world champions were not going to let a 35-year winning streak go against the USA. The last time the Eagles claimed a victory over the Red Roses was in the 1991 Rugby World Cup and since then England have won all 22 matches they have played. The Red Roses got back to winning ways and while their recent losses to Canada displayed the top sides had caught up with the world No 1 team, Friday’s outing against the USA evidenced that outside the top three there is still a gap to be closed.The USA headed into the match in good form with five consecutive wins, including victories over Wales and Ireland, and their No 8 Freda Tafuna has been one of the standouts across all of the teams during the WXV. However, England were able to contain the bright spark and despite good performances from Alev Kelter and Hope Rogers, the hosts did not have enough firepower.Red Roses suffer back-to-back defeats for first time in 10 years as Canada make statementRead moreThere were two key elements to England’s win: Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and a strong second-half performance from the front row. The wing Moloney-MacDonald may have been dropped from the matchday 23 against Canada last time out but she responded perfectly with four tries. It will be the exact retort John Mitchell would have wanted and the head coach praised the Exeter star afterwards for her consistency. Breaks by players such as Maud Muir gave the visitors the extra few percentages they needed.It was far from a polished performance by England though. Wasted chances against Canada contributed to both defeats and an error-strewn attack was on display again in the first half on Friday. The Red Roses had some great plays, namely Moloney-MacDonald’s first try, but they could have punished the USA more often had it not been for knock-ons and rogue passes.A disappointing note throughout the match was the empty-looking stands in the 25,000-capacity stadium in New Jersey. The official attendance was not announced but much of the ground had no fans. That was not helped by a 5pm kick-off time but a game of this magnitude deserves a bigger audience than the one that showed up.The last time these two nations met was in the opening game of the World Cup last year. The Red Roses won that 69-7, and once again England got the scoreboard ticking early on. It was less than five minutes before Moloney-MacDonald acrobatically finished, and she added another shortly after.Rogers got a try back and in doing so closed in on the American women’s all-time points record with the score bringing her just four points away. But it was England who held a 17-7 half-time lead after the captain, Meg Jones, scored and Moloney-MacDonald secured her third and fourth tries early in the second period.Kelter put in a huge hit on Jones and despite the tackle producing momentum for the world’s sixth-ranked side, it was England who went over through Mia Venner. The Gloucester-Hartpury wing has been impressive in her two starts in this away leg of WXV and she will give Mitchell a selection headache in 2027 if she continues her current form.The loss will leave a sour taste for the USA, not just because England’s replacement hooker Bryony Field, Maddie Feaunati and Sadia Kabeya turned a narrow win into a thumping one, but the hosts’ co-captain Georgie Perris-Redding hobbled off with injury.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis game was both teams’ last of the calendar year so the USA will have to wait to bounce back at the 2027 Pacific Four tournament. England will hope they have started a new winning streak to take into the Women’s Six Nations but the important things they will take forward, according to the captain Jones, are the lessons learned from this tour.“We have gained so much feedback from where we want to keep growing and getting better,” she said. “Ultimately teams are getting better, that is the nature of it. It happened in the men’s game, it’s happening in the women’s game and we just have to start being more unpredictable.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's rugby unionEngland women's rugby union teamUSA women's rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alex de Minaur hits career milestone in Vienna to book semi-final date with Zverev | Tennis | The Guardian
description: World No 10 defeats Matteo Berrettini 7-6 (7-4) 6-2 in quarter-final of ATP 500 event to become ninth Australian man to reach 350 tour-level wins
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: World No 10 defeats Matteo Berrettini 7-6 (7-4) 6-2 in quarter-final of ATP 500 event to become ninth Australian man to reach 350 tour-level wins
Content: Alex de Minaur defeated Matteo Berrettini 7-6 (7-4) 6-2 in the quarter-finals of the Vienna Open to set up a semi-final date with Alexander Zverev in Austria.Photograph: Lisa Leutner/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlex de Minaur defeated Matteo Berrettini 7-6 (7-4) 6-2 in the quarter-finals of the Vienna Open to set up a semi-final date with Alexander Zverev in Austria.Photograph: Lisa Leutner/ReutersTennisAlex de Minaur hits career milestone in Vienna to book semi-final date with ZverevWorld No 10 defeats Matteo Berrettini 7-6 (7-4) 6-2 in quarter-final27-year-old becomes ninth Australian man to reach 350 tour-level winsAustralian Associated PressFri 30 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex de Minaur has enjoyed a landmark 350th tour-level win of his career at the Vienna Open, downing an old rival to set up a semi-final date with the world No 1-elect Alexander Zverev.Australia’s main man defeated Matteo Berrettini, the Italian he’s had plenty of trouble with down the years, for the second successive year in the quarter-final of the ATP 500 event at the Wiener Stadthalle.Doubles players sign open letter pleading with tennis chiefs to ‘protect’ formatRead moreNot only did his 7-6 (7-4) 6-2 triumph set “Demon” up for a third duel in just over a month with Zverev on Saturday but it boosted his bid to reach the season-ending men’s championship, the ATP Finals, which still lies in the balance.World No 10 de Minaur found a way to draw first blood in a tight first stanza after saving a set point at 5-6, going on to take control of the tiebreak when the Italian, almost criminally, plonked a simple put-away into the net.De Minaur crucially saved a couple of break points at the start of the next set and cashed in by himself breaking Berrettini for the first time in the next game when the Italian produced an embarrassing air-shot when faced with a straightforward smash.View image in fullscreenAustralia’s Alex de Minaur returns the ball to Italy’s Matteo Berrettini at the Vienna Open.Photograph: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP/Getty ImagesFrom there, there was no way back for the world No 48 as de Minaur raced to victory in an hour and three-quarters to reach the semis of the Austrian indoor hard-court event for the third-straight year.It all came off the back of, statistically, the equal-best serving display by de Minaur all season, getting in 71% of his first serves, as he actually out-aced the boom-serving Berrettini 5-4.“That’s been an emphasis as of late, and I do feel like I’ve got in a good rhythm on serve and feel like I’m confident with what I’m doing,” said de Minaur.“I maybe didn’t serve as well as I would have liked to at the start of the week, but today was a great serving display from me, and you know, hopefully I can keep it going.”It all helped him become the ninth Australian man to reach the 350 match-win landmark after Lleyton Hewitt (616), John Alexander (591), Rod Laver (576), John Newcombe (568), Ken Rosewall (546), Phil Dent (414), Tony Roche (364) and Pat Rafter (358).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut earlier, Zverev, who recently lost to de Minaur in the Laver Cup and defeated him in Shanghai, gave a glimpse of the searing form which has him set to be enthroned as world No 1 on Monday as he powered through his quarter-final against British Wimbledon hero Arthur Fery, 6-0 6-2, in just under an hour.“Yeah, 100 per cent, that’s the aim,” said de Minaur, pondering his latest chance to beat Zverev for the first time in an individual, rather than team, tournament.“That’s the types of matches that you want to be playing, against the best in the world – and right now he’s the best in the world. So I’m excited for that. Another battle.”If de Minaur beats Zverev, he’ll move back into the eighth and last qualifying spot to reach the ATP Finals for a third-straight year, with only the Paris Masters still to come as a qualifying event before the Turin end-of-season showpiece.Earlier on Friday (Saturday AEDT), Daniil Medvedev secured his place ‌at the Finals for the seventh ‌time by outplaying French veteran Adrian Mannarino 6-2 6-3, setting up a last-four clash with world No 3 Carlos Alcaraz, who beat American Tommy Paul 6-4 ​7-6 (7-2).Explore more on these topicsTennisAlex de MinaurAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Araújo key factor in Liverpool’s improvement at set pieces, says Iraola | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: The Uruguayan defender helps with the height and physicality of the team, said the Reds’ head coach in the build-up to Arsenal’s visit on Sunday
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: The Uruguayan defender helps with the height and physicality of the team, said the Reds’ head coach in the build-up to Arsenal’s visit on Sunday
Content: Ronald Araújo has played the majority of his games for Liverpool at right-back.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRonald Araújo has played the majority of his games for Liverpool at right-back.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesLiverpoolAraújo key factor in Liverpool’s improvement at set pieces, says IraolaReds yet to concede set-piece goal in Premier LeagueSzoboszlai and Muñoz could return for Arsenal gameAndy HunterFri 30 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola has cited Ronald Araújo as a key factor in Liverpool’s improvement at set pieces but admitted Arsenal pose the “biggest challenge” to his team’s defensive record on Sunday.Liverpool have not conceded a set-piece goal in the Premier League and have shipped only one overall, Conor Gallagher’s consolation header past Giorgi Mamardashvili in Tottenham’s Carabao Cup defeat at Anfield in September. Liverpool’s resilience stands in stark contrast to last season when Arne Slot’s side conceded 20 non-penalty set-piece goals in the Premier League. That was the joint-most in the competition alongside Crystal Palace and Iraola’s Bournemouth.Are Liverpool in the title race? Their match against Arsenal will tell us a lotRead moreThe Liverpool head coach credits his assistants, Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper, and the club analysts with this season’s set-piece figures, and says the addition of Araújo to his defence has played a major role.“It definitely helps having a centre-back at right-back when we talk about defending set pieces,” said Iraola, who could have Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz back from injury. “It helps with the height and the physicality of the team.“It helps us to defend better but it is true that you also lose a little bit offensively on the other side. Offensively we cannot demand of Ronald the same thing as other full-backs and what they give us, but we have to balance this with other patterns.”Arsenal scored 25 set-piece goals, excluding penalties, en route to winning the title last season but have yet to show the same prowess.“It is very early in the season and they hadn’t scored [from set pieces] until last weekend and now they have scored,” Iraola said. “I hope they stay that way for a while but they are a big threat.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“From set pieces they are a big threat. They have very tall players who are very good headers and they work it very well. They give you a big demand and I think we will have to defend very well. I think we have, touch wood, dealt very well with defending set pieces so far this season. But Arsenal is probably the biggest challenge.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolanewsShareReuse this content

title: Searle makes difference as Leicester battle to Prem top spot at Bristol  | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Leicester scored four tries at Ashton Gate in a 22-16 win against Bristol that took them to the top of the Prem
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Leicester scored four tries at Ashton Gate in a 22-16 win against Bristol that took them to the top of the Prem
Content: Adam Radwan crosses for Leicester’s second try of four.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAdam Radwan crosses for Leicester’s second try of four.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesPrem RugbySearle makes difference as Leicester battle to Prem top spot at BristolBristol 16-22 LeicesterVisitors score four tries in error-strewn gameRobert Kitsonat Ashton GateFri 30 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the end there was a relatively clear winner of this straight shootout for top spot in the Prem.Leicestertook the spoils in an error-strewn contest between two sides who began the night in second and third position, scoring four tries to one and being masterfully steered to a bonus point victory by their alert fly-half Billy Searle.Following on from their commanding second-half display in the wet at home to Northampton, the Tigers were far from perfect but had the game’s outstanding player in Searle, whose left boot set up three of his side’s tries in addition to landing two conversions.Bristol, reduced to 13 players in the second quarter by a brace of yellow cards, had their moments but ultimately coughed up possession far too often.Exeter’s Tom Hooper: ‘Sometimes you’ve just got to suck up a little bit of pain’Read moreThe game’s stylistic highlight was a quite brilliant sixth-minute solo try by Louis Rees-Zammit, back to his sharpest on the wing for the Bears, but it takes more than the occasional flash of talent to tame the Tigers. In Adam Radwan they had their own high-speed danger man, with the former Newcastle wing and full-back Freddie Steward both registering first-half tries.Of the England international contingent on view, though, the most eye-catching was Ellis Genge who was a handful in all areas during his 63 minutes, only for the visitors to ruin the prop’s night with a bonus point try from Jamie Blamire within moments of his departure. Modern-day Leicester are not yet an irresistible force but they still have the ability to grind out crucial results. “That was a good gritty win,” stressed Geoff Parling, Leicester’s head coach. “I’m really proud of the team … we’re really pleased with the spot we’re in.”There was something of a throwback feel to the whole evening, with Bristol’s players wearing old-school letters in tribute to the club legends of yesteryear. Leicester were invited to do the same until league officials stepped in and deemed it too confusing. The Tigers’ rugby alphabet used to run the other way, with ABC denoting the front row rather than the outside backs, and asking them to abandon that tradition was borderline heresy.There was a timeless beauty, either way, to Rees-Zammit’s early score. The England tighthead Joe Heyes – entertainingly listed on the teamsheet as ‘Joy Heyes’ – was minding his own business in midfield when the Welsh wing accelerated past him from a standing start before slaloming all the way to the line.Leicester’s response was clinical in a different way, Searle’s cross-kick finding an unmarked Steward who dived over to mark his 100th Prem start in style. The visitors also had a close-range ‘try’ by Chessum scrubbed out for an earlier knock-on but, for a good while, there was little to separate the teams.If Leicester had a slight edge at the scrums the Bears were the more fluent attacking team and Rees-Zammit came close to adding another stunner to his collection,only for his deft chip ahead to elude his grasp. The momentum soon shifted significantly, though, courtesy of two quickfire yellow cards in three minutes for Matías Moroni and Tom Jordan for misjudged tackles.With a two-man advantage Leicester duly went ahead courtesy of another smart kick by Searle, drilled perfectly in behind the cover for the electric Radwan to outpace the cover and slide over. The half-time score of 12-7, even so, still gave the Bears some wriggle room in the closing 40 minutes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe omens did not look great when the Tigers scored again, Searle’s precise boot this time finding Ollie Hassell-Collins in acres of space on the left. But a penalty from Jimmy Williams provided some breathing space and, now restored to 15 players, a massive penalty for the hosts’ scrum altered the mood again.Blamire’s maul score, however, finally settled things, Searle again having an input with a raking kick to the corner. At a time when England’s fly-half pecking order is once again in the spotlight, here was another reminder of his match-winning qualities.On a night full of frustrating moments for both sides, his contribution was even more striking. Bristol huffed and puffed but chances came and went and the steady boot of Williams was ultimately not enough. While Leicester are now top dogs going into the weekend they will need to perform better than this to remain ahead of the chasing pack through the upcoming winter.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyBristolLeicesterRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iraola tempers Liverpool title talk, Maresca says Donnarumma is droppable, and more – as it happened | Premier League | The Guardian

Content: 11.16 EDT'Not in Disneyland': Arteta's warning for DowmanIn the aftermath of the youngster’sCarabao Cupdismissal, Mikel Arteta believes he has to balance the 16-year-old’s youth with the cold, hard realities of top-tier football.He wanted to be straightforward with Dowman and treat him as he would other players in the squad. “Otherwise, we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in thePremier Leagueat this level and we look after him so much that you cannot imagine,” the Arsenal manager said today.“But at the same time, we’re going to demand from him like anybody else because he needs to earn the right to play. Otherwise, the rest of the boys, what are they going to tell me? You need to be fair.”Arteta also urged the need to be very protective of Dowman, while also being clear about what he expects of players, the team and the club.Regarding Arsenal’srejected appeal against his 85th minute red cardagainst Fleetwood, the Spaniard was “very disappointed, especially with the reckless tackles that he received, and then his reaction is minimal in relation to the action … it could have been really bad, yeah. And we are lucky today that he hasn’t had a broken foot.”Dowman’s absence for Sunday’s match away to Liverpool leaves Arteta with a dearth of wide players.‘We are not in Disneyland’: Arteta warns Dowman of Arsenal’s demandsRead moreMikel Arteta has words for Max Dowman as he walks off the pitch after his red card against FleetwoodPhotograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesShareUpdated at11.52 EDT

title: South Africa all out and set Australia 288 to win decider: third men’s cricket Test, day four – as it happened | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder made fine centuries as South Africa fought back to set up a fascinating final day
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder made fine centuries as South Africa fought back to set up a fascinating final day
Content: 9h ago12.44 EDTDay four reportGeoff LemonIt would be unfair to say that Australia let a winning position slip on the fourth day of the third Test at Cape Town, only because that would undersell how Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder prised it away.Australia’s vaunted four bowlers, owners of 1,674 wickets at day’s beginning, could only raise that to 1678 by day’s end. In the process, a lead of 40 became 287. South Africa had been 40 for 4 in the first innings at Gqeberha and bounced back to win; they were effectively 40 for 4 in the third innings here, and now have a great chance to do the same.Australia set 288 to win after South African centurions turn the tideRead moreShareUpdated at18.07 EDT

title: Breeders’ Cup 2026 day one: Haffner wins Juvenile Turf to complete O’Brien double – as it happened | Breeders' Cup | The Guardian
description: European-trained runners completed a second successive clean sweep of the juvenile events on turf at a Keeneland Breeders’ Cup
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: European-trained runners completed a second successive clean sweep of the juvenile events on turf at a Keeneland Breeders’ Cup
Content: 3h ago18.08 EDTEUROPEAN CLEAN SWEEP ON DAY ONE IN KENTUCKYEuropean-trained runners completed a second successive clean sweep of the juvenile events on turf at a Keeneland Breeders’ Cup on Friday evening as Aidan O’Brien’sHaffner,in the Juvenile Turf, followed up earlier wins for George Boughey’sLibertango,in the Juvenile Turf Sprint, and O’Brien’sSun Goddessin the Juvenile Fillies Turf.Billy Loughnane,the new champion jockey on the Flat, got the meeting underway in thrilling style onLibertango, having been confirmed as a late replacement for Flavien Prat in her saddle only around an hour before the race.Prat was declared to rideLibertangoearlier in the week when it seemed that Loughnane would be unable to shed the necessary pounds to weigh out at 8st 7lb.An extended series of sauna sessions got him down to the necessary weight with only a couple of hours to spare, but the effort was worth it as he broughtLibertangowith a strong run in the stretch to win by a length and a quarter.“I can’t put it into words,” Loughnane said afterwards. I never expected to ride the filly at this weight. Thankfully, they have the saunas here so managed to do the weight. I feel great and a big thank you to George Boughey for putting me back on board.”Ryan Moore produced rides of similar coolness and efficiency aboard bothSun GoddessandHaffner,breaking smartly from the stalls to sit close to the lead before striking for home inside the final quarter-mile.The double on the day nudged Aidan O’Brien one clear in the all-time standings with 23 Breeders’ Cup winners, after he was briefly tied at 22 with Bob Baffert after his coltHughestook the Juvenile earlier on the card.ShareUpdated at18.08 EDT

title: Packers beat Panthers as Green Bay’s Christian Watson returns after mid-game hospital visit | NFL | The Guardian
description: Jordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to beat the Carolina Panthers
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Jordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to beat the Carolina Panthers
Content: Christian Watson is tackled by Carolina Panthers safety Zakee Wheatley.Photograph: Tannen Maury/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenChristian Watson is tackled by Carolina Panthers safety Zakee Wheatley.Photograph: Tannen Maury/UPI/ShutterstockNFLPackers beat Panthers as Green Bay’s Christian Watson returns after mid-game hospital visitCarolina Panthers 19-27 Green Bay PackersPackers WR has 113 receiving yards despite injuryGuardian sportand agenciesThu 29 Oct 2026 23.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to beat theCarolina Panthers27-19 on Thursday night.Love went 30 of 41 for 288 yards with touchdown passes to Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Jacobs plus an interception. Although he rushed for only 39 yards on 21 carries against the NFL’s lowest-ranked run defense, Jacobs scored on a four-yard catch and one-yard run for the Packers (5-3).Bears swing big and trade two first-round picks for star Titans DT Jeffery SimmonsRead moreAfter trailing 27-10 in the third quarter, Carolina cut Green Bay’s lead to 27-19 on Bryce Young’s 26-yard touchdown pass to Jalen Coker on a fourth-and-three play with 5:37 remaining. Young’s ensuing two-point conversion pass was incomplete.The Panthers (3-4) got the ball back at their own 45 before losing the ball on downs at midfield with 2:41 remaining. Carolina got one last chance from their own 20 with 22 seconds and no timeouts remaining, but Dani Dennis-Sutton’s sack essentially ended any comeback hopes.Young went 23 of 31 for 209 yards with one touchdown and one interception. Carolina’s Chuba Hubbard had 22 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown and seven catches for 38 yards.Green Bay’s Christian Watson was involved in a remarkable sequence of events. He hurt his chest making a 53-yard catch in the second quarter. The Packers feared he may have sustained a serious injury, and he was taken to a local hospital. However, after being passed fit by doctors, he returned late in ​the ​third quarter, then caught ​a six-yard pass on the ​opening play of ‌the fourth. He finished as the game’s top receiver with 113 yards on eight receptions.“I never wanted to go [to hospital], I was hoping they’d let me off,” Watson said after the game. “They said there were a couple of signs that made them want to take me over there, so I was just praying it was good enough that I could come back out here. Luckily it was … I’m happy to be out here on a football field. There was no internal bleeding [nothing] that was raising suspicion. I cleared everything and I was able to get back out.”Watson said he had been able to follow the game while he was in hospital. “One of the doctors had his phone out, so I was watching the play-by-play,” he said.Carolina cornerback Will Lee hurt his hamstring while diving to make a tackle on the same play in which Watson was injured, and he was carted into the locker room. Carolina already have three other cornerbacks on injured reserve: Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), Mike Jackson (groin) and Jaycee Horn (quadriceps).Brewers get big welcomeThere was a warm welcome for another Wisconsin team on Thursday night. Several members of the Milwaukee Brewers, including team captain Christian Yelich and Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski, received a huge ovation as they arrived Lambeau Field one night afterwinning the first World Series titlein franchise history.Brewers pitcher Brandon Woodruff held the Commissioner’s Trophy aloft as he emerged from the tunnel during a timeout before the second quarter. A few of the players attempted a Lambeau Leap into the crowd, with outfielder Sal Frelick having the most success.Those Brewers players later were shown on the video board cheering as they wore cheeseheads that included the message, “2026 WS Champions.”Explore more on these topicsNFLGreen Bay PackersCarolina PanthersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’ | Binance | The Guardian
description: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses
Content: North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn from a different exchange last year.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenNorth Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn from a different exchange last year.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersBinanceNorth Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so farQ&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?Dan MilmoandKalyeena MakortoffFri 30 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifyingNorth Koreaas the likely culprit.Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars.Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the$1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.Trump says he doesn’t know who crypto tycoon is despite having pardoned himRead moreTRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack.Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets.The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who wasjailed for four months in 2024after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.Donald Trump pardoned himin 2025.The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”View image in fullscreenBinance was founded by Changpeng Zhao.Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMarkets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.”Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m.The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic.View image in fullscreenRichard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance: ‘Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg/GettyWorld Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers.Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.Share your experienceShare your experiencePlease share your response in the form below, anonymously if you prefer. We will contact you before we publish any of your submission.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhere do you live?Tell us a bit about yourself (e.g. age, background, what you do)OptionalIf you've been directly affected by the Binance hack, we'd like to hear about it herePlease include as much detail as possible.How did you hear about the hack? How has communication been so far?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.Has your confidence in crypto altered in any way?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.Do you have concerns?OptionalPlease include as much detail as possible.If you are happy to, please upload a photo of yourself hereOptionalPlease note, the maximum file size is5.7 MB.Choose fileCan we publish your response?Yes, entirelyYes, but contact me firstYes, but please keep me anonymousNo, this is information onlyPhone numberOptionalYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.You can add more information hereOptionalIf you include other people's names please ask them first.Would you be interested in speaking to our audio and/or video teams?Audio onlyVideo onlyAudio and videoNo, I'm not interestedBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreA spokesperson for the FCA said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.”The Bank of England is also monitoring the hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment.Coinbase, another major cryptocurrency exchange, said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarilyhalted trading after a security incidentinvolving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsBinanceCryptocurrenciesHackingNorth KoreaBitcoinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural | Technology | The Guardian
description: Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned
Content: ‘If you’re using AI, you’re using some sort of language model, what data are you training it on to [determine] what’s a ghost?’Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If you’re using AI, you’re using some sort of language model, what data are you training it on to [determine] what’s a ghost?’Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesTechnologyGhost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernaturalGhost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concernedAW OhlheiserFri 30 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.34 EDTShareGhost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app calledGhostTube Seer, as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”.In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play storelisting.But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like ther/Nosleep subreddit, meant for scary stories, have implementeda strict policyagainst AI-generated material.‘Halloweenmas’: how the spooky one-nighter turned into a month-long spectacularRead moreWaine and Cutting claim their app can generate images depicting the supernatural, using signals from a phone’s built-in magnetometer, identifying words and phrases in those signals, and then running them through an image generator.Fellow paranormal enthusiasts can post the images they generate to a feed and comment on other users’ pictures. Since its release in 2023, Seer has become a regular part of their onscreen work. In arecent videoon their Amy’s Crypt YouTube channel, the pair sat in a carefully selected location in the Winchester Mystery House while running GhostTube Seer.“Can you show us what used to go on in this room?” Cutting asked. The app generated an abstract compilation of wooden walls and golden curtains that the pair suggested could be one of the home’s bedrooms. Seer also generated images of humans and animals while running: a woman reading, another woman with a black shawl, and a flock of white birds flying. Each was interpreted by the pair to have some relevance to the history of the home.The pursuit of ghosts has historically been relatively niche and personal, even after early 2000s TV showslike Ghost Huntersprompted a surge of interest in the hobby. That’s changed in recent years. Ghost stories and sightings, once they find their way online, can become training material for large language models like ChatGPT or Google Gemini, just like any other content.New technologies have always been a part of paranormal history, says Alex Matsuo, a paranormal researcher and author whose day job is in the technology industry. Thomas Edison’s attempt at a “spirit phone” to contact the dead is an early example, one with an ambition not dissimilar to today’s AI-powered “deathbots”. The history of spirit photographs, a hotly debated phenomenon of the 19th and early 20th century, parallels advances in new photography techniques.Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readingsRead moreSome paranormal enthusiasts, though, are concerned that generative AI is more than just another new technology to play with and instead threatens the soul of what they do.“I’m not surprised that AI has been embraced by a lot of people in the ghost hunting community,” said Matsuo.When GhostTube Seer was first released, she tried it out. She is skeptical of what she’s seen so far.“Any time someone’s coming out with a ghost hunting tool using AI, my big question has always been: ‘OK if you’re using AI, you’re using some sort of large language model, what data are you training it on to [determine] what’s a ghost?’” Matsuo said. She also noted that there are ethical concerns: is a generative image tool using copyrighted art to create its own spectres? Are ghost hunting chatbots sending users into their own “paranormal echo chambers”?Other paranormal enthusiasts are embracing the proverbial ghost in the machine. Seer isn’t the only generative AI app designed for ghost hunters. Sean Austin, a paranormal investigator who was featured on a Travel Channel series about ghost hunting, launched an app called Spirit Phone Innovations that uses “advanced AI” to analyze audio signals to detect EVP – electronic voice phenomena – a mainstay of ghost hunting.Matsuo believes the heart of looking for ghosts should remain deeply human.“A lot of us come into the ghost hunting world because we’ve gone through some trauma or grief,” she said. Ghost hunting is, for many, a form of processing loss, she said. “Everyone’s trying to find the next big thing that could give us an answer into the unknown or validating the existence of ghosts.”As AI’s physical footprint expands with the rapid construction of datacenters across the US, ghostly locations are likewise facing the threat of change. A former asylum in Pennsylvania that became a beloved haunted house was sold to a datacenter developer in late 2025 to be torn down. However, local residents banded together and successfully blocked it in May.How the fight over US datacenters is scrambling this state’s politics: ‘We don’t want it’Read moreExplore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsFolklore and mythologyChatGPTOpenAIHalloweenShare

title: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres | Datacentres | The Guardian
description: As thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous conditions and living in fear of speaking out
Author: Mei-Ling McNamara
Headline: As thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous conditions and living in fear of speaking out
Content: Illustration: Guardian Pictures/Alamy/Mei-Ling McNamaraView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Pictures/Alamy/Mei-Ling McNamaraRights and freedomDatacentresElectrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentresAs thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have  uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous conditions and living in fear of speaking outSupported byAbout this contentMei-Ling McNamaraFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSandu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vastGoogledatacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.”The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit.Once in the voltage room, Sandu says the managers confirmed the lines had been de-energised. In the first round, everything went as planned. Then, on the second test, while holding insulated tongs, he linked the cables. But this time, the lines were live.The blast was immediate and catastrophic. In milliseconds, 400 volts and 12,000 amps hit Sandu’s face and across the right side of his body. “I went completely blind,” he says. When doctors received him in the Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, he says he was placed in an induced coma for five days.View image in fullscreenSandu in hospital after electrocution.Photograph: Investigate EuropeHospital records seen by the Guardian and Investigate Europe show that the arc flash electrocution had burned 12% of Sandu’s body, with second-degree burns to the face and neck, as well as third-degree burns across his right shoulder and fingers.When Sandu woke from surgery in the intensive care unit a week later, his wife was at his bedside. He says his entire body felt like a “white-hot blister … It was so much pain. The human heart cannot comprehend it.”Sandu says the regional director of Google, along with a representative from Dornan Engineering, an Irish company that oversaw his contractor, and his recruiter, came to visit. While he lay bandaged in the hospital bed, he says the Google director told him he was lucky to be alive.To date, no company or contractor appears to have been found liable for the accident. The local labour inspectorate closed its investigation in late October and found no wrongdoing.A spokesperson for Dornan Engineering said it was “committed to maintaining safe working conditions, complying with applicable labour laws and continually learning to help prevent incidents like this from happening again”.Sandu’s electrocution appears brutal and harrowing, but far from unique, according to a five-month investigation by Investigate Europe and the Guardian into conditions for migrant workers on datacentre sites acrossSweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands.Europe is in the midst of a datacentre boom, the largest infrastructure surge the continent has seen in decades, withmore than2,300 datacentres rapidly altering the physical and energy landscape of Europe (at least 500 of them in the UK) and hundreds more under construction.But unions say the push for tech sovereignty in Europe is becoming increasingly reliant on the exploitation of migrant workers.View image in fullscreenThe Google datacentre in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.Photograph: Amazing Aerial/AlamyIn dozens of interviews we found evidence of debilitating injuries, squalid living conditions, an unreported infectious outbreak, unpaid wages and exploitative employment practices.In the UK,a general contractor diedwhile working on a datacentre site last year, while another fatality was reportedin 2024 at an electrical substationbeing built for a Microsoft datacentre. Serious accidents have also been recorded this year at projects inItaly,Sweden,NorwayandBelgium, and exploitative labour practices have been found at projects around the world,including in Brazil.On the outskirts of Gävle, a city two hours north of Stockholm, past timber-framed cottages and dense pine forests, lies a smooth road leading to one such site. The remote clearing is part of a 130-hectare,€3bn expansion planbegun in June 2024 to scale up Microsoft’s AI datacentre infrastructure.One subcontractor at the site is the Irish-owned construction company BenBau. It is among 148 firms working under Collen Construction at the Gävle site, including 28 direct subcontractors.For months, there has been a growing sense of outrage among Adrian*, 45, and his colleagues working for BenBau on theMicrosoftsite. They showed evidence of crowded living quarters – 24 people to a kitchen, 14 men to a single bathroom – and say they have reported vermin infestations, broken ventilation systems and lack of heating during the sub-zero Swedish winters, but the problems remain.View image in fullscreenOne worker claims he contracted TB at the Microsoft datacentre construction site at Gävle in Sweden.Photograph: investigate-europe.orgSuch conditions can make the transmission of disease more likely. In February this year, one Romanian worker tested positive for active tuberculosis, medical records show. Shortly after, others living in the same shared housing showed similar symptoms. BenBau initially informed only a few men who shared close quarters with the infected worker and then told the men that testing was optional, according to workers. After the first worker who contracted the disease had left for hospital, Benbau moved another worker into his bedroom.Freedom of information requests made to Sweden’s national work authorities and its Public Health Agency say no outbreak had been reported.The living and working conditions form only part of the story.More than 30 workers have shown hundreds of payslips to the Guardian and Investigate Europe that appear to show some of them working up to 50 or 60 hours a week with no overtime pay and missed holiday pay. With many foreign workers unfamiliar with the laws, unions say inequity can arise quickly.Days before publication of this investigation, the union Solidariska Byggare, representing the 70 Romanian workers at Microsoft’s site in Gävle, brokered a settlement with BenBau, which it says will give workers back pay and allow unions access to sites.A spokesperson for BenBau said the company “takes all concerns regarding the welfare, health and safety of our people extremely seriously” and has “stringent procedures for reporting, investigating and addressing workplace concerns”.Since 2021, Sweden’s Work Environment Authority (AV) has opened 50 cases into working conditions at datacentre sites involving Microsoft and a number of Irish firms, according to a freedom of information request.Earlier this month, a contractor fell through a roof hatch while carrying out maintenance work on a ventilation system at the Microsoft site in Gävle, according to freedom of information request to AV.View image in fullscreenA union meeting at Gävle to announce a settlement between affected workers and one construction company.Photograph: Valeria AltariovaIn October 2021, a forklift allegedly ran over the foot of a supervisor working for Collen at the site. The worker subsequently needed surgery. An incident report submitted by Collen to work authorities says that the wrong machine had been used, the driver had no formal certificate for it and the lift plan was incomplete. Still, it had been signed off. The Work Environment Authority saw no grounds to report the employer to prosecutors.A spokesperson for Collen said: “We are committed to ensuring that every Collen site is a safe, healthy and respectful place to work, where everyone is treated with dignity and their fundamental human rights are protected. We expect the same throughout our supply chain and have zero tolerance for any conduct inconsistent with these principles.“Our projects are subject to rigorous compliance with our own mandatory policies and procedures, our clients’ requirements, all applicable laws and regulations, and recognised industry standards in every jurisdiction in which we operate.”View image in fullscreenA pamphlet circulated at the union negotiation with BenBau at Gävle, Sweden, in September.Photograph: Mei-Ling McNamaraA similar pattern is found throughout Europe, says James McCabe from Unite the Union, an Irish-UK group representing more than 1.2 million workers. “Everywhere we’ve encountered Irish datacentre contractors at tech-giant datacentre sites we’ve learned of lack of normal and meaningful union access … as well as serious concerns of labour crimes and exploitation of workers,” he says.Johan Danielsson, a European parliament rapporteur in charge of regulating subcontracting chains, says: “If people let these big American multinationals come here and import their anti-union business models, then it becomes a problem. Because behind the fence they are abusing workers, and they don’t want anyone to know it.”A spokesperson for Google said: “Our supplier code of conduct and contracts require all suppliers to comply with local labour laws and uphold safe, healthy working conditions. We maintain active dialogue with union leaders and trade groups, and are committed to providing transparent information about our workplace.”A spokesperson for Microsoft said: “In our datacentre construction, we work with contractors and suppliers, with whom we set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining. To ensure our contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies, we have robust processes in place, including audits.”* Names have been changedThis investigation is led by Investigate Europe, a cross-border team of investigative journalists:Lorenzo Buzzoni,Jan Daalder,Pascal Hansens,Ella Joyner,Chris Matthews,Nico SchmidtandAstri Thunold.Explore more on these topicsDatacentresRights and freedomWorkers' rightsUnionsInfrastructureGoogleMicrosoftSwedennewsShareReuse this content

title: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case | Australian law | The Guardian
description: Scraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey says
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Scraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey says
Content: The attorney general, Michelle Rowland (pictured), says the government is committed to supporting creatives even as concern mounts over a possible weakening of Australian copyright laws.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenThe attorney general, Michelle Rowland (pictured), says the government is committed to supporting creatives even as concern mounts over a possible weakening of Australian copyright laws.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPAustralian lawExperts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights caseScraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey saysGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerFri 30 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAltering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide.The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point asthe movie The Castle, the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI.“We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian Australia.Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”.In a rush to lure AI companies, the Australian government risks undoing a creative ecosystem that has taken decades to build | Dan GuthrieRead moreLabor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, haspromised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropicsuggested an “opt-out” modelwhich would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection.A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”.“If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member ofthe federal parliamentary committee on AI.“How we support property rights is core to this.”A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes.Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues.“The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here.Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish celebrities beat AI companies lobbying to get free use of their work. They have a warning for AustraliaRead moreCadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues.Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders.Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”.“It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.”Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals.He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners.“The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said.Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community.“The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said.Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern.“That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders.“The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.”Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks.“There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know whatwillhappen,” Cadell said.“I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian lawAI (artificial intelligence)Australian politicsAustralian musicAustralian booksAustralian filmAustralian televisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Billionaire tax: how a union leader’s ‘crazy’ idea became the defining issue of California’s midterms | California | The Guardian
description: It was an ambitious notion – now Californians will vote on a one-time 5% billionaire tax, and state’s super rich have pulled out all the stops in opposition
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: It was an ambitious notion – now Californians will vote on a one-time 5% billionaire tax, and state’s super rich have pulled out all the stops in opposition
Content: The most vocal critics of the billionaire tax? Billionaires.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe most vocal critics of the billionaire tax? Billionaires.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesCaliforniaBillionaire tax: how a union leader’s ‘crazy’ idea became the defining issue of California’s midtermsIt was an ambitious notion – now Californians will vote on a one-time 5% billionaire tax, and state’s super rich have pulled out all the stops in oppositionDara KerrFri 30 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTShareOne year ago, the idea of a billionaire tax inCaliforniawas still in its infancy.It wasn’t yet one of the most contentious ballot measure fights in state history – pitting Democrats against Democrats, drawing national attention from political heavyweights, and netting hundreds of millions of Silicon Valley dollars to fight it. Back then, it was a bold and desperate answer to Donald Trump’s healthcare cuts.Trump had just signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which dictated a trillion dollars of Medicaid, Affordable Care Act and other healthcare fundingbe cut over the next decadeto offset sweeping tax cuts. When the bill goes into effect in January, that could meanmore than 3.4m Californianswill lose their coverage, including millions of children.“That’s why we were willing to do something that lots of people said was crazy,” said Dave Regan, the divisive architect of the billionaire tax and president of the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW). “To us, what’s crazy is doing nothing and watching millions of people lose coverage.”Now, with the midterms less than a week away, California voters will decide on whether to pass the ballot measure known as Proposition 40. The proposal would levy a one-time 5% tax on billionaires living in the state as of 1 January 2026, the proceeds of which would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.The initiative has its critics, even among Democrats, who point at its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. But its most vocal critics have been billionaires.The idea of taxing the Golden State’s ultra-wealthy has snowballed into a messy brawl over the last year. Progressive politicians have become bedfellows with tech billionaires, opposition ballot measure campaigns have been mounted, Signal chats leaked, and boatloads of money have been spent.Tech billionaires have treated the proposal as an existential threat, dumping upwards of $356m into “independent expenditure-only” political action committees (Super Pacs) to stop it. In the first two weeks of October, according to the most recent campaign filings, the opposition campaign spent more than $42.8m – surpassing $2.5m per day. That moneywent to an army of consultants, who have been tasked with lobbying politicians, blanketing the airwaves with ads and placing op-eds in Latino newspapers across the state.View image in fullscreenAttendees cheer Bernie Sanders at a rally in Los Angeles in February in support of the billionaire tax.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images“This looks like it’s going to be the most expensive ballot measure ever,” said David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University. “Not in California history, but in the history of the world.”Meanwhile, the far-less-funded pro-Prop 40 camp has relied on viral social media campaigns from influencers and actors, including theartist Shepard Faireyandactor Mark Ruffalo, and raucous rallies headlined by leftwing politicians. During one packed event in San Francisco earlier this month, Vermont’s Bernie Sanders said: “The whole country, and frankly people from around the world, are paying attention to what is happening here.”While Prop 40 is just one ballot measure election in one state, it is causing ripple effects nationwide. It comes at a time when affordability is top of mind and thedisparity of wealthin the US hasn’t been so starksince the Great Depression. McCuan said the billionaires’ big spend was partially due to a fear of contagion to other states. Likewise, supporters say they hope the proposed tax is a harbinger for referendums on wealth inequality across the country.Regan and his union got started on their endeavor last summer. After Trump signed his bill on 4 July, Regan’s team began making calls. They put together a working group of policy experts, economists, lawyers, researchers and political consultants, who came up with the one-time 5% tax to keep hospitals open and union healthcare workers in their jobs.Regan is known for using the ballot measure process as a political tool to strongarm deals with lawmakers and push causes important to the SEIU-UHW. Since 2012, the union hassponsored 48 initiatives.
