The strategy with the billionaire tax was to sharpen the focus on inequality.“We worked to come up with something that could draw enough support from voters, and that could avoid a catastrophe,” Regan said. “We just bore down on that.”When their plan became public after the October 2025 filing deadline, the billionaires hatched a working group of their own.‘If there’s an impediment, just buy it’Chris Larsen, a cryptocurrency mogul, hosted a Christmas party in northern California’s swanky Marin county last December, according toBloomberg. It was in a treehouse tucked into a grove of towering redwood trees. The singer Janelle Monáe performed and California governor Gavin Newsom was there, along with Google co-founder Sergey Brin.Newsom’s relationship with Brin goes back decades to when he was mayor of San Francisco. The governor, now a presumed presidential candidate, hadflown on Google’s jet with Brin, and the two men attended each other’s weddings. But a lengthy exchange they reportedly had at Larsen’s party was far from collegial.Brin confronted Newsom about the proposed billionaire tax, according to people who spoke with Newsom, Bloomberg reported. TheGoogleco-founder, currently worth about $245bn, told the governor it was forcing him to leave California.Newsom and Brin did not respond to the Guardian’s detailed list of questions.By that point, more than a dozen tech executives and prominent Silicon Valley venture capitalists had reportedly already joined an encrypted Signal group chat expressly dedicated to burying the billionaire tax, theSan Francisco Standardreported. Brin and Larsen were members, along with venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, PayPal co-founder Max Levchin, Stripe chief executive Patrick Collison and investor Ron Conway, according to people who saw the chats.Larsen and Levchin declined to comment. Brin, Andreessen, Collison and Conway did not return requests for comment.View image in fullscreenGoogle co-founder Sergey Brin at a conference at the renamed Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington earlier this month.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersThe group brainstormed ideas for fighting the tax. Theyreportedlymet every Tuesday for months via video call, debated fleeing the state, and tussled over how much to trust Newsom because of his position as a Democratic governor of a blue state. Newsom has long opposed state wealth taxes and quickly came out against the billionaire tax, repeatedly saying it would “drive a race to the bottom” and stifle innovation as the ultra-wealthy leave.While a handful of those ultra-wealthy have left, the vast majority of thestate’s 200-plus billionaireshave remained – including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who saidhe’s “perfectly fine” with the tax. Initially, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California, but filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission last weekrevealed he struck a dealwith his company’s board to help him foot the bill if Prop 40 passes in exchange for staying in the state.Among others who indicated they’re departing are Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, Trump’s former AI and crypto czar David Sacks, and Google co-founders Larry Page and Brin. Last December, Brinmoved to a $42m mega-mansionon the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe, just steps from California’s border.Brin is the de facto ringleader of the Prop 40 opposition campaign. Through a Super Pac called Building a Better California, he’s contributed at least $102m to the cause – more than any other donor. Brin worked with political operatives and had his family office map out plans to trounce the tax, according to theNew York Times. Brin is also a frequent guest at the White House and wasawarded the National Medal of Scienceby Trump earlier this month.Abby Lunardini, a spokesperson for Building a Better California, said: “Californians deserve to know the facts about a measure that would permanently gut the state’s budget, tax base, and economic advantage, all while making the problem it’s supposed to be fixing – healthcare funding – worse.”Another major early donor to the opposition campaign was Thiel, who gave $3m to the California Business Roundtable Super Pac at the end of December. Larsen has donated more than $23m through various Super Pacs, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has given more than $42m, according to campaign finance filings.At least some of the donations were in cryptocurrency, which had to be converted to dollars under state rules, documents show. Campaign expenditure filings for the tech Super Pacs reveal more than $40,000 has been spent on crypto processing fees alone. Company stock shares given by founders like DoorDash’s Tony Xu reportedlycomprised another significant chunk.View image in fullscreenPeter Thiel leaves the presidential palace in Buenos Aires after a meeting with Argentina’s rightwing president Javier Milei in April.Photograph: Matias Baglietto/ReutersThe opposition campaign’s initial goal was to ensure Prop 40 didn’t make the ballot. They already had Newsompublicly vowingto defeat the proposal. The next step was to go after the signature-gathering process. Anyone can put forward a ballot measure in California if they can gather enough signatures by the filing deadline. Signature-collection firms charge per signature, and the price fluctuates each election based on demand.Opponents to the billionaire tax came up with a strategy to kneecap SEIU-UHW’s signature-gathering process by introducing several ballot measures of their own toboost the price of each signature– the going rate went from $4 per signature to a record-breaking $36.The venture capitalist Conway spelled it out in apodcastin March: “Our job is to get Gavin to negotiate this so that it doesn’t get to the ballot. So maybe they don’t get the signatures.”When the SEIU-UHW used mostly volunteers to amass their signatures, the opposition campaign reportedly attempted another plan – purchase the firm the union used for signature-collection, so that those signatures couldn’t be used, according to Regan. The same idea was floated in the Signal chat, according to the San Francisco Standard, with one participant reportedly messaging: “That’s what you would do in business: If there’s an impediment, just buy it.”Fred Kimball is the president of the signature-gathering firm Kimball Petition Management, which worked with the SEIU-UHW and pioneered this type of business. He said that not only did his company endure denial-of-service cyberattacks, which stalled their signature validation process, but he received two calls from unnamed individuals inquiring about a sale.“It never got any further than that,” Kimball said. “The requirement would be that I’d have to turn over the signatures. Once you do that, it’s all over … My dad started this industry, there’s no way I’d do that.”By the end of April, well before the signature filing deadline in June, the SEIU-UHW took a victory lap, announcingthey’d gathered 1.55m signatures– nearly double the necessary amount to qualify for the ballot.“This is a David versus Goliath battle,” Mayra Castaneda, an executive member of SEIU-UHW, said at a press conference at the time. “David has just won the first round.”The showdownAfter the union’s signature-gathering triumph, the responsibility to kill the billionaire tax rested with Newsom, at least in the eyes of billionaires. Newsom’s objective was toreach a compromisewith the SEIU-UHW to withdraw its proposal before the June deadline. The governor and Regan had been in talks since December, Regan said, but they remained at odds in finding a solution to the impending healthcare crisis.Newsom had brought together a coalition to negotiate a deal, enlisting other unions and interest groups tooppose the tax. The governor also tried to get Regan to his side, according to Regan. He said Newsom’s chief of staff invited the union boss to a press conference, in which the governor would credit Regan for anational wealth tax proposal. Regan said Newsom’s national plan lacked teeth, so he declined.SEIU-UHW offered a counter proposal: they’d drop the one-time tax from 5% to 2% if Newsom endorsed it. In aletter to the governor, the union wrote: “Let’s save patient lives together.”“But that was a non-starter,” Regan said. So SEIU-UHW announced in late June that it was advancing to the ballot, saying: “David won the second round against Goliath”.View image in fullscreenGavin Newsom at a Democratic rally in San Francisco last week.Photograph: Heather Diehl/APTwo billionaire-backed countermeasures also made the ballot, however: Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targets the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 is a general proposal on limiting certain new taxes and would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth. If either measure receives more yes votes than Prop 40, it will stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passes. Regan calls them “poison pills”.After that, the battle entrenched. Flush with tech money, which kept rolling in, the opposition side grew quickly, landing dozens of endorsements. Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the lobbying branch of the healthcare group, joined the cause, as did the influential California Teachers Association, the California Medical Association, and a host of building and trade unions and public safety associations.The newly formed coalition launched an ad campaign calling Prop 40 a “dangerous wealth tax” and “reckless experiment”. The campaign received endorsements from several prominent Democrats, including Xavier Becerra, the gubernatorial candidate; Katie Porter, a former congresswoman; and Daniel Lurie, the mayor of San Francisco. While Porter contends the tax doesn’t fix the underlying system, Lurie argues the tax woulddrive revenue out of California. Becerra says billionaires should pay their fair share, but Prop 40 isn’t how to do it.When asked about No on 40’s campaign strategy, a spokesperson for the campaign instead shared a comment from Jack Chou, the president of the California Medical Association, who said the cause has gained endorsements because the measure “permanently damages our economy and budget while failing to fix our healthcare system, improve care, or lower costs.”The Prop 40 campaign looked doomed as its core allies, Democrats and unions, were jumping ship. But then things took a turn.In August, the California Democratic party held a board meeting in San Diego, where they voted on endorsing Prop 40. At first, the measure lost. But, according to people familiar with the matter, Congresswoman Maxine Waters stepped in and condemned her colleagues for not supporting the tax. A reconsideration was introduced and the votes swung in favor of Prop 40.State filings show that the opposition campaign had donated tens of thousands of dollars to the California Democratic party, along with the Democratic parties of San Diego, Orange county and Los Angeles county. Despite the donations, all of these Democratic parties have endorsed the billionaire tax.View image in fullscreenMembers of the SEIU march during a one-day strike in Sacramento last week.Photograph: Jose Luis Villegas/APRo Khanna, the Democratic congressman who represents the district that includes Silicon Valley, has been astaunch supporter of Prop 40. “It makes no sense to me why any democratically elected official or traditional Democratic allies wouldn’t be supporting this,” he said during a June press conference. “People want folks who are going to stand up to the billionaires and the trillionaires.”Another turning point was the endorsement of the powerful California Federation of Labor Unions AFL-CIO, which lists 1,300 unions in its roster. During its biennial convention in August, its members voted overwhelmingly to endorse Prop 40.Lorena Gonzalez, the president of the federation, described the scene on the floor of the convention center that day. One-by-one, union healthcare workers stood up and spoke passionately about the need to fund hospitals, maternity wards and emergency rooms to ensure they don’t close in the wake of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, she said.“Once you heard that, and heard that billionaires got tax breaks from the big BS bill and that Medi-Cal got cut, it just became a no-brainer,” Gonzalez said. “I’m not going to be a labor movement that bows down to the establishment and is scared of taking on billionaires.”Mudslinging abounds and record-breaking spendingAs the election nears, California residents have witnessed the two campaigns vie for attention and relentlessly demonize each other.Last week, after Newsomendorsed the billionaire’s Prop 42 countermeasure, which would stop the state from ever passing a wealth tax, the Prop 40 campaign released an attack ad on the governor. Likewise, the opposition campaign sent voters across the state a glossy four-page mailer that read: “You’re Next.”Since July, the tech Super Pacs have upped their donations to the committees opposing Prop 40 and supporting Props 41 and 42. The three campaigns have received a total of more than $379.5m – making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history. “We’ve said for months we’re going to get carpet-bombed by these guys,” Regan said. “Their so-called strategy, there’s only one prong to it: we can buy anything we want.”Along with the flood of spending and negative ads, accusations and personal attacks have been flying in all directions. Much of this has been focused on Regan, who’s beencriticized in Democratic and union circlesfor being an aggressive bulldog and spending his union’s resources to push ballot measures.In one specific instance, Courtni Pugh, a former executive director at the SEIU, accused Regan of physically assaulting her in 2009,according to the Los Angeles Times. She said he kicked open her office door, pinned her against a wall and screamed that she was a “dumb ass”. The SEIU investigated the allegations this year and wrote in a report that Pugh’s claim was substantiated. Regan denied the alleged abuse, claiming that the allegations against him are retaliatory for his support of Prop 40. (The union investigation did not substantiate Regan’s retaliation claim.) Law enforcement did not investigate the abuse allegations and no charges were brought.Pugh is now serving as asenior advisor to Becerraand working as a consultant for the No on 40 campaign. Regan told the Guardian: “Courtni Pugh, at Hilltop Solutions, wants to invent accusations about me from 17 years ago on the payroll of the billionaires.”Pugh said Regan’s response “is offensive to the people – especially the women and women of color – who have had to endure his threatening behavior”. A spokesperson for Becerra said Pugh has not advised him on his position on the wealth tax.View image in fullscreenDave Regan, the SEIU-UHW president, during a ‘Yes on 40 for Ballots Over Billionaires’ rally in San Francisco.Photograph: Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesThe newest Democrat to vocally oppose Prop 40 is former congresswoman Porter, who’s known for taking corporate executives to task. She haswritten op-edsin local papers, postedvideoson social media, and is quoted in ads and mailers saying: “Prop 40 does nothing to reform our healthcare system.” After losing a gubernatorial bid to Becerra earlier this year, she said she was retiring from politics. But she’s waded back into the fray with Prop 40. Late last month, Newsom alsoappointed herto a paid position on the board of governors for the state’s community colleges.Despite the controversy and criticism, the SEIU-UHW has brought notable figures to its side. Last month, six Nobel prize-winning economists wrote anopen letterendorsing Prop 40. Doing the math, they wrote that the combined wealth of California’s billionaires is $2.3tn, equal to the entire annual income of all 20m taxpayers in the state. They pointed out that billionaires’ net worth has grown nearly 150% over the past couple of years, fueled by the AI boom. “This tax only partially plays catch-up, but it is a move in the right direction,” the economists wrote.Now it’s up to the voters, who appear to be unswayed by the onslaught of messaging. APolitico polllast week showed that 84% of registered voters said they’d seen campaign ads involving Prop 40 and the majority of them weren’t persuaded into changing their positions. Despite that, the measure has fallen in the polls. While it enjoyed a seven-point lead over the summer, it’s since fallen to a one-point lead.For Regan, win or lose, he said the idea of taxing billionaires isn’t going away.“I think this campaign has already put this issue on the national agenda in a very significant way,” he said. “This issue is going to be at the center of the nominating process for a Democratic candidate in 2028.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWest CoastThe super-richUS politicsSergey BrinGoogleLarry PageShare

title: Buy a wind-up radio – and don’t forget the chocolate: survival experts on how to prepare for an emergency | Emergency planning | The Guardian
description: UK government guidance says we should be ready for the unexpected, but what’s actually helpful to have at home? We ask the specialists
Author: Isabelle Aron
Headline: UK government guidance says we should be ready for the unexpected, but what’s actually helpful to have at home? We ask the specialists
Content: Just in case: a few essential supplies can make all the difference if everyday services are disrupted.Photograph: HanaHa/GettyView image in fullscreenJust in case: a few essential supplies can make all the difference if everyday services are disrupted.Photograph: HanaHa/GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterEmergency planningBuy a wind-up radio – and don’t forget the chocolate: survival experts on how to prepare for an emergencyUK government guidance says we should be ready for the unexpected, but what’s actually helpful to have at home? We ask the specialistsThe best power banks – testedIsabelle AronFri 30 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow prepared are you for an emergency? Do you have a few extra tins of beans in the cupboard, or a full-on preppers’ kit in the cellar? While no one likes to think about worst-case scenarios, you can’t have failed to notice the growing noise around being sensibly, practically ready for floods, power cuts, cyber-attacks and other events.The government launched itsBe Ready campaignin October withguidance on how to prepare for emergencies, including a list of suggested items to have at home.To help you understand what to buy, and where to buy it from, we asked survival, medical and nutritional experts for their advice. “There’s lots of panic about upcoming floods, El Niño and AI attacks, but this emergency preparedness is something we all should be doing anyway. It’s just a good idea to look after yourself and your family like this,” says Hannah Cloke, regius professor of meteorology and climate science at the University of Reading. And if you are in a position to do so, consider donating to a charity likeTrussellto help support one of thealmost one in 10 UK householdsalready experiencing food insecurity.From wind-up radios to water filters, here’s what the experts recommend adding to your list.Are you stocking up onessential items at home? What products have you found useful for past eventssuch as power cutsor being without water?Please let us know how you’re following government advice atthefilter@theguardian.com.What to keep at home in case of emergenciesView image in fullscreenReady for anything: a little planning can help you cope with the unexpected.Photograph: Natalia  Lebedinskaia/GettyFirst aid kit“Top of my list is a good first aid kit with sterile dressings that you can cut to size, not just little plasters, and some kind of tape to secure it with,”says John Hudson, chief survival instructor to the UK military and author ofHow to Survive: Lessons for Everyday Life from the Extreme World. “Zinc oxide tape is good because it’s super sticky and can be used for blisters. Other basics include crepe or elastic roller bandages, sterile eye pads, blunt-ended scissors, tweezers, safety pins or clips, alcohol-free antiseptic wipes and gloves for if you’re helping someone else.Lifeventure makes good travel-sized first aid kits.”Will Duffin, an NHS GP working in urgent care who runs theExtreme MedicInstagram account, also stresses the importance of a good first aid kit. “I recommend buying an off-the-shelf first aid kit, and then you can add bits into that,” he says. “One of the main things for families is a thermometer and some Calpol.” Duffin also suggests having supplies of basic, over-the-counter medication that might come in handy, such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, antihistamines, Imodium and rehydration sachets.“The other day-to-day one is wound care – cuts, aches and sprains. So have some antiseptic, sterile gauze, basic dressings such as plasters and medical tape,” he says. As well as getting the gear, you need to have some idea of what to do with it, which is why Duffin recommends going on a basic first aid course. Organisations such asSt John AmbulanceandBritish Red Crossoffer various options.View image in fullscreenTravellerfirstaidkit£37.99 at Lifeventure£37.99 at LifesystemsView image in fullscreenBraun ThermoScan 7ear thermometer£36 at Lloyds PharmacyFrom £44.85 at AmazonView image in fullscreenTommee Tippee 2-in-1thermometer£14.99 at John Lewis£15 at BootsWind-up radiosIn case channels of communication go down, the government has advised buying a battery or wind-up radio, some of which also have a torch and a USB slot to charge your phone. “It’s such a simple piece of kit. The wind-up versions are great because in an emergency, you can use the power of your own arm to power the battery,” says Cloke.View image in fullscreenImmverwind-upradio with 10,000mAh battery and LED torch£34.02 at B&Q£28.99 at AmazonA wool blanket and jumper“If you haven’t already got some kind of woolly throw or blanket in the house, get one. It doesn’t have to be expensive merino wool or anything like that; it just needs to be wool,” says Hudson. The same goes for woolly jumpers, too. “People have probably got enough clothes in their house, but make sure you have something that’s got a lot of wool in it. A jumper is brilliant because if it’s chucking it down with rain and you get caught out, wool will keep you warm even when it’s wet,” he says. Both are helpful if you have no way to heat your home, and are one of the best ways to keep you warm even if it’s damp.View image in fullscreenRecycledwoolblanket£30 at the RNLISupplies for your car“[Many of us] are in our cars all the time, and what happens if you get stuck? Put some blankets and warm clothes into it, have a torch, some batteries, jump leads, a small shovel, a hi-vis jacket so you can safelyask for help at night, some basic water and long-life food, and a first aid kit. A mini version of what’s in your house,” says Cloke. It’s also a good idea to have a sleeping bag in the boot of your car, so that if you’re driving and you get stuck or your car breaks down, you can stay warm in the car, says Hudson. “The sleeping bag can help stop you from becoming hypothermic. You want a hollow-fibre one because it will still keep you warm if it gets damp.Snugpak does great stuff, and several of its products are used by the military. You can also get secondhand sleeping bags from military surplus stores,” he says.View image in fullscreenSnugpakthesleepingbag£42.95 at Outdoor ActionFrom £41.06 at AmazonView image in fullscreenAAwintercarkit withfoldingsnowshovel£21 at Argos£15.73 at AmazonA torch“Most of us have got torches on our phones, but in an emergency you will want to save the battery for contacting people and other things. A basic torch and some spare batteries are a very useful thing during a power cut,” says Cloke. You can also buywind-up torches, which save on batteries.View image in fullscreenEnergizer 1,000-lumenmetaltorch£20 at Tesco£20 at B&QView image in fullscreenDuracell Plus AAalkalinebatteries (30pack)£27.95 at B&Q£22.49 at AmazonSpace blanket“Some of the cheap space blankets take up no space, but they’re like wrapping yourself in something thinner than a crisp packet, so they will rip if there are any sharp edges or wind. Reinforced ones are really robust. They’re a big sheet that’s silver on one side and brightly coloured on the other, with rivets in the corner, so you can do all sorts with them,” says Hudson. “Space blankets are lined with very thin, highly reflective aluminium so any radiated body heat is reflected back to you rather than being lost to your surroundings. Plus, the orange colour is a great way to get spotted by any potential rescuers if you’re outdoors.”View image in fullscreenRedcampheavy-dutyemergencyblanket£17.99 at AmazonHead torches“Head torches are great because you’re still able to use both hands while being able to see in the dark,” says Hudson. “You can spend a fortune on them, but you don’t have to. I bought an Energizer one recently, and it’s all that you really need. That one needs batteries, but you can get rechargeable ones too – I have one from Everbeam.”View image in fullscreenEnergizer Vision400-lumenheadtorch£19.99 at Argos£24.99 at Robert DyasView image in fullscreenEverbeam650-lumenheadtorch£16.99 at AmazonFor more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest head torchesWater“Having water stored is really important for a whole range of emergencies. The [mains] water might go off or get contaminated in some way. The key thing is to make sure you’ve got enough for the number of people in your household. My advice is to have 10 litres per person per day for hygiene, cooking and drinking,” says Cloke. The governmentguidancesuggests having enough bottled water for three days. It says you should have “three litres per person per day for drinking. More would be needed for other tasks such as cooking and washing”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWater filterHudson recommends a water filter bottle such as Pure Hydration’s Aquapure Traveller, which has a clever purifier cap to reduce harmful substances and microorganisms in water.You put in any fresh water, screw the cap on, and drink the water you squeeze through the purifier. “They’re amazing,” Hudson says. “The filter takes out a lot of the things in water that can harm you, from large things such as pathogens – worms and snail eggs – through to bacteria and tiny viruses, so you can more safely drink from any fresh water source you can find, such as rivers or rainwater. We’ve used them for 20 years in all sorts of environments with the military.” It’s a good idea to buyextra filters, too, although Hudson says they’re “good for 350 litres, so enough water at least 10 days if you’re not somewhere super hot and/or humid”.View image in fullscreenAquapure Traveller£49.50 at Pure HydrationPower bank“I think a power bank is more useful than batteries,” says Hudson. “You can buy big ones [he recommends the size below] that will also jump-start a car, which is quite handy, and also charge things such as head torches and phones. These days the bigger, the better if you don’t have to carry it; so many items need juice.”View image in fullscreenPortablecarbatteryjump-starterpowerpack£39.99 at AmazonFor more, read the Filter’s guide tothe best power banks and battery packs in the UK for reliable charging on the goHand sanitiser“Basic alcohol hand gel is important. If the water supply goes out, things like coughs and colds can spread within the family. Having a supply of hand sanitiser is good preparedness,” says Duffin. Cloke also recommends stocking up on “packets of wet wipes for basic hygiene, particularly if you’ve got babies”.View image in fullscreenCuticuraantibacterialhandgel£1.55 for 100ml at Boots£9.30 for 6 x 100ml at AmazonView image in fullscreenWet Ones Be Fresh Originalantibacterialwipes£2 for 40 wipes at Boots£9.43 for 6 x 12 wipes at AmazonCandles“Candles provide light without burning through your power supply. Go for stocky, fat ones because they’ll fall over less easily and last longer. Tea lights are also good – they don’t burn for ages, but you can buy sackfuls of them for not much money. You need matches too, like the big chunky boxes of Cook’s matches. Don’t leave unattended, and make sure you’ve got a fire extinguisher or a fire blanket,” says Hudson.View image in fullscreenVotivepillarcandles,four pack£3.50 at DunelmPulsesView image in fullscreenCupboard staples: tinned and jarred foods are handy when fresh supplies or cooking facilities are limited.“Tinned beans, chickpeas and lentils all have a long shelf life and are rich in fibre, nutrients and protein,” says Dr Federica Amati, head nutritionist at Zoe, nutrition lead at Imperial College London’s school of medicine and author ofThe Appetite ResetandEvery Body Should Know This. “Getting a variety is good for flavour reasons, but also for micronutrient content. Dried lentils are easy to cook, but if there’s a power cut or a shortage, tinned and jarred lentils will serve you better.” Oh, and don’t forget a tin opener.View image in fullscreenOxoGood Gripssoft-handledtin opener£19 at John Lewis£16.15 at AmazonGrain pouches“Microwaveable pouches are fantastic. If you’ve got a few ready to go, then if for whatever reason you don’t have enough water or can’t use the hob but you have a microwave, you can have these. Some of them you don’t even need to microwave, and you can just eat them out of the packet,” says Amati.View image in fullscreenMerchant Gourmetbrown,redandwildrice,250gx 6£9 at AmazonTinned fish“Get a variety of tinned fish, like mackerel, sardines, anchovies and sprats. Tinned mackerel is one of the easiest to integrate, and you can get them tinned with tomatoes, which a lot of people prefer if they don’t like fish. Find something you like, and then buy a couple more of those in your next shop, so you can build up a supply,” says Amati.Frozen fruit and vegetables“Buy frozen fruit and vegetables, if you have the space. Frozen veg is picked ripe and blanched within hours. Have some frozen berries and veg – broccoli, cauliflower and peas. You can get jars and tins of vegetables too, like roasted peppers, sweetcorn, carrots or beetroot,” says Amati. It’s also worth noting that, in the case of a power outage,food should stay frozen for up to 48 hours in a full freezer, or 24 hours if it’s half full, provided you keep thedoor closed.UHT milk, teabags and chocolate“UHT milk is worth getting, and make sure you have enough teabags, because you might be able to have a cup of tea, and those things are still important. Dark chocolate is also awesome – it keeps for months, needs no cooking or power, and offers plenty of energy in a small square, mostly from cocoa butter fats that sustain you rather than causing a rapid rise and crash in energy,” says Amati. She suggests opting for 70% cocoa or above so that “you also get more fibre, magnesium, iron and cocoa flavanols, plant compounds that support healthy blood vessels”.For more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest supermarket dark chocolateOats“Oats are fantastic,” says Amati. “You can just add hot water, mix them up, and then you’ve got something to eat. And you can eat them raw, mixed into yoghurt or milk.”Vacuum-packed bread“If you can’t buy fresh bread and you can’t freeze it, unopenedvacuum-packed rye bread can last about six months, and it’s super nutritious,” says Amati.View image in fullscreenBionaorganicryebread, 500g£3 at WaitroseOther tipsView image in fullscreenBe prepared: keep your first aid kit stocked and make sure you have enough of your regular medication.Photograph: Riska/GettyHave some cash“If there’s been some kind of tech outage and things are slowly coming back up, you might not be able to use your cards or phone to pay for stuff, so it’s worth having a little bit of cash,” says Hudson.Write down numbers“Everyone’s got people’s numbers in their phones, but what if the phone’s broken? Have some numbers written on a piece of paper, like people that you care about that you want to check in with and a number for a local medical centre in case you need to get your prescription,” Hudson says.Stock up on vital meds“If you’ve got some extra regular medication, that’s great. Sometimes people struggle to get that prescribed for them. But if you can stay a few days ahead, that will really help in case of emergency. I like to suggest having enough for a week or a month if you can, or at least two days if you’re struggling,” says Cloke.Duffin suggests having “at least seven to 14 days of your vital repeat medications in hand”, and that this is a useful thing to do anyway. “Request your script early, not just because of a severe weather event or a nuclear attack. If supply chains become more volatile, the medicine you need may not be in stock and might need to be ordered in.” Thegovernment guidancesays that “it’s important to request prescriptions up to five working days before you need your medicine”. The NHS also has anonline formyou can use to request emergency supplies of prescription medicine if you have run out, but note that they advise against ordering more than needed.For more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest camping stovesand thebest power banksIsabelle Aron is a lifestyle and culture journalist who’s written features on everything from the secrets of superagers to chefs on their favourite kitchen gadgetsExplore more on these topicsEmergency planningThe FilterGadgetsExtreme weatherClimate crisisHackingFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one | Games | The Guardian
description: Voicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a father
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: Voicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a father
Content: Draga, protagonist of Black Tides Draga's Wake, played by Dominik DiamondPhotograph: Strange Creature Factory LtdView image in fullscreenDraga, protagonist of Black Tides Draga's Wake, played by Dominik DiamondPhotograph: Strange Creature Factory LtdGamesAfter 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in oneDominik DiamondVoicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a fatherFri 30 Oct 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTShare“I listen to you on the radio and I keep hearing your voice in my head!”Not a typical opening to a creative partnership, but that is how Greg Strangis introduced himself to me 16 months ago, when he asked me to come to his garage in the middle of nowhere and have a look at a game he was making called Black Tides Draga’s Wake.If this sounds dodgy, remember that when I was 21 years old, a posh bloke asked me to come to a random church in the East End of London and talk saucy in front of him and a couple of other posh blokes. This turned out to be my audition for GamesMaster.So, I go to Greg’s garage. He has a giant yet well groomed beard, eyes that flash with intensity underneath one of those Peaky Blinders caps and talks faster than other humans. He’s basically a hipster Rasputin. He is also a character artist who has worked for Rockstar, Naughty Dog and Guillermo del Toro. He ticks all the genius boxes for me.And then I see the actual game. It is gorgeously dark and twisted: a survival horror game set on a decaying 1900s steamship after a heist gone wrong. The titular Draga is a big, tough-as-hell sailor with a dark past, infected by an ancient god that grows within him.View image in fullscreenGorgeously dark and twisted … Black Tides Draga’s Wake.Photograph: Strange Creature Factory Ltd.It sounds exciting, it sounds original, it sounds terrifying. And he wants me to be in it.But it sounds nothing like me. I am not a sailor. I am not big and tough as hell, and the only ancient god I have ever been infected with is gout. (Trust me, the pain is biblical.)I am going to have to …act.I did study drama at university, but this was the University of Bristol in the early 90s, so it was less about high kicking on stage to Oklahoma or learning Shakespearean monologues and more about poring over some obscure Russian play where potatoes are a metaphor for gender politics, written by a bloke who once gave Gorky a lift.I never told Greg this at the time, but when I see my first attempts at voice acting play out in the game, I don’t like it. I see this amazing badass character smashing disgustingly huge monsters with my tinny tones coming out of him. So I lower my voice ever so slightly and stop trying to act so much. And it works! Helpfully, Greg’s direction always makes me feel comfortable and encouraged.Every time I turn up for a session I am inspired by the work done by the team, who are in different corners of the world, doing this in their spare time. I see their message threads with all kinds of ideas, pictures and animations. It reminds me of the bedroom programming culture of the ZX Spectrum, fuelled by the unshakeable belief in an idea and a passion for gaming. In an age where huge publishers are decimating studios all over the world, it is a reminder of how vibrant game-making can still be.View image in fullscreenExistential crisis … Dominik as a survival horror action hero.Photograph: Dominik DiamondI don’t want to be the weak link in this chain. I don’t want my performance to be something that takes a prospective publisher out of the moment. I learn to love pushing and pulling the words in different directions. The biggest challenge is improvising fight noises that Greg and the team can add in wherever and whenever they want. During the game this is supposed to seem natural, but in reality it is a Scottish dad in his 50s making the kinds of noises he hasn’t made since his honeymoon. In a garage. In the middle of rural Nova Scotia. With another guy telling him he has to be more aggressive.It’s unbearably weird when I play the game. I feel distraught when I die, because itisme. I feel equally bad when I see other people playing the game, leading to uncomfortable new thoughts about video game characters’ lack of free will. It’s all a bit of an existential crisis.But then I play clips for my kids without telling them I am in it. I see their faces break out into wide grins as they realise it’s their grumpy old Scottish dad playing a survival horror action hero. It’s one of my favourite ever moments as a parent.It has also made me appreciate voice acting in games, something that didn’t register with me before, because for me it always felt like thecharactertalking – which is testament to the quality of voice acting and directing in games. Or at least games since the original Resident Evil. I now truly appreciate performances like Nolan North as Nathan Drake, Ashley Johnson in The Last of Us, and every single actor who says any of the words in Expedition 33.The announcement trailer for Black Tides Draga’s Wake dropped a month ago. It got 200,000 views in the first couple of days. Greg is in discussions with assorted publishers. I still have to pinch myself that after playing games for 50 years, I am finally going to be in one.Explore more on these topicsGamescommentShareReuse this content

title: The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead | Mark Wolfe | The Guardian
description: Congress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the season
Author: Mark Wolfe
Headline: Congress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the season
Content: ‘Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives.’Photograph: John Taggart/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives.’Photograph: John Taggart/EPAOpinionUS CongressThe Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is aheadMark WolfeCongress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the seasonFri 30 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTShareHeating oil may be the clearest warning yet of how the war in Iran is deepening the US’s energy affordability crisis. Families who heat their homes with oil are facing bills that could be50% higherthis winter, adding nearly $900 to the cost of keeping their homes warm. These families were already struggling before the war began.As the Guardianrecently reported, research by my organization found that electricity shutoffs in 10 states had increased 28% over the past two years. Millions of Americans were already falling behind on their utility bills, forced to choose between paying for energy, food, medicine and rent. Now they face another round of increases in gasoline, electricity and home heating costs.The war didn’t create America’s energy affordability crisis. But it is making a bad situation much worse.For families living on social security, minimum-wage workers and others with little room in their budgets, higher energy prices are taking an especially heavy toll. Even middle-class families are struggling to absorb another $100 or $150 a month for gasoline, groceries and home heating.Heating oil is the canary in the coalmine for the broader affordability crisis.Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon TisdallRead moreHeating oil and diesel are essentially the same petroleum product, and both have been hit hard by the disruption to global energy markets. Higher diesel prices increase the cost of moving food, delivering goods and operating farms and construction equipment. Those costs eventually find their way into the prices families pay.But for the millions of households that rely on heating oil, the impact is much more immediate. Unlike gasoline, which families can sometimes conserve by driving less, heating oil is essential for keeping homes warm. Families cannot simply stop filling their tanks when prices rise.Trump described higher oil prices resulting from the war as “a very small price to payfor USA, and world, safety and peace”. But there is nothing small about anadditional $878in heating costs for a family living on social security or working for minimum wage. The president has also said that fuel prices will fall “like a rock” when the war ends. I hope he is right.Even if the war ended tomorrow, energy prices would not necessarily return to their previous levels. Damaged refineries need repairs, shipping routes must reopen, and depleted petroleum inventories need to be replenished. That could take months. Families cannot postpone paying their heating bills while the oil market recovers.Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives. We are calling on lawmakers to add $3bn to the Low Income HomeEnergyAssistance Program (Liheap), which helps low-income families pay their heating bills.This would allow states to provide families with supplemental assistance to cover rising heating oil and electricity prices before the start of the winter heating season.The problem extends beyond the poorest families. Many working families earn too much to qualify for assistance but still struggle to pay their energy bills. Congress should consider temporarily expanding eligibility for Liheap to struggling middle-class families, with additional funding to ensure that assistance to the lowest-income households is not reduced.A recent survey conducted byConsumer Reportsfound that more than a quarter of all families reported reduced the heating and cooling in their homes to uncomfortable levels to save money and 19% cutback on groceries or switched to less expensive food options.double quotation markProducing more energy at home hasn’t protected the US families from price shocks caused by wars overseasWithout additional energy assistance, families will fall further behind, and some will face the possibility of losing heat during the coldest months of the year.But Congress also needs to address the larger problem. For too long, we’ve measured America’s energy security by how much oil and natural gas we produce. Yet producing more energy at home hasn’t protected the US families from price shocks caused by wars overseas.We need to think about energy security differently. That means expanding energy sources, including wind and solar, whose fuel costs cannot be driven up by a war. There is no strait of Hormuz for solar power.That is the longer-term challenge. Right now, millions of families are heading into winter facing energy bills they cannot afford.At some point, the war in Iran will end, but the affordability crisis will not end with it. Washington needs to help families get through this winter and make sure the next war thousands of miles away doesn’t once again determine whether they can afford to heat their homes.Mark Wolfe is an energy economist and serves as the executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (Neada) representing the state directors of the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the co-director of the Center on Energy Poverty and Climate (CEPC). He also serves as an adjunct professor at the George Washington University public policy schoolExplore more on these topicsUS CongressOpinionEnergyOilGasUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: The world needs the United Nations more than ever. It needs a new lease on life | Alex Rondos and Mark Medish | The Guardian
description: We need neither ‘peace in our time’ nor ‘perpetual peace’ – but enough peace to keep civilization
Author: Mark Medish
Headline: We need neither ‘peace in our time’ nor ‘perpetual peace’ – but enough peace to keep civilization
Content: ‘The resort to war over dialogue and diplomacy has reared its head again.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreen‘The resort to war over dialogue and diplomacy has reared its head again.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAOpinionUnited NationsThe world needs the United Nations more than ever. It needs a new lease on lifeAlex Rondos andMark MedishWe need neither ‘peace in our time’ nor ‘perpetual peace’ – but enough peace to keep civilizationFri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.38 EDTShareTo save theUnited Nationsfrom the irrelevance in which it now wallows, the next secretary general will require the concerted backing of the few powers that govern the security council.The paradox is that the great powers who created the institution in the 1940s and recently treat it with a cavalier cynicism are now the ones who need it most, as does the rest of the world.This is not about nostalgia for what was created after the second world war. That world has changed. We are no longer in the cold war. But it is carelessness of high order to assume that some mystical process will create a world while, in the meantime, the most powerful give license to some dangerous pathologies that have brought us to ruin in the past.The resort to war over dialogue and diplomacy has reared its head again. Restraint has given way to calculated recklessness. Changing facts on the ground before talking now creates leverage, and that is why we see an unprecedented multiplication of centers of violence. Militias and mercenaries abound.As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve BloomfieldRead moreCollective security to which all commit to be effective is now supplanted by a petulant isolationism. Revolutionary new technologies have spurred a rush to secure minerals and supply routes upending traditional notions of sovereignty. Drone warfare has made violence much more affordable. Frontiers are now up for grabs.The permanent members of the security council, anachronistically still composed of the victors of the second world war, have a tall order. Quarrels that are as old as tribes, communities and nations now have new, more lethal weapons.Civil wars, border wars and the return of imperial ambition are not relics. They drive the war in Ukraine, the drift toward conflict in the Horn of Africa, the instability around the Gulf and the Red Sea, and the standoff over Taiwan.These conflicts are now multiplying at a scale and speed in a time when global regulatory arrangements over existential threats are denigrated. Proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, pandemics, climate change will either be fueled or managed by artificial intelligence.As AI is woven into military planning, early warning and command systems, it compresses the time leaders have to think before they act, and it multiplies the tools of deception and destabilization. A world that learned, slowly and at great risk, to live with nuclear weapons must now learn to live with machines that may shape decisions about using them.These dangers can only be contained if we dispense with some misplaced assumptions.The first is that the UN is a club of the like-minded. It was never meant to be. The UN exists so that states that distrust or even detest one another have somewhere to meet – a place that offers hospitality to adversaries.If the hard conversations about war and technology do not happen there, where else will they happen in a way that protects the rest of humanity? It is about co-existence, not convergence.The second assumption is that power can be evenly distributed. It cannot. Pretending otherwise is idealism to the point of fault. A handful of states possess the disproportionate capacity to contain these dangers or to unleash them. In practice, today this means the United States, China and Russia.But there is no reason to exclude India or a better-integratedEuropean Union. Even if they do not trust one another, they need only recognize a shared interest in a world that remains manageable.This harsh reality should temper the fashionable faith in “middle powers”. Their activism is understandable, even admirable: they see the great powers changing character and are trying to respond. But they are called middle powers for a reason. They cannot, on their own, end a major war or govern a technology developed mostly elsewhere.War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess | Nesrine MalikRead moreThis does not mean that might makes right. Neither does it mean that complicated times need simple answers which would be a repudiation of politics at the international level. Power checked by reasonable deliberation, negotiation and diplomacy is a core principle that inspired the charter of the United Nations. This moment calls for a rededication to principled pragmatism.History has much to teach. When the plague swept Europe in the 14th century, the city states of Italy established the practice of quarantines and an early form of health certification. The science may have been wrong and the system imperfect. But it worked well enough, and it rested on self-interest, not virtue.Since the mid-20th century, in a radically different technological era, nuclear proliferation and the risk of nuclear war have been contained, so far, through a lengthy process of negotiation and agreements.Imagine a renewed UN that is a problem-solver rather than a bystander, a credible forum rather than a costly talking shop, and the prime instrument for collective action.None of this happens unless the great powers want it to. Choosing a secretary general is one of the few moments when they must agree on a qualified person and a timely agenda. The superpowers, middle powers and emerging powers of the global south may each have reasons for skepticism. But they share a stronger reason to make this effort.We need neither “peace in our time” nor “perpetual peace” – but enough peace to keep civilization.Alex Rondos is a former envoy of the European Union. Mark Medish is a former senior US national security and treasury officialExplore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionUS politicsEuropean UnioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Mary Peltola made a mistake. But her Republican opponent would be a disaster for Alaska | Kim Heacox | The Guardian
description: Trump and Senator Dan Sullivan have put my home state on the chopping block. But Peltola understands Alaskans
Author: Kim Heacox
Headline: Trump and Senator Dan Sullivan have put my home state on the chopping block. But Peltola understands Alaskans
Content: ‘She’s a lifelong Alaskan who knows how to listen and who understands what she calls “kitchen table issues”.’Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘She’s a lifelong Alaskan who knows how to listen and who understands what she calls “kitchen table issues”.’Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Mary Peltola made a mistake. But her Republican opponent would be a disaster for AlaskaKim HeacoxTrump and Senator Dan Sullivan have put my home state on the chopping block. But Peltola understands AlaskansFri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTShareDonald Trump’s trip to Alaska earlier this month was a real doozy.Should I be surprised? The previous time he visited my home state, in August 2025, he ordered the US military toroll out a red carpet for Russia’s Vladimir Putin. The two billionaire oligarchs chummed it up and posed for cameras, then talked about the war in Ukraine and achieved no formal ceasefire and no peace agreement.I was curious to see what Trump would do this time. If our economy is so good, as he says it is, and if Republicans are so superior to Democrats, as he says they are, then why fly 3,400 miles to hold a rally for Dan Sullivan, Alaska’s junior Republican senator running for his third term?Sullivan is in a tight race with his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola. That’s why. Control of the US Senate for the next two years could come down to Alaska.A week ago, Trump made a desperate move. Hedirected the US Department of Justiceto file a lawsuit against the state of Alaska because a second Dan Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher from the coastal fishing town of Petersburg, is also on the ballot.On Wednesday, the plot thickened when theNew York Timesreported that back in the summer of 2025, Democratic operatives began to engineer ways to get a spoiler on the Alaska ballot, according to interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager and longtime aide, Elisa Rios, who was fired in a staff shake-up in August. Other sources included texts.Alaska Senate race: what to know about Democrats’ alleged ballot-stacking effortRead moreRios said Peltola was not directly involved in the operation but was aware of it. Last week, Rios contacted the Times and retracted all statements “made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race”. She added: “I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity.”A spokesperson for the Democratic Senate campaign armtold the Guardian: “Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns.”Trump’s justice department lawsuit, however, is unprecedented. It seeks to block a Peltola win “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan”. Meanwhile, the justice department hasreportedly issued subpoenasover the matter.Four months ago, the Alaska supreme courtapproved both Sullivans on the ballot. The Alaska division of elections lists the Petersburg candidate as “Sullivan, Daniel J Jr” without a party affiliation, and the senator, Dan S Sullivan, as the incumbent Republican.Criticism of the lawsuit has been deep and wide. “Attention Alaska,” wroteLibby Bakalar, the municipal attorney for Bethel and a former assistant attorney general. “Donald Trump is abusing the judicial system in an attempt to personally appoint your next United States senator. Don’t let him.” (Following theTimes story, she told KTOO: “Not a single illegal thing happened here.”)Which brings us back to the rally on 13 October. The Wasilla sports center – not so large but easy to fill – thrummed with excitement as Trump and Sullivan shared the stage and appeared to have a good time, playing to all the flags and phones and red hats.Sullivan said nothing about Alaska’s federal employees who lost their jobs due to government cuts, many of them highly educated scientists. He also made no appeal to the many Alaskans in remote villages who struggle with some of thehighest prices in the state’s history: home heating fuel at $7-$9/gallon, milk at $25-$30/gallon.And if that weren’t enough, he said nothing about the estimated30,000 Alaskanswho have lost, or will soon lose, their medical coverage.Instead, Sullivan stood with the man responsible for those problems and told the crowd what he had said to Trump privately: “Mr President, I just really want to thank you for all that you’re doing for Alaska.”Really?Was I missing something? I’ve lived in Alaska for nearly 50 years – have been charged by bears, surrounded by caribou, charmed by whales and inspired by glaciers.I can’t imagine my heart and soul thriving anywhere else. A young ranger with the US National Park Service back in the 1970s, I came north for adventure and beauty and found both. The wild America I was born too late to see down south, awaited me up north. For that, I will always be grateful.Blame it on Henry David Thoreau, Edward Abbey and Rachel Carson, American authors who convinced me that nothing is more valuable than wildness, curiosity and a sense of wonder.As such, it’s not bears that frighten me. It’s men like Sullivan and Trump who can hear a dollar bill fall on the tundra. Men who get excited by 1)drilling for oilinthe Arctic national wildlife refuge2)reducing the western Brooks Rangeto amassive mining districtand reaching those mines by slicing a cut-and-fill road throughGates of the Arctic national park, and 3)repealingthe US Forest Service’sRoadless Rulethat will enable clearcut logging in the Tongass national forest – a temperate rainforest, one of the rarest biomes on Earth – where massive, ancient trees and a thick understorystore more carbon than any other national forest in the country. Of the roughly 1.6m responses, more than 99%opposed the repeal. Americans appreciate the life-giving value of their trees.What a travesty then, to witness Alaska on the chopping block.Trump and Sullivan make a destructive bromance. Sullivan has voted with Trump’s stated positionsmore than 95% of the time, including, more recently,14 votesagainst resolutions aimed at curtailing the president’s military authority or against removing US forces from Iran. No wonder Trump wants to keep him around. Drill, dig, fill and kill.And where was Mary Peltola during this rally?Off the road system, listening to village Alaskans express their concerns about, well … everything. The cost of fuel and food, their warming world and declining numbers of caribou and fish; thenorthern rivers turning rustic orange-yellow, laced with toxic metals leached from thawing permafrost. Their homes sinking into swamps orfalling into the seathat no longer freezes in autumn, which allows ocean storms to tear down protective bluffs and eat away their villages.Trump took a jab at Peltola but saved his best for other matters.DoJ reportedly issues subpoenas over same name Alaska candidatesRead more“Bring on the pardons,” he announced, and the beneficiaries stepped forward:two Anchorage mechanicswho had pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act through a business that disabled pollution control devices on diesel engines. “They want to put them in jail for 10 years because they fixed an engine,” Trumptold the crowd. “How sick.” He proceeded to talk about trucking and “all of the environmental crap” that allegedly makes vehicles expensive and inefficient.This is where we find ourselves. In a landscape and ecosystem butcher shop run by Trump and Sullivan and other Republicans doing their best to defeat “environmental crap”.And Mary Peltola? She needs to do what Trump has never done: apologize.Come clean with the people she seeks to represent. Stand strong and promise to take the high ground. She’s alifelong Alaskanwho knows how to listen and who understands what she calls “kitchen table issues”.Sullivan, by stark contrast, is a corporate shill. If re-elected, he will continue to bend the knee to our wannabe king. The choice is clear.Can Peltola unseat Sullivan on 3 November? Yes. Alaska will be counted last, but don’t count us out. My forecast from the land of caribou, whales and bears: cloudy with a chance of better days ahead.Kim Heacox is the author of many books, including The Only Kayak and Jimmy Bluefeather, both winners of the National Outdoor Book Award. He is a former ranger at Alaska’s Glacier Bay, Denali and Katmai national parksExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionAlaskaDonald TrumpUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump vowed to reduce prices, but his policies have fueled US inflation | Steven Greenhouse in New York | The Guardian
description: ‘Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them’
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: ‘Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them’
Content: A local shopper searches for meat products on 21 September 2026 at the Market 32 supermarket in South Burlington, Vermont.Photograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA local shopper searches for meat products on 21 September 2026 at the Market 32 supermarket in South Burlington, Vermont.Photograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Trump vowed to reduce prices, but his policies have fueled US inflationSteven Greenhousein New York‘Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them’Fri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.53 EDTShareDonald Trumpsuccessfully campaigned for his second term two years ago promising toreduce prices on day one, but ever since he returned to the White House, he has done little to fight inflation or reduce prices. Instead, some of his most important policy decisions – most notably hiswar against Iranand his tariff wars – have increased inflation instead of reducing it. This helps explainwhy more than one in five Americans who voted for Trumpnow disapprove of the job he’s doing.Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them during his second term. Indeed, the “liberation day” tariffs he imposed soon after returning to office increased the price of hundreds of goods, includingcitrus fruits, steel, bananas, beef and auto parts. When the supreme court overturned those tariffs as illegal, Trump immediately imposednew 10% across-the-board tariffsthat again helped push up prices (a lower courtfound those tariffs unlawful, too). Time and again, Trump has slapped on new tariffs even though they inherently push up prices because tariffs are a tax on imported goods. Little wonder that a Fox News poll this month found that77% of Americans disapproveof how Trump has handled tariffs.Candidate Trump pledged to slash“energy and electricity prices by half”, to get“gasoline below $2 a gallon”,and to bring down “airfares and housing costs”. He has failed to do any of those things. Gas now averages $4.28 a gallon nationally, according toAAA.Yale Budget Labsays Trump’s tariffs will cost the average household $1,100 this year, whileMoody’s Analyticssays the war with Iran has already cost US households about $2,000 from higher energy, fuel and transportation costs and from higher interest rates.Worsening Americans’ affordability problems, prices have been rising faster than workers’ wages in recent months. As a result, Americans haveseen no real wage growth on averagesince Trump returned to office – both average hourly pay and prices have risen by 5.4% since January 2025.Matthew Middleton, a White House spokesman, defended Trump’s record on inflation and critiqued Joe Biden’s, saying: “President Trump has implemented an aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda that has blunted Biden’s historic 40-year high inflation crisis, driven economic growth, increased wages and created private-sector jobs in areas that had been hollowed out and shipped overseas.”After returning to the White House, Trumphelped push up electricity pricesbyending federal subsidies for low-cost renewable energy. His gung-ho cheerleading for datacenters, along withhis speeding up of federal permitting to build them, has helped fuel a datacenter construction boom that is expected to increaseelectricity costs to consumers by more than $6bn. Trump and the Republican-led Congress further hit consumers by raising the cost ofmany electric vehicles by $7,500when they ended EV subsidies.When Trump plunged into war against Iran eight months ago, he showed little concern about what that war would mean for inflation back home. He ignored warnings that the war would cause Iran toclose the strait of Hormuz, which in turn would cause oil and gas prices to soar. Since the war began, US gas prices have risen by over 40%, diesel prices by nearly 70%, andsome fertilizer prices by 20%. Record diesel prices have pushed airfares skyward, while soaring diesel and fertilizer prices have created a sea of red ink for US farmers.In one tiff over inflation, after Trump said last June “I love the inflation,”Senator Bernie Sanders responded, “You know who doesn’t love inflation, Mr President? Working families struggling to afford gas, groceries and other necessities because of your disastrous actions.”Further defending Trump’s record on inflation, White House spokesman Middleton said: “The President has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but this administration will continue to deliver economic wins for the American people over the next two years. While Democrats pretend to care about ‘affordability’, this administration has delivered tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families: President Trump signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals and will continue to put American workers first.”A White House official added that Trump’s policies “have created an environment for sustained increase in energy supply and lower costs for American households and businesses”. Those policies have included making it easier to drill for oil and reducing business and environmental regulations.Trump’s moves have further worsened Americans’ affordability woes by pushing up interest rates. By the time Biden left office, inflation, which had soared to a painful 9% during the pandemic,had slid to 3.0%and was heading lower. But Trump’s policies have played a major role in pushing inflationback up to 3.7%. That has caused the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, while also pushing mortgage rates higher. Thirty-year fixedmortgage rates have climbed to 7.4%,making it considerably harder for young and non-affluent Americans to buy homes. (As for Trump’s 2024 promise to reduce housing costs,he refused to sign a bipartisan billthat sought to speed housing construction with the aim of making housing more affordable.)Under Trump, not only has the national debt climbed above $40tn, but this year’s federal budget deficit will reach $2tn. That worsening fiscal picture has worried bond investors and pushed up interest rates. (In 2019, Trump promisedto eliminate the entire national debtwithin eight years.)Trump’s policies have increased healthcare costs for millions of Americans. By pushing Congress to cut Medicaid by $1tn and to not extend Obamacare subsidies, Trump helpedcause more than 20 million people to losehealth coverage or pay more out-of-pocket for healthcare. Americans who pay for their own health insurance saw their premiumsjump by 25% this year, with many households paying not just hundreds of dollars more, but thousands more.To be sure, Trump has taken several steps to fight inflation, but most have been minor. HisTrumpRX program has offered many drugsat lower prices, and that was one factor among many that contributed to the4.5% drop in prescription drug pricesover the past year. In August, Trump announced hewould import 660m pounds of ground beeffrom Latin America to reduce beef prices – that move (which angered ranchers) was a direct response to the public outcry over the higher beef prices resulting from his tariffs. Last November, in a sharp about-face aimed at reducing prices, Trumprescinded his tariffs on coffee and tropical fruitsafter consumers had grown angry that coffee and citrus prices had soared due to Trump’s tariffs.With his promise to pay $5,000 to every adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, Trump is essentially saying he will make it up to voters for pushing up prices and worsening affordability problems. Trump saysthe money for those payments could come from tariff revenues, but guess where those tariffs revenues come from? They come from the money that US consumers have had to pay on Trump’s tariffs – on his taxes on imports. Some might say that Trump wants to pay Peter by first robbing Peter.Trump keeps saying thataffordability problems are “a hoax”. But whenever average Americans go to a supermarket or gas station, they know that the affordability squeeze is real and a big issue in their lives. Many can see that Trump, despite his campaign promises, has done precious little to reduce inflation. Indeed, in very bad news for Republicans in the midterm elections, a recent Reuters/Ipsospollfound that 78% ofAmericans blame Trump’s policiesfor pushing up prices.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionInflationEconomicsUS politicsUS-Israel war on IranTrump tariffsTariffscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a gen Z voter. Content creators have far less power than politicians think | Alex Bronzini-Vender | The Guardian
description: Both US parties scramble to win young voters via influencer operations. The evidence doesn’t support their efforts
Author: Alex Bronzini-Vender
Headline: Both US parties scramble to win young voters via influencer operations. The evidence doesn’t support their efforts
Content: ‘The podcast-interview format itself isn’t magic.’Photograph: Call Her Daddy/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The podcast-interview format itself isn’t magic.’Photograph: Call Her Daddy/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026I’m a gen Z voter. Content creators have far less power than politicians thinkAlex Bronzini-VenderBoth US parties scramble to win young voters via influencer operations. The evidence doesn’t support their effortsFri 30 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.38 EDTShareIn tight races, any group that shifts a few points can be called decisive. In 2024, however, gen Z voters actually earned the spotlight.Take Michigan, where Donald Trump won by about 1.4 points: he and Kamala Harris evenlysplitthe youth vote, a 24-point collapse in the Democratic edge since 2020. If young voters made up just 15% of the state’s electorate, their swing toward the president would be worth roughly 3.6 points, larger than Trump’s entire margin of victory.Ever since, both parties have scrambled to court the tastemakers who seem to have gen Z’s ear.At her debut briefing, the former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt reserved a “new media seat” in the briefing room, inviting podcasters, influencers and content creators to apply for credentials. The NRCC, House Republicans’ campaign arm, haspaidmore than $120,000 to a network of conservative influencers, listing the expense simply as “media”.Not to be outdone, the Democratic National Committee haspartneredwith more than 500 online personalities through its “Influencer & Creative” operation – and has lately floated the idea of a creator-hosted debate during the 2028 primaries.The same wishful theory undergirds all these efforts: both parties seem to think online creators can simply upload political opinions straight into our heads.As a zoomer myself, I find this theory rather patronizing. More to the point, it isn’t true: there’s little evidence that online creators play much of a role in how zoomers actually vote. And if young voters decide these midterms, influencers shouldn’t get the credit.Plenty of people watch influencers, but very few people deeply trust them.In a survey this year by the Media Insight Project, 63% of 18-to-34-year-oldssaidthey get news from influencers “at least sometimes”. Yet among teens and adults who actually receive news from these people, just 9% report having a great deal of confidence in what they are being told. (AI chatbots enjoy a nearly identical rate of trust, at 10%.)Other polls have found much the same thing: when YouGovsurveyedyoung voters across eight battleground states in September on whom they actually turn to for political advice, half named a family member and three in 10 named a friend. Just 6% named an influencer.In another survey of young peoplereleasedthis spring by Circle, a civic-engagement research center at Tufts, just 9% of respondents said they got political information from social media posts by influencers and celebrities. Another 14% pointed to podcasts hosted by influencers, artists, comedians or other celebrities.By contrast, 45% of respondents – the largest share – got their information from political, advocacy or community organizations they follow, while nearly a third cited conversations with family and friends.To whatever extent that internet personalities actually persuade people, their powers rest entirely on the illusion that they speak for themselves. Naturally, both parties have responded by shattering that illusion.Campaigns and their allies increasingly pay for those voices, often at exorbitant prices. In this year’s race for California governor, Tom Steyerpaidat least 17 influencers $5,000 or more apiece, while Katie Porter’s campaign paid one lifestyle creator $25,000 for what appeared to be a single post. A TikTok creator with 1.7 million followerssaida Republican-affiliated group hadoffered her $36,000for a video, and a company with deep Republican ties oncepaida squad of gen Z creators to defend Ken Paxton, now Texas’s Republican Senate nominee, on X.Some influencers attempt to keep these “partnerships” hidden. The New York Timesfoundthat Josh Greene, a progressive creator with nearly 800,000 followers, had not always disclosed the fact that he’d taken money from at least seven candidates and allied groups this cycle.Paid influencers are everywhere in US politics. We need transparency | Martin J Riedl and Samuel WoolleyRead moreAnd when the payments do come to light – as they tend to – they risk destroying the very credibility that campaigns were trying to buy. As the Rainey Center for Public Policyfoundthis summer, 47% of voters said they’d trust a creator less after learning a political post had been paid for by a campaign; only 11% said they’d trust them more.Obviously, the internet matters. Zohran Mamdani, who won young men by roughly 40 points in last year’s New York mayoral race, hassaidmany New Yorkers he met knew him only from his appearances on podcasts such as Flagrant, hosted by the comedian Andrew Schulz. (As Mamdani put it, Democrats should “stop treating young people and young men with the condescension that we often see and hear in our politics”.) And Trump’s tour of the podcasting sphere in 2024 had racked up more than 100m YouTube views by the day after the election that year.Still, both appearances wereinterviews, not simply paid content. Even if the questioning is friendly, the candidates still do most of the talking. And the podcast-interview format itself isn’t magic: Kamala Harris’s appearance on Call Her Daddy seems to have done little to move young voters.Every older generation finds the next one inscrutable, and gen Z is an especially tough read. Older Americans can be forgiven for struggling to grasp what it means to come of age in the era of social media. (Our memes are, admittedly, really weird.)Still, if you ignore our screen time, we’re pretty normal after all. Like swing voters twice our age, we’ve ditched the Republican party because prices remain stubbornly high. For all the money Washington is spending to decode our political decision-making, the most surprising thing about gen Z voters may be just how boringly ordinary we are.Alex Bronzini-Vender is a writer living in New YorkExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsYoung peopleRepublicansDemocratscommentShareReuse this content

title: British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Financial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us all, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: Financial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us all, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: Thomas Clarkson addresses a meeting of the world anti-slavery convention in Exeter Hall, London, June 1840.Illustration: Pictures from History/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThomas Clarkson addresses a meeting of the world anti-slavery convention in Exeter Hall, London, June 1840.Illustration: Pictures from History/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesOpinionSlaveryBritish people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated historyAndy BurnhamFinancial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us allAndy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave tradeFri 30 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 20.54 EDTShareOn 28 October 1787, Thomas Clarkson pushed through the crowds to reach the pulpit of Manchester Cathedral. A campaigner for abolishing slavery, hespoke urgently about the horrors of the slave tradeand the humanity of enslaved people. “He drinks the cup of sorrow,” Clarkson said. “And he drinks it at our hands.”DuringBlack History Month, these are the stories it is important to remember. They show us the complicated truth of our history. Thousands of people in Manchester signed a petition against slavery after Clarkson’s sermon. And yet Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people. There are similar stories up and down the nation. We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives.The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people.
