They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.Our history is intertwined with countries that are now our allies, particularly in the Commonwealth. Next week, I will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests: a beacon of stability, strength and security. Together we can face down shared challenges. We can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration. We can strengthen our respective countries and share our values to build a safer world for us all.But facing a changing world together requires us to stand on firm foundations. To meet those challenges of the future, we need to face up to the past. For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.So we are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.My focus is on building a future where people at home and abroad live in greater peace and prosperity.So we will bring to the Chogm our determination to tackle the issues that affect people across our Commonwealth family and beyond.Today, debt-servicing costs in the poorest and most vulnerable countries are at their highest in more than 25 years. More than 40% of these countries spendmore on interest repayments than on health. I want to launch a new drive on debt, working with our global partners to help those countries repay over a longer time period and with better rates. That is why the chancellor, foreign secretary and I have asked Gordon Brown, who will join us at the Chogm, to help with this work.We will also support the energy transition in the face of the climate crisis. And we will build on the incredible work being done to educate women and girls, give smaller countries a louder voice on the world stage, and end global poverty and inequality.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI want us to build stronger relationships with each other and renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.We stand on the shoulders of those such as Thomas Clarkson and the many ordinary people who spoke out for justice and humanity.In 1862, at the height of the American civil war, Manchester was the cotton capital of the world. In a vote at the Free Trade Hall, the humble cotton workers resolved that they wouldno longer handle slave-picked cotton. Their actions helped end the civil war, prompting Abraham Lincoln to write to them praising their “sublime Christian heroism”.It is so often the case in British history that huge injustices ignored by the powers-that-be are eventually overturned by ordinary people. Those Manchester cotton workers represent that proud British tradition, and I will take inspiration from them as we go forward into our new dialogue.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorse | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: From surgeons to senior civil servants, even the most decent people can make disastrous mistakes. But these gaffes require honesty, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: From surgeons to senior civil servants, even the most decent people can make disastrous mistakes. But these gaffes require honesty, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: ‘There is something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure.’ Liz Truss on stage in February 2025.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreen‘There is something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure.’ Liz Truss on stage in February 2025.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APOpinionMental healthHow do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorseGaby HinsliffFrom surgeons to senior civil servants, even the most decent people can make disastrous mistakes. But these gaffes require honestyFri 30 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTShareGabriel Weston made a mistake at work this summer. It doesn’t define her – she was and is a well-regarded NHS surgeon and author – but it was serious enough, as she explained in an extraordinarily candid series ofInstagramandSubstackposts this month, to prompt an investigation that left her feeling“ashamed and alone and really quite nervous”. Whatever went wrong in the operating theatre was bad enough to be classed a “never event” (something that should never be able to happen if the process is working properly) and triggered a nagging anxiety that she might somehow do it again, unless she figured out where she had unexpectedly gone wrong.It’s a fascinating insight into a process that most people never have the courage to talk about openly. But it also highlights why it’s so hard in practice for doctors and other professionals to acknowledge and learn from mistakes – as every public inquiry into every public scandal ends up recommending, only to repeat it all over again after the next one – rather than close ranks and cover up. Weston says she only spoke up out of frustration with what she saw as her employers’ failure to support her (she had asked to reduce what she considered an overloaded operating list to take some pressure off, which she says has now happened, leaving her full of praise for the hospital’s ultimate response). Judging by the responses to her posts, she’s not alone.I thought of Weston this week when Liz Truss published Bank Job, the second book she has written in two years circling the drain of her career. This one seems if anything even less self-aware, blaming the Bank of England, not herself, for the spectacular failure of her mini-budget (even her old cheerleaders at the Telegraph called itderanged). But it’s also oddly sad. There’s something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure, as if the truth would shatter her. She can’t seem to leave the whole episode alone – can’t withdraw, as Keir Starmer has, into stony silence about his own prematurely curtailed time in Downing Street – yet can’t really face it head-on either.Could 2026 be the year that democracy fought back? | David Van ReybrouckRead moreHow does anyone learn from cataclysmic failure? I don’t mean the frothy, early-career kind that seemed the end of the world at the time, but which you can laugh about now from the security of knowing that eventually everything turned out fine. Those aren’t the kind of failures the state really cares about avoiding. Nor do I mean the kind whose authors somehow manage to fail upwards anyway – or at least onwards, like Truss, into some strange reincarnation on YouTube. The failures that most haunt their authors, but which often hold the most useful lessons for preventing such a thing ever happening again, are often of the “there but for the grace of God go you and I” kind, involving formerly blameless and conscientious people who make one inexplicably dumb mistake, often under pressure or when exhausted.Richard Jacksonwas a high-flying civil servant working on counter-terrorism, who one night accidentally scooped up two classified documents that should never have left the building along with some routine papers he was taking home. Realising his error that night, he fatally compounded it by deciding to sneak the files back before their absence was noticed, only to accidentally leave them on the train – where they were found and handed into a BBC reporter, resulting in a security scandal that cost Jackson his job and left him close to suicide. The advice on coping he shared in a recent episode of BBC Radio 4’s Life Changing series – get dark thoughts out of your head by writing them down or telling someone; keep a note of all the nice things people have ever said to you; don’t let your life be defined by one mistake – seems useful for individuals in the eye of the storm. But so perhaps is what Weston calls a degree of professional “care and acceptance” for good people who have failed, and want help working out why.Shamelessness has a deservedly terrible reputation in public life, and for some mistakes forgiveness can be too much to ask.But it’s shame that prevents thoughtful people learning from failure; shame that drives the cover-up; shame that ruins, and sometimes even ends, lives. People willing to honestly examine their own mistakes for others’ benefit deserve some grace in return. The true shame lies with those refusing to offer it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. title: This is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop nationalist populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rules | Jonathan Freedland in Tel Aviv | The Guardian
description: The opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in power, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in power, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Partnership for Peace (Shutafut LaShalom) calls for the Yashar party leader, Gadi Eisenkot, to form an alliance with Israel's Arab parties, Herzliya, 29 October 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPartnership for Peace (Shutafut LaShalom) calls for the Yashar party leader, Gadi Eisenkot, to form an alliance with Israel's Arab parties, Herzliya, 29 October 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelThis is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop nationalist populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rulesJonathan Freedlandin Tel AvivThe opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in powerFri 30 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.59 EDTShareIt’s less an election result than a philosophical puzzle: what happens when a win contains a loss, a loss contains a win and the two collide? That’s the question posed by the confused and confusing outcome of this week’s Israeli election, one that, despite its murky uncertainty, offers clear, sharp lessons – both for that country and for those locked in combat with nationalist populists across the globe.Start with the result that has simultaneously handed Benjamin Netanyahu a devastating defeat and a strong chance of staying on as prime minister, extending a run that has seen him lead Israel, on and off, for more than 19 of the past 30 years. The defeat is clear enough. At a stroke, his parliamentary majority was wiped out. Before Tuesday, the parties that together comprised his ruling coalition controlled 68 of the Knesset’s 120 seats: that tallyhas now shrunk to just 53, far short of the 61 seats needed for power. That’s a loss in anybody’s language.And yet, Netanyahu does not look or sound like a man defeated. That’s because he knows that while the parties arrayed against him won many more seats than he did – 67 to his 53 – their chances of forming a government are slim. If they fail, one or two of them might peel away and enter a so-called national-unity government – under Netanyahu as PM – or there will have to be fresh elections, ones from which, most analysts agree, Netanyahu would emerge stronger.The opposition’s problem is not arithmetical. It goes much deeper. Put simply, a big chunk of the anti-Netanyahu seats were won by parties that chiefly represent the one in five Israeli citizens who are Palestinian. This was the big twist of Tuesday’s election, a huge surge in turnout for what Israelis refer to as the Arab parties. Usually, far more Jewish than Arab Israelis participate in the country’s elections, but this year that pattern was flipped:turnout in Palestinian communities inside Israel hit 80%. The result is a record total of 19 seats for Arab-led parties. The anti-Netanyahu bloc cannot form a government without them. In today’s Israel, Palestinian politicians are the kingmakers.On paper, the next step might look straightforward enough. All Netanyahu’s Jewish opponents need do is team up with their Arab colleagues and they can send the PM packing. But such an alliance would mark a watershed in Israeli history. It would mean breaking a taboo that has endured, with only fleeting exceptions, since the founding of the state, a taboo rooted in mutual suspicion.On the one hand, Israel’s Jewish-led parties have long shunned the mainly Arab parties because the latter identify as anti- or non-Zionist, meaning they reject Israel’s self-definition as a Jewish state. For that same reason, Arab-led parties have maintained a boycott, refusing to legitimate the Israeli state by participating in its government.In 2021, a short-lived “government of change” broke the taboo by including in its ranks Ra’am, an Islamist party regarded, improbably enough, as the most moderate of the Arab groupings. But after the Hamas massacres of 7 October 2023, the taboo was restored – and hardened. Netanyahu cast Palestinian-Israeli politicians as an enemy within, as tacit allies of the Hamas killers, a framing buttressed by a crude anti-Arab racism voiced most explicitly by his coalition allies – the likes of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – and which sought to delegitimise Israel’s entire Arab minority.This was Netanyahu’s core message throughout the campaign: you can’t trust my opponents because, when the moment comes, they will sit with “the Arabs”. In recent days, he and his allies have doubled down on that message, claiming high Palestinian turnout means that “the Arabs are stealing the election” – rather than merely exercising their democratic rights – and, on Thursday,alleging that Qatar paid Palestinian-Israeli citizens to vote, thereby rendering the entire result void.Instead of challenging Netanyahu’s framing, and insisting that the vote of every citizen, Arab or Jewish, is of equal worth, most of the main opposition parties –Yair Golan’s Democrats were the exception– bowed to it, pledging that they would not forge a coalition with the largely Arab parties, and certainly not with any group more radical than Ra’am. Now they find themselves in a bind. On their own, the Jewish-led opposition cannot form a government. Unless they somehow manage to lure defectors from Netanyahu’s bloc –perhaps one or both of the ultra-Orthodox parties– even Ra’am’s support won’t be enough to reach the magic number of 61. They need Arab partners – and probably several of them.This, then, is the big lesson for Israel. That group that has long opposed Netanyahu – Jewish-Israelis who despise a PM on trial for corruption, who has mounted serial assaults on Israel’s institutions, including the supreme court, and brought isolation, if not pariah status, upon the country – are now confronted with a fact that has long been true but which they have preferred not to see: that they are a minority in the land they once dominated. As Aluf Benn, editor of the liberal daily Haaretz, told me: “The Jewish vote is predominantly rightwing in Israel and has been for decades.”That means the Jewish Israeli opposition cannot win alone. This week stands as proof, because this was their perfect opportunity. Netanyahu was at his lowest ebb, the leader on whose watch the most calamitous day in Israeli history took place, the leader who promised to destroy Hamas in Gaza, but who succeeded only in turning that place into a ruin, killing tens of thousands and, in the process, destroying Israel’s standing in the world. He faced in Gadi Eisenkot, his lead challenger, a decorated former general rooted in the Mizrahi working class, a man universally regarded as honest and decent, a bereaved father whose own son fell in the Gaza war – a man, in other words, who might have been designed to appeal to the very voters who for so long have been beyond the opposition’s reach. And yet none of that was enough to win.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe only way the opposition can succeed is by making common cause with their Palestinian fellow citizens, just as Democrats in the US –who have not won a majority of the white vote since 1964– could never win the presidency without the support of Black Americans. No one should underestimate the scale of the task, which requires a deep cultural shift as much as a political one. It should have been the work of decades, rather than a panicked scramble in a few rushed weeks of coalition horse-trading. It demands a reshaping of Israeli society, breaking a pattern of systemic discrimination and inequality within the country that has existed since the founding of the state (to say nothing of the post-1967 occupied territories where, of course, millions of Palestinians have no vote at all in Israeli elections). That task was always essential, but this week has confirmed that, if the right’s lock on power is ever to be broken, it can be delayed no longer.Much of this is peculiar to the unique political terrain of Israel. But there are broader lessons for all those fighting nationalist populism, whether that be Donald Trump innext week’s US midterms, Marine Le Pen in France or Nigel Farage in Britain. First, don’t accept the terms laid down by the other side: that was the cardinal error made by Netanyahu’s challengers. Second, mere opposition and criticism is not enough. The nationalist populists will always tell a compelling story; you have to tell an equally compelling one of your own. And, last, you need to be every bit as determined as they are. Too often you play by gentlemen’s rules, when those you are fighting are anything but gentlemen. Netanyahu is without shame and will do anything – cross every line, cut any deal – to keep power. The opponents of such a man will prevail only if they show an equal resolve in seizing it.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael-Gaza warcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Dumplings are the ultimate proof of our common humanity | Joseph de Weck | The Guardian
description: Across nations and classes, there is one thing we can all agree on – that putting delicious things inside dough is a good idea, says writer Joseph de Weck
Author: Joseph de Weck
Headline: Across nations and classes, there is one thing we can all agree on – that putting delicious things inside dough is a good idea, says writer Joseph de Weck
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onComfort foodThe hill I will die on: Dumplings are the ultimate proof of our common humanityJoseph de WeckAcross nations and classes, there is one thing we can all agree on – that putting delicious things inside dough is a good ideaFri 30 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTShareOn a recent Saturday morning in Paris, I made a life-changing discovery. It came in the frozen aisle of an Asian supermarket: you can buy premade dumpling wrappers. Take a moment to think about the implications of this. Chinese shrimp wontons? Ukrainian potato varenyky? Italian veal ravioli? You’re halfway there before you’ve even chopped an onion (as long as you’re not precious about usingexactlythe right dough for each recipe).Since then, I’ve fallen into a full-blown dumpling rabbit hole, my nights spent on YouTube, watching grandmothers sitting in circles, pinching dough. So many shapes. So many techniques. Team inward pleats or outward?Columbia University Press has just publishedThe Epic History of Macaroni and Cheese: From Ancient Rome to Modern America. But clearly someone should also write The Long Arc of Putting Things in Dough: A Transcultural History. Because what does it say about humanity that all around the globe, at various points in history, people have invented some version ofadelicious thing wrapped in dough?Perhaps we all secretly long to be dumplings; there is certainly something reassuring about being enclosed. The French philosopher Claire Marin calls this a nostalgia for our “lost envelopment” – a longing to return to that primordial experience of being fully embraced in the womb.Indeed, how fortunate is a filling’s existence: held, knowing it is exactly where it belongs. Desired, yet protected. And entirely individual, but never alone; dumplings are herd beings. Plus, they’re cute. So much so thatsquishy mystery dumplingshave become the latest trend toy. The Labubu is so 2025.Perhaps we need to go back to the stone age to understand the worldwide dumpling craze.In her 1986 essayThe Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction, the American novelist Ursula K Le Guin suggested that our narrative of human history may be badly skewed. We picture early humans as men chasing bison. Yet the first human tool may have been a basket, not a spear. Gathering probably provided most of the calories; hunting was more often a hobby to kill time. And the fact that we say “hunter-gatherers” rather than “gatherer-hunters” is probably another vestige of the patriarchy.“It is a human thing to do,” Le Guin writes, “to put something you want, because it’s useful, edible or beautiful, into a bag … and then take it home with you.”Dumplings, those lovely edible containers, take this human instinct and make it culinary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Comedians should not be hot | Amy AnnetteRead moreWhatever the reasons for the dumpling’s global triumph, it fills me with hope. Every time I eat Afghan mantu, Argentinian empanadas or Austrian kasnudeln, I feel that these little envelopes are trying to teach me a small lesson in universalism.Forget the clash of civilisations. Dumplings, whether you like them or not, are the ultimate proof of our common humanity.Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zürich and ParisExplore more on these topicsComfort foodThe hill I will die onChinese food and drinkFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: Opening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do it | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address it, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: Andy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address it, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: A pro-EU demonstration outside the Houses of Parliament, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA pro-EU demonstration outside the Houses of Parliament, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOpinionBrexitOpening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do itSimon JenkinsAndy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address itFri 30 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTShareAndy Burnham’sopening debateon whether Britain should rejoin the EU is divisive, painful and politically risky. That is why it should be welcomed. To jeopardise his popularity so soon after coming to office might seem reckless, but the issue is urgent and not going away. Brexit is continuing to damage the nation’s economy. The prime minister’s job is to challenge, if not reform it.The Brexit decade has evoked a bizarre sense of guilt among Britons.Opinion pollsshow nearly 60% regard it as a mistake, with just a third still in favour. Almost a quarter of those who voted for Brexit now regret it. While early forecasts of economic disaster wereproved wrong, the accumulated cost of cutting links with Britain’s biggest trading partner is estimated at6-8% of GDP.This is huge. It must rank as the greatest act of self-harm by a British government in modern times.A year ago Keir Starmer began to ease some of the barriers, with modest deals on youth exchange and meat exports. Burnham wants to take this further, with negotiations resuming in Brussels next month. Yesterday in the Commons he cited damage tothe car industry, while agriculture remains mired in dozens of pages of regulation.Fish rotsin inspection sheds, and cars and passengers queue for hours at borders.Yet if something must be done, the question remains: what? Burnham emphasises that he would not renege on Labour’s 2024 election pledge tohonour the referendumin this parliament. But he certainly wants a revival of the debate and has a personal hope to see Brexit reversed one day. For now he seeks “an honest discussion … an open conversation” on where future negotiations might lead. He murmured the possibility of free movement of people for EU passport holders. The subject’s delicacy was demonstrated as Westminster Brexiters reacted like scalded cats.“Betrayal … catastrophe”, cried Reform UK’s Nigel Farage.A reason for Burnham to proceed cautiously is that the public’s regret overBrexitis not matched by agreement on what should take its place. While 55% of all Britons would support rejoining the EU, that falls to 35% if the condition is surrendering the UK’s previous opt-outs – which would mean joining the euro and participating in the Schengen passport-free travel zone.There could be a middle-ground Brexit model, including a bespoke place for Britain within a wider European economic area. But this in turn might be unacceptable to some existing EU countries. An alternative could include membership of the European Free Trade Association or a customs union.The truth is Britain has always been ambivalent in its attitude to European unions. Ireland and Denmark had in the past reversed anti-EU referendums by negotiating opt-outs with Brussels. David Cameron attempted no such remedy in 2016. He simply resigned.During the post-referendum Commons debates it was clear that many MPs would have favoured a “soft Brexit” option, its form as yet unclear. A responsible parliament at the time might have formed a coalition to pursue such an option. As it was, Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party preferred to exploit Theresa May’s internal divisions and leave the way open for Boris Johnson and his “hard Brexiters”. Manning Westminster’s party barricades took precedence over seeking a sensible compromise with Brussels.Burnham must therefore tread with care. Westminster’s political culture slithers instinctively into conflict mode without thought for the message that this sends to the outside world. Plenty of Europeans remain sceptical of whether Britain truly wants to rejoin the EU, and will resist any demand for extensive opt-outs or concessions. But that is for another day. For now, Labour is committed to honour its referendum manifesto promise.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham is right to open the conversation. But he must first detoxify Brexit and diminish its prominence – and that of the party whose existence depends on it, Reform. For the time being, as there is no question of rejoining the EU, there is no issue of British sovereignty. The negotiations should be boring, over regulations, conventions and protocols. These would inevitably involve compromise – but compromise that ensures both parties come away with something gained.One solution would be to do what was not done after 2016: establish a strong cross-party Commons committee to monitor the November talks and take Burnham’s conversation forward. This should concentrate on reducing barriers to trade and growth, and promoting cultural and security relations with Europe. To put it mildly, Europe needs such concentration, and badly. On that, surely Westminster can agree.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionForeign policyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: We must protect Jewish Australians without casting suspicion on legitimate concern for Palestinians | George Newhouse | The Guardian
description: There is much in Jillian Segal’s report that deserves support. But sincere humanitarian concern and susceptibility to antisemitism are not the same things
Author: George Newhouse
Headline: There is much in Jillian Segal’s report that deserves support. But sincere humanitarian concern and susceptibility to antisemitism are not the same things
Content: ‘Criticism of Israel can cross into antisemitism, and vigilance is essential’, writes George Newhouse. ‘But distinguishing prejudice from legitimate political criticism … is equally important.’Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreen‘Criticism of Israel can cross into antisemitism, and vigilance is essential’, writes George Newhouse. ‘But distinguishing prejudice from legitimate political criticism … is equally important.’Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPOpinionAntisemitismWe must protect Jewish Australians without casting suspicion on legitimate concern for PalestiniansGeorge NewhouseThere is much in Jillian Segal’s report that deserves support. But sincere humanitarian concern and susceptibility to antisemitism are not the same thingsAntisemitism envoy proposes ‘external ombudsman’ to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of Israel and Middle EastFri 30 Oct 2026 01.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 02.17 EDTShareThe antisemitic massacre at Bondi exposed a terrifying truth: that Jewish Australians can no longer take their safety for granted. The doxing, cancellation, threats and vilification of Jewish artists, lawyers, doctors, nurses, patients and academics since October 2023 have been virulent and traumatising for many Jews. Combating hatred, intimidation and violence against Jewish Australians is an urgent national responsibility.That makes thereport from Australia’s special envoy to combat antisemitism, Jillian Segal, an important intervention. But a strategy motivated by legitimate fears can still risk making the problem harder to solve.Antisemitism envoy proposes ‘external ombudsman’ to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of Israel and Middle EastRead moreSegal identifies antisemitism on the far right, among Islamist extremists and on the radical left. She goes on to describe “modern, progressive antisemitism” as its most pervasive manifestation in Australia, arguing that extremist ideas gain respectability through the language of human rights and social justice.Antisemitism can certainly masquerade as anti-Zionism. Jewish Australians must never be held responsible for the actions of Israel’s government. Conspiracy theories about Jewish power, harassment and threats against Jewish people or institutions are indefensible.Some extremists may exploit concern for Palestinian human rights to promote antisemitism, and I acknowledge that some institutions have become hostile environments for Jewish people. But to suggest that concern for human rights is being exploited by radical activists as a “gateway” to draw well-meaning Australians towards anti-Jewish propaganda strikes me as too simplistic.Segal’s analysis gives insufficient weight to another explanation. Many mainstream Australians are genuinely distressed by the suffering of civilians in Gaza and attacks on Palestinian communities in the West Bank. Their concerns are often shared byIsraelis who protest their own government’s policiesin harsh terms. These reactions arise from what people have witnessed and their sense of injustice, not necessarily from extremist influence or manipulation.Nor should the language of human rights be treated with suspicion. Allegations of war crimes, collective punishment, discrimination, ethnic cleansing or worse raise serious questions of international law that must remain open to evidence, debate and scrutiny.Criticism ofIsraelcan cross into antisemitism, and vigilance is essential. But distinguishing prejudice from legitimate political criticism, as Segal herself acknowledges, is equally important.That distinction is important when considering her recommendations for stronger institutional regulation and restrictions affecting protest. Threats, intimidation, hate and unlawful vilification must be confronted, and existing laws must be effectively enforced. But any additional restrictions on political expression must be demonstrably necessary, proportionate and consistent with democratic freedoms.There is much in Segal’s report that deserves support. Jewish Australians should feel safe and welcome in workplaces, universities, hospitals, cultural institutions and in public life. Protecting them from discrimination, harassment and violence should unite Australians across political divisions.But sincere humanitarian concern and susceptibility to antisemitic narratives are not the same, even where they may overlap. Confusing them risks misunderstanding the motivations of ordinary Australians and alienating potential allies in confronting antisemitism.A successful national response must protect Jewish Australians without casting suspicion on legitimate concern for Palestinians. It should uphold human rights consistently, defend freedom of expression and confront prejudice wherever it appears.The strongest answer to antisemitism is not to narrow the space for disagreement, but to build a shared commitment to human dignity, equality and freedom from hatred and violence.George Newhouse AM is a human rights lawyer and former mayor of Waverley council in SydneyExplore more on these topicsAntisemitismOpinionHuman rightsIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: Could 2026 be the year that democracy fought back? | David Van Reybrouck | The Guardian
description: Elections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark times, says Belgian author and philosopher David Van Reybrouck
Author: David Van Reybrouck
Headline: Elections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark times, says Belgian author and philosopher David Van Reybrouck
Content: Supporters of Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrate in Rio de Janeiro, 25 October 2026.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAView image in fullscreenSupporters of Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrate in Rio de Janeiro, 25 October 2026.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAOpinionSerbiaCould 2026 be the year that democracy fought back?David Van ReybrouckElections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark timesFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTShareIt is undoubtedly too early to declare victory, but the recent electoral defeats ofViktor Orbán,Aleksandar VučićandFlávio Bolsonaromake me wonder: is 2026 turning out to be the year democracy slowly, but surely, fought back?Even inIsrael, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reigning bloc lost its parliamentary majority and saw the spectacular rise of Arab parties. Though the opposition may not be able to form a government yet, it does have the larger parliamentary bloc.The shift began with an astonishing election result in Hungary in April. Against all odds, Orbán, the EU’s most deeply entrenched autocrat, was unseated by challengerPéter Magyar. Over his long years in office, Orbán had done everything possible to consolidate and perpetuate his authoritarian grip on power. The media were in his pocket, the judiciary ate from his hand and academic freedom was systematically curtailed. Yet a broad civic movement coalesced around Magyar’s party and succeeded in ousting him. The banks of the Danube witnessed theirmost exuberant night of celebrationthis century.Joy wasequally palpablelast Sunday night, 300km down the river in Belgrade. There in Serbia, the Student List, a bottom-up alliance of students, academics and angry citizens, unexpectedly sent Vučić packing. Vučić had held a tight grip on power since 2014, first as prime minister, then president, relying on a familiar cocktail of far-right bravado,financial scandalsand contempt for the rule of law: the winning formula of recent years. But there seems to be a limit to what citizens are ready to accept. Vučić’s fate was sealed after the newly constructed roof canopy of theNovi Sad train station collapsed in 2024, killing 16 people and triggering widespread public fury against systemic corruption.Then came the biggest news of all on Monday morning, whenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvadefied expectations to emerge victorious in Brazil’s presidential election. In the first round, Flávio Bolsonaro had been in the lead, and almost every poll predicted he would win the run-off. Many Brazilians braced themselves for an administration at least as radical-right as his father’s. Instead, Lula, the son of poor, illiterate farmers and a former factory worker himself, surprised friend and foe alike by winning the presidency of Latin America’s largest economy for the fourth time.Commentators were quick to point out that Lula’s victory halted a winning streak for rightwing populists across Latin America. That is certainly true, but zooming out reveals a broader pattern. This is not primarily a story of left v right, but rather of democrats v post-democrats. Hungary’s Magyar is by no means a leftist; he is a centre-right leader who was once a member of Orbán’s own party. In Serbia, the Student List washeaded by Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist and university professor with no pronounced ideological profile. While he champions liberal values such as press freedom and the rule of law, his stance on Kosovo aligns with traditional Serbian nationalism: it should not be independent.What Magyar, Srdanović and Lula share – despite significant political differences – is a fundamental belief that the rules of the democratic game must be respected. Elections must be fair, judges and journalists must work independently, and checks and balances exist for a reason.Post-democrats, by contrast, treat laws and international agreements as mere suggestions, a convenient menu of policy options from which they can cherrypick. They use elections to gain power, only to hollow out democratic institutions once they are in office and maximise their private business profits. As corruption is key, they have to remain in power to stay out of jail. Opposing voices must be muzzled and critical media prosecuted. Post-democrats only keep the outer shell of democracy. Bolsonaro Jr took a page fromDonald Trump’s playbook: election results are declared unimpeachable when he wins, andrigged when he loses. Similarly, Netanyahu is now attempting to discredit the Israeli election outcome, by suggesting Qatar interfered on behalf of the Palestinian parties.Post-democrats have been on the rise for years, and it is terrifying. Since 2000, we have witnessed a steady, deliberate dismantling of democratic achievements across every continent. Anyone reading the latest internationalDemocracy Report, produced by the V-Dem Institute, could easily despair. In terms of overall democratic health, it finds that we have effectively regressed to the levels of 1978. Only 7% of the world’s population live in liberal democracies.Yet after years of alarming headlines about global democratic backsliding, the news from Budapest, Belgrade and Brasília offers rays of hope in dark times. So does the massive wave of Gen Z protests this year, from India and the Philippines to Albania, Argentina and Chile. Huge crowds of young people have taken to the streets to challenge autocratic power and corruption in their countries.Could liberal democracy be finding its second wind? Is it actually possible to defeat autocrats and authoritarian regimes after all? Could this mark the beginning of a democratic revival that might extend to the US next week? Most polls suggest that the Democrats stand a strong chance of reclaiming at least the House of Representatives in the upcoming US midterms.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, thedelegitimisation of Arab votersin Israel this week reminds us of the limitations of change via the ballot box. Elections can help us get rid of post-democrats, but in deeply divided societies they are not enough to heal. The individual, silent act of voting must be complemented with collective processes of deliberation.Nonetheless, globally, 2026 may come to rank as the best year for democracy in more than a quarter of a century. Could this be the turning point?What this tells usahead of critical electionsin some of the EU’s largest member states in the year ahead – France, Spain, Germany and Poland – remains anyone’s guess. Looking at the momentum of the AfD in Germany, rightwing populist parties with post-democratic tendencies remain very much alive in Europe. AndVox could be part of a People’s party-led governmentin Spain in a matter of weeks. But Hungary, Serbia and Brazil have delivered a vital reminder: the rise of autocratsand their permanence in power are not immutable laws of nature. Soon enough, post-democracies may start to feel passé.David Van Reybrouck is a Belgian author and philosopher laureate for the Low Countries. He is the author of Against Elections: The Case for Democracy, and the initiator ofDemocracy27Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaOpinionBrazilHungaryProtestLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroViktor OrbáncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Patrick Stewart brought virile star power to the stage, from clowns to kings to wounded lions’ | Stage | The Guardian
description: With his striking voice, so rich and resonant, the actor blazed through the RSC – and his time in Hollywood only enriched him. Yet he was a great team player, capable of anything, as his double acts with Ian McKellen showed
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: With his striking voice, so rich and resonant, the actor blazed through the RSC – and his time in Hollywood only enriched him. Yet he was a great team player, capable of anything, as his double acts with Ian McKellen showed
Content: ‘The best since Michael Redgrave’ … Patrick Stewart as Mark Antony in Antony and Cleopatra at the Swan theatre, Stratford, in 2006.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The best since Michael Redgrave’ … Patrick Stewart as Mark Antony in Antony and Cleopatra at the Swan theatre, Stratford, in 2006.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStage‘Patrick Stewart brought virile star power to the stage, from clowns to kings to wounded lions’With his striking voice, so rich and resonant, the actor blazed through the RSC – and his time in Hollywood only enriched him. Yet he was a great team player, capable of anything, as his double acts with Ian McKellen showedMichael BillingtonFri 30 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 15.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Stewart, who has died aged 86, was a classic example of the company actor who becomes a star: a natural Enobarbus who winds up playing Mark Antony. It would be easy to say that he had fame thrust upon him through his roles in Star Trek and X-Men, but I would argue that it was a two-way process.As Peter Bradshaw points out, Stewart brought his RSC-trained gravitas to the screen, but his roles in popular franchises gave him an extra layer of confidence and authority on stage. He became, in short, an even more powerful actor.I felt a particular fascination with Stewart’s career, since he was in the first play I ever reviewed for a national paper. He was Warwick in George Bernard Shaw’s Saint Joan at the Bristol Old Vic in May 1965 and I was instantly struck by his rich, resonant voice. Once he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966, I followed his progress eagerly. He seemed the perfect team player, capable of anything: Shakespearean clowns such as Touchstone in As You Like It and Launce in The Two Gentlemen of Verona, or more muscular figures such as Cornwall in King Lear and Hector in Troilus and Cressida.But it was one particular season in 1971-72 that convinced me he had star power. He began by playing a ruthless Bulgarian communist in Trevor Griffiths’s terrific political drama,Occupations (a work overdue for revival). Then he played pivotal roles in Trevor Nunn’s four-play Stratford season, The Romans. He was a virile, grim-visaged Aufidius in Coriolanus. He followed that as a volatile, unstable Cassius in Julius Caesar, seething at the arrogant idealism of John Wood’s Brutus. In Antony and Cleopatra, his Enobarbus was a grizzled old sweat, and he took over as the murderous Aaron in Titus Andronicus when the whole cycle moved to London.9:59Shakespeare to Star Trek: Patrick Stewart’s extraordinary life - The LatestStewart’s career at the RSC went from strength to strength – he was Astrov in Uncle Vanya and Ejlert Løvborg in Hedda Gabler – but there was always another side to his life. Having profited from the tuition of the RSC’s great verse-speaking guru, John Barton, he became passionate about passing on what he had learned. It started with his talking to US students in London each year, a study group led by a Shakespearean devotee calledHomer “Murph” Swanderto whom, as I saw when I once joined them, he was visibly devoted.This developed into Stewart becoming a key figure in Actors in Residence, which toured American colleges performing Shakespeare. Eventually, this missionary work changed his life. One day in 1986, Stewart was lecturing and acting in LA, and in the audience was a producer, Robert H Justman, who was involved in a revival of Star Trek. Listening to Stewart, he turned to his wife and said: “We’ve found our captain.”View image in fullscreenStewart as Claudius and David Tennant as Hamlet, at the Courtyard theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, in 2008.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStewart first signed up for six years on Star Trek and there were English colleagues who thought he was crazy to abandon theatre. But I would argue that Stewart’s time in Hollywood, which included his role as Professor X in X-Men, enriched him personally and professionally. You could see the benefits when he returned to the British stage. In 2006, he was back with the RSC in Gregory Doran’s production of Antony and Cleopatra, playing opposite Harriet Walter; the following year,I wrote thathe was the best Mark Antony since Michael Redgrave. He gave us a magnificently wounded lion haunted by the memory that he had once been king of the jungle.That capacity to remind us of a Shakespearean character’s self-awareness was also apparent in a stunning performance of Macbeth in a Rupert Goold production first at Chichester in 2007 andthen in the West End. Stewart’s Macbeth had all the paranoia that accompanies power but, very much like Olivier before him, he allowed his voice to soar in agony when describing the “troops of friends” that he would never live to enjoy. A year later, Stewart was back with the RSC playing Claudius to David Tennant’s Hamlet in another Gregory Doran production. Instead of the usual stage villain, Stewart’s Claudius was a composed, calculating killer. The great moment came at the end of the play scene when, instead of rising in panic, Stewart strode over to Hamlet and pityingly shook his head as if to say: “You’ve really blown it now.”View image in fullscreenStewart plays Vladimir – opposite Ian McKellen as Estragon – in Waiting for Godot at the Theatre Royal Haymarket, in 2009.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAfter X-Men, Stewart formed a close bond with his co-star, Ian McKellen: both northerners with a Shakespearean hinterland. I wasn’t as wild as everyone else about their performances inWaiting for Godot, partly because I disliked their performing an old Flanagan and Allen number at curtain-call. But they were both superb in a West End revival ofPinter’s No Man’s Land. While McKellen caught perfectly the chattering anxiety and desperate desire to please of Spooner, the pub-poet, Stewart – as the famous writer, Hirst – exuded an infinite weariness and desperate isolation as he drank himself into oblivion. Coming from opposite sides of the Pennines, the two actors even allowed their voices to blend in a musical harmony that is essential to Pinter. Having followed Stewart’s career from its beginnings, I was delighted to see him relishing the star status he had so justly earned.Explore more on these topicsStagePatrick StewartfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: To baldly go: Patrick Stewart was an icon for bald men everywhere | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: The actor was an exemplary bald, unapologetically embracing his hairloss and setting the scalp-based bar for all other men with receding hairlines
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The actor was an exemplary bald, unapologetically embracing his hairloss and setting the scalp-based bar for all other men with receding hairlines
Content: Undeniable sex appeal … Patrick Stewart as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: Insurrection (1998).Photograph: Paramount Pictures/Elliott Marks/AllstarView image in fullscreenUndeniable sex appeal … Patrick Stewart as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: Insurrection (1998).Photograph: Paramount Pictures/Elliott Marks/AllstarPatrick StewartTo baldly go: Patrick Stewart was an icon for bald men everywhereStuart HeritageThe actor was an exemplary bald star, embracing his hair loss and the freedoms it brought. He didn’t go grey or recede – and he didn’t wear a wig like William Shatner as Captain KirkPatrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.29 EDTSharePatrick Stewart managed to be lots of different things at once. He was a towering figure on stage. He was a literal superhero onscreen. And, at times, he wasn’t above sending himself up. It also needs to be said that he was a bald man.And a pioneering one at that. Nowhere was this more clear than during his stint on Star Trek: The Next Generation. Previously, Star Trek had been a kind of space-set action show, where the relentlessly virile Captain Kirk would beam down to new planets to either punch or get off with all the aliens there. But then came its successor, and Kirk was replaced by a nonviolent intellectual called Jean-Luc. Worse still, he didn’t have any hair. What a sign of weakness.View image in fullscreenThe captains … Stewart and Shatner in Star Trek: Generations (1994).Photograph: Paramount/AllstarBut Patrick Stewart made it work. Not only was his cool temperament a nice change of pace from the 1960s take, but his sex appeal was undeniable. Indeed, in 1992 TV Guide readers voted him television’s “most bodacious” man. Stewart received 54% of the vote, putting him ahead of much hairier contenders including Luke Perry and Burt Reynolds.Not that he didn’t have his critics. When Picard’s casting was announced to the world, it is said that a reporter complained to Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry that it didn’t make any sense. After all, the show was set in a future where space travel and teleportation were accepted as the norm, so wouldn’t it stand to reason that humanity would have created a cure for male pattern baldness? According to Stewart, Roddenberry’s response was that, by the 24th century, humanity will have evolved to the point where it no longer cares about baldness.Stewart lost his hair in his teens, and was open about the effect this had on his psyche, telling Rolling Stone that he was so worried about how baldness might affect his love life that he spent more than he could afford on a wig. However, by ditching the hairpiece, Stewart became an icon for the bald.When you lose your hair, you begin casting around for other bald men, because in a small way this helps normalise it. Stewart found himself a magnet for this, telling The New Yorker in 2023, “How many times have I been spoken to in the street by somebody who would pull off his cap, revealing a bald head, and say, ‘You saved my life!’”Again, this is because Stewart was an exemplary bald. So often when men go bald they end up overcompensating by inflating themselves to preemptively ward off negative comments. Look at The Rock, and how much more aggressively he bulked out after he lost his hair. Look at Jeff Bezos, who reacted to baldness by pumping iron and building willy-shaped space rockets. Now compare this to Stewart, who pointed towards a different path of culture and elegance and refinement, embracing his baldness without ever apologising for it.More than anything, though, you just have to look at the reactions to his death to see the real legacy of Patrick Stewart’s baldness. People were generally staggered to learn that he was 86 years old. This is because, as all bald people know, losing your hair ages you, but only temporarily. He was 47 years old when Star Trek: The Next Generation premiered in 1987, but he arguably looked a decade older than that. But then he carried on looking that age for decades afterwards. He didn’t go grey, or recede, or adopt an unflattering dye job, or any of the other things that makes men look old, because he didn’t have any hair. And unlike Captain Kirk, he never worea high-end hairpiece. Patrick Stewart played the long game, and he won. O captain, my captain.Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartcommentShareReuse this content
