title: ‘It really was the idiots in charge’: inside the TV sketch show that launched a generation of stars | Television | The Guardian
description: It influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its due
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its due
Content: Astonishingly talented cast … back row, L-R: Catherine O’Hara, Joe Flaherty, John Candy, Dave Thomas and Harold Ramis. Front row, Andrea Martin and Eugene Levy.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenAstonishingly talented cast … back row, L-R: Catherine O’Hara, Joe Flaherty, John Candy, Dave Thomas and Harold Ramis. Front row, Andrea Martin and Eugene Levy.Photograph: NetflixTelevision‘It really was the idiots in charge’: inside the TV sketch show that launched a generation of starsIt influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its dueDale ShawFri 30 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSCTV – short for Second CityTelevision– is one of most influential comedy shows ever created. In the 1970s and 80s, while North American comedy fans worshipped at the altar of Saturday Night Live, the comedy nerds loved SCTV. The Canadian sketch show was weird. It was dark. It was multilayered and years ahead of its time.Dave Thomas, head writer and an original cast member, was there from the start. “Conan O’Brien said that he used to watch and he thought, ‘This show is being written specifically for me,’” Thomas tells me. “There were references in it that he was absolutely sure only he got. We wrote at the top of our reference level. And the idea was to see if the audience would meet us there.”Thomas was part of an astonishingly talented cast that included John Candy,Eugene Levy,Catherine O’Hara, Rick Moranis, Joe Flaherty, Martin Short, Harold Ramis and Andrea Martin. They wrote and starred in the series, which ran intermittently in Canada from 1976 to 1984. At a time when American shows dominated the airwaves, and homegrown content tended to be earnest factual programmes along the lines ofHinterland Who’s Who, Canadian audiences were delighted to see a show that reflected their culture while being – to everyone’s surprise – actually funny. It even went on tofind a late-night audience in the US.View image in fullscreenFormer cast members Catherine O’Hara (left) and Andrea Martin in SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of.Photograph: NetflixTo celebrate its legacy, Netflix has just added 134 episodes of SCTV to coincide with its release of a new documentary – SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of. Like many of the show’s fans, Thomas isn’t exactly enamoured with the title.“Yeah, the title is kind of insulting in a way,” he says.That’s not the only problem. While it’s a decent primer for revisiting the show, featuring new interviews with the surviving cast members, including Thomas, the documentary could have been so much more. Many things are skipped over, such as the musical acts, including bands like the Boomtown Rats and the Plasmatics, who didn’t just perform but also appeared in sketches. And while the cast took care of the writing in the show’s early days, they were later joined by talented staff. These omissions rankle with Thomas.“Tom Hanks and Bob Odenkirk doing the narrative on how it was written? I thought, what the fuck? Why don’t you ask some of the people who wrote it? We had some really good writers on that show.”SCTV’s Leave It to Beaver parodyThere is a cracking story to be told. For the uninitiated: the cast of Chicago’s legendary Second City improv theatre had already been plundered by producer Lorne Michaels to create Saturday Night Live in 1975. It seemed to make perfect sense to use Second City’sTorontooutpost to create a Canadian version of SNL. Gilda Radner and Dan Aykroyd had already been poached by Michaels, so the remaining cast members were asked to make a television sketch show without knowing the first thing about it.“For the first two seasons, SCTV was a failure,” Thomas remembers. “It was the poor brother of SNL. Our greatest weakness was that our show looked cheap as shit. So we made it about a small television station, and that’s why it looks so cheap.”Each episode of SCTV covered one broadcast day for a run-down TV station in the fictional rural Canadian town of Melonville. As well as parodying the film and TV of the time, the backstage dramas of the station also played a part.“We were learning,” Thomas tells me. “We were being paid to learn how to produce television while doing it. It really was the idiots running the asylum for the first two years. There are a lot of things we got credit for that were just horrible mistakes.”View image in fullscreenJohn Candy, who would later go on to star in Planes, Trains and Automobiles with Steve Martin.Photograph: NetflixThe naivety of the cast and the low budget, paradoxically, freed up the sketch-writers: without shiny sets and special effects, they focused on characters. There was the overbearing station managerGuy Caballero, the cheapskate’s cheapskate; the garrulous variety starJohnny LaRue, who was an extension of John Candy’s party-loving nature; Catherine O’Hara’s showgirlLola Heatherton; Eugene Levy’s appalling standup,Bobby Bittman; and Harry, the Guy With a Snake on his Face. Sketches were smart, sharp and featured startlingly accurate impressions (Thomas’s Bob Hopewas a standout).As time went on, the show found its feet, started gaining an audience, increased its budget and grew more sophisticated.“I was particularly proud of the evolution of the comedy,” Thomas remembers. “Like the parody of the television show Fantasy Island, which was also a parody of Casablanca, and also a parody of Road to Morocco, and also a parody of The Wizard of Oz, all weaved in and out. A lot of the Simpsons writers said that’s what they loved about SCTV, that it brought in a kind of a multilayered writing. And they said: that’s the way we write The Simpsons.”But as the money came in, the creators’ freedom dwindled. Used to having everything their own way, the cast and writers baulked when threatened with any outside interference.“I remember one of the producers that NBC had sent up was in the cafeteria one morning, crying,” recalls Thomas. “I said, ‘What’s the matter?’ He goes, ‘The goddamn cast, they shut me out. They stonewall me. I’ve got a good mind to quit.’ And I said, ‘Well, you probably should quit because you’re here in the cafeteria, crying. Is that what you had in mind when you got into showbiz?’”View image in fullscreen‘We thought, screw this press conference, let’s go to Studio 54!’ … Dave Thomas.Photograph: NetflixBeing produced in isolation gave SCTV a distinct personality and a legion of devoted fans. But the team were still very much on the outside.“We went to New York for a press conference,” Thomas says. “There were only three people there and two of them were student journalists. But we thought, well, screw this press conference, let’s go to Studio 54. We’re on television. We should be able to get in. They wouldn’t let us in.”Thomas and Rick Moranis (later to star in Ghostbusters, with Harold Ramis, and Honey, I Shrunk the Kids) were part of SCTV’s most surprising breakout success. Asked to include more specifically Canadian content in the series, they improvised two-minute pieces to camera featuring two dim-witted, beer-swilling, hockey-watching Canucks, Bob and Doug McKenzie. The characters caught on: Canadians, so used to watching American stereotypes played for laughs on TV, loved seeing two of their own get the same treatment. The documentary shows Beatles-like levels of hysteria at McKenzie brother appearances. They went on to record albums and make a film.Not everyone in the cast was delighted by all this, as Thomas admits. “There’s no question that the success of the McKenzie brothers was a divisive factor and played a role in Rick and I leaving. There were little things like that which definitely sowed some seeds of division, but we were still family.”The show shifted networks, time slots and cast members until it eventually fizzled out in 1984. But the SCTV family went on to greater heights. John Candy became a Hollywood star. Eugene Levy and Catherine O’Hara featured in many of Christopher Guest’s comedies (including Best in Show and A Mighty Wind), as well as starring in Schitt’s Creek together. Martin Short is, well, Martin Short.And Thomas has a wildly varied career: he starred in the sitcom Grace Under Fire, wrote Spies Like Us with Dan Aykroyd, started an animation company and is now developing an Amazon show with his son. But Thomas will always be fiercely proud of his SCTV achievements.“I loved that show because, I thought, nobody’s doing this. Nobody is doing a show like this. There was a network tendency to dumb everything down to the stupidest person in the room. And we didn’t do that.”SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of streams on Netflix from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionCanadaTV comedyTorontoCatherine O'HarafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sky-high ratings – for a lacklustre series: The Celebrity Traitors has become too nice for its own good | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Too many recruitments, frustrating confessions and an underwhelming murder in plain sight … this series has failed to take off
Author: Louis Staples
Headline: Too many recruitments, frustrating confessions and an underwhelming murder in plain sight … this series has failed to take off
Content: At the round table … James Acaster.Photograph: Euan Cherry/PAView image in fullscreenAt the round table … James Acaster.Photograph: Euan Cherry/PAThe TraitorsSky-high ratings – for a lacklustre series: The Celebrity Traitors has become too nice for its own goodToo many recruitments, frustrating confessions and an underwhelming murder in plain sight … this series has failed to take offLouis StaplesFri 30 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis article contains spoilers for theepisode of The Celebrity Traitors on 29 October. Do not read on if you have not seen it.What happens when a game that revolves around secrets and lies gets derailed by the truth? That’s what played out last night in the penultimate episode of The Celebrity Traitors, when – spoilers ahead! –James Acasterwas dramatically confronted at the round table about his role in murdering Ross Kemp. After being grilled by Michael Sheen in a soliloquy that felt borderline Shakespearean, Acaster did something we have never seen before on this show: he fessed up to the entire thing, falling on his sword and revealing his true identity.Acaster’s reveal is one of the defining scenes in a series that has broken the show’s sky-high ratings records. Yet watching the episode – and this celebrity series as a whole – I can’t shake the feeling that it’s been underwhelming. The grand finale could provide some big twists, but the show so far has felt tentative and lacked a certain spark. If Acaster’s confession had happened last year, it would have been merely a blip. But here, it feels emblematic of a series that, no matter what happens in the final, hasn’t quite lived up to the hype.The selection of the Traitors is one of the most important parts of the game because these players have an outsized influence on its direction and, as a result, often take up more airtime. They also become the unofficial narrators of the show as they are the only ones who know what is really going on.Part of the reason this series has felt lacklustre is because most of the Traitors were selected by the Traitors themselves, rather than producers who make a living from creating addictive TV. It all started with Richard E Grant’s epic blunder in episode one, when he told Joe Lycett that he was a Traitor and was quickly banished from the game. Not only did this deprive the audience of watching Grant and fellow Traitor Maya Jama scheming in the turret, but it set in motion a chain of events in which most of the Traitors were recruitments.The problem here is that some of the recruited Traitors didn’t seem up to the task of murder and betrayal. Acaster made no secret of the fact that he didn’t want to be a Traitor, and Hannah Fry didn’t seem fully comfortable in the role, either. I have no problem with these players being authentically themselves, but it’s more fun to watch characters such as Alan Carr (from the 2025 series) gleefully plotting in the shadows – to witness supposedly “nice” celebrities mastering the dark side. That’s what the game is about.The number of recruitments has also made the show feel stilted. Being a Faithful is a tricky task at the best of times, but it’s borderline impossible to have consistent theories or a sense of momentum when someone is being recruited every few episodes, rendering many events from earlier in the game null and void. The “original” Traitors making it deep into the game isn’t just satisfying for the audience; it’s also important for how the game functions. Too many recruitments can erode narrative cohesion.As a format,The Traitorsis close to being the perfect gameshow, which is why it has become a smash hit in almost all its international versions. But one flaw that’s baked into the game is that the biggest characters are often murdered or banished first, because they are seen as a threat to either the Traitors or the Faithful.This has an even greater impact on the celebrity version because we already know the players. For the audience, there is a sense of disappointment when a celebrity they really like gets eliminated early on. (Myha’la, I will avenge you!) This doesn’t exist in the same way on the civilian version, because we don’t necessarily know what we’re missing out on.Richard E Grant admits Traitors mistakes: ‘I never thought they would take me seriously’Read moreI can’t shake the feeling that the celebrities are just a little too nice to each other. Perhaps this is because they have been on TV before and are wary of how they will be perceived, or don’t want to fall out with someone they might see again in a professional setting. As someone who watches many international versions of The Traitors, I prefer the charm of the British show to the American version: the latter is far more conflict-filled and glitzy. But with this series, we’ve gone too far in the opposite direction. It’s become too nice and Acaster falling on his sword encapsulates that.On social media, there is a lot of anger towards Acaster, with some accusing him of making a mockery of the game. That was my initial reaction, too – and his confession has somewhat taken the wind out of the show’s sails ahead of the finale. But nobody watching at home can know how they would react in such a high-pressure situation.The backlash against the comedian is really misplaced frustration that this series hasn’t delivered many of those “OMG!” moments we have been accustomed to. Even the murder in plain sight – usually a box-office highlight – felt underwhelming. You can fill a castle with celebrities and engineer all kinds of twists, but sometimes it just doesn’t pan out the way you would hope. That’s reality TV for you.The Celebrity Traitors finale airs on BBC One at 8pm on 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsThe TraitorsTelevisionRichard E GrantJames AcasterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ceilidh renaissance’ lures gen Z offline in search of real-life joy | Folk music | The Guardian
description: Young dancers at the Ivy House in south-east London join the older crowd amid a renewed appetite for authentic, community events
Author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
Headline: Young dancers at the Ivy House in south-east London join the older crowd amid a renewed appetite for authentic, community events
Content: ‘It’s really lovely to come together in spaces with lots of different people,’ said one dancer at the ceilidh at the Ivy House in Nunhead, south-east London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s really lovely to come together in spaces with lots of different people,’ said one dancer at the ceilidh at the Ivy House in Nunhead, south-east London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianFolk music‘Ceilidh renaissance’ lures gen Z offline in search of real-life joyYoung dancers at the Ivy House in south-east London join the older crowd amid a renewed appetite for authentic, community eventsRosie Peters-McDonaldFri 30 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheIvy House pubin Nunhead, south-east London, has long been associated with raucous music, with the rock legends Ian Dury and Elvis Costello gracing its stage in the 70s, and indie favouritescarolineandKiran Leonardpulling in crowds today. But last Friday, it was a traditional Scottish ceilidh dance rather than a grassroots gig luring London’s cool kids to its sticky dancefloor.The event is emblematic of a renewed appetite for analogue, in-person experiences among a younger generationplagued by a loneliness epidemicandfatigued by meeting people on dating apps.“We spend a lot of time looking at screens,” said Matt, who saw the event as a refreshing way to spend time offline. “It’s really lovely to come together in spaces with lots of different people.”View image in fullscreen‘It just makes you feel alive.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianThe popularity of the ceilidh is evidenced by the launch of Ceilidh the Musical, which promises a “heart-warming party” with no experience required and started its tour at Shoreditch town hall, eastLondon, last week.According to the ticketing platform Eventbrite, from 2024-25 ticket sales for ceilidh events in the UK grew by 16%, while there was 15% growth globally. Page Dudley, a spokesperson for the platform, said young people were looking for events that were “communal and a lot less polished”.“It’s my first time at a proper ceilidh,” said George, 35, at the Ivy House. “I just like how silly it can be. It just makes you feel alive.”His partner, Louise, 32, was also a ceilidh first-timer. She said she liked how nobody was judging other people’s dance abilities. “It’s nice that it’s all ages,” she said. “When you strip away the ego, everyone just becomes their childlike selves.”View image in fullscreen‘Everyone just becomes their childlike selves.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianJamie, 19, is a seasoned ceilidh attender and said they were becoming much more popular among his peers. He has even bumped into schoolfriends unexpectedly at ceilidhs. “Everyone is just laughing at the same stuff, especially when people get confused [with the dance moves],” he said.Anna Spree, the communications, events and fundraising assistant atLink Age Southwark, which raised money from ticket sales at the Ivy House dance, said the “ceilidh renaissance” had allowed the local anti-loneliness charity to reach new people.“[The dances] were accessible enough that anyone could join in, but also slightly complex, which made them a lot more fun,” she added.View image in fullscreen‘It’s nice that it’s all ages.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianCeilidh, which comes from the Gaelic word for “visit” or “gathering”,originatedin Scotland and Ireland in the 19th century.“I’ve noticed the ceilidhs we’ve been putting on have been attended by a lot of under-30s,” said Alison Craig, a guitarist in the South East London Folk Orchestra (SELFolk), which provided the music on Friday.The ceilidh was organised after a successful dance in the same pub last year, which Craig recalls was bustling with young ceilidh newcomers. “The last time I saw the Ivy House bouncing like that was in about 1975,” she said.Although this particular ceilidh took place in a bar, Craig maintained that ceilidhs could be good for dry nights out, too: “You think, bloody hell, I’ve just had a Saturday night out and not had a drink.”View image in fullscreenSELfolk – the South East London Folk Orchestra – provided the music.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianEd McCabe, the founder ofLondon Ceilidh Club, has also noticed the shift. “Ever since Covid, it’s really boomed,” he said. “People just want to be in a room together.” He believes ceilidhs have “low barriers to entry” and are a great place to meet new people – or even find love.“There’s a whole aspect that you can’t look cool while you’re doing it,” he said. “You’re sweaty, you can’t stop smiling … it’s a great place to meet someone.”Craig echoed this: “It’s not about trying to look sexy or really cool,” she said. “Not to say ceilidhs aren’t sexy or cool, because they can be. You just need to get into it and enjoy it.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s the opposite of not being picked for sports at school.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianRichard Jones, who plays the accordion in SELFolk, suggested another great thing about ceilidhs was that they weren’t heteronormative. “It’s non-gender, if you like,” he said.His bandmate Neil McLean, who plays the flute, agreed. “We don’t really do men and women, we do ones and twos,” he said. “It’s the opposite of not being picked for sports at school.”SELFolk hosts regular ceilidhs which attract a crowd across all ages, according to Jones. “[People] know it’s safe, they know they can have a good time, and they don’t need to come in groups,” he said. “Very quickly the group becomes its own community.”Explore more on these topicsFolk musicFolk dancingYoung peopleLondonPubsLonelinessCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandma | Television | The Guardian
description: The star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filming
Author: Coco Khan
Headline: The star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filming
Content: Food for thought … Awkwafina aka Nora Lum.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFood for thought … Awkwafina aka Nora Lum.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTelevision‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandmaThe star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filmingCoco KhanFri 30 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m embarrassed I didn’t bring anything. It’s 10-something in the morning, and I’m meeting Nora Lum, 38 – best known as rapper, comic actor and writer Awkwafina – the morning after the Bafta TV awards. I feel that I should have brought her a pastry pick-me-up. Yet here I am empty-handed. “It could have been Chinese buns,” she playfully suggests.Yes, it could have been. Especially because we are meeting to discuss her new series on Apple TV, Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook. It sees the star of box-office hits Crazy Rich Asians and Marvel’s Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings travel across the US to learn from a new generation of Asian American chefs, in the hope that she might revive her own family’s long-closed Cantonese restaurant. But there’s one problem: she can’t cook.Or so she says. “Unlikely” cook? There’s nothing unlikely about it, I wager. Sure, in the first episode, Lum looks genuinely alarmed by the triple threat of hot oil, high heat and sharp knives in wok cooking. But she does very well. She clearly has a knack for food.“Well, I think it was the easiest knack to develop, because all it really takes is to eat at a ton of restaurants and order food constantly,” she pushes back.“But look, I was raised by immigrant Chinese people – I did eat all the weird Chinese stuff,” she says, understating her family’s impressive culinary credentials. The full story is thus: back in the 50s, Lum’s great-grandfather Jimmy opened one of New York’s first Chinese-American restaurants in Flushing, Queens. Called Lum’s, it became something of an institution, helping to popularise the Chinese-American food beloved today (think: orange chicken and BBQ ribs).“The restaurant is how we came to this country,” she explains. “It closed in 1982, so I wasn’t born. But it was so important. The way they talk about it is like a family member that passed away.”View image in fullscreenHigh steaks … Awkwafina and Jimmy O Yang (right) with Andrew Samia of Curry Boys BBQ in The Unlikely Cook.Photograph: Christina Belle/Apple TVLum’s new TV show about it is pleasingly warm and personal, with much of its gentle humour coming less from the supposedly awkward personality that inspired Lum’s stage name than her deep appreciation for food and hospitality. Have you ever seen someone scream “Oh my God, not the cilantro!” in ecstatic anticipation of a herb? I have, and it’s charming. But ultimately, Unlikely Cook is a love letter to Lum’s magnetic, occasionally foul-mouthed, paternal grandmother; the woman who raised her when she lost her mother at just four years old.Several months after I meet Lum, I see the Instagram post announcing her grandmother’s death. But, for now, I ask about the woman who has loomed so large over her creative work, and regularly steals the show in Unlikely Cook. How easy is it working with your own grandma?“It’s crazy. I’ve been asking my grandma to be in things since my first [TV] job, which was on MTV’s Girl Code,” Lum explains. Grandma obliged, starring in the brilliantly named episode Bad Sex, Grandparents, Eating Habits.“I’m always a little worried, thinking: ‘Oh my God, what are you going to say?’ But she has such a lovely on-camera affect. It just kind of clicks.”“With this [project], she’s calling me at all hours of the night, we’re staying up talking. Actually, she called me a week ago and was like, ‘I’m just thinking about the menu, and we should put a pu pu platter – but we shouldn’t call it pu pu, because, you know, it means shit so we should call it the volcano platter.’ It’s giving her excitement again.”View image in fullscreenFry hard … Awkwafina in The Unlikely Cook.Photograph: Christina Belle/Courtesy of AppleBetween the family appearances and actor Jimmy O Yang’s star turn (Lum’s real-life best friend) Unlikely Cook may be Lum’s most biographical work yet. Which is saying something given her hit 2020 comedy television show was literally called Awkwafina Is Nora from Queens, and starred her as directionless, awkward Nora living in – you guessed it – Flushing, with her widowed father and boisterous grandmother.For fans of Nora from Queens, there may be a particular, parasocial joy in watching Unlikely Cook. The sitcom could be absurd (Nora’s grandma accidentally growing cannabis, for instance), but you always sensed some emotional truth beneath it. Now we get the real Nora Lum.“Oh my God, yeah,” she exclaims. She refers to an episode where she is stressed. “That episode was bizarre to watch. Because I have never seen myself be serious, be panicked. That’s never been recorded.”“There was something about it where I actually felt bad. I felt bad for my exes, my friends. I was watching myself back like, ‘Chill out, girl!’”I didn’t have her pegged as the self-conscious type, I say, what with working so frequently from her real life. “I’ve never been documentarised in quite this way,” she explains. “There’s a part of me that’s like, oh my God, you let people see this crazy, unbridled version of you?! I still don’t know how to deal with that. But I do feel that whatever is honest, it can’t be the worst.”To be fair, foodisemotional stuff, and so often bound up in questions of identity, history and, especially in the immigrant context, family sacrifice. I ask Lum about her observation in the documentary that a generation of elders grafted in restaurants so their kids didn’t have to. They could be lawyers instead.“The truth is that a lot of the [older] people we met didn’t want their children to go back into the restaurant business. For my great-grandpa’s generation, when they came over they were relegated to either laundromats or restaurants, cooking food that has historically been demonised,” Lum says. “But then again, it’s also something that people love. There are more Chinese restaurants in America than there are McDonald’s, KFC, Burger King, all of that.”But while the restaurant business gave Lum’s family life, it also took a lot of it. Her grandmother had her own restaurant for a time, but when it failed, Lum’s grandparents were forced to file for bankruptcy, losing both their business and home. For a while, the whole family lived in a one-bedroom apartment.View image in fullscreenAll smiles … Awkwafina.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian“I think her business failing was really hard on her. She would fold the napkins in the back. She would launder napkins in our home. And she would be the most amazing maître d’ that the whole town knew. I don’t think she ever really recovered from it.”Would opening a permanent Lum’s be a way of rewriting that history?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I think giving back – if I’m in a position to do that – does feel like this full-circle moment where I could still make my family proud in that way. It would definitely be something for her.”All this talk of making family proud and honouring their sacrifices is something I know well, having also been raised in an immigrant household. Did Lum agonise over her choice of a creative career as much as I did when I chose English lit over law – something I loved over something that might more reliably make good on what my family gave me?“No, because I don’t think I was smart enough to get into law school,” she laughs.“Oh, I doubt that’s true,” I reply.“I’m actually not a good student. I went to summer school for gym.For gym. If you fail a class during the year, you can make it up over the summer. But it’s like a punishment, right? Every day I was taking two periods of gym, because I had failed so many times.”She continues: “Do you know what Earth science is? The rock one? It’s the easy rock one. It’s not even chemistry. I had to take the Earth science [exam] five times, dude.“So I think my family were just thinking, well, she has nothing to lose. Besides I wasn’t doing it off their dime, so I think maybe they were just happy I was doing something. But my dad really wanted me to be a meat inspector. I’m still on those government job registries that he signed me up for. He’s like, “Meat inspector, that’s a really good job.”“Itisa good job,” I concur.“It is! Great entry level salary. And you always, always need a meat inspector,” she says.“You could start now,” I offer.“I know, I know,” she laughs, and I wonder if she has the same idea I have.Awkwafina is the Meat Inspector, coming soon to Apple TV.OK, back to business. Watching Unlikely Cook, I couldn’t help thinking about the politics of America right now. After all, a show celebrating the work of immigrants feels significant in the age of Trump and ICE. Was that intentional?“No, not at all. But if you want to tell the story of Chinese-American food, immigrant culture is something you can’t ignore. It’s also a deep part of our identity as second-generation Asian Americans, it’s part of how we see the world. And it’s a hard thing to see right now in America.”Our time is nearly up. But wait, I’m still not sure, does this mean someday there will be a permanent Lum’s? “It’s still in the works of being figured out,” she says.But clearly, in Nora Lum herself, something has stuck. “After this show, I did start dabbling a little,” she says. While shooting a film in Kentucky, she took to cooking her own breakfast, “a four-egg omelette with spinach and cheese”, she says with faint pride. It’s not quite as impressive as Chinese buns. But maybe they’ll come soon.Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook is on Apple TV from Friday.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionFood TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one | Games | The Guardian
description: Voicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a father
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: Voicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a father
Content: Draga, protagonist of Black Tides Draga's Wake, played by Dominik DiamondPhotograph: Strange Creature Factory LtdView image in fullscreenDraga, protagonist of Black Tides Draga's Wake, played by Dominik DiamondPhotograph: Strange Creature Factory LtdGamesAfter 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in oneDominik DiamondVoicing the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake led to me making the kinds of noises I haven’t made since my honeymoon but also one of my favourite moments as a fatherFri 30 Oct 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTShare“I listen to you on the radio and I keep hearing your voice in my head!”Not a typical opening to a creative partnership, but that is how Greg Strangis introduced himself to me 16 months ago, when he asked me to come to his garage in the middle of nowhere and have a look at a game he was making called Black Tides Draga’s Wake.If this sounds dodgy, remember that when I was 21 years old, a posh bloke asked me to come to a random church in the East End of London and talk saucy in front of him and a couple of other posh blokes. This turned out to be my audition for GamesMaster.So, I go to Greg’s garage. He has a giant yet well groomed beard, eyes that flash with intensity underneath one of those Peaky Blinders caps and talks faster than other humans. He’s basically a hipster Rasputin. He is also a character artist who has worked for Rockstar, Naughty Dog and Guillermo del Toro. He ticks all the genius boxes for me.And then I see the actual game. It is gorgeously dark and twisted: a survival horror game set on a decaying 1900s steamship after a heist gone wrong. The titular Draga is a big, tough-as-hell sailor with a dark past, infected by an ancient god that grows within him.View image in fullscreenGorgeously dark and twisted … Black Tides Draga’s Wake.Photograph: Strange Creature Factory Ltd.It sounds exciting, it sounds original, it sounds terrifying. And he wants me to be in it.But it sounds nothing like me. I am not a sailor. I am not big and tough as hell, and the only ancient god I have ever been infected with is gout. (Trust me, the pain is biblical.)I am going to have to …act.I did study drama at university, but this was the University of Bristol in the early 90s, so it was less about high kicking on stage to Oklahoma or learning Shakespearean monologues and more about poring over some obscure Russian play where potatoes are a metaphor for gender politics, written by a bloke who once gave Gorky a lift.I never told Greg this at the time, but when I see my first attempts at voice acting play out in the game, I don’t like it. I see this amazing badass character smashing disgustingly huge monsters with my tinny tones coming out of him. So I lower my voice ever so slightly and stop trying to act so much. And it works! Helpfully, Greg’s direction always makes me feel comfortable and encouraged.Every time I turn up for a session I am inspired by the work done by the team, who are in different corners of the world, doing this in their spare time. I see their message threads with all kinds of ideas, pictures and animations. It reminds me of the bedroom programming culture of the ZX Spectrum, fuelled by the unshakeable belief in an idea and a passion for gaming. In an age where huge publishers are decimating studios all over the world, it is a reminder of how vibrant game-making can still be.View image in fullscreenExistential crisis … Dominik as a survival horror action hero.Photograph: Dominik DiamondI don’t want to be the weak link in this chain. I don’t want my performance to be something that takes a prospective publisher out of the moment. I learn to love pushing and pulling the words in different directions. The biggest challenge is improvising fight noises that Greg and the team can add in wherever and whenever they want. During the game this is supposed to seem natural, but in reality it is a Scottish dad in his 50s making the kinds of noises he hasn’t made since his honeymoon. In a garage. In the middle of rural Nova Scotia. With another guy telling him he has to be more aggressive.It’s unbearably weird when I play the game. I feel distraught when I die, because itisme. I feel equally bad when I see other people playing the game, leading to uncomfortable new thoughts about video game characters’ lack of free will. It’s all a bit of an existential crisis.But then I play clips for my kids without telling them I am in it. I see their faces break out into wide grins as they realise it’s their grumpy old Scottish dad playing a survival horror action hero. It’s one of my favourite ever moments as a parent.It has also made me appreciate voice acting in games, something that didn’t register with me before, because for me it always felt like thecharactertalking – which is testament to the quality of voice acting and directing in games. Or at least games since the original Resident Evil. I now truly appreciate performances like Nolan North as Nathan Drake, Ashley Johnson in The Last of Us, and every single actor who says any of the words in Expedition 33.The announcement trailer for Black Tides Draga’s Wake dropped a month ago. It got 200,000 views in the first couple of days. Greg is in discussions with assorted publishers. I still have to pinch myself that after playing games for 50 years, I am finally going to be in one.Explore more on these topicsGamescommentShareReuse this content

title: Susan Saint James obituary | US television | The Guardian
description: US TV star known for the sitcom Kate & Allie and for starring opposite Rock Hudson in McMillan & Wife
Author: Anthony Hayward
Headline: US TV star known for the sitcom Kate & Allie and for starring opposite Rock Hudson in McMillan & Wife
Content: Susan Saint James with Rock Hudson as McMillan & Wife. Their screen relationship was a hit with global audiences.Photograph: ABC/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSusan Saint James with Rock Hudson as McMillan & Wife. Their screen relationship was a hit with global audiences.Photograph: ABC/Everett/ShutterstockUS televisionObituarySusan Saint James obituaryUS TV star known for the sitcom Kate & Allie and for starring opposite Rock Hudson in McMillan & WifeAnthony HaywardFri 30 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSusan Saint James, who has died of pancreatic cancer aged 80, was a major star onUS televisionfor two decades, shooting to worldwide fame alongside Rock Hudson in the police drama McMillan & Wife and playing one of two divorced single mums in the female “odd couple” sitcom Kate & Allie.Saint James was cast as McMillan’s wife, Sally, after being spotted in a 1970 episode of another crime series, McCloud, playing a police officer on the trail of a serial killer. The role of Stewart McMillan, or “Mac”, a debonair San Francisco police commissioner, was Hudson’s first in a TV series after more than two decades as a movie heart-throb in Hollywood’s so-called golden age, alongside sex symbols such asGina LollobrigidaandDoris Day. The husky-voiced Saint James more than held her own in the show, in which she starred for five years from 1971.View image in fullscreenSaint James, left, as Kate, and Jane Curtin as Allie in the 1980s sitcom Kate & Allie, about two divorced single mothers who move in together.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockThe programme’s winning twist is that the apparently scatter-brained Sally is more shrewd than she appears, and often steps in to help her husband, as well as uncovering new crimes. The couple’s social invitations to dinner parties and charity events invariably lead them to discover robbery or murder, too, while at other times Sally herself is targeted by criminals, kidnapped more than once and, predictably, rescued by her loving husband.The screen relationship made McMillan & Wife a hit with global audiences – and its demise came when Saint James left after five series following a contractual dispute. Sally was killed off in a plane crash and the programme returned titled simply McMillan, surviving for only one more series.Saint James switched to comedy for Kate & Allie (1984-89). She played Kate McArdle alongside Jane Curtin as Allie Lowell, two divorcees and former high-school buddies with three children between them who move into a Greenwich Village apartment together to ease their financial and emotional burdens. The two actors had previously played suburban housewives in the 1980 film comedy How to Beat the High Cost of Living and Saint James herself had already gone through two failed marriages.The producers of the show made clear that there was no sexual relationship – the pair’s separate bedrooms with single beds were highly visible.“This is not a statement saying, ‘Girls, leave the guys and go live with your best friend,’” said Saint James. “Kate and Allie didn’t plan this. It’s just the best solution they could think of, and their friendship sustains them.”Like McMillan & Wife, Kate & Allie thrived through the on-screen relationship between the characters, while the sitcom saw the friends go on to start their own catering business as their children grow up.When it ended, Saint James mostly retired from acting – returning to the screen just a handful of times – to bring up her own children and concentrate on voluntary work withSpecial Olympics, an organisation providing opportunities for children and adults with learning disabilities. She also co-owned the soft-rock radio station WZBG based in Litchfield, Connecticut, from its launch in 1992 until its sale in 2024.View image in fullscreenSaint James in the 1977 film Outlaw Blues, co-starring Peter Fonda.Photograph: Warner Bros/Kobal/ShutterstockBorn in Los Angeles, she was the daughter of Constance (nee Geiger), a teacher, and Charles Miller, a toolmaker with a newsreel and movie camera manufacturer. The family moved to Rockford, Illinois, when Charles became president of the model kits and hobby products company Testor.After boarding at a Catholic school, the Woodlands Academy of the Sacred Heart, in Lake Forest, Illinois, Susan had plans to study at Connecticut College, but ditched them when a Life magazine photographer at her brother’s wedding told her she would make a professional model. Moving to New York, she landed a contract with a leading agency.She then spent 18 months modelling in Paris, where she was also a stagehand at L’Olympia music hall, work that included assisting the French singer-actorCharles Aznavour, who encouraged her to act.On returning to the US in 1966, she took acting classes, changed her name to Susan Saint James and, aged 19, signed a seven-year contract with Universal Studios.She walked straight into a part in a TV pilot, Fame Is the Name of the Game (1966), playing Peggy, an editorial assistant, alongside Tony Franciosa as an investigative reporter. It ran as a series titled The Name of the Game (1968-71) and won Saint James a Primetime Emmy award in 1969 (followed by two more nominations). She earned further Emmy nominations for McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie.In between those programmes, she acted in run-of-the-mill TV movies while enjoying film roles asPeter Fonda’s girlfriend in Outlaw Blues (1977) and, with her dark hair dyed blond, the love interest of Dracula (George Hamilton) in the hit 1979 vampire spoof Love at First Bite. (“Even industry people didn’t recognise me as the blond model, though I shared top billing,” she said.)View image in fullscreenGeorge Hamilton and Saint James in the spoof vampire film Love at First Bite, 1979.Photograph: American International Pictures/Everett/ShutterstockShe was also seen as a war correspondent in a 1980 episode of the sitcom M*A*S*H, and had a brief relationship with the musician Stephen Stills of Crosby Stills & Nash.In later years Saint James occasionally appeared on television in series such as Law & Order: Special Victims Unit (in 2006), Suits (in 2011) and Upload (2020-22).Her first two marriages, to the scriptwriter Richard Neubert (1967-68) and Tom Lucas, a make-up artist (1971-77), ended in divorce. In 1981, she married Dick Ebersol, a television executive. Their son Teddy died in 2004.Ebersol and their other sons, Charlie and Willie, survive her, along with Sunshine and Harmony, the children from her second marriage, a sister, Mercedes, and seven grandchildren.Susan Saint James (Susan Jane Miller), actor, born 14 August 1946; died 26 October 2026Explore more on these topicsUS televisionTelevisionobituariesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: who will win Celebrity Traitors? It’s time to find out | Television | The Guardian
description: Miranda Hart, Ross Kemp and James Acaster shone through Alan Carr’s shadow. Plus: a visit to a farm worked by people with disabilities. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Miranda Hart, Ross Kemp and James Acaster shone through Alan Carr’s shadow. Plus: a visit to a farm worked by people with disabilities. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: All will be revealed … Claudia Winkleman in The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryView image in fullscreenAll will be revealed … Claudia Winkleman in The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: who will win Celebrity Traitors? It’s time to find outMiranda Hart, Ross Kemp and James Acaster shone through Alan Carr’s shadow. Plus: a visit to a farm worked by people with disabilities. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Graeme Virtue,Hannah J DaviesandEllen E JonesFri 30 Oct 2026 02.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Celebrity Traitors Finale8pm, BBC OneAnd just like that, the second Celebrity Traitors has reached its finale! It might not have had Alan Carr, but Miranda Hart warmed hearts, Ross Kemp upped the paranoia and James Acaster became a sex symbol. There’s one more round table, then the finalists learn their fates in the flames.Hollie RichardsonLandward7.30pm, BBC TwoDougie Vipond visits Aberdeenshire to meet Mike Duxbury. After losing his sight at six years old, he became one of the first blind students to be accepted into agricultural college. After hundreds of job rejections, he and his partner, Ness, founded the Inclusive Farm, for people with disabilities and diverse needs.Priya ElanGardeners’ World8pm, BBC TwoIt’s the penultimate episode before Monty Don waves a green-fingered goodbye. In advance of that, Adam Frost is making finishing touches to his new garden before the growing season ends, while Rachel de Thame celebrates the chrysanthemum.HRThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneAfter last week’s alternative reality detour, it’s back to blood-spattered business as usual in zombified New York. Bourbon-voiced brigand Negan (Jeffrey Dean Morgan) is holed up in a dive bar after his latest rage-induced murder. Can Maggie (Lauren Cohan) convince him to surrender before a trigger-happy posse comes a-knockin’?Graeme VirtueWar9pm, Sky AtlanticMore of the glossy divorce drama that arguably prioritises style over substance. Carla (Sienna Miller) goes public about her split from Morgan (Dominic West) with an outburst on live TV that gets her trending online. Or, as she puts it: “This is a talkshow, so let me bloody talk!”Hannah J DaviesThe Graham Norton Show10.40pm, BBC OneIt’s a “bunny boiler” reunion in the studio this week, as Michael Douglas takes a seat beside Glenn Close on the red sofa. They’re joined by Kieran Culkin (with whom Close stars in the new Hunger Games film) and Naomi Ackie. Music comes from Sugababes.HRFilm choiceThe End of Oak Street(David Robert Mitchell, 2026),9.10am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenUnhappy families …Anne Hathaway and three kids in The End Of Oak Street.Photograph: Warner Bros. Pictures/PictureLux/AvalonIt’s 1982 and the Platt family – dad (Ewan McGregor), mum (Anne Hathaway) and two anxious kids – are existing in a state of suburban stasis, until the stakes are raised by a bunch of dinosaurs stomping through their neighbourhood. How and why these dinos have suddenly appeared are questions for a different movie. This one – made by Mitchell, director of 2014’s cult horror hit It Follows – is mostly concerned with big, silly blockbuster fun, Spielberg references and the resilience of an unhappy family forced to band together.Ellen E JonesApocalypse Z: New World (Carles Torrens, 2026),Prime VideoThe Spanish-language zombie flick Apocalypse Z: The Beginning of the End was a huge international hit for Prime Video in 2024. In this sequel, also directed by Torrens, much of the population has taken refuge in the Canary Islands, after the outbreak of the blood-borne TSJ virus. Roberto (Carlos Alcaide) joins a special return mission to the mainland, which soon becomes a scramble for survival as the infected hordes march on. Perhaps returning fan favourite Lúculo the cat (still played by Pedrito the cat) can come to the rescue?EEJExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best recent translated fiction – review roundup | Books | The Guardian
description: Minihorror by Barbi Marković; Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch; Hafni Says by Helle Helle; Googling for Soul by Hamid Ismailov
Author: John Self
Headline: Minihorror by Barbi Marković; Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch; Hafni Says by Helle Helle; Googling for Soul by Hamid Ismailov
Content: Antic energy … Barbi Marković.Photograph: /Apollonia T. BitzanView image in fullscreenAntic energy … Barbi Marković.Photograph: /Apollonia T. BitzanTranslated fiction roundupBooksReviewThe best recent translated fiction – review roundupMinihorror by Barbi Marković; Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch; Hafni Says by Helle Helle; Googling for Soul by Hamid IsmailovJohn SelfFri 30 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinihorrorby Barbi Marković, translated by Jen Calleja (Faber, £14.99)This eccentric and fantastical collection of very short stories is bursting with weird life. Mini and Miki (the Disney mouse names in Serbian) are a sometime boyfriend and girlfriend living in Austria. They visit Mini’s family, who gather round a pit and make her climb down into it (when she told Miki “they’re dragging me down”, he thought it was a metaphor). They visit Miki’s family, where a dog Mini draws on a card comes alive and attacks her. Things swing from hopeful – “they’re having fun like a couple in an advert” – to dismal: a hair dye goes wrong and “Mini looks like a 13-year-old dog”. Minihorror combines a Bernhardian comic gloom (“in summary, everything’s tainted, and existence is a particular hardship”) with antic energy. “Miki isn’t sure what to think about life. Is it good? Is it bad?” It’s everything, just like this book.Paradise Burnsby Pol Guasch, translated by Mara Faye Lethem (Peninsula, £12.99)“Stories, if you give them an order, aren’t stories but lies.” Catalan author Guasch makes the point vividly in this novel which flits briskly from present to past and from narrator to narrator. It’s set in a changed climate – “One only knows it’s winter now by the shrunken days and long nights” – where young men join a firefighting service and fight “wildfire simulations of blazes that could not be put out”. The central characters are friends Rita and Líton, but Líton is dead when the book begins – “twenty-four short years, a life as fleeting as a shooting comet” – so the story goes backward, to find out why. The jumpy narrative ranges from Rita’s childhood diary, to three “crafty old biddies” in the neighbourhood, to Líton and his lover René. But inside the hectic structure is a tribute to the value of friendship, and how a friend “has to be the net beneath the tightrope that is life”.Hafni Saysby Helle Helle, translated by Martin Aitken (Akoya, £12.99)Hafni, at 48, is leaving her husband – literally, by taking a road trip through Denmark. “Many’s the time he’d cycle off and I’d be standing at the kitchen window wishing the wind would take him.” Now it’s her turn to go. Alongside details of life away from home – washing her pants in the sink, opening beer bottles with a metal comb – she reflects on how liberating it is to be free of a sense of obligation. The rules she has lived by can be abandoned, if not forgotten. “No more phrases like ‘you shouldn’t have’.” She meets new people – such as a dying woman who sees it as her duty to keep everyone around her cheerful – and wobbles between hope and fear. But ultimately this is a subtle, affecting story of what happens when a woman stuck in her life says, “I don’t want to be me. I want to change who I am.”View image in fullscreenGoogling for Soulby Hamid Ismailov, translated by Shelley Fairweather-Vega, Dani Ismailov, Irina Buss-Zolotareva and Andrew Bromfield (Glagoslav, £17.99)This sequence of stories about Uzbeks, often exiled in Russia, is full of rampant action, blunt comedy and real horror. In the title story, a man believes his life is echoing the events of Andrey Platonov’s story Soul, and also believes that Hamid Ismailov, the author of this book, has been arrested on terrorism charges. (In reality, Ismailov was forced to flee Uzbekistan in 1992.) Other stories include a man driven to penury by the escapades of a nephew he’s never met before; two in-laws thrown together by fate; and a girl with a precious doll (her story seems more subdued than the others until her drunk father chases her with a knife). Ismailov’s characters have a lively line in insults: “You have the complexion of a fart,” says a father telling his son to eat better. “It’s as if the world had rejected seriousness,” says one character – but Ismailov’s blend of seriousness and sparkle is a seductive combination.Explore more on these topicsBooksTranslated fiction roundupFiction in translationHorror booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Attention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo review – a slippery liar’s tale | Books | The Guardian
description: Shortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Shortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answers
Content: Brilliant and breathless … Aea Varfis-van Warmelo.Photograph: Naomi Joanne DelormeView image in fullscreenBrilliant and breathless … Aea Varfis-van Warmelo.Photograph: Naomi Joanne DelormeBook of the dayBooksReviewAttention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo review – a slippery liar’s taleShortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answersAimée WalshFri 30 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 04.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Goldsmiths prize-shortlisted debut from British-Greek author Aea Varfis-van Warmelo opens with a confession: “I have never told this story before.” The narrator, who bears the author’s name, goes on to tell the reader that she is a liar. From Humbert Humbert’s self-justifying account of abuse in Lolita to the devastating misinterpretation at the heart of Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the trope of the unreliable narrator exposes the dangerous gap between the stories we tell and the truths they obscure. In Attention Seeking Behaviour, the reader is asked to examine their own capacity for trust.A young woman aspires to be a writer – yet she has paused her postgraduate degree in poetry. She works unfulfilling jobs that demand little from her and has a lot of sex, which she describes as offering her “solitude”. She does all this while lying compulsively. She lies for fun, to flirt, to steal, for sympathy. She lies out of a desire to hurt others, but also to preserve her own privacy. Lying is, as the narrator claims, universal, though success at lying is not. She regards fraudsters and scammers with derision: they are “divorced from reality” and give her “second hand embarrassment”. In her eyes, her own lies are somehow purer.Grief and trauma pulse beneath the story, as the narrator is haunted by the dead bodies she sees in parks and floating in canals. She says she has called emergency services, but her account is slippery: the harder we try to grasp it, the more it slips through our fingers. Can we believe a word she says?double quotation markThe reader may find their own response to the narrator’s story as unsettling as the story itselfAttention Seeking Behaviour draws the reader through personal confession and a gripping narrative of misadventures while dating, but the novel loses some of its momentum in its discussions of deceit. An essay on Paul Ekman’s Facial Action Coding System for classifying facial movements to determine deception disrupts the narrative drive. When this bleeds into the narrative, her boyfriend says: “No more. Please.” These sections interrupt the flow and lack the immediacy achieved elsewhere.In the book’s second part, questions of credibility become more acute. Acting on behalf of a journalist, the narrator copies files at a legal firm relating to a rape case in which a lecturer is accused of assaulting his student. The victim bares her soul, giving first her phone over to the police, then her laptop. Eventually, after police question her for signs of deception, she withdraws her participation in the investigation. The case is closed.Complainants often anticipate the difficulties of a police investigation. Their testimony is the evidence, their body a crime scene. The narrator says: “We are ambiently aware of what is believable – of what people think is true, whether or not it is real.” Victims of sexual violence are judged in courts and beyond, for what they wore on the night in question, for what they did or did not do in the aftermath. Here lies the book’s genius: it turns the question of reliability back on the reader, exposing the expectations we place on women. Must an account of rape be consistent, coherent or complete to be worthy of belief? Should a woman’s past, including what she has said and done, have any bearing on whether she is believed? The reader may find their own response to the narrator’s story as unsettling as the story itself. The narrator cannot name the trauma that happened with her ex-boyfriend Isaac. Instead, she unravels it “like a police report”, recounting what she said (nothing) and what she felt (numb). The book asks, unflinchingly, do you believe her?Brilliant and breathless, Attention Seeking Behaviour brings no easy resolutions to questions of memory, truth and justice. Yet, as the narrator tells us again and again, all she wants is to be believed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
