To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBooksBook of the dayFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Few Good Men review – Aaron Sorkin’s legal drama makes unwelcome return to stage | Broadway | The Guardian
description: Unconvincing performances and an ill-fitting big stage make a retooled version of the classic courtroom drama feel like a missed opportunity
Author: Richard Lawson
Headline: Unconvincing performances and an ill-fitting big stage make a retooled version of the classic courtroom drama feel like a missed opportunity
Content: Tom Blyth and Nick Blaemire in A Few Good Men.Photograph: Emilio MadridView image in fullscreenTom Blyth and Nick Blaemire in A Few Good Men.Photograph: Emilio MadridBroadwayReviewA Few Good Men review – Aaron Sorkin’s legal drama makes unwelcome return to stageVivian Beaumont theater, New York CityUnconvincing performances and an ill-fitting big stage make a retooled version of the classic courtroom drama feel like a missed opportunityRichard LawsonThu 29 Oct 2026 23.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGiven the current state of the US military brass, it makes some sense that audiences would want to drift back to an older, nobler idea of the armed services, in which bad actors exist but are rooted out by the good guys in uniform. That perhaps explains the Broadway revival of A Few Good Men, Aaron Sorkin’s 1989 courtroom drama about a cocky military attorney defending two young marines who followed an illegal order with fatal results. The play is at once sharp and misty-eyed, critiquing a hallowed institution while reverently imbuing it with a certain dignity – in some ways, it does for the military what Sorkin’s The West Wing did for the Oval Office.860 review – Billy Crystal’s charisma powers rambling one-man playRead moreA Few Good Men was turned into a hit Oscar-nominated film in 1992, starring a then boyish Tom Cruise in the role of recalcitrant navy lawyer Daniel Kaffee and a frightening Jack Nicholson as Kaffee’s ultimate enemy, Colonel Jessep, the hardliner in command of theUS militarybase at Guantánamo Bay, where a marine has died under troubling circumstances. Directed by Rob Reiner, the film is a clever, old-fashioned crowd pleaser, culminating in a classic trial scene punctuated by the line. “You can’t handle the truth!”, Jessep memorably bellows at Kaffee just before confessing to his misdeeds. Those in search of crackling drama and sentimentality about the military should just watch that film, rather than plunking down a considerable sum of money to see the play in its current form at Lincoln Center’s Vivian Beaumont theater.The production is helmed by Michael Arden, an actor turned director who is no stranger to courtroom intrigue: he was behind the lovely 2023 revival of the musical Parade, about a wrongly accused man standing trial for murder. But that show had songs to rely on, whereas A Few Good Men has only its complicated Sorkin dialogue to propel it along. Arden proves less adept at turning that fast talk into music; in his hands, the play is lurching and awkward, rarely finding the rhythm necessary to keep Sorkin’s verbosity afloat.View image in fullscreenBradley Whitford in A Few Good Men.Photograph: Emilio MadridIt doesn’t help that the Beaumont is an enormous space, and Arden and scenic designer Dane Laffrey do nothing to make it more intimate. They use nearly the whole depth of the stage, and highlight the proscenium’s height with looming beams and a guard tower meant to evoke Jessep’s outpost in Cuba. That volume effectively swallows up the rapid, close chatter of the play, rendering it all quiet and tinny. We feel little of the propulsive charge of the story, as Kaffee navigates setbacks and, in the process, finds the principled conviction his career had previously lacked. There is a curious diffuseness to this A Few Good Men, the sense that we are watching the dim memory of something that was once exciting, rather than the thing itself.Perhaps an actor of sturdier stock than Tom Blyth could have made things more resonant. As Kaffee, Blyth – a 31-year-old Briton most famous for a 2023 Hunger Games prequel film – has the arrogant, golden-boy strut down pretty well. But he struggles to convincingly convey Kaffee’s legal acumen, his cunning in getting the desired result from a cornered witness. As dogged internal affairs attorney Joanne Galloway (played by Demi Moore in the film), musical theater mainstay Krysta Rodriguez has similar problems of gravitas – she’s a bright presence, but one does begin to wonder what a plucky ingenue from a 1940s romp is doing at a court-martial.The real sore spot in the ensemble, though, is a direly miscast Bradley Whitford as Jessep, a role that should radiate imperious menace, but in Whitford’s rendition comes across confused and unfocused. Whitford totters around the stage with his legs wide apart, as if he is doing a creaky John Wayne impression. He half mumbles and half growls his lines, a strained simulation of macho might. Whitford proved in two separate television series that he can more than handle Sorkin’s signature patter. (He’s also now doing great work on the Sorkin-esque series The Diplomat.) But Jessep is not one of Sorkin’s zippy smart guys. He’s a bull, a bear, something atavistic and scary. That’s not exactly in Whitford’s wheelhouse, it seems.This clash of actor and part would be more tolerable if, in the performance I saw, Whitford seemed more confident with his lines. Blyth also struggled in that regard, particularly in the climactic scene in which Kaffee provokes Jessep into disclosing the real truth of the matter on the stand. While attempting to summit the peak of the play, both actors stumbled over their words and, on a few occasions, seemed to go blank for a moment. Which killed any momentum that Arden had managed to whip up; the scene came and went at a limping stagger and then the story huffed to a close. Hopefully Whitford and Blyth have fared better at other performances, but even then I doubt that this A Few Good Men generated much heat or electricity. It’s a starchy, listless production that never finds a proper sense of scale.Not all is lost, though. There are some great turns from actors in smaller roles, including Nick Blaemire as a wise-cracking and morally concerned second-chair lawyer; Thom Sesma as a conflicted lieutenant colonel; and Michael Oberholtzer as the lead prosecutor on the case. They find the right cadence and timbre to make Sorkin’s ornate language sound casual and credible. If only they were in a smaller theater – where audiences could really feel the cramp of the courtroom, the pressure of a military base – and led by more suitable stars. As is, they are but a few good players in a production disappointingly derelict in its duty.A Few Good Men is at Vivian Beaumont theater, New York City, until 10 January 2027Explore more on these topicsBroadwayAaron SorkinUS theaterTheatreUS militaryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sampa the Great: Nu Zamrock review – a full-circle moment for a world-class act | Music | The Guardian
description: Sampa Tembo’s genre-hopping third album meets the moment with charisma and cheek
Author: Caitlin Welsh
Headline: Sampa Tembo’s genre-hopping third album meets the moment with charisma and cheek
Content: Sampa the Great’s new album Nu Zamrock is out now.Photograph: Abu DumbuyaView image in fullscreenSampa the Great’s new album Nu Zamrock is out now.Photograph: Abu DumbuyaMusicReviewSampa the Great: Nu Zamrock review – a full-circle moment for a world-class actSampa Tembo’s genre-hopping third album meets the moment with charisma and cheekCaitlin WelshFri 30 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2019, as Sampa the Great, Sampa Tembo became the first woman to win an Australian Recording Industry Association award for hip-hop or rap; she’s also the first (and only) person to win theAustralian musicprize twice. But she’s said consistently over the past decade that, while her music career began in Australia – when she was based here between 2013 and 2019 – she is still Zambian-born, Botswana-raised.Having returned to Africa to live and record,she told the Guardian in 2022: “I was constantly being called Australian. I felt that I really had to defend Zambia and Zambian music and culture. The fact I was raised in Botswana and heard this music as I was being raised there fell to the wayside.”Does Australia’s eagerness to claim her as Our Sampa come in the same earnestly admiring spirit as we claim other imports whose careers took off from an Australian launchpad, like, say, Crowded House or Rebecca Gibney? Or is there an ugly, acquisitive streak in the disproportionately white Australian music industry that rushes to congratulate itself for “producing” “diaspora artists” like Tembo, who make our national creative output feel less stale and pale?View image in fullscreenTembo’s blend of blends ‘settles in beautifully on repeat listens’Photograph: Loma Vista Recordings/PAWith the sounds of amapiano and Afrobeats entering the global pop charts via artists like Tyla and Burna Boy, mainstream western audiences are beginning to have a better grasp of the unique qualities and context of African pop and rock fusion genres, not to mention a better understanding that music was not invented in Liverpool in 1960.In Nu Zamrock, Tembo also seems to call out peers who only start repping the culture when the mainstream catches on: “You’ll find me in Africa winding my waist / You ever been global? You just in the States,” she sneers on Location, nodding to her own explorations of the world: “Switching the game like a young relocation / Find me in Ghana and not on vacation.”Her move back toZambia, and her discovery of her family connection to Zamrock codifiers WITCH, also heavily informed and framed her 2022 album, As Above, So Below, and at first it’s a little hard to discern what is supposed to be “Nu” about her approach. But the full-circle feeling of her blend of blends – the tidal wave of psych-rock influence that has travelled the globe from the UK and the US in the 60s, to 70s Zambia, to Australia, through modern jazz and soul, all the way back to southern Africa – settles in beautifully on repeat listens, tumbling even more of those distinctive polyrhythms, kalindula and raw, high-gain guitar fuzz in alongside the self-possessed snap of her lyrical style. Collapsing genre further, she stacks repeated references to being an African and Zambian “rock star”. It’s as though she has relaxed a little as both a performer and producer – the way you can when surrounded by people for whom you don’t have to perform an identity – without sacrificing any discipline.Through her sonic evolution she remains thematically consistent: Nu Zamrock is at least the third of her records to contain lyrical nods to the concept of “a seat at the table”, and she gives us an update on the “demons” she described at her heels on Shadows, the opening track to As Above, in the stomping Simon Says: “I say all my demons is dead.”Briggs swaps rap for punk with Big Noter: ‘I’m the same guy with the same middle finger!’Read moreThe early single Can’t Hold Us is a sync-ready anthem about resilience featuring her sister Mwanje; the unflinching Canary hits like a truck; while the lush Catch If You Can lets the listener catch a breath. A guest spot from Sia in Supernova fits surprisingly well – there is a rat-a-tat quality to their respective deliveries that works beautifully – but not even Sampa’s charisma is a match for the pop juggernaut’s steamrolling, blocky toplines. Tembo has never sought commercial approval but the softer tracks here remove any doubt that she could crush pop music if she wanted to.Later, on Star, she croons affirmation to someone who might be wondering how to get from the crowd to the stage: “Did you know you could be just the way you are, love / To be someone like me?”Nu Zamrock is the sound of Tembo telling the industry that how it chooses to perceive her is none of her business.Whereas back in 2018 she wondered “How you supposed to be Black down under?” on Simon Says she now shrugs cheekily: “Sampa the Great is the problem I’m waiting for them to solve.” For her, delivering a world-class view of a widescreen world is no problem at all.Nu Zamrock by Sampa the Great is out now through Loma Vista recordingsExplore more on these topicsMusicHip-hopPop and rockAustralian musicZambiaAfricareviewsShareReuse this content

title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racket | Music | The Guardian
description: The Rotterdam band are a riot of sound, look and attitude led by Eva Kah, who is as much a living artwork as she is a phenomenal live performer
Author: Richard Foster
Headline: The Rotterdam band are a riot of sound, look and attitude led by Eva Kah, who is as much a living artwork as she is a phenomenal live performer
Content: ‘In your face’ … Eva Kah of Bombstrap.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘In your face’ … Eva Kah of Bombstrap.Photograph: PRAdd to playlistMusicThe week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racketThe Rotterdam band are a riot of sound, look and attitude led by Eva Kah, who is as much a living artwork as she is a phenomenal live performerRichard FosterFri 30 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromRotterdam, the NetherlandsRecommended if you likeGnod, Discharge, GwarUp nextDebut album Big Enemy out now via Tartarus, playing Le Guess Who festivalRotterdam’sBombstrapare a riotous and theatrical fusion of sound, look and attitude. An embodied version of John Milton’s Pandæmonium with the amp turned up to 11, the band revel in hardcore alternative living, internet wormholes, art-school pretensions and a gungy form of hardcore. Based in and drawing succour from one of the most famous squatted centres in the city, Het Poortgebouw, Bombstrap are a noisy counterblast to the increasing and overwhelmingly witless “circuses-and-bread” gentrification of Rotterdam.Visual artist and singer Eva Kah is a living artwork and phenomenal live performer, whose in-your-face act illuminates those grey areas between righteous anger, nihilistic energy and teeth-grating bad taste. Kah’s vocals ape the warning screams and ululations a crone would make over the grave of Achilles. A natural extension of the look, obviously.Some of the uncompromising attitudes heard in debut album Big Enemy also betray their links to Manchester’s punk and squat scenes; previous members of the extendedGnodfamily have played with them. But the sound is a shifting, amorphous one, permanently up for grabs in the listener’s interpretation. The gravelly mix of chopped-up rhythms and raw, high-decibel punk guitars could even hark back to ancient prog-punk gonzoids such as the Pink Fairies. They are one of the last cries of homegrown, communal, anarcho hippy-punkdom and have all the social and sonic baggage that that entails. There is no career path in sight.Richard FosterThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenDeep and dramatic … Clementine Douglas.Photograph: Lily AjaibClementine Douglas​ – So PreciousSelf-penned, and gorgeously self-produced with a ribbon of synth melody pirouetting from the bottom of the mix, this is deep and dramatic vocal house from the British singer normally found belting alongside Calvin Harris, Dom Dolla et al.​DJ Heartstring – 3am/4am (ft Monk, 3ndles5 & Crazymike)The German dance duo get their countryman Monk to flow over their breakbeat euphoria, while there are shades of Real Lies’ nocturnal social realism to 3ndles5’s spoken English-language verse.Josh Johnson – Jazz Chord PossessionJazz saxophonist Johnson is sideman to Jeff Parker and producer to Meshell Ndegeocello and Flea. His own latest single has two sweetly swaying melodic motifs set against each other, plus analogue synth burbling out back.​Isaac Kniveton​ – Love GrooveLike a colourful plastic playground with its edges melting in the sun, there’s a bright psychedelia to the way the British producer’s Kompakt-style techno-pop unfolds, peppy and woozy all at once.Anamanaguchi – Sucker PunchThe New Yorkers pair crunching, muscular chords with delicate electronic detailing, building up a dense bank of shoegaze that’s illuminated from within by a thousand points of neon light.​Metoronori – Lights of the BayDreampop is an overused phrase, but it’s appropriate for the otherworldly beauty and wrongfooting shifts in the Japanese singer-producer’s new album, Forgot Reef Number: this track has a music-box prettiness.Waterbaby – CreekWe loved her albumMemory Be a Bladeearlier this year, and the Stockholm singer-songwriter is back with this waltzing lullaby, full of her trademark blend of wounded emotion and stoic endurance.Ben Beaumont-ThomasSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistNetherlandsEuropeSquattingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kali Malone: Burning Song review – drone composer wields Bach’s organ to breathtaking effect | Experimental music | The Guardian
description: The US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpiece
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpiece
Content: Acute attention … Kali Malone.Photograph: © Kingsley IfillView image in fullscreenAcute attention … Kali Malone.Photograph: © Kingsley IfillExperimental musicReviewKali Malone: Burning Song review – drone composer wields Bach’s organ to breathtaking effect(Ideologic Organ)The US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpieceLaura SnapesFri 30 Oct 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn drone world, Burning Song is Kali Malone’s pop record. These pieces are significantly shorter than the lengthy ones that made the US composer’s name, and she takes a newfound emotional approach to composition, forsaking the contrapuntal canon form.View image in fullscreenKali Malone: Burning SongIn some arcane land, this probably constitutes unforgivable selling out. In more rational circles, the result is still 40 minutes of beautiful, plaintive tonality, with Lucy Railton on cello and Stephen O’Malley of Sunn O))) (also Malone’s husband) on bowed acoustic guitar. Malone plays the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche, where the composer was cantor for his last 27 years. Rather than a saint, it’s him who is buried under the altar. “That made it feel like a church for music,” Malone toldBlackbird Spyplane.‘I want an indescribable feeling’: composer Kali Malone on her search for the sublimeRead moreIf Malone’s longer pieces are music to get lost in, the compact forms and liberated mood shifts of Burning Song command acute attention. The trio play in synchronicity, their crackle and breath and scrape simmering intensely. They start Grieving Figure with a sustained note that sounds like a distant ship’s horn, then brightens like blazing final moments of a fierce sunset. Bells on a Branch starts sounding like a swarm of bees and ends utterly parched; Railton’s cello circles ominously amid the drama of Crawling Ashore.As for emotion, it’s no Max Richter-style lunge for the cheap seats. The heavy opening notes of Map the Path are solemn yet startlingly direct for Malone, feeling for the first time as if she’s lifting her fingers from the keys and shaking the listener by the shoulders.Explore more on these topicsExperimental musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: LSO/Pappano review – Kendall’s engaging new work has a tea kettle, tremolo and slam-dunks of timpani | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The British composer’s ‘i have discovered the secret of death’ was beguiling and compelling, the centrepiece of a programme that saw Pappano and the London Symphony Orchestra firing on all cylinders
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: The British composer’s ‘i have discovered the secret of death’ was beguiling and compelling, the centrepiece of a programme that saw Pappano and the London Symphony Orchestra firing on all cylinders
Content: Communicating with disturbing clarity … Fleur Barron and Hannah Kendall at the composer’s world premiere at the Barbican on 29 October.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenCommunicating with disturbing clarity … Fleur Barron and Hannah Kendall at the composer’s world premiere at the Barbican on 29 October.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewLSO/Pappano review – Kendall’s engaging new work has a tea kettle, tremolo and slam-dunks of timpaniBarbican, LondonThe British composer’s ‘i have discovered the secret of death’ was beguiling and compelling, the centrepiece of a programme that saw Pappano and the London Symphony Orchestra firing on all cylindersFlora WillsonFri 30 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStage resets between musical works are a standard feature of orchestral concerts: pianos are moved around, additional players file on or off. But I’ve never before seen a tea kettle brought on and placed ceremoniously at the front of the stage, as occurred ahead of the world premiere ofHannah Kendall’s LSO commission I have discovered the secret of death. But thenKendall’s music is vibrantly unconventional, often incorporating noise-makers from beyond classical music’s usual lineup.Her latest work was exceptionally engaging, the beguiling textures of its opening – scratches and whistles, jingles and nervous twitches of piano tremolo – periodically interrupted by violent slam-dunks of timpani, double bass pizzicato, low brass. Later there were music boxes (a hallmark of Kendall’s scoring) and the narrow whine of woodwind reeds detached from instruments.Mezzo-sopranoFleur Barronwas amplified but positioned less as a soloist, more as another line within the orchestra as she sang through her hands, a harmonica and that whistling tea kettle. Her diction was crystalline, her tone urgently compelling, but only certain words and phrases – by Guyanese poet and activistMartin Carter– were audible through these physical barriers. Kendall’s long programme note explained the significance of kettles in the history of slavery as a means of resistance. But what communicated with disturbing clarity through her music alone was struggle: to speak and even to breathe.The rest of the programme could hardly have been more different. Under Antonio Pappano, Liadov’s maximalist miniature The Enchanted Lake was all glistening surface – as exquisitely saccharine as if Wagner’s Tristan had procreated with a candyfloss machine. After the interval,Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No 5 was served as a vast dollop of heart-on-sleeve romanticism. The fine print was mostly present and correct: passages of rustic oompah in the first movement, a deliciously tender horn solo in the second, witty phrasing in the waltz of the third. But for long stretches, Pappano had the LSO firing on all cylinders, Tchaikovsky’s countermelodies and rhythmic chugging as prominent as any big tune, the climaxes turned up to brash. It certainly wasn’t subtle – but when as polished as this, the primary-colours approach is also a lot of fun.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicLondon Symphony OrchestraAntonio PappanoExperimental musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Carmen review – Costa-Jackson’s smouldering heroine blazes brightly  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Ginger Costa-Jackson is an elemental and powerful Carmen in this revival of Damiano Michieletto’s 2024 staging that relocates the drama to Franco’s Spain
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Ginger Costa-Jackson is an elemental and powerful Carmen in this revival of Damiano Michieletto’s 2024 staging that relocates the drama to Franco’s Spain
Content: Emotional and thrilling … Ginger Costa-Jackson and Russell Thomas in Carmen.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenEmotional and thrilling … Ginger Costa-Jackson and Russell Thomas in Carmen.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicOperaReviewCarmen review – Costa-Jackson’s smouldering heroine blazes brightlyRoyal Opera House, LondonGinger Costa-Jackson is an elemental and powerful Carmen in this revival of Damiano Michieletto’s 2024 staging that relocates the drama to Franco’s SpainClive PagetFri 30 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDamiano Michieletto’s Carmen has plenty going for it. The Italian director’scolourful 2024 staging,revived here for the second time already, is an effective update of a work where sexual violence can feel normalised if not handled with care. Here, it’s a subtle combination of emotional immaturity, relentless heat and habitual boredom that eventually blows the lid off the pressure cooker.With the action relocated to Franco’s Spain, the oppressive police presence and reactive societal lawlessness ring true, even if Michieletto glosses over the era’s darker elements. In a remote rural community, Carmen and her smuggler associates may be merely kicking against the pricks, but their antiestablishment chutzpah wins hearts and minds from the get-go. None of them are actually freedom fighters, but we root for them as if they were.View image in fullscreenHer fate is on the cards … CarmenPhotograph: Mihaela BodlovicIsolated within a barren Mediterranean landscape, Paolo Fantin’s confining, Hopper-esque buildings heighten the claustrophobic mood. Alessandro Carletti’s torrid lighting does the rest. Carla Teti’s gaudy 70s costumes seem a little stagy – such brightly clad smugglers would be shot on sight – but the vibe is, on the whole, authentic. Within this Latin nowheresville, Carmen, the only local with a bit of get-up-and-go, almost wills the unfolding tragedy – a change, after all, is as good as a rest.The production has its faults. Don José’s mother popping up as a symbol of fate is overused and over literal (and why can only Carmen see her?). Worse, though, is the cutesy parade of children during the entr’actes, which ruins some of Bizet’s most charming music, while their comedic presence is increasingly at odds with the onstage brutality. But then Michieletto seems keener on pointing to a certain picaresque quality to be found in Prosper Mérimée’s original novella.It’s a complex staging and Dan Dooner’s revival is a bit rough around the edges. The blocking occasionally feels purposeless, but the chorus, and especially the children, sing well, and Sesto Quatrini’s lively conducting grows bolder as the evening progresses.At the heart of this production isGinger Costa-Jackson’s elemental Carmen, an emotional powder keg, smouldering, smoking and frequently raging against her destiny. Her mounting frustration rarely disturbs the voice, however, which is dark and velvety with a battering ram lower register. Russell Thomas produces a thrilling stream of sound as Don José, rising to an electrifying final scene. Earlier, though, the spark between them sputters, not helped by his having to sing The Flower Song to a brick wall.Adriana González’s phrasing and dynamics lend vocal appeal to Michieletto’s mousey, myopic Micaëla, and Alexander Vinogradov brings swagger and style to the neon-suited toreador. The night, though, belongs to Costa-Jackson, a Carmen who blazes as brightly as any, before inevitably going down in flames.Carmen is at the Royal Opera House, London until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicRoyal Opera HousereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Expect goosebumps!’: to celebrate Halloween, readers choose the spookiest places in the UK | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: From a ghostly hill fort on the South Downs to a haunted farmhouse in remote Northern Ireland, you guide us to some frightfully scary places
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From a ghostly hill fort on the South Downs to a haunted farmhouse in remote Northern Ireland, you guide us to some frightfully scary places
Content: ‘Wonderfully spooky’ Dunnottar Castle.Photograph: Charlotte Graham/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Wonderfully spooky’ Dunnottar Castle.Photograph: Charlotte Graham/ShutterstockReaders' travel tipsUnited Kingdom holidays‘Expect goosebumps!’: to celebrate Halloween, readers choose the spookiest places in the UKFrom a ghostly hill fort on the South Downs to a haunted farmhouse in remote Northern Ireland, you guide us to some frightfully scary placesTell us about an escape in the wilds of Scotland– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 30 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 04.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinning tip: an eerie clifftop castle near AberdeenDunnottar Castle, perched on cliffs above the crashing North Sea, is one of Scotland’s eeriest places. The most haunting part is the Whigs Vault, where more than 160 prisoners were confined in dreadful conditions in 1685. Standing in that dark chamber, it’s impossible not to imagine their fear and suffering. With my Fraser ancestry, the castle’s history feels especially poignant. The names of multiple Frasers are recorded, their details written on the wall. The wind whistles through the stonework, the waves thunder below, and there’s a sense that the past hasn’t quite left. It’s beautiful, tragic and wonderfully spooky, especially beneath Aberdeenshire’s brooding grey skies.RosieA Neolithic burial chamber in PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenPentre Ifan.Photograph: Louise France/AlamyMy dad and I reachedPentre Ifanon a November evening, just before dark. The burial chamber defies explanation: 16 tons of weathered capstone, barely touching three sharp stone points, as though something unseen was holding it up. There was a low hum from somewhere; I hoped it was the wind spilling over the Preseli hills. As the daylight crept away, the chamber beneath grew darker than the settling dusk around us. My dad, who has an explanation for everything, stood silent. I think we walked back to the car a little faster than we had come.TomHaunted by criminals in SomersetView image in fullscreenShepton Mallet prison.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianMy recommendation isShepton Mallet prison, or “the Mallet” as it used to be called, back when it was used as a military prison. It opened in 1625, and you can still crawl through a wall into an original cell. The prison has three Victorian blocks and umpteen stories of past prisoners, including the Kray twins. You can have a daytime tour, or a night-time ghost tour, where you’ll hear stories of spooks and ghouls witnessed by many visitors and staff over the years. You can even stay the night in a real, cold, grim prison cell. The staff are friendly and all great characters, I can’t recommend it enough!CharlieHollowed out tower in West YorkshireView image in fullscreenSt Thomas à Becket church, Heptonstall.Photograph: Philip Silverman/AlamyPerched high above Hebden Bridge in the historic hilltop village of Heptonstall lies the roofless shell of St Thomas à Becket church. Raked into ruin by a storm in 1847, this 13th-century structure was left to decay alongside its19th-century successor, creating a rare site where two parish churches share a single churchyard. Gaunt, towering arches frame open skies, and the hollowed-out stone tower feels like the Tower tarot card made real. Expect goosebumps!Finbarre SnareyA pub night you won’t forget in StaffordshireView image in fullscreenThe Four Crosses Inn.Photograph: Alex Telfer/The ObserverTheFour Crosses Innis the most haunted pub in England – and I should know: it was in my mother’s family for many generations! I grew up hearing about all the ghostly goings on. It was also one of the oldest pubs (it’s onlyopen for toursnow), and family lore has it Dr Johnson stayed there. On the edge of creepy Cannock Chase moor in Staffordshire, the scene of many murders, it has dank cellars and creaking attics for you to get really scared in.RobPoltergeist stories in County FermanaghView image in fullscreenFivemiletown, Northern Ireland.Photograph: Bonzo/AlamyCooneen Ghost House, near Fivemiletown, is one of Northern Ireland’s eeriest places. The abandoned farmhouse is private, but it can be glimpsed from the road, which somehow makes its old poltergeist stories feel even more unsettling. NearbyCrocknagrally Forestis perfect for a cold-weather ramble to make a day of it, especially on a misty winter afternoon when the tracks are wonderfully secluded and it all feels very remote and spooky. The kind of walk where folklore seems woven into the landscape: dark trees, lonely roads and an old haunted house just out of reach. There are loads of stories around this place that locals will share.Christina Haweskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRomantic tragedy on Llŷn peninsulaView image in fullscreenAbandoned works at the Cae’r Nant quarry above Nant Gwrtheyrn.Photograph: Peter Martin Rhind/AlamyThe once abandoned quarrying village ofNant Gwrtheyrn, on Llŷn peninsula, lies at the foot of Yr Eifl, down a terrifyingly steep and winding road. On a misty autumn day, with the crashing waves below you and the unsettling presence of a wild goat peering down at you from the cliffs above, it can be truly eerie. The woods in the valley are home to the tale ofRhys and Meinir– a traditional prenuptial game of hide and seek gone awry, with the skeletal remains of a bride-to-be revealed by a bolt of lightning. The site is free to visit.SionedCrashing waves and call of rooks in AberdeenshireView image in fullscreenSlains Castle.Photograph: AlamyOn a cold grey daySlains Castleon the east coast of Scotland, north of Aberdeen, certainly has a spooky air. Although rumours about the castle inspiring Bram Stoker when writing Dracula are apparently untrue, the castle ruins bring to mind bats pouring out of windows and unsavoury aristocrats lurking around corners. It is precariously located on cliffs above the North Sea and the crashing waves and calls of rooks and jackdaws provide an evocatively eerie soundtrack to your visit.Joel RawlingsUnexplained screams on the South DownsView image in fullscreenChanctonbury Ring.Photograph: Veronique Stone/AlamyChanctonbury Ring is an iron age hill fort ringed by beech trees, on the South Downs in West Sussex. Folklore claims that by walking or running around the ring seven times you’ll see the devil. Writer Robert Macfarlane certainly had an unnerving experience there while camping, as recounted in his 2012 bookThe Old Ways: A Journey on Foot, when awakened in the dead of night by terrifying human-sounding screams high above him in the tree canopy, which seemed to divide and converge before swooping down upon him. Accessible only on foot, who dares follow in Macfarlane’s footsteps to check out the myth?Kirsty McHattieGothic atmosphere in WhitbyView image in fullscreenWhitby Abbey.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyMy favourite spooky spot isWhitby Abbey, perched high above the Yorkshire coast. Its ruined arches and weathered stone look dramatic in daylight, but imagine them at dusk, with mist drifting in from the North Sea and the wind moving through the empty windows. Whitby’s narrow streets and harbour add another layer of atmosphere, especially when the lamps come on and the town grows quiet. It is easy to see why Bram Stoker found inspiration here for Dracula. I would love to explore the abbey as the light fades, then wander down towards the harbour, listening to the waves and letting my imagination do the rest. The best spooky places are where history, landscape and legend meet – and Whitby has all three. Its magic endures.EmilioExplore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysReaders' travel tipsHalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Ayllu’s sakura no hana – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: An elegant and slightly flamboyant Japanese-Peruvian fusion with delicate, floral notes and a fruity finish
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An elegant and slightly flamboyant Japanese-Peruvian fusion with delicate, floral notes and a fruity finish
Content: Ayllu’s sakura no hana.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenAyllu’s sakura no hana.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Ayllu’s sakura no hana – recipeAn elegant and slightly flamboyant Japanese-Peruvian fusion with delicate, floral notes and a fruity finishShak NematulloevFri 30 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInspired by our restaurant’s Japanese-Peruvian roots, and to mark the 1-2 November Day of the Dead celebrations, this drink combines white rum and sake with a dash of bitters and a red-wine float: the result is a light, layered cocktail with delicate, floral notes, juicy berry fruit and just enough theatre to impress without being hard to make.Sakura no hanaServes150ml white rum– we use Bacardi25ml sake10ml standard 1:1 sugar syrup2 dashes bitters– we use Angostura15ml red wine, ideally malbec, to float on top1 edible flower(we use a cherry blossom when it’s in season), to garnish (optional)Fill an old fashioned glass with ice, then add all the liquids except the wine and stir to combine. Slowly pour in the malbec, so it sits as a separate layer on top of everything else, garnish with the edible flower, if using, and serve.Shak Nematulloev, bar manager,Ayllu, London W2Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodJapanese food and drinkWinerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s miso-toffee apple hand pies – recipe | Bonfire Night | The Guardian
description: Warm your hands on these sweet little pastries – perfect Bonfire Night fodder!
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: Warm your hands on these sweet little pastries – perfect Bonfire Night fodder!
Content: Helen Goh’s toffee apple hand pies.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s toffee apple hand pies.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotBonfire NightHelen Goh’s miso-toffee apple hand pies – recipeWarm your hands on these sweet little envelopes of gently spiced, toffee-glossed apples wrapped in puff pastry. Perfect Bonfire Night fodderHelen GohFri 30 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese plump and rustic little parcels are perfect for Bonfire Night: warming, portable and, wrapped in a napkin and held in one hand, easy to eat outdoors. Filled with gently spiced, toffee-glossed apples, they are deliberately more homely hand pies than anything overly neat or patisserie-like. The small amount of miso in the filling deepens the toffee flavour and rounds out the sweetness, without making it taste too savoury or funky.Miso-toffee apple hand piesPrep10 minMacerate30 minCook1 hr 15 min, plus chilling and coolingMakes8800g apples, ideally a mixture of granny smith and pink lady (about 3 of each), peeled, cored and cut into 1½-2cm pieces (650g net)80g light brown sugar2tbsp apple cider vinegar1 tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ground nutmeg¼ tsp fine sea salt, plus a generous pinch for the egg wash50g unsalted butter20g white miso1 tsp vanilla extract1 small egg50g plain flour2320g packs shop-bought puff pastry1tbsp demerara sugarPut the apple pieces in a large bowl with the brown sugar, vinegar, cinnamon, nutmeg and salt, and toss to combine. Leave to macerate at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, tossing occasionally.Strain the apples, reserving the liquid; you should have about 100ml. Melt the butter in a large, wide frying pan on a medium-high heat. Add the strained apples and cook, tossing occasionally, for four to five minutes, until they begin to soften. Pour in the reserved liquid and cook for a further three to four minutes, until the liquid reduces and a glossy caramel forms around the apples. Stir in the miso and vanilla until evenly incorporated, then take off the heat. Spread the filling over a tray or large plate, so it can cool quickly, then refrigerate until completely cold.To assemble, lightly beat the egg with a generous pinch of salt and put the flour in a small dish. Unroll one sheet of pastry, leaving it on the baking paper it comes with, and cut into four equal rectangles. Keep the second sheet refrigerated while you assemble the first four pies.Spoon about 60g filling on one half of each pastry rectangle, leaving a 1½cm border around three outer edges surrounding the filling, then brush these borders lightly with egg, keeping the egg wash just inside the cut edges (brushing it over the sides can seal the pastry layers and prevent them from rising properly). Fold the uncovered half of pastry over the filling and gently press the three edges together. Dip the tines of a fork in the flour, then use this to crimp all around the edges to seal.Slide the four pies on their baking paper bases on to an oven tray and refrigerate while you repeat with the second pastry sheet and the rest of the filling on a second tray. Refrigerate both trays for 20-30 minutes, until the pies are cold and firm.Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Brush the tops of the pies with the remaining egg wash and sprinkle with demerara sugar. Using the tip of a small, sharp knife, cut three slashes in the top of each pie, so the steam can escape, then bake for about 30 minutes, swapping the trays around halfway through cooking if necessary, until puffed and deeply golden. Leave the pies on the trays for 10 minutes, then transfer to a rack. Serve warm or at room temperature.Explore more on these topicsBonfire NightThe sweet spotFoodBakingSnacksPastryFruitHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Gherkins galore! 17 delicious ways to enjoy pickles – from frickles to pickletinis | Food | The Guardian
description: One of the UK budget’s big surprises? A discount on gherkins. And while they’ll always be good on a burger, there are many more unusual ways to indulge, from fried cheese treats to savoury ice-cream
Author: Leah Harper
Headline: One of the UK budget’s big surprises? A discount on gherkins. And while they’ll always be good on a burger, there are many more unusual ways to indulge, from fried cheese treats to savoury ice-cream
Content: A fine pickle … fried pickles with spicy dipping sauce.Photograph: LauriPatterson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fine pickle … fried pickles with spicy dipping sauce.Photograph: LauriPatterson/Getty ImagesFoodGherkins galore! 17 delicious ways to enjoy pickles – from frickles to pickletinisOne of the UK budget’s big surprises? A discount on gherkins. And while they’ll always be good on a burger, there are many more unusual ways to indulge, from fried cheese treats to savoury ice-creamLeah HarperFri 30 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn John Healey’s first budget as chancellor this week, he announced that he will remove import tariffs on more than 100 products – including, crucially, gherkins. Baked beans and boiled sweets, too, butgherkins stole the limelight, perhaps due to gen Z’s long-heldobsession with all things pickled, including cucumbers.But for those who think of a gherkin as either something to be chomped straight from the jar or swiftly removed from a Big Mac, do not worry: there are, in fact, plenty of ways to get more bang for your newly discounted gherkin buck.If you’re unsure about gherkins in general, let me ease you in with a gateway dish:the frickle, AKA a fried pickle. Deep frying almost any foodstuff will make it taste better and pickles – as gherkins are commonly known in the US – are no exception. Remember to pat dry your gherkins, which typically come swimming in their own brine. Then it’s simply a case of making a batter, dredging, frying and trying not to get grease all over your chin.View image in fullscreenPickle your fancy … deep-fried pickles at a barbecue restaurant in Kentucky.Photograph: Yarvin Market Journeys/AlamyFrickles are usually paired with a creamy dipping sauce such as aioli or ranch dressing – but why not go double gherkin and make your own tartare?Nigel Slater’s classic tartare sauceuses gherkins to cut through greasiness, allowing us “to continue eating”. You don’t have to ask me twice.Alternatively, there’s alsogherkin ketchup: Tom Kerridge’s recipepromises that “your guests will think you’re a pickling genius” – despite the fact that you are essentially serving up pureed gherkins.Now that you’re a gherkin convert, time to try something a little more adventurous. Sophie Wyburd’s recipe forbaked camembert with spicy pickle dressingis a tangy twist on a classic comfort food, adding gherkins to the more traditional dressing components of oil, rosemary and chilli. Plus, I would challenge anyone to turn down the “croissant crouton” dippers, which she serves in place of the usual crusty bread.Cosy indulgence not the vibe? Why not freeze your gherkins to make something altogether fresher. Recipe developer Emily Bonner blitzes her frosty pickles to create a kind of savoury granita, thenuses it to top a burrata.View image in fullscreenAdded zip … Nashville-style chicken burger with pickles.Photograph: Nazar Abbas/GettyThe cheese and gherkin pairings don’t end there: Nicola Lamb combines gherkins with cheddar for herflaky cheese and pickle scones, whileMatt Tebbutt adds them to a gruyère and salami toastie, intended to accompany french onion soup – although I’d venture it’s tasty eaten alone, too. Is the viral TikTok “chickle” snack – yes, that’s gherkins wrapped in fried cheese – an upgrade on the frickle? I couldn’t possibly say.Hamish Ruia and Max Desoutter – AKA the Flavour Fellas – use a grated gherkin and dill mixture to turn the traditional Spanish dishpan con tomateinto “pan con pickle”. And, while at first glanceAlexa Weibel’s fried chicken sandwichmay appear to simply use gherkins as a garnish, she also uses the brine to marinate the meat as well as chopped gherkins to “add zip” to her coleslaw.If this is all sounding a little bready, how about Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’s super-tangypotato and egg salad with gherkins and capers– orTamsin Burnett-Hall’s dill pickle macaroni salad. They’re both described as a side dish, but perhaps now is the time to make them the main event?View image in fullscreenDill or no dill … Tom Hunt’s gherkin brine ice-cream.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianOK, let’s get weird: can I interest you in apickletini? Sure, it’s like an appletini, except … yes, I’m afraid it’s gherkins. Brine and garnish – plus vodka and vermouth; classier than apickleback– whiskey “chased” with a shot of pickle juice – if not necessarily more enjoyable. Alternatively, there’sDua Lipa’s spicy diet coke: the singer mixes pickle and jalapeno “juice” with the carbonated soft drink, before topping with a couple of slices of each. That pickletini’s not sounding so bad now, huh?Tom Hunt describes hispickled cucumber and vodka ice-creamas “one for the true gherkin fanatic” – but you’ve come this far, so I can only assume you’d be willing to give it a go. He suggests you “serve in cones and top with a gherkin” – but to my mind that rather ruins the fun of asking guests to guess the flavour.If you do want to be upfront about it, you might as well servechocolate-covered mini gherkins– optional toppings include sea salt, chilli flakes and freeze-dried raspberries, none of which do much to disguise the fact that these are, in effect, gherkins dipped in Dairy Milk. The recipe describes them as “quirky canapés … or party conversation starters” – which I imagine is certainly true. Pair with marmalade or garlic to really make the most of those post-budget bargainsExplore more on these topicsFoodPickling, fermenting and preservingSauces and graviesCocktailsfeaturesShareReuse this content
